artigo.texto: CATL licenses its technology to Ford's factories, bans cannot hold back Chinese enterprises' overseas expansion, and the Chinese battery industry has crossed the high wall of trade bans. Ford's mass production of LFP cells using CATL's licensed technology reflects that China's new energy industry's overseas expansion has shifted from product sales to technology licensing, as a means to evade tariffs and equity reviews. Energy Foresight learned that on November 24, Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan launched mass production of prismatic LFP cells using licensed technology from CATL, with a production line output of 40 cells per minute, and the first batch of cells was sent to Louisville for Fathom prototype vehicles. Ford holds no equity stake, and CATL collects licensing fees. The production line churns out 40 cells per minute, which Ford says is one of the fastest prismatic LFP lines outside China. The factory's property rights, machinery, workers and depreciation all belong to Ford. CATL does not hold any shares, only dispatches engineers, provides process technology, and gets paid per unit of cell produced. In the past few years, the script for China's new energy industry going global has been flipped: tariffs block products, rules of origin block production capacity, and equity reviews block joint ventures, so companies are choosing to license their technical expertise instead. From selling goods to selling factories and then to selling process technology, restrictions have never really stopped anyone, they have only changed the way of charging. People cannot cross that wall, but technology can There is a partition inside the factory, with the cell workshop and the battery pack assembly workshop on opposite sides. Only materials are allowed to pass through the door, no personnel. CATL's engineers can stay on the cell production side to adjust parameters and support production ramp-up, while the work behind the adjacent door belongs to Ford. This wall is more honest than any statement, drawing a clear line on the ground between "what can be provided" and "what cannot be provided". Is Ford buying the formula? The chemical system of lithium iron phosphate was published publicly in 1996, core patents have expired one after another, and the formula is no longer a secret. What Ford cannot really buy is the set of practical know-how that keeps the defect rate as low as one part per billion at a beat of 40 cells per minute: electrode coating parameters, winding tension, formation and grading curves, and the anomaly handling manual tested by hundreds of millions of cells. After buying a full set of cooking utensils and recipes, you still need to hire a chef to stand by and supervise the heat control. Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development, mentioned that after looking around battery manufacturers, CATL is "the fastest way to build affordable electric vehicles in the United States". As the old saying goes, give a man a fish and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime. The current version is to teach people how to fish, charge by each catch, and the fish pond and nets all belong to the other party. What CATL offers is LRS — License, Royalty paid by volume, and Engineering Service. I teach you how to do it, and you give me a share of the revenue for each cell you produce. Capital expenditure, idle production capacity and raw material price fluctuations remain on Ford's books, while CATL gets licensing fees that come with almost no cost. The same set of process technology can be charged repeatedly in factories invested by different customers. Who should be nervous? Ford's electric vehicle division Model e posted a loss of 1.058 billion US dollars in the third quarter, revenue fell 31% year-on-year to about 1.2 billion US dollars, and the loss ratio expanded from -79.1% to -86.5%. Fathom is scheduled to be launched in the fourth quarter of 2027, with the standard version starting at $28,350, about $25,000 lower than the average price of electric vehicles in the United States at that time. For vehicles at this price point, batteries account for 30% to 40% of the total cost. If the cell cost cannot be brought down, even the most sophisticated platform will only be a concept car on the exhibition stand. The letter from the Secretary of Transportation used the phrase "deeply shocked", but shock cannot reduce costs. From selling goods to selling technical expertise, there is more than one path The roadmap for China's new energy industry going global is not a single dead-end path, but more like a three-way intersection with all lanes open at the same time. The first path is selling goods. In 2025, the export of the "three new major categories" reached 1.28 trillion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 27.1%. This path is the most straightforward, but also the most vulnerable to tariff interception. Under Section 301, the tariff rate for Chinese lithium batteries is 25%, and that for electric vehicles is 100%. Before the goods even arrive at the port, the accounts are already unprofitable. The second path is to move factories overseas. CATL built a 14GWh facility in Thuringia, Germany, planned a 100GWh facility in Debrecen, Hungary, and established a 50:50 joint venture with Stellantis in Spain; Gotion High-Tech and Volkswagen PowerCo set up three joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. Moving factories overseas can avoid tariffs, but cannot bypass local content requirements and equity reviews. artigo.texto: SK On said Friday it is set to supply batteries for energy storage projects totaling 443 megawatts in South Korea's largest energy storage tender to date, expanding its market presence as it converts electric vehicle battery production lines for stationary energy storage. SK On accounted for 37.1 percent of the capacity selected in the third round of the government's energy storage system, or ESS, procurement program. While its share fell from 50.3 percent in the previous round, its supply volume increased by 56 percent. SK On will supply five sites, including in Soseong, North Jeolla Province, and Gangjin, South Jeolla Province. Samsung SDI took the largest share, with 751 megawatts, or 62.9 percent of the total 1,194 megawatts, across nine projects, including sites in Yeongam, South Jeolla Province, and Muju, North Jeolla Province, as well as two on Jeju Island. LG Energy Solution did not participate in the latest round. The Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and the Korea Power Exchange selected 14 ESS projects for priority negotiations Thursday, with final awards due Dec. 4. The combined power capacity exceeds that of the first two rounds combined. Successful developers must obtain power generation licenses by August 2027 and complete installation by February 2029. The government plans to hold a fourth tender in the first half of 2027. The state-led ESS program aims to store surplus electricity and feed it back into the grid when needed, helping balance supply and demand as renewable power generation grows. The latest round would bring SK On's total allocation under the program to 727 megawatts. In February, it secured 284 megawatts across three sites in South Jeolla Province, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027. SK On is converting 3 gigawatt-hours of its Seosan plant's 7 gigawatt-hours of production capacity to manufacture lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries for energy storage. It plans to complete equipment replacement and trial production by year-end. The company plans to source cathode materials, electrolytes and separators from domestic suppliers, including cathode materials from L&F. The tender placed significant weight on nonprice factors, including fire safety and contributions to domestic industry. SK On said its ESS batteries passed a large-scale fire test conducted by CSA Group in October under the UL 9540A testing standard. The company is also converting production lines at its Georgia facility to manufacture LFP batteries for energy storage. These lines will supply a Massachusetts project under a 1-gigawatt-hour agreement signed with renewable energy developer Flatiron Energy Development in September 2025. In a separate deal announced in August, SK On agreed to supply US energy storage company NeoVolta Power with 9 gigawatt-hours of LFP pouch cells manufactured in Georgia over five years starting in 2027. sahn@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: Battery storage system could power 170,000 homes Plans to build a battery storage system capable of powering more than 170,000 homes have been recommended for approval. CONNECTID 2 Ltd has applied to install the infrastructure on land west of the A140 at Red House Farm in Yaxley, near Eye, Suffolk. However, the application has been opposed by Yaxley, Thrandeston and Mellis parish councils over concerns including flooding and fire safety. Mid Suffolk District Council will make its final decision at a planning meeting on 2 December. Blueprints showed the storage system would consist of 448 battery container units and be built on 10.4 hectares (25.7 acres) of mostly agricultural land. The facilities enable electricity from renewable sources, such as solar and wind, to be stored outside of national and local networks and then released into the grid when power is required. According to planning documents, the development would have 520MW of storage - enough energy to power 176,100 homes a day. If permission is granted, the site will be returned to agricultural use after 40 years or if it goes six months without operating. Similar proposals at land south of Eye Airfield Industrial Estate were approved by the council in July 2025. The local authority is run by a Green, independent and Liberal Democrat coalition. artigo.texto: The American public really hates data centers. We should know. Over the past year, we’ve watched data center fights flare up in hundreds of towns nationwide and dominate the midterm elections. Our polling shows that 71% of Americans would now oppose a data center being built near their home — up from 42% last year. So it’s little wonder that data centers have become a big part of the debate over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting reform bill that now awaits a vote in the House of Representatives. BAAJA would make it easier to build many types of big and small projects in the United States, including transmission lines, pipelines and public transit. But when criticizing the bill, opponents have fixated on one type of project in particular: data centers. Earthjustice, an environmental litigation group, has warned that the bill will “fast-track the dirty data center buildout.” In an interview last month, a powerful House Democrat claimed that the bill is really “about” data centers and the energy infrastructure needed to power them. This didn’t happen by accident. Within hours of the bill’s release, opponents planned to link it to data centers in their messaging criticizing the legislation, according to a transcript leaked to Punchbowl News. In response, the bill’s supporters have argued that BAAJA penalizes data centers and would force them to protect Americans from higher electricity bills — a policy that many winning Democrats just ran on. Some supporters have gone further, asserting that the bill won’t help data centers in any way. That isn’t true. But it’s also not true that the bill would be an unqualified gift to the data center industry. The big four policies While BAAJA is a long bill, it has four big policies that would affect data centers in some way. It’s worth holding all four in your head at the same time. First, it would build out the country’s electricity transmission grid, requiring utilities and grid operators to plan and build a much larger grid than exists right now. This would help data centers because data centers need a lot of electricity. But it would also help everything else that uses electricity, too — including the electric vehicles, heat pumps, and electric infrastructure essential to fight climate change. And it would help renewables, whose growth is limited by insufficient power-line capacity to bring electricity to cities and suburbs. For this reason, some green critics of the overall bill, such as Earthjustice, “strongly support” the transmission section. Second, BAAJA would write tough new ratepayer protection provisions applying to data centers and crypto mines into federal electricity law. If BAAJA passes, then the Federal Power Act would discriminate against AI and crypto data centers as it discriminates against no other type of industrial energy user. These policies aim to protect Americans from seeing their electricity bills rise due to data centers, and they go much further than President Trump’s voluntary “pledges.” They would force data center developers to pay for grid upgrades upfront, so that if a project requires grid infrastructure improvements and then fails, it doesn’t impose costs on everyone. These provisions would allow states or utilities to write their own stricter rules and, for instance, auction off spare capacity on the grid to data centers instead of giving it away to whoever is first in line. States could then use those savings to cut Americans’ power bills further. On top of these rules, the bill would require data centers, crypto miners, and other large computing facilities to report their energy use to the federal government. This has been a longstanding priority for climate groups; disclosing this information is already required for most other kinds of large energy consumers, but it has been voluntary for the AI and crypto industries. Third, the bill would ease permitting for natural gas pipelines at a time when new ones are being developed specifically to serve data center demand growth. BAAJA would narrow and limit states’ ability under the Clean Water Act to block permits for natural gas pipelines that cross major rivers or wetlands, and it extends permits granted under the law from five to 10 years. It also significantly curtails a provision that has allowed some Democratic governors to block gas pipelines that pass through their states. Data centers run on electricity, not natural gas. But because it has been so hard for new facilities to connect to the electricity grid, many data center developers have planned to build big on-site natural gas plants to power their projects. The bill’s changes could make it easier for gas pipelines to expand to service these planned facilities. Finally, the bill would make it easier to build big projects of all kinds that have any kind of federal permitting nexus. BAAJA limits the scope of certain environmental review laws, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It imposes new deadlines on outside litigants’ ability to sue under those laws. And it limits the scope of Clean Water Act wetlands permitting and allows states to take over Endangered Species Act reviews. The bill also makes it much harder to undo permitting decisions lawfully made by a previous president. This last set of changes, taken together, would make it easier for large construction projects of all kinds to break ground and reach completion, especially in places where federal wetlands and species permitting could take a long time. That could help factories, wind and solar farms, mines, transmission lines, public transit, pipelines, warehouses, retailers, and — yes — data centers. What this all means The bill, in other words, isn’t simply good or bad for data centers. artigo.texto: Car battery gigafactory builder drops out - Published The company building the UK's biggest electric vehicle (EV) battery factory has said its opening remains "on track", despite a major contractor stepping away from the project for the second time in six months. The gigafactory near Bridgwater in Somerset, is being led by Agratas and built on the site of a former ordinance factory, creating around 4,600 jobs once open. Contractor TSL, which is building the factory's exterior, will step down, external once that work is complete, but the company has declined to say why and it is unclear if it had planned further involvement. Buckinghamshire-based TSL only joined the project in June after previous lead contractor Sir Robert McAlpine ended its involvement. Agratas, part of the Tata Group which owns Jaguar Land Rover, said it will not need to replace TSL as it is already working with another contractor - NG Bailey - who will carry out the remaining work fitting out the inside of the factory. More from Somerset - 'Stunning' sculpture could replace M5 Willow Man - Published20 hours ago - Hopes damaged tower could reopen to visitors - Published21 hours ago - Loss of farm school land to have 'massive impact' - Published1 day ago A spokesperson for Agratas said: "We are on track to meet our customer requirements. "The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility's launch phase." Construction of the factory on the 616 acre (249.2 hectare) brownfield location near Bridgwater was expected to take two years, with about 2,000 people working on site this year. Project leader Agratas said in the summer the original 2026 factory opening date had been pushed back to 2027, and has now confirmed it will be the end of that year. The company said 1,500 operational jobs would be created in 2027, with 4,600 jobs on offer once it expands across the whole site. The Federal Communications Commission's approval on Wednesday of SpaceX's plan to deploy one million orbital data center satellites into space by 2040 was not "just irresponsible," said one environmental advocate. "It’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.” Whitehouse was among the critics who noted that the approval had been granted without an environmental review, which is required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the deployment of one million "orbital space modules," which SpaceX has said would form a new data center constellation called "Starmind," would open "a bold new frontier" and allow the US to lead "the world into the era of super intelligence." The satellites would process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth, according to SpaceX, the space exploration company led by Republican megadonor Elon Musk. The environmental legal group Earthjustice said they also risk "changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky," and denounced the commission for releasing the decision as families across the US were preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving. “Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.” "Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals." The number of satellites in space has already grown rapidly in the last several years, with 15,000 satellites in orbit in 2026—up from 1,400 just over a decade ago. Satellites cause emissions as they are placed in space through rocket launches, and other environmental impacts include debris from potential collisions—especially as the number of satellites grows—degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution. Astronomers spoke out against SpaceX's plan earlier this year, saying it would prevent scientists from studying the night sky with modern telescopes, as well as disrupting ecosystems and humans' biological clocks due to extreme light pollution. On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's licensing of Musk's plan. "The proposed constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky," said the group. "The intended and unintended radio emissions from a constellation of such unprecedented size would imperil radio astronomy research, and the waste heat generated by the data centers would produce a thermal signature that would increase the infrared background of the sky and threaten the efficacy of sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research. In addition, atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy." "The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world," the AAS added. Earthjustice emphasized that the approval came as Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the permitting reform bill that would prevent future administrations from revoking licenses for projects including data centers and would block courts from enforcing environmental review laws for such projects if they had been violated previously. “This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of [President Donald] Trump,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president of Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”

artigo.texto: Jareeporn Jarukornsakul, Chairman of the Executive Committee and Group Chief Executive Officer of WHA Corporation Public Company Limited (SET: WHA), said the company has received assurances from its data center customers that a proposed U.S. policy to tax American companies investing in data center projects overseas would not affect their investment plans. The comment came in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s idea of imposing tariffs on U.S. companies that develop data centers outside the United States. Jareeporn said WHA’s customers have confirmed that the policy has not altered their investment strategies. However, if the measure were to restrict U.S. operators from directly investing in data center construction in Thailand, WHA would be prepared to develop data center projects itself and lease the facilities to customers. The approach would provide another option to accommodate investment demand from foreign clients, she said. Regarding DAMAC Digital’s cancellation of its investment plan in Malaysia, Jareeporn said discussions with data center customers currently in negotiations with WHA have not indicated any impact or delay to investment plans in Thailand. On foreign direct investment (FDI), WHA believes Thailand remains at an advantage in terms of U.S. import tariff rates compared to key competitors such as China and Vietnam. If Thailand can maintain a competitive tariff level, such as around 18%, the impact of the trade war on Thai industries would be limited, while the country would remain attractive to foreign investors. The U.S., meanwhile, could face higher goods costs as a result of such measures. Thailand also continues to serve as a “safe zone” for Chinese investors, supported by its strong trade and industrial ecosystem, Jareeporn said. Regardless of changes in U.S. political direction, China is expected to continue facing pressure from trade measures, encouraging Chinese manufacturers to relocate production bases and expand investment in Thailand. WHA is now beginning to see signs of renewed investment expansion from customers in the U.S., Japan, and Europe, particularly Germany. This reflects opportunities to broaden the customer base of the company’s industrial estate and logistics businesses going forward, Jareeporn said. She added that WHA’s operating performance in the fourth quarter of 2026 remains solid and is expected to support full-year results reaching a new all-time high for the fifth consecutive year. Business momentum in 2027 is also expected to remain strong, driven by the company’s existing backlog and continued investment demand from customers across a wide range of industries. For its logistics business expansion, WHA is continuing to develop warehouse and logistics space to meet leasing demand from both domestic and international customers. The WHA Mega Logistics Center Theparak KM.21, the largest logistics project under WHA Logistics, covers more than 640,000 square meters and has an estimated project value of approximately THB 8 billion. The project currently has an overall occupancy rate of about 86%. The remaining space is in newly completed buildings, which WHA expects to fully lease by early 2027, reflecting continued strong demand for warehouse and logistics space. WHA also plans to develop the WHA Mega Logistics Center Chonlaharnpichit KM.4 Project 2 on a total area of 720,000 square meters, with an estimated project value of about THB 10 billion. The development is expected to take around four to five years and will support long-term industrial expansion and logistics space demand. WHA continues to expand its customer base into new industries. Most recently, the company concluded negotiations to lease around 52,000 square meters of space to a major Japanese fashion business customer, and signed an additional lease agreement with DHL, a global logistics service provider. These developments will help diversify its customer base and support recurring revenue growth in the future, Jareeporn said.

artigo.texto: As the midterm results rolled in a few weeks ago, making clear that Democrats were headed for a huge night, the world’s richest person, the largest individual midterm donor, and one of X’s most relentless posters was focused on his latest extraterrestrial scheme: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk wrote on the social media platform he owns. It was his first public reaction to the election results, which amounted to a harsh rebuke of the MAGA messaging he’d spent the past four years underwriting. A self-serving take? Absolutely. SpaceX aims to launch a huge amount of AI processing capacity into orbit, with the goal of eventually deploying 100 gigawatts of solar-powered computing satellites every year. But does Musk have a point? Maybe. As the midterms proved — and as Heatmap has long been tracking — anti-data center sentiment is exploding. Our most recent polling found that 71% of survey respondents would oppose a data center near where they live, which is actually down slightly from 75% a few months earlier. The overwhelming majority of congressional and gubernatorial candidates who won this year favored cracking down on these facilities through stronger regulations or even moratoria. That’s all to say that Musk is hardly the only entrepreneur betting the moment is ripe for AI infrastructure to reach far flung corners of the planet and beyond. So far, the middle of the ocean and low Earth orbit look like the leading frontiers. Wave energy startup Panthalassa, for instance, is building ocean-based data centers, while other space-based data center hopefuls such as Cowboy Space, Starcloud and Orbital are also jockeying for a share of the market alongside bigger players like Google and Blue Origin. “When we first embarked, there was probably more skepticism than there was conviction,” Joseph Yaffe, COO of data center startup Cowboy Space, told me. “Now I think the balance has changed, and there’s more conviction than there is skepticism.” Yaffe originally founded the startup with the goal of beaming solar power down to Earth, but pivoted to data centers this spring when the company raised a $275 million Series B at a $2 billion valuation. Unlike other startups in this industry, Cowboy Space doesn’t want to rely on SpaceX to get its satellites into orbit — it plans to build its own rockets. While taking on Musk’s nearly $2 trillion rocket-slash-AI company may sound like a fool’s errand, Yaffe sees this as the startup’s edge, in part because the midterms revealed the deep unpopularity of Musk’s priorities. “We’re operating in an industry that’s dominated by one single polarizing company, or really a company with a polarizing leader. His side lost,” Yaffe told me. “People who are thinking a lot about space as a new commercial frontier would like to have other ways to get access to space.” Cowboy Space’s rockets are purpose-built to house its 1-megawatt orbital data centers, with an upper section designed to detach and double as the GPU-packed satellite. By contrast, Starship, Musk’s next-generation rocket, still requires a separate satellite to house AI chips. And if an outside company wants to hitch a ride, they’ll have to pay SpaceX for the privilege; if Cowboy Space’s rocket design proves skyworthy, it avoids that. The company thinks these advantages will eventually make its computing as cheap as anything on Earth, if not cheaper in the long run. “But not 20 years — we think five years,” Yaffe told me. It’s targeting first launch by the end of 2028. No major customer has yet committed to buying compute from orbital data centers at scale, though some are testing the waters. Starcloud says its next satellite, slated to launch by year’s end, will run workloads for Crusoe, and it has partnerships with AWS and Google Cloud. But Yaffe expects to see more action within the next year. “People, understandably, are now in the place of, Well, do we wait and see if they can put a one-megawatt data center in orbit, or do we commit and try to at least have first dibs on the first 10 gigawatts in orbit now?” Orbital, a pre-seed space-based data center startup founded earlier this year, also sees the midterms as a gift of sorts. “I guess folks are going down the same research journey that I did like a year ago, and realizing that this is not at all that crazy of an idea,” Euwyn Poon, the company’s CEO, told me. Orbital is targeting its first launch for next summer, aboard a SpaceX rocket, with plans to begin scaling by the end of the decade. Neither Yaffe nor Poon, however, views community opposition as the primary constraint on the AI buildout. Both support building on land, they just don’t think terrestrial energy supply can keep pace. But they’re split on what comes next. Poon thinks orbit will become “the dominant way of capturing energy and running AI compute,” while Yaffe expects the majority of computing capacity to stay on Earth. In the broader context of the industry, however, this is a fairly minor point of disagreement. After all, plenty of investors still view the prospect of scrappy startups building orbital data centers as a wildly expensive and exceedingly unlikely proposition in the first place, including Mike Schroepfer, founder of Gigascale Capital and former Meta CTO. “It’s a trap. I’m just amused by how many people are falling for it,” Schroepfer told me. “Elon’s so good at this. He’s convincing everyone this is the thing, so everyone’s going to invest in it and build the supply chain. And he is best positioned to build space-based data centers, so I don’t know how anyone’s going to compete against SpaceX on this.” Schroepfer thinks Musk will put AI infrastructure in orbit, but that the economics of this approach will still look pretty poor compared with his favored alternative: deploying data centers in the open ocean. artigo.texto: The world's first 600-MW-class expander for a compressed air energy storage system Photo: Courtesy of the Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences China has completed the development and testing of the world's first 600-MW-class expander for a compressed air energy storage (CAES) system, marking a major step forward in the development of large-scale energy storage equipment, the Institute of Engineering Thermophysics (IET) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) announced on Thursday. The IET and Zhongchu Guoneng (Beijing) Technology Co announced that the jointly developed expander has completed the integrated testing and successfully rolled off the production line. A compressed air energy storage system mainly consists of a compressor, an expander and a thermal energy storage heat exchanger, among other components. An expander is a key component of a compressed air energy storage system, converting the energy stored in compressed air into mechanical work. The system works much like a giant rechargeable battery: During periods of low electricity demand, excess power is used to compress air for storage. When electricity demand rises, the compressed air is released to drive an expander, which drives a generator to produce electricity. As a core component of the system, the expander is often compared to its "heart," with its performance having a significant impact on the efficiency of the entire system. After nearly two years of intensive research and development, the research team overcame several technical challenges involved in designing a 600-MW-class expander capable of variable-speed operation, wide load-range performance and high efficiency. Key breakthroughs included the fully three-dimensional aerodynamic design across the expander's entire operating range, the complex structural design of an ultra-long multistage shaft system, and coordinated dynamic control of variable geometry and rotational speed. The team subsequently developed the world's first 600-MW-class compressed air energy storage expander with fully independent intellectual property rights, according to the institute. The expander has completed the integrated assembly and mechanical testing, with all test results meeting or exceeding design targets, the institute said. Advantages of the device include a high degree of integration, high efficiency, rapid startup and shutdown times, long service life and ease of maintenance. The 600-MW-class system represents a doubling in scale compared with a 300-MW-class system. According to the team, scaling up the system is expected to reduce costs per unit of power capacity by 20 percent to 30 percent and improve overall system efficiency by 3 to 5 percentage points. The successful development of the expander marks an important milestone for compressed air energy storage technology worldwide and significant progress in the world's first 600-MW-class CAES national demonstration project, the institute said. The IET began researching CAES technology in 2005, becoming one of the earliest institutions in China to undertake research in this field. It pioneered a new principle for advanced CAES technology, overcoming key limitations of conventional systems, including their reliance on fossil fuels for supplementary combustion and low energy efficiency. After 20 years of research and development, the institute was the first in the world to propose the concept of "matching storage and discharge with cycle operation," establishing a design theory based on corresponding operating points within energy storage systems. It has also clarified the internal flow and heat transfer mechanisms of key CAES components and made breakthroughs in wide-load compression, high-load expansion turbines, high-efficiency compact thermal storage and heat exchange, and system design and control under all operating conditions. These advances have enabled the development of an independent technology and research system. The institute has successfully developed China's first demonstration systems at the 1.5-MW, 10-MW, 100-MW and 300-MW scales, establishing China's leading position internationally in compressed air energy storage technology. Long-duration, large-scale energy storage is essential to building a new energy system. As renewable energy capacity continues to expand, the inherent intermittency and fluctuations of wind and solar power are expected to pose growing challenges to the safe and stable operation of power grids. As one of the most promising technologies for large-scale, long-duration energy storage, CAES is expected to play an increasingly important role in safeguarding energy security and strengthening the power system's ability to maintain stability and balance supply and demand, according to the institute.

artigo.texto: AI's next data center boom is moving into cities, and into people's homes As demand for computing power grows, developers are finding ways to install servers in office towers, industrial buildings and even private residences. The shift promises faster connections and new revenue streams, but also raises questions about electricity, noise, water consumption and regulation. In recent weeks, residents of the Colonial Hills neighborhood in Southaven, Mississippi, have been receiving unexpected house calls. Real estate agents hired by xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company, have been going door to door, offering to buy residents' homes and urging them to leave the area quickly. The logic behind the move is as straightforward as it is ruthless: in an effort to prevent homeowners from joining a lawsuit already filed against the company over noise generated by a power plant supplying electricity to a nearby xAI data center, Musk has apparently decided that buying their homes would be cheaper. According to one recorded conversation, the company aims to acquire 418 homes in the neighborhood. So far, 18 homeowners have agreed to sell. This remarkable story is just one example of the unusual challenges arising from the ever-growing demand for the computing resources that power the artificial intelligence revolution. To generate responses quickly, AI models require ever-increasing numbers of servers. The result is a global construction boom in massive data centers, typically built in remote areas or on the outskirts of towns, whose construction and operation can take a toll on the environment, wildlife and local communities. In Finland, Google was ordered last month to halt infrastructure and construction work on two data centers after it emerged that the company had illegally felled approximately a quarter of a million trees to clear the sites. In Talavada, India, local residents are campaigning against the construction of a massive data center, a joint project by Google and the Adani Group, arguing that it threatens the local water supply and regional wildlife. Meanwhile, in the United States, Republican voters are increasingly paying attention to environmental issues, in this case because of the impact data centers are having on their own communities. Residents are complaining about the constant "white noise" generated by data centers and their adjacent power plants, as well as the enormous quantities of water consumed to cool the servers inside them. And what about Israel? The Electricity Authority was recently forced to intervene and regulate the flood of applications to establish data centers. While the Authority sought to manage the facilities' electricity consumption, setting a limit of 200 megawatts for each new facility, one question remains unresolved: how much land is actually available in such a small, densely populated country to accommodate these enormous server complexes? These challenges have helped drive a new development in the industry: the construction of data centers within urban areas. Some are designed to meet the computing needs of an entire building, reducing reliance on remote server farms; others occupy entire floors of office towers. Some companies are even offering to install servers in vacant rooms in residential buildings, generating rental income for apartment owners. The shift is already underway and is expected to accelerate. The main reason for bringing data centers into cities is that building them in remote locations can take years, due to the need to establish transmission infrastructure, clear land, navigate regulatory hurdles and contend with public opposition. Cities, by contrast, already have established power infrastructure. Integrating data centers into existing buildings through mixed-use development can also help overcome planning and land-acquisition barriers. The trend is also being driven by forecasts about how the technology industry will evolve. Until now, much of the AI industry's focus has been on training models, a process that requires enormous computing power but does not necessarily require servers to be close to end users. Consulting firm McKinsey predicts that the industry's focus will increasingly shift toward "inference": the actual execution of models when a user asks a question, an autonomous vehicle detects a pedestrian or a robot makes a decision. Unlike training, inference often requires rapid response times, making it advantageous to locate computing infrastructure closer to users. A server for every tenant The trend is still in its early stages, but research firm The Insight Partners estimates that approximately $10.9 billion was invested in urban data centers in 2025. It projects that the figure will reach $118.8 billion by 2034, representing annual growth of about 30%. According to the study, spatial constraints will be a key driver, with a shortage of available sites accelerating the migration toward urban centers. The EdgeUp AI project by Switchup, a company that manages approximately 300,000 square meters of office space, is among the first attempts to bring this model to Israel. The complex, currently under construction in Tel Aviv, is expected to combine office space with infrastructure facilities, including data centers. Ben Braverman, a managing partner at Switchup, says the company is building a facility in which parts of the space were initially allocated to 16 servers. Their computing power will be made available to companies renting offices in the building. According to Braverman, having servers nearby will significantly reduce the gap between simulation and real-world execution while lowering costs for tenants. Braverman says the model will spare companies the need to establish and operate their own server infrastructure. He describes a broader vision: "We will take a floor or half a floor in a building, divide it into units of about 50 square meters, and companies that rent labs from us will get server farms

artigo.texto: German chemical company BASF is restructuring its battery materials business to focus on cathode materials. It is divesting its battery recycling business and exploring external partnerships for its precursor business. The company aims to strengthen its competitiveness in cathode materials through collaboration with China's CATL, the world's largest battery manufacturer. BASF said on Nov. 27 that it had begun supplying CATL with cathode materials produced at its plant in Schwarzheide, Germany. The facility is BASF's second supply base for CATL after its plant in Changsha, China. The Schwarzheide plant is Germany's only cathode materials production facility. BASF and CATL signed a global framework agreement for cathode materials supply in July last year. CATL selected BASF as a key supplier of cathode materials. The companies jointly developed products tailored to battery performance and technical requirements. Local production in Germany has also established a supply chain within Europe. Specific supply volumes and cathode material compositions were not disclosed. Cathode materials are key components of a battery's positive electrode and determine major performance characteristics, including energy density, power output and lifespan. Common cathode materials include ternary chemistries such as nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) and nickel-cobalt-aluminum (NCA), as well as lithium iron phosphate (LFP). BASF focuses primarily on nickel-based cathode materials. BASF operates cathode materials production facilities in China and Japan as well as Germany. In China, it supplies CATL with cathode materials produced at its Changsha plant. In Japan, BASF TODA oversees the cathode materials business. Major customers include Panasonic and Prime Planet Energy & Solutions (PPES), a battery joint venture between Toyota and Panasonic. Since 2024, BASF has adjusted its investment plans and business structure in response to changing conditions in the electric vehicle and battery markets. It has reduced costs and capital expenditure in its battery materials business while securing long-term supply agreements with major customers. During the restructuring process, BASF identified cathode materials as offering the greatest profitability and growth potential. On Nov. 20, the company signed an agreement to sell its battery recycling business to German battery recycling specialist cylib. The transaction covers recycling operations in Europe and North America, including the black mass production plant and battery recycling pilot facility in Schwarzheide, Germany, as well as intellectual property and customer contracts. The companies expect to complete the transaction between the second and third quarters of 2027. Financial terms were not disclosed. BASF is also seeking external partners that can utilize existing equipment and technology at its idled production facility in Battle Creek, Michigan, and precursor plant in Harjavalta, Finland. “Cathode materials are critical to battery performance, safety and cost,” said Daniel Schönfelder, president of BASF's Battery Materials division. “We will concentrate our resources on areas where BASF's chemistry expertise can deliver the greatest value to customers.”

artigo.texto: Órgão regulador de telecomunicações dos Estados Unidos, a Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC, na sigla em inglês) autorizou na quarta-feira (25) a SpaceX a lançar até 1 milhão de satélites como parte de seu projeto de centros de dados no espaço, o que gerou preocupação entre alguns especialistas. Embora a instalação dos data centers no espaço tenha vantagens, como a possibilidade de captar continuamente energia solar, também pode perturbar a observação do céu noturno e as pesquisas astronômicas. A FCC indicou que a constelação Starmind processará "quantidades massivas de dados para que sejam usados aqui na Terra". A autorização concedida à SpaceX vai até 2040, segundo um documento publicado no site do órgão. O presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, destacou o jargão que costuma ser utilizado pelo presidente americano Donald Trump quando fala de inteligência artificial: — Os Estados Unidos estão conduzindo o mundo à era da superinteligência. Carr acrescentou que os centros de dados serão para os americanos: — Essenciais para apoiar a liderança dos Estados Unidos na área de superinteligência. Aumento de data centers no espaço Desde o ano passado, multiplicaram-se os projetos de data centers em órbita. Além da SpaceX e de sua constelação Starmind, o Google desenvolve o programa Suncatcher, enquanto a Blue Origin apresentou à FCC um pedido para o seu Project Sunrise. Outras empresas emergentes também têm projetos em andamento, em especial a Starcloud, que colocou em funcionamento com sucesso, no fim de 2025, um processador de última geração a partir de um satélite. Em outubro, o Google também alcançou resultado semelhante. A SpaceX tem a vantagem de contar com os seus próprios foguetes, que já realizaram centenas de missões. Em agosto, Elon Musk, o CEO da SpaceX, prometeu o primeiro lançamento no quarto trimestre de 2027 e uma aceleração do ritmo em 2028. A empresa firmou um acordo com a Nvidia, que fornecerá processadores de última geração Vera Rubin, projetados especialmente para operar no espaço. A maior parte dos programas de centros de dados espaciais segue uma arquitetura semelhante: uma constelação de satélites em órbita baixa, posicionados próximos uns dos outros para garantir uma conexão confiável. No caso do Starmind, os satélites se comunicarão com os da constelação de internet Starlink, também da SpaceX, responsável pela transmissão dos dados. Outros concorrentes planejam receber dados diretamente da Terra e devolvê-los ao planeta por meio de laser. Mas especialistas alertaram para possíveis obstáculos técnicos e para os problemas ambientais que podem ser provocados por esta tecnologia. Entre os desafios ainda não solucionados, está a capacidade dos processadores de suportar os elevados níveis de radiação do espaço. Analistas também destacaram a dificuldade de suportar temperaturas extremas ou de evitar danos causados por detritos espaciais ou micrometeoritos. Desânimo e consternação A Sociedade Astronômica Americana (AAS, na sigla em inglês) afirmou que está "desanimada e consternada" com a decisão. "A constelação proposta significaria minar décadas de investimentos federais em instalações astronômicas e a capacidade dos astrônomos e do público de apreciar e estudar o céu noturno." A sociedade apontou que a constelação implica "objetos maiores (e, portanto, mais brilhantes) e em maior número", de modo que os satélites serão "visíveis, por serem objetos extremamente brilhantes, durante longos períodos no céu noturno". Jan Hasselman, advogado veterano da ONG Earthjustice, alertou que os satélites podem afetar o planeta Terra: — Expandir drasticamente o número de satélites no espaço tem um impacto direto na vida cotidiana das pessoas e também no futuro do nosso planeta.

artigo.texto: Most Americans do not like data centers. They made that very clear in the midterm elections, when local communities overwhelmingly approved moratoriums and restrictions on data center construction. Still, Congress is now debating a bill that would make it easier to build them — and that bill passed the Senate last week. The case against these facilities is well-established. Less common is an ardent voice of support. Ted Neitzke is one of those rare proponents. He's mayor of the formerly industrial Wisconsin city of Port Washington, north of Milwaukee and adjacent to Lake Michigan. "Every revolution has brought an evolution, and that's what I think is happening," Neitzke told NPR last month. "We are living in the early 20th century, just remodeled again. We have Zuckerberg. They had J.P. Morgan. We have Elon Musk. They had Rockefeller." As mayor, Nietzke supports a controversial data center the size of 500 football fields that's being built on former farm land in Port Washington. Opponents of the project believe it will harm the community. But Mayor Neitzke thinks he's figured out a way to reap its benefits and minimize its downsides. "I don't understand why a community like ours, who grew up in an industrial base, would fight the fact that we would need this back again," he said. Even after the midterms delivered a decisive rebuke of data center projects, Mayor Neitzke says his city's data center deal could be a national model, one that resolves many of the concerns Americans have about them. "There is no better square-foot-value industrial development than a data center," he added, "and a lot of people will get very upset when I say that." artigo.texto: U.S. data centers are driving greater power demand, and with it, more pollution from coal and gas power plants. Researchers estimate that worsening pollution is leading to hundreds of early deaths. The new modeling study finds that, in 2023, the added power demand from data centers led to an estimated 650 early deaths across the U.S. Given the rapid buildout of data centers, their impact would likely be even greater today, authors say. The study further suggests that pollution is often intensifying far from where data centers are located. For instance, data centers in Virginia — which are connected to a large regional power grid — might spur power plants in the Midwest to ramp up. As their power output grows, so does particulate pollution, a contaminant linked to heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease. “Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” said coauthor Noelle Selin, head of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy at MIT. The findings were published in Environmental Research Letters. A separate study, published this month in Nature Sustainability, looks at the impact of more than 400 hyperscale data centers across the U.S. It found the facilities are using as much electricity as 8 million homes. In Oregon and Virginia, two data center hotspots, they are consuming more than 15 percent of the electricity sold in each state. artigo.texto: A Tecto Data Centers anunciou nesta quarta-feira, 25, a construção de seu primeiro data center em Pernambuco. Localizado em Recife, o empreendimento, denominado TREC1, terá capacidade inicial de 1 MW, com possibilidade de expansão para até 6 MW. O início das operações está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto integra o plano de investimentos de US$ 2 bilhões da companhia, anunciado em abril deste ano, que contempla obras e novos empreendimentos até 2028. O valor destinado especificamente à unidade pernambucana não foi divulgado. A instalação atenderá operadoras de telecomunicações, hyperscalers, provedores de nuvem e de conteúdo, além de clientes corporativos. Entre os serviços previstos estão colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados. Integração O novo data center será interligado à infraestrutura da companhia em Fortaleza (CE), um dos principais pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos internacionais ao Brasil. A integração permitirá que clientes distribuam suas operações entre as duas capitais, inclusive para recuperação de dados em caso de desastres e continuidade dos negócios. "Com o TREC1, a região passa a contar com dois polos da nossa rede, afinal, acreditamos que Recife está para Fortaleza, assim como o Rio de Janeiro está para São Paulo. Essa é a lógica da nossa estratégia AI Grid, que conecta data centers, levando capacidade de processamento para perto das empresas e complementando as grandes estruturas do AI Factory", afirmou Tito Costa, CRO da Tecto Data Centers. Com a unidade de Recife, a companhia prevê alcançar oito data centers em operação na América Latina até 2027, sendo cinco no Brasil e três na Colômbia. A empresa também desenvolve outros dois projetos no mercado brasileiro: um de 200 MW em Santana de Parnaíba (SP) e outro de 20 MW em Porto Alegre (RS).

artigo.texto: EU and UK Finalize Deal to Link Emissions Trading Systems, With Interchangeable Allowances From January 2028 Why It MattersLinking the two carbon markets shifts airline compliance toward one pooled allowance market with a single UK authority, while the EU's separate plan for long-haul flights keeps its external reach contested. What happened The European Union and the United Kingdom have finalized negotiations to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS), with the deal announced at the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Nov. 20, 2026. The UK ETS was created in 2021 following Brexit, and businesses called for it to be linked to the EU ETS from the outset. Negotiations began in late 2025. The European Commission's Directorate General for Climate Action said the agreement will ensure the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading applies in the EU and the UK. If ratified on both sides, the deal is expected to simplify airline compliance and create a larger market with more stable carbon pricing. The UK will also introduce a "one-stop shop," so airlines deal with a single authority for both schemes rather than separate UK and EU regulators. Work is underway to operationalize the agreement, with any necessary legislation to be passed in 2027 and procedures to be enacted in January 2028. According to the UK government, from Jan. 1, 2028, UK and EU allowances can be used interchangeably across both schemes. The first surrender deadline at which allowances from both systems will be accepted is Sept. 30, 2028, covering operators' obligations for the 2027 compliance year. The two systems will continue to operate separately, with "dynamic alignment," and the UK government said it will have an early "decision-shaping role" when the EU develops new EU ETS policies. The aviation scope dispute In July 2026, the European Commission announced plans to extend the EU ETS to cover flights between the EU and non-EU countries within a 5,000 km (3,100 mi.) range. The proposal drew strong opposition from aviation stakeholders, who view it as extraterritorial and as undermining global efforts through Corsia, the International Civil Aviation Organization's program to stabilize net CO2 emissions from international flights. The UK Department for Transport acknowledged the draft EU proposal and said it is aligning with "elements" of the EU ETS, including the scope of aviation coverage. The EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland's ETS since Jan. 1, 2020. Industry impact & what to watch For airlines and business-aviation operators flying between the UK and the EU, the practical change is administrative as much as financial. Two separate carbon regimes, each with its own regulator and allowance pool, are set to become one interchangeable pool with a single UK point of contact. Operators that today hold and track allowances separately for each scheme would be working from a common stock, and a larger linked market is expected to steady carbon pricing. The link also ties UK aviation policy more closely to Brussels. With dynamic alignment, the UK follows the EU's rule changes while keeping a separate system, and its early role in shaping new EU policy sits alongside its stated alignment with elements of the EU's aviation coverage. That makes the EU's July proposal on flights to non-EU countries within 5,000 km a live question for UK-linked operators, and it keeps the objections tied to Corsia in play. The next dated milestones are legislation in 2027, procedures in January 2028, and the Sept. 30, 2028 surrender deadline for the 2027 compliance year. Ratification on both sides is the condition on which the deal's benefits depend.

artigo.texto: SpaceX gets FCC approval for 1 million satellites to build data centers in space, Brendan Carr says The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday greenlit SpaceX's request to put 1 million satellites in space that will create orbital data centers, bringing CEO Elon Musk closer to his goal of harnessing the sun to generate computing power. "Today, in a historic first, the FCC approved SpaceX's request for 1 million satellites (orbital compute modules) to create data centers in space," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a post on X. Musk responded by saying, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." SpaceX's satellites will conduct telemetry, tracking and command operations, and will connect with other satellites, including those in SpaceX's Starlink system, the FCC said in a February filing. SpaceX filed a request with the FCC to put data centers in space in January. In its application, it said that deploying data centers in space would be the "first step towards becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization," referring to a threshold Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev proposed at which a civilization could tap the entire energy output of its star. When it filed its initial public offering in May, SpaceX said that orbital data centers would be able to handle intense demand from the AI sector and generate energy more efficiently than land-based facilities, which have become a flashpoint across the U.S. Thousands of data centers are being built, sparking backlash from communities who argue the facilities will transform their cities, create unwanted noise and drive up electricity and water use. In the midterms, American voters approved dozens of proposals aimed at restricting data centers. In its IPO filing, SpaceX said it expects to begin deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028.

artigo.texto: - 1A WEG obteve o credenciamento de seu pack de baterias de lítio junto ao BNDES e chega habilitada ao primeiro leilão de armazenamento de energia do Brasil. - 2Enquadrada na rota 2 pelo conteúdo local, a fabricante permite aos investidores financiar até 100% dos itens elegíveis por meio do Fundo Clima no leilão. - 3Para atender à demanda, a WEG investe R$ 330 milhões em uma nova fábrica em Itajaí, projetada para operar a partir do segundo semestre de 2027. Resumo e áudio gerados por inteligência artificial a partir do texto desta matéria. A WEG obteve o credenciamento de seu pack de baterias de lítio junto ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social, o BNDES, e chega habilitada ao primeiro leilão de armazenamento de energia do Brasil, que começa na próxima quarta-feira (2). Com o registro, investidores que adotarem a solução da fabricante de Jaraguá do Sul (SC) passam a ter acesso a condições diferenciadas em linhas, como a de Financiamento de Máquinas e Equipamentos, e a do Fundo Clima. O Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de 2026 será dividido em duas etapas. Em 2 de dezembro ocorre a disputa de armazenamento nacional, restrita a soluções que cumprem requisitos de conteúdo local. Entre no grupo Em 4 de dezembro, a modalidade de armazenamento geral abre espaço também para sistemas sem nacionalização. Os contratos dos vencedores terão duração de 15 anos, com início de operação previsto a partir de agosto de 2028. Diferença no financiamento A WEG foi enquadrada na rota 2 de credenciamento, mais complexa que a rota 1, por exigir etapas de fabricação dos packs no Brasil. Dentro dessa classificação há diferenças de profundidade industrial: parte das soluções se limita a integrar módulos e conjuntos já montados, enquanto outras partem das células para processos mais complexos de fabricação e montagem. “É justamente nessa segunda abordagem que nos diferenciamos estrategicamente no mercado. A WEG está indo além da estratégia de nacionalização a partir das células e do atendimento regulatório, pois está contribuindo para estabelecer uma indústria brasileira de armazenamento com maior conteúdo tecnológico, competitividade e autonomia ao mercado”, diz o diretor de Vendas Solar, BESS e Building da WEG, Harry Schmelzer Neto. A classificação pesa no custo dos projetos. Pelo Fundo Clima, empreendimentos na rota 2 podem financiar até 100% dos itens elegíveis, ante o limite de 80% na rota 1. Em projetos de grande porte, nos quais custo de capital, prazo de financiamento e previsibilidade de receitas são determinantes, a diferença tende a influenciar a escolha de fornecedores. “Nossa participação no leilão terá grande importância, pois contribuiremos para atender o sistema energético naquilo que ele precisa, aumentando sua estabilidade e garantindo o uso das fontes renováveis para a transição energética”, completa Harry Schmelzer Neto. Nova fábrica em Itajaí Para atender à demanda por sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, a WEG amplia o parque fabril de Itajaí, no Litoral Norte catarinense, com uma nova fábrica de 4 GWh de capacidade anual. O investimento de R$ 330 milhões é feito por meio do programa BNDES Mais Inovação, e a operação deve começar no segundo semestre de 2027, cerca de um ano antes do início previsto dos contratos do leilão.

artigo.texto: Korean POSCO Group has strengthened its relationship with battery manufacturer CATL through a long-term lithium supply agreement covering the 2026-2028 period. The deal will see POSCO supply lithium for use in electric vehicle battery production, further deepening cooperation between the two companies as demand for battery raw materials continues to grow. Supporting Battery Production CATL is the world’s largest EV battery producer, accounting for around 40% of the global electric vehicle battery market. The company supplies batteries to major vehicle manufacturers in China and international markets. Under the agreement, POSCO Group will provide lithium required for CATL’s battery manufacturing operations between 2026 and 2028. The companies have also committed to strengthening their long-term partnership and cooperating to support a stable supply of battery raw materials. According to the announcement, deliveries under the contract have already begun. Expanding POSCO’s Lithium Business The agreement forms part of POSCO Group’s broader strategy to grow its lithium business, building on capabilities developed through its long-standing experience in securing and developing raw materials for its steel operations. The company has established a production base through the early acquisition of high-quality lithium resources and believes the CATL agreement will reinforce its sales position in China while enhancing its standing in the global lithium market. The deal also aligns with the strategic direction of POSCO Holdings Chief Executive Chang In Hwa, which focuses on securing high-quality resources and developing long-term relationships with leading global customers. Focus on Supply Chain Stability POSCO said it plans to continue improving the production stability and sales competitiveness of its lithium resources in an effort to strengthen profitability. The company also highlighted its role as a major Korean supplier of critical minerals, stating that it aims to contribute to greater stability across global supply chains for key battery materials. For the battery sector, the agreement underlines the importance of long-term raw material partnerships as manufacturers and suppliers seek to secure reliable lithium supplies to support continued growth in electric vehicle battery production.

artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday. Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI. Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan." The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval. Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October. In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January. Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday. "Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense." SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

artigo.texto: O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou que a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) está em fase final de conclusão e deve sair "nos próximos dias". A expectativa foi sinalizada em conversa com jornalistas, durante o Fórum dig.ia, realizado em Brasília, nesta quarta-feira, 25. "O mais difícil foi conseguir aprovar [o Redata] no Congresso Nacional. Está agora na fase final do processo de regulamentação. É uma discussão entre ministérios, Casa Civil e presidência da República. A gente acredita que nos próximos dias isso será resolvido, até pela importância do tema", disse o ministro. A lei do Redata foi sancionada em setembro. A regulamentação, que deve trazer uma lista de equipamentos contemplados com redução de impostos, é aguardada pelo mercado como forma de ampliar os investimentos no setor de infraestrutura digital aproveitando o benefício fiscal. "Sabemos que é muito importante para atração de novos data centers. A gente vai assumir esse papel de ser um grande hub de data centers para inteligência artificial", destacou Siqueira Filho. Políticas adiadas para 2027 Se a regulamentação do Redata pode sair em breve, o mesmo não se pode dizer das políticas nacionais de cabos submarinos e data centers. Ambas eram esperadas para este ano, mas o ministro, questionado por TELETIME, confirmou que vão ficar para 2027. "Isso vai ficar para 2027. A política de data centers se soma ao Redata, justamente por reduzir a burocracia e favorecer a interação com estados e municípios com relação aos licenciamentos. É isso que estamos propondo para dar mais visibilidade e segurança jurídica para quem decide investir no Brasil", pontuou. Norma 4 O ministro também afirmou que ainda deve conversar com a Anatel sobre a extinção da Norma 4. A previsão é de que a medida que distingue serviços de telecomunicações do Serviço de Conexão à Internet (SCI) seja revogada em janeiro de 2027, o que contraria entidades de provedores de Internet. "Não tratei desse assunto particularmente ainda. Em breve, a gente vai conversar com a Anatel para entender quais são as motivações, o que a Anatel está pensando, qual o objetivo disso. E também ouvir o mercado, os provedores, as empresas que fazem acontecer no nosso setor para que a gente tenha uma posição que seja justa no tempo correto atendendo a todos", disse Siqueira Filho.

artigo.texto: Justiça nega suspensão do leilão de baterias Justiça Federal nega suspensão do leilão A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal negou nesta quarta-feira (25) um pedido de tutela de urgência que buscava suspender a realização do primeiro leilão para contratação de baterias para o setor elétrico brasileiro, marcado para a próxima semana. A decisão foi proferida pelo juiz Diego Câmara, que analisou a ação civil pública apresentada pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (ABEEólica). O magistrado entendeu que não estavam presentes no caso os requisitos para a concessão da medida, como perigo de dano ou o risco ao resultado útil do processo. A negativa mantém o cronograma do certame, que é aguardado com expectativa pelo setor elétrico. A decisão representa um revés para a entidade eólica, que buscava barrar a realização do leilão antes mesmo de sua ocorrência. Com isso, o processo segue seu curso normal, e a disputa deverá ocorrer conforme planejado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). ABEEólica questionava custeio das baterias Na ação civil pública, a ABEEólica questionava principalmente o custeio da contratação das baterias, que por definição legal foi imputado aos geradores de energia. Segundo a entidade, a lei que impôs o ônus aos geradores é inconstitucional. Esse ponto central da argumentação da associação eólica não foi acolhido pelo juiz, que considerou ausentes os requisitos para a tutela de urgência. Além disso, a ABEEólica apontava “vícios” na estruturação do certame de baterias pela Aneel, citando a falta de uma regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos entre os diferentes geradores. A entidade defendia que, sem essa definição prévia, o leilão não poderia ser realizado de forma justa e transparente. No entanto, o juiz entendeu que não há norma legal ou regulamentar que condicione a realização do leilão à definição prévia pela agência reguladora do rateio do encargo. Decisão destaca ausência de dano iminente O juiz considerou ainda que não há dano iminente aos geradores associado ao leilão, já que a disputa marcada para a próxima semana não corresponde ao início da cobrança de encargos. Segundo a decisão, a cobrança somente ocorreria com a entrada em operação dos projetos, em 1º de agosto de 2028. Esse entendimento foi fundamental para afastar o perigo de dano alegado pela ABEEólica. Dessa forma, o magistrado concluiu que a realização do leilão não traria prejuízos imediatos aos geradores, uma vez que os efeitos financeiros só seriam sentidos anos depois. A decisão reforça a ideia de que o certame é uma etapa necessária para garantir a segurança energética do país, sem antecipar ônus indevidos aos agentes do setor. Governo cita risco de déficit de potência O juiz citou ainda em sua decisão elementos trazidos em defesa da manutenção do leilão pelo governo, como o risco de déficit de potência já a partir do próximo ano. Esse argumento foi apresentado pelo poder público para justificar a urgência na contratação de baterias, que são vistas como essenciais para garantir a estabilidade do sistema elétrico diante do crescimento da geração intermitente, como a eólica e a solar. A menção ao risco de déficit de potência reforça a importância do leilão para o planejamento energético nacional. A decisão judicial, portanto, alinha-se à necessidade de assegurar o suprimento de energia no curto e médio prazo, evitando possíveis crises de abastecimento que poderiam afetar consumidores e empresas em todo o país. Impacto para o setor elétrico e consumidores A manutenção do leilão de baterias tem implicações diretas para o setor elétrico brasileiro. A contratação de sistemas de armazenamento é considerada estratégica para dar flexibilidade ao sistema, especialmente com o avanço das fontes renováveis. Para os geradores, a decisão significa que deverão se preparar para participar do certame e, futuramente, arcar com os custos definidos em lei, ainda que a discussão sobre a constitucionalidade continue em tramitação. Para os consumidores, especialmente os empresários e comerciantes do interior paulista, a realização do leilão pode trazer benefícios a longo prazo, como maior confiabilidade no fornecimento de energia e redução de riscos de interrupções. No entanto, há também a preocupação com o repasse dos custos dos encargos, que podem impactar as tarifas de energia. A decisão judicial não encerra o debate, mas garante a continuidade do processo de contratação, que é visto como essencial para a modernização do setor. A fonte não detalhou os próximos passos da ação civil pública, mas a decisão desta quarta-feira representa um marco importante para o leilão de baterias, que segue confirmado para a próxima semana. O setor elétrico acompanha atentamente os desdobramentos, enquanto a ABEEólica avalia as possibilidades de recurso. Perguntas Frequentes Por que a Justiça Federal negou o pedido de suspensão do leilão de baterias? O juiz Diego Câmara entendeu que não estavam presentes os requisitos para a concessão da medida, como perigo de dano ou risco ao resultado útil do processo. Quais eram os principais questionamentos da ABEEólica contra o leilão de baterias? A ABEEólica questionava o custeio da contratação das baterias imputado aos geradores de energia, alegando inconstitucionalidade da lei, e apontava vícios na estruturação do certame, como a falta de regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos. Quando os geradores começarão a pagar os encargos das baterias contratadas no leilão? A cobrança de encargos somente ocorrerá com a entrada em operação dos projetos, em 1º de agosto de 2028.
