artigo.texto: POSTECH Develops Solid-State Battery That Runs at Room Temperature Without Pressure Equipment South Korean researchers have demonstrated an all-solid-state lithium metal battery that operates at room temperature under low pressure, without heavy pressurization equipment. The achievement sharply lowers the high-pressure operating conditions long seen as the biggest obstacle to commercializing solid-state batteries, opening a path to reducing the weight and volume of battery packs. POSTECH announced on the 26th that a research team led by Park Soo-jin, a professor in the Department of Chemistry, together with Dr. Lee Hyung-seok and integrated-program student Sung Ji-hoon, developed the all-solid-state lithium metal battery in collaboration with researchers from Chung-Ang University, the Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States. The battery operates stably at room temperature under pressures of 0.3 MPa (megapascals) or less. The results were published on the 7th (local time) in the international journal Nature Communications. Solid-state batteries are a next-generation technology that replaces flammable liquid electrolytes with solid ones, lowering the risk of fire. Using a lithium metal anode can significantly boost energy density, but during charging, deposited lithium causes the electrode to expand in volume, opening gaps between the electrode and the electrolyte. Needle-like lithium crystals known as dendrites grow through these gaps and, if they pierce the electrolyte, can cause internal short circuits. Previously, preventing such gaps required pressing the battery firmly with massive equipment at high temperatures. The pressurization equipment itself was a major contributor to the weight and volume of battery packs. The research team tackled the two problems — electrolyte cracking and lithium expansion — with separate materials. First, they added thioctic acid (TA) to the sulfide-based solid electrolyte, which is vulnerable to impact, to form a dense polymer network structure. This network binds tightly with the electrolyte and holds cracks together like safety glass in automobiles, suppressing cracking and dendrite penetration, the team confirmed. The expansion problem was solved by using a porous carbon material with numerous microscopic pores as the anode current collector. In effect, the collector is pre-equipped with buffer space inside to accommodate the lithium that swells during charging. According to the team, the force of the expanding lithium is not concentrated toward the electrolyte but is distributed evenly through the pores of the current collector. The team used the Pohang Light Source (PLS-II) to observe the interior of the battery in three dimensions in real time during charging and discharging. They confirmed that expansion stress is absorbed as lithium fills and empties the pores of the current collector, and that repeated charge-discharge cycles produced no short circuits or distortion at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Cells using the technology operated stably at room temperature and pressures of 0.3 MPa or less even in a full-cell configuration with an NCM811 ternary cathode, widely used in actual electric vehicles. The team said this is the first time such low-pressure operation has been achieved in a sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium metal full cell with a capacity of 2.4 mAh/㎠. "The limitations of brittle sulfide-based solid electrolytes were addressed with a polymer network, and the expansion stress of lithium with a porous current collector," Park said. "These results came from close collaboration with South Korean researchers." Dr. Lee Hyung-seok, a co-first author, said, "Eliminating the massive pressurization equipment makes it possible to reduce the volume and weight of battery packs," adding, "It is expected to be recognized as a core mechanism that accelerates the commercialization of solid-state batteries." Solid-state batteries are regarded as a technology that can secure both energy density and safety at the same time, and global automakers and battery companies are competing to commercialize them. However, the brittleness of sulfide-based electrolytes, the expansion of lithium metal anodes and high-pressure operating requirements have been cited as bottlenecks for mass production. Because this study lowered the pressure requirement through material combinations alone, it is expected to serve as a reference for future cell design and pack lightweighting research on solid-state batteries. Still, as the work is at the laboratory-scale full-cell validation stage, further verification is needed for scale-up, long-term cycle life and application to production processes. The researchers expect the achievement to help bring forward the commercialization timeline for sulfide-based solid-state batteries. artigo.texto: CONWAY — At the ninth hearing on BlueWave Solar’s proposed solar array on Roaring Brook Road, Planning Board members and residents voiced concerns with the fire safety of the proposed battery energy storage system. After the company agreed to revise its original application to remove 20% of the panels, the proposed solar array’s updated design entails a 4.05-megawatt, dual-use system, allowing landowner Ronald Boyden to continue using the site for farming, with animals able to graze under the panels. “I believe the decision that’s before this board is going to be the most consequential land-use decision this town has made,” Selectboard Chair Christopher Waldo said at the start of the Nov. 18 public hearing. “It’s going to set a precedent for how industrial developers look at Conway. It’ll set a precedent for how we as board members, committees [and] citizens protect Conway.” Waldo said the town lacks the infrastructure to respond to fires originating at battery energy storage systems, including the water supply and force of firefighters, given that the Conway Fire Department consists of volunteers. “Where are we going to get that water supply? Where are we going to get the firefighters?” Waldo asked. “We all support green energy, we all support solar. … Unfortunately, Conway cannot be a host to such an industrial facility, because we can’t in good conscience say that we could protect our citizens and our schoolchildren if a fire breaks out.” Kevin LaMalva, an engineer at Fire & Risk Alliance working with BlueWave Solar, said using water to extinguish a battery energy storage system fire is discouraged and would only exacerbate the issue. Fire Chief Christopher Herrmann clarified that the firefighters would use water to control the fire if it spread to surrounding areas, like the nearby barn. With water being discouraged, “You’re pretty much stuck with, like Chris [Waldo] said, letting the battery burn out,” Herrmann said. For the fire chief, his concerns relate to the potential of a fire releasing harmful chemicals from the batteries into the air and water. According to LaMalva, the levels of hydrogen fluoride, one of the chemicals in the lithium-ion batteries, that would be released in a fire would be similar to a structure fire igniting from “ordinary items.” “That’s when the emergency response plan comes in,” LaMalva said. According to LaMalva, the emergency response plan for the battery energy storage system, which BlueWave Solar has not yet created, will recommend air monitoring after a fire to track any gasses from the fire’s plumes. In response to Herrmann and Selectboard member Elaine Campbell’s concern about emissions from the fire reaching the Conway Grammar School — the town’s emergency shelter — across the street from the proposed solar array, LaMalva said the school sits outside the area that would raise concern based on plume modeling data from other projects. “That is truly a worst-case outcome, because these are highly, highly regulated and tested pieces of equipment,” LaMalva said. “The system itself is intrinsically designed to burn itself out safely without leading to further fire spread.” He described the battery energy storage system’s fire safety system as a “defense and depth” approach, with multiple layers of prevention. A battery management system and thermal management system monitor the batteries for signs of thermal runaway and adjust the voltage and temperature. Thermal runaway occurs when a battery overcharges, short-circuits or undergoes damage that heats up the battery and can cause fires or explosions. If thermal runaway does occur, pressure relief vents in the cells work to stop the runaway. To prevent an overheated cell from overheating another nearby cell, insulators also separate the cells within the module. If thermal runaway spreads to other cells, an explosion control system within the battery energy storage system container kicks in. Other safeguards are in place if the runaway continues to escalate, LaMalva said. “It’s not relying on one safety system to prevent the bad outcomes,” LaMalva said. “It’s a series of barriers that are in place to prevent that really bad outcome. It starts at the micro-level and it gets more macro-level.” According to the Electric Power Research Institute, while battery energy storage systems continue to experience safety failures, the rate of safety failures has decreased by 98% between 2018 and 2025. Nevertheless, residents have heard of fires at solar projects close to home, including in Shutesbury, where a fire started in an inverter at a 5.6-megawatt solar array in April. Along with recommended tactics, the emergency response plan will list critical firefighting equipment if the battery energy storage system catches fire. An expert on battery energy storage systems will be available to help train firefighters and familiarize them with the emergency response plan. artigo.texto: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered plans for a wave of new data-center construction following Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s digital infrastructure. The directive, issued after a September trip to Vladivostok, calls for new projects in Kemerovo (Kuzbass) and Yakutia (Sakha Republic), two of Russia's largest coal-producing regions. Kemerovo, located in southwestern Siberia, sits atop the Kuzbass coal basin and accounts for a significant portion of Russia's coal production. Yakutia, which lies farther east, is the largest federal subject of Russia by area and has emerged as one of the country's fastest-growing coal regions, if not of the same size. Read More on World Putin ordered his prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, to oversee the development of the plans by the end of the year and "ensure the implementation of the program." Why Russia Wants New Data Centers Russian officials and industry groups say demand for computing capacity is increasing as AI becomes more widespread across the globe. Russian officials have increasingly argued that the country needs more computing infrastructure to support domestic AI development. On September 1, Russia’s first federal artificial intelligence (AI) law came into effect, establishing sovereign AI, state support for Russian AI developers, and overseas promotion as national goals. Some provisions do not take effect until March 1, 2027. The facilities have become a center of focus for Ukrainian strikes in recent weeks, with sites linked to Yandex, VK and Sberbank being targeted in the last few weeks. As a result, officials have suggested making infrastructure harder to target. One proposal from Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev would place new data centers underground, including in former coal mines. "It's clear that they need to dig in," Shadayev said at the CNews Forum. "Given the choice between moving abroad or going underground, we, of course, favor moving them underground rather than relocating them." Kemerovo Governor Ilya Seredyuk has also suggested placing data centers in former mines, arguing abandoned underground sites could provide natural cooling and added protection from strikes. Back in July, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged during a speech at the "Territory of Meanings" youth educational forum, that Russia "cannot compete with the leading American language models." However, he said the country was "among the five countries in the race." "And I hope that, through superhuman efforts, we will narrow the gap," he added. Russia’s Data Center Portfolio Analysts told Newsweek that Russia's total number of data centers is difficult to determine because public information is limited and often outdated. However, estimates by DC Market Insights say there are 111 facilities in Russia as of November 19, 2026. This would put Russia in the top 15 countries by facility count, according to the source-linked tracker of data centers. However, it falls far short of the U.S. with 1,341 sites. Datacenter Atlas mapping suggests the majority of Russia's facilities are concentrated around Moscow and St. Petersburg. The facilities affected by the October strikes accounted for approximately 11 percent of Russia’s data center capacity, according to an estimation by the Moscow Times. Yandex confirmed on November 10 that it had restored access to roughly 97.16 percent, with 2.84 percent permanently lost. Another challenge is electricity. Industry reports have pointed to growing power constraints around Moscow, where much of the country's digital infrastructure is concentrated. But the coal-producing regions mentioned in Putin's plan could provide access to large energy supplies and available land. However, Eldar Murtazin, an analyst at Mobile Research Group, told the Moscow Times that building a new data center in a former mine could cost two to five times as much as building above ground. Murtazin noted that costs would likely be inflated due to high building costs, pumping out groundwater and staffing issues. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and James Debens

artigo.texto: A discussão em torno do modelo de financiamento para o armazenamento de energia no Brasil coloca em evidência os impactos econômicos e regulatórios das regras de custeio. Enquanto fontes tradicionais dividem despesas entre os consumidores, a legislação recente aplicou uma dinâmica diferente para as baterias. A situação gera debates sobre a transparência dos preços e a segurança jurídica para os investidores do setor. A diferença no modelo de financiamento Historicamente, a reserva de capacidade destinada a garantir potência nos horários de maior demanda utiliza recursos rateados entre os consumidores de forma direta. No entanto, a Lei 15.269/2025 estabeleceu que o custo das baterias seja suportado exclusivamente pelos geradores. Especialistas e agentes do setor questionam a coerência de adotar critérios distintos para serviços com a mesma finalidade no sistema elétrico nacional. Impactos na formação de preços O deslocamento da cobrança para os geradores não significa a eliminação do gasto para o consumidor final. Todo novo encargo inserido na cadeia produtiva acaba por influenciar a formação do preço do produto. Nos contratos do mercado livre, o investimento sofre forte pressão, enquanto nos leilões regulados a Aneel já projeta o repasse às distribuidoras, resultando em reflexos nas tarifas de energia elétrica. Incerteza regulatória e novos leilões Com os leilões de baterias agendados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026, o mercado lida com um cenário de indefinição. Tramita no Congresso Nacional o Projeto de Lei 3.716/2026, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), que visa revogar a exclusividade do custeio pelos geradores. A dualidade entre a lei vigente e a proposta legislativa adiciona riscos para empreendimentos de longo prazo, que dependem de contratos de 15 anos e de receitas previsíveis para atrair financiamento. Desafios para a competição e a modicidade tarifária A inclusão do risco regulatório nas propostas tende a encarecer os projetos e pode afastar potenciais investidores, reduzindo a competitividade dos certames. A tentativa inicial de proteger o consumidor de cobranças diretas corre o risco de produzir o efeito oposto, encarecendo a energia por vias indiretas. Garantir segurança regulatória é apontado por analistas como um passo fundamental para viabilizar o armazenamento de energia no país sem elevar os custos finais.

artigo.texto: Data centers: o que aprender com Singapura? A seleção de projetos em Singapura traz lições e alertas sobre eficiência e valor econômico para a infraestrutura digital no Brasil. Por Victor Arnaud* – Um data center pode atrair investimento e disputar energia, água e espaço com outras atividades. Singapura decidiu comparar as propostas pelo que entregariam ao país. Ao Brasil, interessa entender essa escolha e seus riscos. Na inauguração da primeira instalação, Tan Kiat How, ministro de Estado sênior para Desenvolvimento Digital e Informação de Singapura, defendeu gerar mais valor com a capacidade computacional, em vez de apenas aumentar seu volume. Após pausar a expansão em 2019, Singapura lançou o piloto do Data Centre Call for Application, o DC-CFA, em 2022. EDB e IMDA, agências de desenvolvimento econômico e digital, compararam eficiência, conectividade e contribuição econômica. Em julho de 2023, alocaram provisoriamente cerca de 80 MW a quatro propostas. A primeira instalação do piloto foi inaugurada em 6 de novembro de 2026, com 8 MW iniciais e até 20 MW previstos na expansão completa. A segunda chamada abriu em dezembro de 2025 e alocou provisoriamente 200 MW a quatro operadores em agosto de 2026. O PUE máximo caiu de 1,3 para 1,25, ambos a plena carga de TI. Esse índice mede o consumo total da instalação por unidade de energia usada pela TI. Exigiu-se também abastecer ao menos metade da nova capacidade por vias elegíveis de baixo carbono. Os selecionados deverão informar o consumo e comprovar essa parcela. O mérito é explicitar a relação entre acesso a recursos e compromissos de entrega. O risco aparece quando “contribuição econômica” se torna um critério tão amplo que favorece quem promete o maior pacote. Sem justificativas claras e possibilidade de contestação, a seleção pode proteger empresas estabelecidas. Um projeto eficiente no papel também precisa demonstrar desempenho em operação. O Digital Infrastructure Act, aprovado em 2026, permitirá incorporar compromissos da candidatura às condições de licença. A vigência é esperada para 2027, com implantação gradual. Os próximos passos serão executar os projetos e detalhar as regras. Outra rodada poderá ser considerada, mas não está garantida. Singapura tem pouco território e depende fortemente de gás importado para gerar eletricidade. O Brasil tem matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e gargalos distintos entre regiões. Energia disponível não significa conexão pronta no local do projeto. Transmissão, água e autorizações exigem avaliação local, em vez de uma restrição nacional copiada de outro contexto. No “AI Cake”, Jensen Huang descreve cinco camadas: energia, chips, infraestrutura, modelos e aplicações. A imagem ajuda a pensar a política brasileira: como os data centers permitirão desenvolver e usar modelos, formar profissionais e levar aplicações às empresas e aos serviços públicos? Essa ligação deve orientar a expansão. O Redata é uma das peças desse esforço. A Lei 15.504/2026 prevê suspensão de tributos sobre bens elegíveis, nos termos legais, com contrapartidas de energia, eficiência hídrica, pesquisa e atendimento ao mercado interno. Exige relatório público de sustentabilidade e atribui ao MDIC e à Fazenda a avaliação dos benefícios. Até 25 de novembro, o regulamento operacional não havia sido localizado nos registros oficiais consultados. A lição de Singapura deve orientar o conjunto da política de infraestrutura digital: coordenar recursos, definir critérios e acompanhar a entrega. O cuidado é evitar exigências vagas que acrescentem espera e favoreçam poucos. Para o Brasil, o resultado precisa aparecer no acesso à capacidade computacional, no desenvolvimento tecnológico e no uso produtivo dessa infraestrutura. O Redata deve ser avaliado por sua contribuição a esses objetivos. A qualidade da política estará na ligação entre os projetos aprovados e o que empresas, pesquisadores e serviços públicos conseguem realizar com eles. *Victor Arnaud, presidente da Equinix no Brasil, escreve mensalmente a Coluna do Arnaud no Tele.Síntese, com sua visão sobre presente e futuro da infraestrutura digital, soluções e IA .

artigo.texto: [Exclusive] "Hyundai Motor-Invested" U.S. Battery Firm Sues Korean Battery Maker That Partnered With POSCO Over Patent SES AI Files Patent Infringement Lawsuit Against BEI in U.S. Court "Claims Infringement of Two Anode-Free Lithium-Metal Battery Patents" Technology Plates Lithium Metal Directly onto Current Collector Without An Anode Material... For Use in Drones a The complaint in a patent lawsuit filed by U.S. battery company SES AI against South Korean battery company BEI. View original image U.S.-based battery company SES AI has filed a lawsuit against South Korean battery company BEI, alleging that BEI infringed its patents for anode-free lithium-metal batteries. According to the battery industry on November 25, SES AI filed a patent infringement lawsuit against BEI under U.S. patent law in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on November 18. SES AI alleges that at least two products developed by BEI, including the "Maximus UL17B" and "Maximus UL20A," infringe its anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. The two patents SES AI claims were infringed are a patent on "the design and performance of a battery in which the anode capacity is lower than the cathode capacity" (U.S. Patent No. 9,887,415) and a patent on "a high-capacity battery in which a metal coating forms on the anode surface during initial charging" (U.S. Patent No. 10,727,483). Both concern anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. Images and specifications of BEI-developed batteries "MUL 17B" and "MUL 20A." Screenshot from BEI's website. View original image The patents were registered to Singapore-based Viking Power Systems Pte. Ltd., a wholly owned subsidiary of SES AI. The second patent is also registered with the Korean Intellectual Property Office as "Electrochemical Cell and Method for Manufacturing the Same" (Registration No. 1025884540000). Lithium-metal batteries, which use lithium metal instead of graphite for the anode, are lighter and have a higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion batteries, and are being developed primarily for aerial mobility applications such as drones. Anode-free lithium-metal batteries, which have recently attracted attention as a next-generation battery technology, are exactly what their name suggests: batteries without an anode material. During charging, lithium ions from the cathode combine with electrons and plate directly onto the current collector as lithium metal, thereby forming the anode. During discharge, the lithium metal loses electrons and moves back to the cathode in the form of lithium ions. The battery operates through an electrochemical process in which the anode forms and then disappears. Because anode-free lithium-metal batteries do not contain an anode material, they can have thinner cells and store more energy in the same volume. They can also simplify the manufacturing process and reduce costs. Since its establishment in 2020, BEI has manufactured batteries for drones, defense applications, and robots. In particular, the company is expanding its business, including through an MOU signed in March with POSCO Future M and Kumho Petrochemical to jointly develop anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. BEI is preparing for a KOSDAQ listing in 2028 and has selected Samsung Securities and Mirae Asset Securities as lead underwriters. Posco Future M signed an MOU with Kumho Petrochemical and BEI at the POSCO Center in Seoul on March 25 to jointly develop anode-free lithium metal battery technology. (From left) Ko Younghoon, head of Kumho Petrochemical’s Central Research Institute; Hong Youngjun, head of Posco Future M’s Technology Research Institute; and Bae Changdeuk, CEO of BEI. View original image SES AI has also recently been expanding its drone battery business. In 2021, SES AI established a lithium-metal battery production facility at its plant in Chungju, North Chungcheong Province, and is developing it into a key production base for drone batteries. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plant's annual production capacity from around 200,000 units to 1 million units by the end of 2026. In its complaint, SES AI alleged that "some of BEI's employees were former senior executives of SES AI" and that they would have been familiar with SES AI's patents. According to LinkedIn, at least four BEI employees previously worked at SES AI. SES AI's patent lawsuit appears to signal its determination to actively protect its intellectual property, as anode-free lithium-metal batteries have recently drawn attention as a next-generation battery technology. SES AI said, "SES AI has groundbreaking proprietary technology and patents that can enhance the competitiveness of military drones and drone batteries, and plans to strongly protect its intellectual property rights." It added, "If infringement is confirmed in the future, we will continue to take active steps to protect our intellectual property rights." BEI also said it would contest the matter through legal channels. BEI said, "We are currently reviewing the scope of the claims and the technical specifications of the patents in question," adding, "We are consulting with a U.S. law firm specializing in patent litigation on how to respond." artigo.texto: On Battery Storage Facilities To the editor: Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) installations are vital for stabilizing and reducing the cost of power. For example, during the short period of the 2024 winter freeze, BESS facilities saved about $750 million in day-ahead market costs (Aurora Energy Research), helped maintain normal levels of service and prevent outages. Scare tactics in communications against BESS installations are deplorable. BESS facilities need to be distributed in order to provide the most benefit. Centralizing them does NOT provide the ability to relieve transmission bottlenecks, reduce grid power losses, stabilize local voltage, and eliminate single points of failure across the entire grid. The Warda BESS connects to the LCRA 138 kV transmission system at the Warda substation. The LCRA T170 138 kV Transmission Circuit, rated at 580 MVA, directly connects the Warda Substation to the Winchester Substation. Both the Warda and Winchester substations have stepdown transformers providing 12.7 kV power for the distribution networks for both the Bluebonnet Electric and Fayette Electric cooperatives. The Winchester Volunteer Fire Department normally receives power from the Winchester Substation via Bluebonnet. Both the St. Mark’s Medical Office Building and the new Progressive Health of Fayette hospital receive power from the Fayette Electric Cooperative through the connections to these two substations. To better understand how power from the Warda BESS powers local loads, consider a simple example of 100 MW flowing into the Warda Substation on one 138 kV line and 100 MW exiting on another 138 kV line while the BESS is putting 25 MW into the substation at 138 kV and Bluebonnet and Fayette together are withdrawing 25 MW via 12.7 kV interconnections. Thus, the BESS is supplying the entire local load of 25 MW in this example. Through the T170 interconnect, the BESS also helps power loads in the Winchester area, including the Winchester Volunteer Fire Department. When the Warda BESS produces more power than the immediate area is consuming, it also supports the grid for other counties. Weirdly, we hear some say that because people in adjoining counties to Fayette County can benefit, that makes the BESS a bad thing for Fayette County. Please reference Matthew 22:39 “Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.” A prime source of inexpensive charging power for the BESS is the 7V Solar Ranch with an output of 240 MW nearby in Muldoon here in Fayette County. There are other solar facilities reasonably close, for example: Bastrop County has the Big Star Solar near Rosansky with an output of 200 MW (plus it has an old 80 MW/120 MWh BESS with it); The Weberville Solar Farm output is 30 MW; and Milam County has more than 1400 MW of solar capability interconnecting with LCRA. The claim that “there isn’t enough water in the area to fight a fire in the area” is absurd. Not much water is needed following a thermal event because the batteries used are Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFe-PO4 or LFP).

artigo.texto: The case for data centers Most Americans do not like data centers. They made that very clear in the midterm elections, when local communities overwhelmingly approved moratoriums and restrictions on data center construction. Still, Congress is now debating a bill that would make it easier to build them — and that bill passed the Senate last week. The case against these facilities is well-established. Less common is an ardent voice of support. Ted Neitzke is one of those rare proponents. He's mayor of the formerly industrial Wisconsin city of Port Washington, north of Milwaukee and adjacent to Lake Michigan. "Every revolution has brought an evolution, and that's what I think is happening," Neitzke told NPR last month. "We are living in the early 20th century, just remodeled again. We have Zuckerberg. They had J.P. Morgan. We have Elon Musk. They had Rockefeller." As mayor, Nietzke supports a controversial data center the size of 500 football fields that's being built on former farm land in Port Washington. Opponents of the project believe it will harm the community. But Mayor Neitzke thinks he's figured out a way to reap its benefits and minimize its downsides. "I don't understand why a community like ours, who grew up in an industrial base, would fight the fact that we would need this back again," he said. Even after the midterms delivered a decisive rebuke of data center projects, Mayor Neitzke says his city's data center deal could be a national model, one that resolves many of the concerns Americans have about them. "There is no better square-foot-value industrial development than a data center," he added, "and a lot of people will get very upset when I say that." artigo.texto: Coweta County voters will decide in January whether to overturn the rezoning that approved Project Sail and prohibit future data center development throughout unincorporated Coweta County. On November 23, Coweta County Probate Court Judge Carrie B. Markham issued two orders clearing the way for a January 12, 2027, special election, following months of organized opposition to the proposed data center campus in western Coweta County. While opposition to Project Sail initially centered on the rezoning of approximately 829 acres of Rural Conservation land near Welcome to Sargent Road and Wagers Mill Road, the referendum extends well beyond that particular development. The proposed changes to Coweta County’s zoning ordinances would prohibit data centers even in areas already zoned for industrial use. More than 11,000 signatures verified The citizens’ petition, filed October 16, was brought under Article IX, Section II, Paragraph I(b)(2) of the Georgia Constitution, which provides a mechanism for citizens to bring county government decisions before voters. In counties with populations exceeding 50,000, the process requires signatures from at least 10% of the registered voters in the last general election. In Coweta County, that meant petitioners needed 10,971 valid signatures. As of November 20, county election officials had reviewed 11,551 signatures and certified 11,065 as valid, with additional signatures remaining to be reviewed. Markham declared the petition valid and ordered the special election, the expense of which will be borne by Coweta County. In a separate order, Markham dismissed an objection filed October 23 by Atlas Development LLC. The judge cited a 2023 Georgia Supreme Court decision involving Camden County establishing that parties do not have legal standing to object to this type of citizens’ petition in Probate Court. A ban beyond Project Sail The referendum combines the repeal of the Project Sail rezoning with changes to the county’s zoning ordinances in a single ballot question. According to the court order, the question will read: “Shall the action of the Coweta County Board of Commissioners on April 7, 2026 approving REZONE 24-019 be repealed, and Appendix A. Zoning and Development of the Coweta County Code of Ordinances be amended to delete data centers and data center campuses as permitted and conditional uses in all zoning districts and to prohibit data centers, data center campuses, cryptocurrency data centers, and cryptocurrency mining operations in all zoning districts of Coweta County?” Voters will not be asked to decide separately whether to reverse the Project Sail rezoning and whether to prohibit future data center development. The two proposals are combined. The ballot language does not distinguish between Rural Conservation land and existing industrial areas. It remains unclear what effect the measure would have on previously approved data center projects other than Project Sail. Months of organized opposition The Coweta County Commission approved the Project Sail rezoning in a 3–2 vote on April 7. Commissioners Al Smith, Jeff Fisher, and John Reidelbach voted in favor, while Chairman Bill McKenzie and Commissioner Bob Blackburn voted against it. The decision followed months of public meetings and organized opposition, with residents raising concerns about water and electricity consumption, traffic, environmental impacts, property values, and the preservation of Coweta County’s rural character. In May, a group of residents filed a separate lawsuit in Coweta County Superior Court seeking to invalidate the rezoning. Steve Swope, co-founder of Citizens for Rural Coweta, welcomed Monday’s Probate Court rulings in an email. “The Coweta County Commission does not have the last vote on the massive data center called Project Sail in an area of our county that has long been zoned for Rural Conservation, we the Citizens do!” Swope wrote. From restricting locations to prohibiting development In a March interview with The Citizen, Swope distinguished his organization’s opposition to Project Sail from opposition to the data center industry itself. “We’re not opposed to AI and we’re not opposed to data centers,” Swope said at the time. Swope advocated locating data centers in existing industrial corridors, including areas along Interstate 85, rather than converting rural conservation land to industrial use. The proposed zoning changes, however, would prohibit data centers in both. In an extensive June interview with The Citizen, Fisher discussed his reasons for supporting Project Sail, including his concerns that Coweta could lose the opportunity to benefit financially from data center development if opposition extended to existing industrial areas. Fisher estimated that Project Sail could eventually generate more than $100 million annually in combined county and school property tax revenue. Swope has previously disputed the scale of those projections, citing tax revenues generated by existing Georgia data centers. Fisher also argued that industrial tax revenue could reduce the county’s reliance on residential growth and provide funding for infrastructure, public safety, and land conservation. In August, Fisher joined the other four commissioners in unanimously rejecting another proposed data center, Project Oak, on property already zoned industrial. “I’ve tried to look at each data center proposal on its own merits,” Fisher wrote in a statement published by The Citizen. The proposed ordinance changes would remove data centers as an allowable land use throughout the county’s zoning districts rather than leaving future proposals to be considered individually by commissioners under the current ordinances. The Citizen reached out to Fisher and Reidelbach late Wednesday for comment on the court rulings. Neither had responded as of publication. The decision goes to voters The January special election will precede the next regularly scheduled elections for the three commission

artigo.texto: Dear reader: unless you are like RANGE writer Aaron Hedge who doesn’t have a life, you may be about to sit down at a glorious Thanksgiving feast with family. Congratulations. But implied in that eventuality is a poison pill: you will get sucked by your “just asking questions about people’s right to bodily autonomy” Uncle/Granddad/Father-figure Bill/Dave/Jim-Bob or your delusional Hillary dead-ender aunt into a … POLITICAL DEBATE, dun, dun, duuuuunnnn!!! (Yeah, we know: family bigots can come in all shapes, genders, sexual preferences, colors and ages.) What we’re saying is: no matter how much we all do the performative “no politics around the turkey!” thing, someone always ends up throwing just a little bit of shade from last night’s episode of Maddow or Gutfeld! (his exclamation, not ours), and then we’re racing to the bottom. But really, how many more times can we all endure that? We’re now entering year 12 of Trump’s stranglehold on the discourse, and your friends at RANGE are more than a little tired of reheating the same family discourse the way America is about to reheat all this damn stuffing. So what’s a locally engaged civic edgelord like you to do?Well, you can just wait around for Grandpa Bob to start asking your genderfluid niece, “what’s up with girl's sports?" Or, as a die-hard RANGE reader, you can short-circuit the national partisanship that we all find so exhausting by bringing up some local controversies that have much more complicated and interesting lines of discussion than just “Boy, Elon sure spent a lot of money in Texas, huh, kid?”And — bonus! — not only are the local issues below the sorts of things people like second cousin Cletus could actually work to change, they are the kind of things you, as your family’s RANGE reader (who’s about to convert the entire unit), already know like the back of your hand. This vaunted status places you in an ideal position to Dungeon-Master tomorrow’s little table-top brawl. That way, your antifa-loving ass can *team up* with your back-to-the-gold-standard uncle to mock your meme-stock cousin who is really dying to just “turn down the heat on the whole data center controversy” because his whippets dealer dared him to buy a bunch of Avista stock. In doing so, you may learn a little something about that uncle (other than why he doesn’t trust the World Bank) and, if you’re lucky, you’ll delay the evening’s annual title-card rematch — the battle for the most reasonable centrist: your never-Trump uncle (who likes to trot out the old saw about how Obamacare is basically just right-wing Romneycare) and your mom, who is still listening to “Mueller, She Wrote,” for some reason — juuuuuust long enough that one of them falls asleep in grandpa’s favorite recliner. (Again, if it makes you feel any better, Hedge does not have to worry about this.) Here, we’re suggesting five RANGE stories/products with which you can gird your rhetorical loins on a number of salient issues in prep for your inevitable fight with your familial political nemeses. Here they are: Who doesn’t want to be a millionaire? There was even a ballot measure backed by similar talking points attempting to repeal the tax that failed in the last election. Curley Qs Next, the media industry is embroiled in a turmoil that has come home in the form of Spokane’s most visible Disney stan, Rob Curley. Curley, the now-former editor of The Spokesman-Review, is no longer at the paper after a lengthy process that has thrown the paper of record and the nonprofit that was supposed to absorb it into a stage of intense uncertainty. Read Daisy Zavala Magaña’s and Wilson Criscione’s initial investigation, showing the newsroom had lost faith in Curley, accusing him of a history of abuses, here. Read the current status of the newspaper’s transfer to the Comma Community Journalism Lab here. (Spoiler: it’s kinda dead.) Eat your heart out, Schwarzenegger The artificial intelligence revolution has come for our souls, but it isn’t the inefficient slugfest between Arnold and Robert Patrick everyone used to think it’d amount to. It’s a lot dumber than that. And while President Donald Trump thinks anyone who opposes infrastructure that supports AI is a troglodyte (we’d love to hear him try to say that word), RANGE has covered the trend in-depth, calling out public officials and, yes, other journalists, for using the technology without disclosing it. Brush up on it with in-depth articles by Erin Sellers and Walters Power politics Not unrelated to the AI stuff, some Spokane County officials and the local power utility have been trying to bring a large data center to the environmentally beleaguered West Plains and the area northeast of Spokane, saying it’ll benefit the economy. (That’s probably not true.) Local folks are furious about it and have been calling for accountability for the secretive conversations power brokers are having with developers. Read our stories, starting with rumors of Avista Corp.’s mysterious “large-load customer,” then uncovering the backroom talks between commissioner Al French and data center developers over the last two years and then read about how our community feels about data centers. artigo.texto: Blue Elephant Energy has acquired a 95% stake in the 40MW/160MWh Zuidvelde battery energy storage system (BESS) project in the Netherlands. The system will be co-located with the existing Zuidvelde solar park in Noordenveld, Drenthe, and is scheduled to be commissioned in the third quarter of 2027. The project will use the solar park’s existing grid connection under a cable pooling agreement. The battery is intended to store solar generation during the middle of the day and discharge electricity to the grid when demand is higher. This approach makes use of existing connection capacity in a country where grid congestion is constraining new projects. Construction is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. TPSolar will manage the build and take responsibility for maintenance once the system is operational. The company sold the project stake to Blue Elephant Energy. “BESS Zuidvelde is our entry into the Dutch battery storage market – and it’s exactly how we believe it should be done: right inside an existing solar park, using grid capacity that is already there,” said Tim Kallas, chief investment officer of Blue Elephant Energy. The company said the project continues its collaboration with TPSolar and could be followed by storage developments at other sites in its portfolio. ING Netherlands is financing the project. The bank also financed the neighbouring solar park. Gino Schuur, head of sustainable finance at ING Business Banking NL, said: “BESS Zuidvelde shows how battery storage can combine renewable energy, flexibility and smarter use of existing grid infrastructure.” The project marks Blue Elephant Energy’s entry into the Dutch battery storage market. TPSolar described it as its largest battery project to date. Image: AI visualisation of the battery storage and Zuidvelde solar park. Credit: Blue Elephant.

artigo.texto: City staff estimate a 50 megawatt data center would use as much electricity as 25,000 new homes. San Francisco’s moratorium on new data centers has been extended to next fall, Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office said Tuesday. In extending the moratorium, San Francisco — like Oakland and Seattle — is giving city staff more time to study data centers and their impacts. “We will continue listening to our communities and labor partners, collaborating across city government, and drawing on the best available data to develop a policy that keeps electricity rates low, protects the clean water and air our residents deserve, and supports the technology infrastructure our hospitals, universities, and government rely on,” Lurie said in a statement. The Board of Supervisors last week unanimously approved an extension to the zoning moratorium until September. Lurie signed the moratorium Monday, his office said. Although the Planning Department shared some of its findings with the public in a report two weeks ago, it was only an initial assessment identifying areas needing more research. That includes understanding how many data centers there are citywide — besides three “standalone” facilities — as well as how much water they use. The initial report did have some clarity, though. It found that San Francisco’s electricity transmission is near capacity and that data centers would be competing with other developments that also need electricity, including housing. The report estimated that a 50 megawatt data center in San Francisco would demand the same electricity as 25,000 new homes. Additionally, two of the three “standalone” data centers in San Francisco identified by city staff are in the Bayview, and one of them has “five active notices of violation” issued this year by the Bay Area Air District over diesel-powered generators out of compliance with permit conditions, operating with expired permits, and exceeding run-time limits of 35 hours. Southeast San Francisco, with its industrial zoning, has been identified as a part of the city that faces environmental burdens and elevated levels of air pollution. The initial 45-day moratorium, as well as the extension (opens in new tab), were proposed by Supervisor Shamann Walton. He terms out in January, making his efforts to curb and study data centers among his final actions as supervisor. He will be replaced on the board by Theo Ellington. While campaigning, Ellington endorsed the idea of a data center moratorium specifically for District 10, which stretches from Dogpatch and Potrero Hill to the Bayview and Visitacion Valley. Land in District 10 has been the subject of speculation. The lobbyist for a private equity firm known for developing data centers met with city officials in August about building and planning permits for a big plot of land in Dogpatch. The moratorium doesn’t allow for the city to process building or planning permits to establish new data centers. Right now, there are no such applications before the city’s Planning Department. “The absence of pending applications is not a reason to let the moratorium expire,” Walton said at a Nov. 16 committee meeting. “The city must proactively evaluate future development and its potential impacts.” More about the author Omar Rashad reports on San Francisco government and politics.

artigo.texto: Chint Power announced an investment of 821 million yuan to install a plant in China uninterruptible power supply systems (UPS) the high-power factory will have a capacity of 2 GWh per year and will meet the backup power demands of data centers. EVE Energy, for its part, will redirect a ternary cylindrical battery project towards the manufacture of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the revised plan provides for a capacity of 8 GWh for storage and light mobility applications. Chint Power will invest 821 million yuan in a UPS plant The investment, equivalent to approximately $122.9 million, will see the plant located in Haining, Jiaxing City, Zhejiang Province, To begin operations, the company will lease and adapt existing industrial facilities. Construction is expected to take two years. The project, titled Haining Chint Digital Intelligence Energy Co., Ltd. 2GWh Annual High-Power UPS Project, will be carried out by the subsidiary Haining Chint Digital Intelligence Energy Co., Ltd. According to company documents, the subsidiary was established on July 7, 2026, with a share capital of 100 million yuan. Chint Power owns 100 % of the company, and the project marks Chint Power’s entry into the data center backup power market. The expansion of these facilities is increasing the demand for systems that can keep critical loads powered during power outages. With this plant, the company aims to expand its product portfolio, generate new revenue streams, and strengthen its presence in the high-power UPS market. EVE Energy modifies its cylindrical battery project On November 20, EVE Energy informed the Shenzhen Stock Exchange of changes to several capital-funded projects, one of which involved manufacturing large-format ternary cylindrical batteries, the company will now dedicate that production line to LFP cylindrical batteries. The revision reduces the planned capacity from 21 GWh to 8 GWh and the total investment from 5.203 billion to 2.801 billion yuan, the project will now be called the Chengdu EVE Energy High-Energy Density Cylindrical Battery Industrialisation Project. EVE Energy will allocate 1.871 billion yuan to the revised plan, which had been left unallocated in the original project, the rest of the investment will be covered with its own resources, the new line will be geared towards low-power equipment, light electric vehicles and small-scale storage, among the intended uses are residential storage and power backup for base stations. LFP technology expands its industrial applications According to EVE Energy, LFP batteries are gaining market share compared to lead-acid and nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries. The company highlights their competitive costs, extended lifespan, and safety level. It also points out that this chemistry facilitates the standardization of cylindrical cells. One of the challenges in large-format LFP cells is improving electrical conductivity EVE Energy it uses a full-tab design to reduce internal resistance, according to the company. This configuration allows large-diameter cells to support sustained fast charging and deliver high currents. These features open up applications in energy storage and light mobility, as well as their use in electric passenger vehicles. Two strategies to expand the energy storage industry The two projects respond to different demands of the Chinese market; Chint Power is directing its new manufacturing capacity to support critical loads in data centers, while EVE Energy is adjusting the production volume and chemistry of its cells to serve light mobility and small-scale storage. artigo.texto: Rolling Meadows approves data center tax incentive for development over residents' objections The Rolling Meadows City Council approved support for the county to give a data center a tax incentive to develop land, despite passionate opposition from residents at their meeting Tuesday night. The meeting exemplified the different approaches Chicago suburbs are taking different to the data center dilemma, with one facing opposition to a project while another welcomes the developments. In Rolling Meadows, neighbors brought signs and packed city chambers as its city council weighed bringing in a data center. A former office space that sits on 40 acres off the tollway on Route 53 has been vacant for years, and that's where the Rolling Meadows data center would end up if approved. But residents raised many questions at Tuesday night's meeting, including the impact to nearby Bussey Woods and its wildlife. But the biggest concern is about nearby homes. "To also state the nearest home is 2,000 feet away is also a huge dismissal," one resident told the council at the meeting. "Two thousand feet isn't far." Residents are worried about the noise, environmental issues both known and unknown, and what a data center could do to the community. Most of the residents in attendance said they believed they should have a vote and a voice in whether the data center is built. While the vast majority wanted the Rolling Meadows City Council to vote against the project, some in the room showed support, saying they would bring jobs and economic benefits. Other communities are not willing to close the door completely to data centers. In Zion on the North Shore, Mayor Billy McKinney said nothing is off the table. He pointed out the village was approached previously about a data center but that deal lacked vision. "I want to make this point, being cautious does not mean that we are opposed to progress. That is the big key," he said. "The plan was so inconclusive, and it raised more questions." McKinney said he understands community concerns, but is not willing to implement a data center ban. "But also know that whatever decision we make, it has to protect our community and future generations," he said. In the end, the Rolling Meadows City Council voted four-two to approve their support for the county giving a tax incentive to develop the land with a data center.

artigo.texto: The growing demand for electric vehicles, renewable energy storage and reliable power backup solutions has increased the importance of battery manufacturing in India. From automotive batteries used in conventional vehicles to advanced lithium-ion systems powering electric scooters, cars and industrial equipment, battery manufacturers play an important role in the country’s energy and mobility ecosystem. As the country moves towards domestic battery manufacturing, companies are expanding their capabilities across battery cells, packs, energy storage systems and recycling. Here is a look at some of the leading battery manufacturing companies in India, their products and their presence across different battery segments. Top Battery Manufacturing Companies in India: Quick Overview These companies operate across different parts of the battery value chain. Their manufacturing capabilities, technology and target applications vary. 1. Exide Industries Founded in 1947, Exide Industries is one of India’s most established battery manufacturers. The company has a significant presence in automotive, industrial and stationary energy storage markets. Its product portfolio includes automotive batteries for two-wheelers and four-wheelers, industrial batteries, inverter batteries and energy storage solutions. Exide also operates multiple manufacturing facilities across India and serves both original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and replacement markets. The company is expanding into lithium-ion battery manufacturing through its wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions Limited (EESL). Its planned lithium-ion manufacturing ecosystem includes a cell manufacturing facility in Bengaluru and battery module and pack manufacturing capabilities at Prantij, Gujarat. According to its FY2025-26 annual report, the Bengaluru cell facility progressed through installation, process validation and customer sampling activities. This investment reflects Exide’s strategy to expand beyond conventional lead-acid batteries and participate in India’s growing electric mobility and energy storage markets. 2. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility Amara Raja Energy & Mobility is another major name among Indian battery manufacturers. The company operates under the Amara Raja Group and is widely recognised for its automotive battery brand, Amaron. Its business includes automotive batteries, industrial energy storage, UPS batteries and advanced lithium-ion battery solutions. The company’s lithium-ion expansion is being undertaken through its Giga Corridor project in Telangana. In July 2026, Amara Raja commissioned a Customer Qualification Plant for lithium-ion cells with an investment of approximately ₹500 crore. The facility supports the development and qualification of different cell formats and chemistries. The company has targeted commercial-scale cell production beginning in 2027. Amara Raja is also developing battery packs and charging solutions for electric mobility applications. Its established automotive battery distribution network and investment in advanced cell technology position it as an important participant in India’s evolving battery industry. 3. Tata AutoComp Gotion Green Energy Solutions Tata AutoComp Gotion Green Energy Solutions is a joint venture between Tata AutoComp Systems and China’s Gotion. Established in 2020, the company focuses on designing and manufacturing lithium-ion battery packs for electric mobility and energy storage applications. Its product portfolio covers several segments: - Electric two-wheelers and three-wheelers. - Passenger electric vehicles. - Commercial vehicles and electric buses. - Industrial equipment. - Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The company uses lithium-ion technology, including Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) chemistry, with integrated battery management systems and thermal management solutions. An important distinction is that Tata AutoComp Gotion focuses on battery pack manufacturing rather than being India’s primary lithium-ion cell manufacturing business. Battery packs combine individual cells with electronics, safety systems and protective enclosures. Its capabilities make it an important supplier within India’s electric vehicle battery supply chain. 4. Ola Electric Ola Electric has entered the battery manufacturing industry through its gigafactory in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu. The company is developing indigenous lithium-ion cell technology under its Bharat Cell programme. Its manufacturing ambitions include producing advanced 4680-format cells for electric mobility applications. Ola’s investment in battery production is intended to strengthen its control over the electric vehicle supply chain and reduce dependence on externally sourced battery cells. The company’s battery operations are particularly relevant to the electric two-wheeler market, where battery cost, energy density, charging performance and safety influence vehicle economics. However, announced manufacturing capacity should not be confused with actual commercial output. The Ministry of Heavy Industries reported that Ola had installed 1 GWh of capacity and started pilot production, while working towards stabilising full-scale commercial operations as of December 2025. 5. artigo.texto: Alguns credores adiaram a decisão enquanto fazem uma análise mais detalhada de um empréstimo ampliado de US$ 6,6 bilhões pedido pela Bridge Data Centres (BDC), controlada pela Bain Capital, segundo pessoas envolvidas nas negociações. Os data centers da empresa na Malásia atendem clientes como a ByteDance. A Bain encaminhou as perguntas à BDC, que não quis comentar. A ByteDance não respondeu ao pedido de comentário. Um banco desistiu de participar de um empréstimo de US$ 372 milhões, com subscrição integral, para a Digital Halo, apoiada pelo Partners Group, e outros estão fazendo mais perguntas, segundo pessoas a par das conversas. Os recursos são para um data center na Malásia que atende a Alibaba e outros clientes. Vários bancos também estavam reavaliando um empréstimo de US$ 480 milhões para a Aolani, neocloud com sede em Singapura que tem a ByteDance como cliente, disseram outras pessoas a par do assunto na semana passada. Digital Halo, Aolani e Alibaba não responderam às perguntas. O Partners Group não quis comentar. Novas regras incluem o Brasil As restrições impostas em 2022 pelo governo Biden à exportação de chips americanos avançados deram origem a um ecossistema de empresas no Sudeste Asiático que ajudam companhias chinesas de tecnologia a acessar esse hardware remotamente. Os empréstimos a data centers na região dispararam nos anos seguintes, e o financiamento de chips começou a ganhar força mais recentemente, à medida que os bancos passaram a aceitar operações mais arriscadas. Isso mudou depois que os EUA anunciaram, na semana passada, que empresas de Singapura, Malásia, Indonésia, Tailândia e Brasil vão precisar de licença do governo americano para comprar chips avançados de IA de fabricantes do país. No mundo todo, data centers que já alugam capacidade de computação relevante para empresas chinesas vão precisar de uma licença específica para continuar com esses contratos e terão 90 dias para obtê-la. Mais de uma dúzia de banqueiros disseram que suas equipes aguardam respostas sobre como as novas restrições vão afetar os tomadores de crédito, o que deve no mínimo atrasar o fechamento de operações. Credores como Citigroup e Standard Chartered, além dos principais bancos de Singapura, iniciaram uma revisão ampla de seus clientes do setor de data centers, segundo pessoas a par do assunto. Bancos tentam reduzir exposição Alguns bancos querem diminuir parte da exposição a dívidas de IA e de data centers, inclusive com a venda de empréstimos no mercado secundário e com operações de transferência significativa de risco (SRT, na sigla em inglês). O United Overseas Bank (UOB), de Singapura, busca uma operação de SRT de cerca de US$ 1 bilhão para repassar riscos ligados a empréstimos para data centers e infraestrutura, entre outros setores, segundo pessoas a par do assunto. Uma delas disse que o noticiário atual está atrasando o andamento e que os detalhes ainda não estão definidos e podem mudar. Um representante do UOB não quis comentar, citando a confidencialidade da operação. Os credores privados, que eram os mais agressivos na busca pelos retornos mais altos do financiamento de GPUs, também estão mais cautelosos. Pelo menos um fundo decidiu não participar de um empréstimo de US$ 300 milhões para a GMI Cloud, parceira de nuvem da Nvidia, destinado à compra de chips para um data center na Tailândia que seria usado pela Tencent, segundo uma pessoa a par do assunto. GMI Cloud e Tencent não responderam aos pedidos de comentário. O efeito vai além do crédito. A DayOne Data Centers, que tem a ByteDance como maior cliente, suspendeu os planos de abrir capital nos EUA, segundo pessoas a par do assunto. Um consórcio que inclui a BlackRock avalia reduzir sua oferta por uma carteira de data centers na Ásia-Pacífico, segundo outras fontes. Para Ben Kostrzewa, advogado de comércio internacional do Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, não é ruim que as novas restrições tenham forçado uma reavaliação ampla das operações. Desde 2023, os empréstimos a empresas de data center na Ásia-Pacífico saíram de praticamente zero para mais de US$ 49 bilhões, segundo dados compilados pela Bloomberg. “Pode ser uma boa pausa para fazer um balanço e revisar esses projetos, considerando o quanto o mercado está aquecido há algum tempo”, disse Kostrzewa. “Isso não vai impedir a construção desses data centers nem parar o mercado, mas vai desacelerar tudo.”

artigo.texto: Nocera Inc (Nocera), a construction engineering company, has signed a binding letter of intent (LOI) to invest US$ 22 million in Calgary-based BitRock Ltd., an AI data center developer. The proposed investment would give Nocera 44 percent stake in BitRock, based on a post investment valuation of US$ 50 million, along with the right to appoint directors and participate in major corporate decisions. According to a press release, the funds will support construction of BitRock’s first AI data center in Alberta, Canada, with 10 MW of IT capacity across four 2.5 MW computing modules. The company plans to expand the site to 200 MW in additional 10 MW phases based on customer demand. The facility will operate under a colocation model, providing powered data hall space and operational services to customers supplying their own computing equipment, and has reported signing memoranda of understanding (MoU) for hosting services. Andrew Teng, Asia Director, Nocera, said, “Power is the scarce asset in AI infrastructure, and BitRock is built around its, we are putting capital into a facility designed to generate its own electricity, in a province that has asked developers to do exactly that, and we are doing it one 10 MW unit at a time. This is a measured entry into North American compute with a meaningful ownership position and a voice on the board.” The investment comes as Alberta faces constraints on grid capacity for large-scale data center projects. The province’s interim allocation of 1,200 MW for large-load developments has been fully committed, increasing the importance of alternative power sources. The LOI was signed on November 19, 2026 and the investment remains subject to due diligence, a definitive agreement, required approvals and other closing conditions while both companies have not guaranteed that the transaction will be completed.

artigo.texto: Virginia data center deals face transparency tests BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - From Botetourt County to Northern Virginia, fights over how local governments approve data center projects are playing out in court. In Botetourt, one such challenge has brought construction on Google’s data center to a halt. The cases involve different projects and different alleged violations, but they raise a common question: Did local governments give the public the access and notice required by law before making decisions? Megan Rhyne, executive director of the Virginia Coalition for Open Government, said challenges to government decisions have focused on alleged Freedom of Information Act and public notice violations. “There already are lawsuits around the state that are trying to change this, change decisions based on either FOIA violations or public notice violations,” Rhyne said. “Most well known is up in Prince William County.” A public notice case in Northern Virginia In Prince William County, a court threw out rezonings for the Digital Gateway data center project after finding that the county had not properly advertised the public hearing. The Court of Appeals upheld that ruling, and the last developer pursuing an appeal later dropped it. Rhyne said transparency rules apply regardless of what a government decides. “These rules of transparency exist no matter what the decision is,” she said. “All decisions that the government made have to follow these procedures and these rules.” In Botetourt, a judge found that supervisors agreed to the Google data center deal behind closed doors and then failed to adequately identify it when they voted in public. Court records say the Board of Supervisors discussed a performance agreement with Google in closed session in June 2025, then returned to open session and approved what board members called “walk-on item number one.” Google’s announcement followed the vote. The judge voided the initial action on procedural grounds and ordered new construction to stop. Crews had begun grading the site and moving dirt in September. Rhyne said the violation affected the public’s ability to see its government make decisions. “This technical violation has resulted in undermining the very thing that FOIA is supposed to protect, which is their access, the public’s right to see their government making its decisions that impact them,” she said. On Tuesday, the Board of Supervisors took action to stop items related to Google’s investments, including a museum and library renovations, while the county evaluates its next steps. The agreement also included investments in first responder equipment and athletic infrastructure; some projects have already been completed. Questions about another project Tim Dooley, the attorney who represented the plaintiff in the Botetourt case, said the ruling raises questions about the process used for another data center project at Wood Haven in Roanoke County. “I think if you scrutinize the process the Western Virginia Regional Industrial Facility Authority, the process they used, you’ll see some striking similarities between that and what happened in Botetourt,” Dooley said. Rhyne said the Botetourt ruling is not binding on other judges, although they could look to it for guidance in future cases. Botetourt County could appeal. The judge also said the board could hold a new public hearing that follows the law. Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Graphene Manufacturing Group (GMG) has signed an initial service agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre (UKBIC) to manufacture and form its G®CELLS battery cells in Coventry. GMG will develop and supply the battery materials from its Battery Development Centre in Brisbane, Australia. UKBIC will initially make pouch cells using its existing industrial-scale equipment. GMG said the arrangement will support cell scale-up and process development while allowing it to defer investment in its own large-format manufacturing capacity. The agreement adds UKBIC to GMG’s cell development work with the Battery Innovation Center of Indiana (BIC Indiana), alongside its own facility in Brisbane. The company expects the three locations to increase production capacity, allow cell formats to be developed in parallel and bring sample cells closer to prospective customers in the UK and Europe. These are expected benefits; the announcement did not give production volumes or a schedule for the first UK-made cells. GMG will pay UKBIC for its services and retain the intellectual property from the development work, according to the company’s announcement. “UKBIC was established to help battery innovators bridge the gap between promising laboratory and pilot results and industrial-scale manufacturing. We’re pleased to be applying our production lines, process engineering and formation capability to build cells using GMG’s materials,” said Sean Gilgunn, UKBIC’s managing director. G®CELLS are a developing battery technology. The company’s latest quarterly report puts the technology at Battery Technology Readiness Level 4, indicating laboratory validation. The UKBIC agreement is intended to support further scale-up; it does not establish commercial production. Image: Tab welder. Credit: UK BIC.

artigo.texto: BerlinerLuft amplia oferta de climatização para data centers Fabricante produz em Alvorada (RS) equipamentos de ar-condicionado de precisão para salas de servidores e instalações de telecomunicações. A fabricante alemã BerlinerLuft está ampliando sua atuação no mercado brasileiro de data centers com uma linha de climatização produzida em Alvorada (RS). Segundo a revista RTI, a empresa passou a concentrar esforços no segmento no segundo semestre de 2025, com base na experiência em ambientes que exigem controle de temperatura, como laboratórios e instalações da indústria farmacêutica. De acordo com Cristiane Marques, coordenadora de Engenharia de Produto e Aplicação da BerlinerLuft, a linha já está disponível no mercado brasileiro. O portfólio inclui a família DataCond, de aparelhos de ar-condicionado de precisão com configuração modular. A série DataCond DEEX, voltada a salas de servidores e instalações de telecomunicações, tem sistema de expansão direta integrado e está disponível em sete tamanhos, com vazões de ar de 3.750 a 20 mil m³/h. Entre os recursos da série estão ventiladores EC, que permitem ajustar continuamente a vazão de ar, e a opção de free cooling direto, que aproveita o ar externo para resfriamento quando as condições ambientais são favoráveis. A fabricante também oferece equipamentos com água gelada e configurações que combinam tecnologias de refrigeração. – Resumen (español) BerlinerLuft amplía su presencia en el mercado brasileño de centros de datos con equipos de climatización fabricados en Alvorada, en el estado de Rio Grande do Sul. La oferta incluye la serie DataCond DEEX, con unidades de aire acondicionado de precisión por expansión directa para salas de servidores e instalaciones de telecomunicaciones. Summary (English) BerlinerLuft is expanding its presence in Brazil’s data center market with cooling equipment manufactured in Alvorada, Rio Grande do Sul. Its portfolio includes the DataCond DEEX series of direct-expansion precision air conditioning units for server rooms and telecommunications facilities.

artigo.texto: Korean researchers have developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates reliably at room temperature under low pressure. The technology could ease the high-pressure requirements that are one of the barriers to commercializing all-solid-state batteries and could be used to reduce their weight and size. A team led by Park Su-jin, a chemistry professor at Pohang University of Science and Technology POSTECH, said on the 26th that it had developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates at room temperature under pressure of 0.3 megapascals (MPa) or less. The team worked with researchers at Chung-Ang University, Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States. The findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications on the 7th, local time. All-solid-state batteries are attracting attention as a next-generation technology that can reduce fire risks by using a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. Using lithium metal in the anode can increase energy density, but the lithium expands during charging, creating gaps between the electrode and the electrolyte. In this process, branchlike growths called lithium dendrites can penetrate the electrolyte and cause an internal short circuit. High pressure has been applied to batteries to prevent this, but the equipment needed adds weight and bulk. The researchers addressed the problem by preventing cracks in the solid electrolyte and distributing the pressure caused by lithium expansion. They added thioctic acid (TA) to a sulfide-based solid electrolyte to form a polymer network, suppressing cracks in the electrolyte and the penetration of lithium dendrites. They also applied a porous carbon material with many tiny holes to the anode current collector to provide space for lithium to accumulate. The design distributes the force generated by lithium expansion during charging within the current collector, reducing the strain on the electrolyte. The researchers used the Pohang Light Source to observe the inside of the battery in 3D during charging and discharging. They found that stress from expansion was relieved as lithium filled and left the pores of the current collector. A battery using the technology operated reliably at room temperature and under pressure of 0.3 MPa or less, even in a full cell using a ternary cathode material (NCM811) for electric vehicles. The researchers said it was the first time in the world that such low-pressure operation had been achieved in a sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium-metal full cell with an areal capacity of 2.4 mAh/㎠. "We addressed both the limitations of the brittle sulfide-based solid electrolyte with a polymer network and the stress caused by lithium expansion with a porous current collector," Park said. "This result came from close collaboration with Korean researchers." References Nature Communications(2026), DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-79393-w
