artigo.texto: Megarevo Energy Storage Solutions Enter Jamaican Market By: , November 26, 2026 The Full Story The introduction of Megarevo inverter and battery energy storage solutions to Jamaica by CESCO Limited will help diversify the country’s energy sector and foster a more resilient energy landscape. These energy storage solutions are being made available locally through CESCO’s exclusive distributorship arrangement, further expanding access to advanced renewable energy technologies. Minister of Energy, Transport and Telecommunications, Hon. Daryl Vaz, who welcomed the technology, congratulated CESCO Limited on the initiative, noting that its partnership with Megarevo presents a valuable opportunity to combine local industry expertise with international leadership in advanced inverter technology, battery energy storage systems and integrated microgrid solutions. “We need electricity systems that are dependable, technologies that improve efficiency and investments that provide lasting economic value. These priorities are essential to our national energy security and the competitiveness of Jamaican businesses,” he stated. The Minister was addressing Tuesday’s (November) Corporate Stakeholders’ Energy Product Launch and Business Forum, hosted by CESCO Limited in partnership with Megarevo and Pacific Energy Solutions, at The Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston. Mr. Vaz noted that recent extreme weather events have highlighted the need to protect critical infrastructure and maintain essential services when electricity supply is disrupted, adding that technologies such as battery energy storage systems and microgrids can make a meaningful contribution to strengthening energy resilience. “Hospitals, water supply systems, telecommunications facilities, emergency services and commercial operations all depend on reliable power. For these facilities, interruptions can have serious operational and economic consequences,” he pointed out. Minister Vaz noted that CESCO Limited spent approximately two years collaborating with Megarevo to develop and refine inverter solutions designed specifically to meet Jamaica’s electricity supply requirements. This includes compatibility with Jamaica’s single-phase and three-phase electricity supply configurations. “CESCO has explained that some existing three-phase inverter technologies may require additional transformers or other modifications to operate within Jamaica’s electricity supply arrangements. The new designs are intended to address this challenge in suitable applications, potentially reducing additional equipment requirements, simplifying installation and lowering overall project costs,” the Minister noted. He said CESCO has also indicated that the systems incorporate grid-forming capabilities and are designed to support applications ranging from approximately 30 kilowatts (kW) to 10 megawatts (MW). “This positions the solutions for consideration across a range of commercial and industrial applications,” Mr. Vaz added. The Minister commended the companies for recognising that technology must be adapted to the specific operating conditions of the markets in which it is introduced. “As these products enter the Jamaican market, I encourage the companies to maintain appropriate technical certification, comply with applicable safety standards and provide dependable after-sales support,” he urged. Mr. Vaz emphasised that investment in local technical training will be essential to building the capacity of Jamaican professionals to instal, maintain and service these systems effectively. Managing Director of CESCO Limited, André Chambers, said that harnessing Jamaica’s natural resources through advanced technology can help reduce the country’s reliance on imported fuels, bolster industrial competitiveness and enhance national energy security. “Through CESCO’s microgrid 360 concept, we are integrating solar generation, battery storage, utility power, standby generator, and intelligent energy management into one comprehensive solution,” he outlined. Mr. Chambers emphasised that technology alone cannot drive this transformation, noting that success will depend on strong collaboration among government, industry, the engineering community and financial institutions. He said the devastating effects of Hurricane Melissa serve as a stark reminder of the country’s dependence on a reliable electricity supply. “Energy resilience is not simply an operational consideration. It is fundamental to business continuity, economic competitiveness and national development. We must think differently about how we generate, store and manage energy,” the Managing Director pointed out. CESCO is now an established provider of electrical supplies and energy solutions, supporting Jamaica’s banking, mining, manufacturing and maritime infrastructure sectors. “Our capabilities expand to include the design, engineering and custom manufacturing of switchgear and power distribution systems supporting essential services providers such as JPS (Jamaica Public Service Company Limited) and National Water Commission (NWC),” Mr. Chambers said. The technology is being introduced to Jamaica and the wider Caribbean by CESCO Limited in partnership with Megarevo, Pacific Energy Solutions and Schneider Electric.

artigo.texto: Australia is hurtling toward a 100% renewable grid, but keeping the lights on through multi-day weather lulls remains a key challenge. An iron-air battery solution arriving in Australia could solve this long-duration bottleneck. Developed globally by leaders like Form Energy, these multi-day systems utilise basic rust chemistry to store grid power affordably. You can easily browse home solar systems through Energy Matters to pair household clean generation with broader grid modernisation. Quick answer: What Australians should know - Iron-air batteries use the reversible process of iron rusting and returning to metallic iron to store and release electricity. They are designed to provide electricity for up to 100 hours. - The technology could complement solar, wind and conventional lithium-ion batteries by supplying electricity during extended periods of low renewable generation. - Iron-air batteries are not yet an established Australian household product. However, international commercial projects are progressing, making the technology worth watching as Australia expands its renewable energy storage capacity. What is an iron-air battery and why does it matter for Australian homes? An iron-air battery is a rechargeable energy storage system that uses iron, oxygen and an electrolyte to store and release electricity. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on lithium-based electrochemical reactions, iron-air systems use the chemistry of rusting. During discharge, iron reacts with oxygen to form iron oxide or hydroxide, releasing electrical energy. When electricity is supplied to recharge the battery, the process reverses, converting the iron compound back into metallic iron. The technology is particularly interesting because it targets long-duration energy storage rather than simply storing a few hours of electricity. Expert insight: Iron-air technology is not designed to replace every battery. Its potential value lies in storing large quantities of electricity for longer periods, complementing shorter-duration batteries and renewable generation. Key terminology Understanding the language surrounding iron-air storage makes it easier to evaluate its potential. - Long-duration energy storage (LDES): Energy storage capable of delivering electricity for extended periods, generally eight hours or longer. - Iron-air chemistry: A rechargeable electrochemical process based on the reversible oxidation and reduction of iron. - Round-trip efficiency: The percentage of electricity recovered after accounting for the energy required to charge a battery. - Grid-scale storage: Large battery installations connected to electricity networks rather than individual homes. - Multi-day storage: Systems designed to supply electricity over several consecutive days. Why this matters right now in Australia Australia’s renewable electricity generation is growing rapidly, but solar and wind production do not always match consumer demand. The Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) 2026 Integrated System Plan reinforces the importance of renewable generation supported by storage and other flexible resources as coal-fired power stations retire. AEMO identifies storage as central to a reliable, lower-cost electricity system through to 2050. For Australian households, this matters because better storage can help reduce renewable energy waste, improve electricity supply reliability and potentially reduce wholesale price volatility. How iron-air battery technology works The central idea behind iron-air batteries is surprisingly simple. They use a controlled version of the same chemical process that causes rust to form on exposed metal. However, engineering this reaction into a rechargeable battery that can operate reliably for years is far more complicated. Technical explanation Iron-air batteries generally contain three important components: - Iron electrodes: Store energy through chemical reactions involving iron. - Air electrode: Allows oxygen from the surrounding air to participate in the reaction. - Water-based electrolyte: Helps facilitate the electrochemical process. The battery operates through two main stages. 1. Discharging: Iron rusts. Oxygen enters the battery and reacts with iron, forming rust-like iron compounds and releasing electrons, which generate electricity. 2. Charging: Rust becomes iron again. Electricity reverses the reaction, converting the iron compounds back into metallic iron so the battery can store energy again. The major advantage is the ability to store energy for much longer than conventional short-duration batteries. US-based manufacturer Form Energy is developing systems designed to deliver electricity continuously for up to 100 hours. However, the trade-off is efficiency. Form Energy’s published planning assumptions indicate a round-trip efficiency of about 40% to 45%, meaning the system requires considerably more electricity to charge than it ultimately delivers. Australian examples and data No established commercial iron-air battery installation currently operates on Australia’s electricity grid. However, international developments suggest the technology is moving beyond laboratory research. Form Energy’s progress includes: - 2025: Deployment of its first iron-air system for commercial demonstration in partnership with Great River Energy. - 2026: Testing across thousands of full-scale cells and more than 170 battery modules. - March 2026: Announcement of its first international deployment, a 10 MW / 1,000 MWh project in Ireland, expected to begin operating in 2029. - 2026: Announcement of a proposed 300 MW / 30 GWh project with Xcel Energy in Minnesota. These developments demonstrate growing commercial interest, although announced projects should not be confused with fully operational installations. The Australian connection is currently more about market opportunity than local deployment. As renewable penetration increases, iron-air storage could become an option for deve

artigo.texto: Polarium Energy Solutions AB has been declared bankrupt by the Stockholm District Court The company more than halved operating expenses since 2024 but remained under financial pressure Chairman Harald Mix is exploring a potential acquisition by his private investment company Mounting financial pressures have forced Swedish battery energy storage company Polarium Energy Solutions AB into bankruptcy. The Stockholm District Court declared bankruptcy after the company concluded that it could not continue operating in its current form. The company attributed its bankruptcy to several factors, including sharply declining battery prices amid growing competition from Chinese suppliers, reduced investments by telecom operators and tower companies, and delays in some distributed BESS development projects. Overcapacity from the Chinese suppliers and a shift to cheaper battery chemistry is pushing down prices for every player in the supply chain leading to sharply lower gross margins. “Like the auto industry, several European battery and energy storage companies have been hit hard by the dramatic increase in competition from Chinese players, and a number of European manufacturers have been forced to file for bankruptcy or restructure financially,” said Harald Mix, Chairman of Polarium. Morrow Batteries and sonnen are some of the European battery companies to have walked the same path (see Germany’s sonnen GmbH Faces Insolvency As US Business Expands and Europe’s Morrow Batteries Files For Bankruptcy). Earlier another Swedish battery manufacturer Northvolt filed for bankruptcy. Its recycling patents were acquired by Refinyx (see Refinyx Acquires Northvolt’s 134 Battery Recycling Patents). These developments, explains Polarium, weakened its financial position despite efforts to reduce costs and restructure its operations. The company claims it had more than halved its operating expenses since 2024, but demand remains “too low relative to costs” leading to an unstainable financial situation. It also made changes to its strategy, business model and organizational structure in an effort to improve profitability. The company had explored options to secure its future, including finding a buyer for all or parts of the business and a court-supervised reorganization, but concluded that bankruptcy was the only remaining option. Polarium’s bankruptcy follows a strategic transformation initiated in 2025. In August 2026, Polarium announced a sharper focus on telecom power solutions and distributed energy storage, areas it identified as having stronger growth and profitability potential. The company also sought to reduce costs, improve margins, strengthen its presence in local markets and move closer to key suppliers. As part of the transformation, Polarium reported that its 2025 net sales declined to SEK 896 million from SEK 1.332 billion in 2024. However, gross profit improved to SEK 114 million from a loss of SEK 46 million, while its EBITDA loss narrowed to SEK 61 million from SEK 270 million. The decision to file for bankruptcy follows the October 1, 2026 appointment of company EVP and Head of the Residential and C&I business segments Pontus Winberg as Polarium’s new CEO. Winberg succeeded Leif Ottosson who retired after leading the transformation and strategic renewal of Polarium. Polarium Chairman Harald Mix said he intends to engage with the bankruptcy trustee to explore whether parts of the business can continue. He has also indicated that he is prepared to consider financing a potential acquisition by his private investment company. According to the company’s announcement, the bankruptcy trustee, Mikael Kubu of Ackordscentralen, has now taken over the company and will determine how its assets and business will be handled, including the possibility of a sale and continued operations.

artigo.texto: A instalação de mega data centers em Campinas e seus possíveis impactos ambientais, econômicos e sociais foram discutidos nesta terça-feira (24) durante um debate público na Câmara Municipal. Especialistas e ambientalistas questionaram a capacidade da legislação vigente de regulamentar empreendimentos desse porte e alertaram para consequências que vão além do elevado consumo de água e energia. - Clique aqui para fazer parte da comunidade do Porque Campinas no WhatsApp e receber notícias em primeira mão. Mediado pelo vereador Wagner Romão (PT), o encontro teve como um dos principais pontos de discussão o Campus Campinas, mega data center voltado à inteligência artificial da Terranova em parceria com a gestora britânica Actis, previsto para a Fazenda Pau d’Alho, em Barão Geraldo, dentro do Polo de Inovação para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável (PIDS). Presidente do Instituto Brasileiro de Proteção Ambiental (PROAM), Carlos Bocuhy chamou a atenção para a dimensão física da infraestrutura necessária ao funcionamento das ferramentas de inteligência artificial e seus impactos sobre o meio ambiente. “A inteligência artificial, da forma como ela se insere, precisa de gigantescos data centers, e ela não está nas nuvens. Ela precisa de uma base física. Ela estimula a mineração, a construção de novos chips, materiais. Data centers consomem energia, consomem água”, afirmou. Ruídos de baixa frequência preocupam especialistas Professora titular da Faculdade de Engenharia Civil, Arquitetura e Urbanismo da Unicamp, Emília Rutkowski destacou a necessidade de diferenciar os centros de processamento de dados convencionais dos megaempreendimentos destinados a atender grandes operações tecnológicas. Durante sua apresentação, a pesquisadora reproduziu uma gravação do ruído emitido por um mega data center e explicou que equipamentos como ventiladores de resfriamento, transformadores elétricos e geradores de emergência são fontes de sons de baixa frequência. “Esse é o grande problema, porque a gente vai ficar ouvindo isto 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, 365 ou 366 dias por ano”, afirmou. Segundo Emília, as características de propagação desses ruídos representam desafios tanto para a instalação de barreiras acústicas quanto para a fiscalização dos empreendimentos. A professora também questionou os possíveis efeitos sobre a fauna, a vegetação e as comunidades próximas. A pesquisadora ressaltou que os data centers são estruturas fundamentais para a produção de conhecimento, mas questionou a concentração dessas operações em empreendimentos de grandes dimensões. “Não vamos discutir ‘não quero data center’. Eu não quero mega data center, porque o que ele está fazendo é economia de escala para quem detém essa informação de nuvem, ou para quem quer treinar a sua IA”, declarou. Proximidade com o Sirius gera questionamentos A localização do empreendimento também foi alvo de preocupação durante o debate. Além de áreas residenciais de Barão Geraldo, como Jardim Miriam, Guará e Alphaville, o entorno reúne importantes instituições de ensino, ciência e tecnologia, entre elas Unicamp, PUC-Campinas, CPqD e o Centro Nacional de Pesquisa em Energia e Materiais (CNPEM), onde está instalado o acelerador de partículas Sirius. Wagner Romão destacou a sensibilidade dos equipamentos científicos do CNPEM a interferências externas e lembrou que, durante as discussões sobre a implantação do PIDS, até mesmo a circulação de caminhões nas proximidades da instituição foi motivo de preocupação. O parlamentar questionou a compatibilidade entre a instalação do mega data center e as atividades científicas desenvolvidas na região, além dos possíveis efeitos sobre a ocupação urbana prevista para o entorno. Legislação ambiental e benefícios fiscais são questionados Outro ponto levantado por Romão foi a regulamentação ambiental desses empreendimentos. O vereador apresentou uma resposta da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) a um inquérito civil do Ministério Público, segundo a qual a atividade de data center não está entre as fontes de poluição previstas em um decreto estadual de 1976 e, por essa razão, dispensa licenciamento ambiental no âmbito da companhia. “O mega data center, sobretudo, expõe não uma lacuna. É uma gigantesca cratera de meteoro na nossa legislação e na capacidade do poder público de regular esse tipo de empreendimento”, afirmou o parlamentar. Romão também questionou a inclusão dos data centers no programa municipal de incentivos fiscais destinado à atração de investimentos e à geração de empregos. Já o advogado Leonardo Pilon, mestre em Direitos Digitais e Sustentabilidade pela Universidade Federal de Santa Maria (UFSM), chamou a atenção para os possíveis impactos térmicos dessas estruturas e defendeu que o planejamento urbano priorize a adaptação das cidades às mudanças climáticas. “A corrida que a gente realmente deveria estar correndo é a adaptação à emergência climática”, afirmou. Conselho de Meio Ambiente acompanha o caso Conforme noticiado anteriormente pelo Porque Campinas, o Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) busca a participação de instituições científicas e tecnológicas na avaliação dos possíveis impactos do empreendimento. Entre as preocupações estão a demanda por água e energia, a emissão de calor, os ruídos e as vibrações, além de eventuais interferências nas atividades desenvolvidas pelos centros de pesquisa instalados na região. O debate desta terça-feira foi transmitido pela TV Câmara Campinas e está disponível na íntegra no canal oficial do Legislativo no YouTube.

artigo.texto: AI has turned data centers into one of the fastest-growing electricity users on the planet. In its Energy and AI report, the IEA estimates that data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of the world’s electricity. In its Base Case, this becomes about 945 TWh by 2030 and about 1,200 TWh by 2035. In the US, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory counted 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4% of the country’s electricity, and expects 325 to 580 TWh by 2028. That would be 6.7% to 12% of all US electricity. Every one of those kilowatt-hours goes through power supplies before it reaches a chip, usually more than one. So here is a question I keep asking: who checks how efficient those power supplies really are? The honest answer is the manufacturer itself, or a voluntary label it chose to apply for. As far as I can find, no law anywhere requires an independent lab to verify the efficiency of a data center PSU. Someone buying an 850 W PSU for a gaming PC has more independent efficiency data to choose from than an operator buying thousands of server modules that run 24/7. Before I go further, you should know where I stand. I run HWBusters and the Cybenetics lab, and Cybenetics would gain from what I propose here, because we test and certify power supplies for a living. Keep that in mind and check my sources. Every number below is linked. Where the power goes In a typical data center, electricity from the grid passes through a transformer, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), and power distribution units (PDUs). Then the server PSU, or a power shelf that feeds a whole rack, converts it to a low DC voltage, and converters on the board step it down again for the CPU or GPU. Every step loses a little. The server PSU is the one stage that every server has, and it never switches off. The diagram shows the uncomfortable part. Transformers have mandatory EU efficiency rules. The UPS has only voluntary programs. The server PSU has a minimum in the EU that the manufacturer declares itself, and nothing mandatory in the US. DC and high-voltage DC (HVDC) supplies, where the industry is heading, have no rules at all. What the rules already do Credit where it is due. The EU has had minimum efficiency rules for server PSUs since 2020, in Regulation (EU) 2019/424. Since 1 January 2023, a single-output server PSU must reach 90% efficiency at 10% load, 94% at 20%, 96% at 50% and 91% at 100%, with a power factor of at least 0.95 at half load. Multi-output units need 90%, 94% and 91% at 20%, 50% and 100% load. Those are demanding numbers. Three details matter, though. Compliance is self-declared under CE marking, so no independent lab has to confirm the numbers before a product goes on sale. The PSU limits exclude DC-powered servers. And the regulation exempts several server types, including servers with more than four processor sockets, large servers, fully fault-tolerant servers and network servers. The Commission was supposed to review the regulation by March 2022. More than four and a half years later, its own website still lists it as “under review”. In the US, I could not find any federal minimum for server power supplies. ENERGY STAR includes PSU efficiency and power factor tables in its Computer Servers v4.0 specification, and it requires independent certification: an EPA-recognized certification body accredited to ISO/IEC 17065 by an IAF MLA signatory, using data from an ISO/IEC 17025 lab. That is the right model. The catch is that it is voluntary, and it nearly disappeared. The administration’s FY2026 budget request zeroed the program, and Congress restored full funding in a law signed on 23 January 2026, with votes of 397-28 in the House and 82-15 in the Senate. In March 2026, EPA and DOE signed an agreement that makes DOE the lead agency. Then there is 80 PLUS, run by CLEAResult. It is voluntary too, but it has categories for 230 V, 277 V, 480 V, and 380 V DC redundant data center PSUs, and a new Ruby level that CLEAResult describes as ultimate efficiency for AI data centers. I found no 800 V DC category. Its test method comes from the EPRI/Ecova Generalized Internal Power Supply Efficiency Test Protocol, which checks a handful of fixed load points. China went another way. Its GB 43630-2023 standard sets mandatory efficiency limits and grades for tower and rack servers, and servers now need a China energy label. But it rates the whole server with a benchmark; it does not test the PSU on its own, and it covers general-purpose one- and two-socket machines. Blade, multi-node, full-cabinet and HPC systems are left out. Facility rules are moving faster. Germany’s Energy Efficiency Act requires new data centers that start operating from 1 July 2026 to reach a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2 or better, with limits of 1.5 from July 2027 and 1.3 from July 2030 for existing sites, although an amendment that may relax them is being debated. In the EU, data centers with at least 500 kW of IT power already report their energy performance, and on 21 September 2026 the Commission adopted an A to G rating and label based on PUE, water use and other indicators. The first labels are expected in 2027. Three blind spots The first is the metric itself. PUE, defined in ISO/IEC 30134-2, divides the total energy of the facility by the energy of the IT equipment. The PSU is part of the IT equipment. So a watt wasted inside a server PSU counts as IT energy, exactly like a watt spent on computing. PUE tells you how efficient the building is. It cannot tell you how much your power supplies waste, and neither can a label based on it. The second is how efficiency is measured. The EU rule and 80 PLUS check a few fixed load points. That is fine as a minimum, but redundant PSUs share the load with a partner module, so they can spend long periods at light load, and nothing below 10% load is checked at all. In our redundant server PSU protocol, we apply more than 1,450 load combinations from 2% to 100% of the operating range in a hotbox

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. – Construction on Google’s planned data center campus in Botetourt County has been halted following a circuit court judge’s ruling Monday evening, a decision that some residents are celebrating as a victory for transparency and government accountability. The ruling has drawn praise from residents who have opposed the project since its inception. “He (plaintiff Robert Dallas) basically gave Google a black eye. He hit a giant in the face and knocked him down. So that’s something important,” said Chad Bean, a Botetourt County resident. The decision comes after county resident Robert Dallas sued Botetourt County and a company associated with Google, arguing that county officials failed to adequately disclose that they were voting on the project’s performance agreement during a June 2025 meeting. Transparency has been a central concern among opponents of the project. “FOIA does matter. And we showed that. There is a desperate need for transparency with the county,” Bean said. The judge’s ruling halts construction, voids the performance agreement and rescinds all actions taken on the data center since the June 2025 meeting. The decision creates new complications for the county and Google, as construction has already begun and money has changed hands. Dr. Mac Scothorn, chair of the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors, provided an update on the project during a regularly scheduled board of supervisors meeting Tuesday. “The county is reviewing the ruling carefully with our legal counsel. Construction activities will be minimal for destabilization into the holidays to ensure this site is in compliance with the permits,” Scothorn said. Google also responded to the ruling Tuesday, saying their considering their options moving forward. “We are evaluating yesterday’s ruling by the court. We remain committed to working transparently with Botetourt County and the community in full compliance with all legal and regulatory requirements,” a company spokesperson wrote. While many celebrate, Botetourt County resident Danny Goad says this isn’t the end of the fight. “I think over the next three or four weeks, you’re going to see many things come out of the groups that oppose this. We want the people’s voice to be heard,” Goad said. The ruling does not necessarily mean the data center project is dead. The county could move forward by holding a public hearing and taking another vote on the performance agreement.

artigo.texto: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX’s request to launch as many as 1 million satellites for the creation of a network of data centers in orbit for complex artificial intelligence computing. The agency’s first-ever authorization of data centers in space makes way for a concept that was central to Elon Musk’s pitch to investors ahead of SpaceX’s initial public offering in June. The company has cautioned that orbital AI data centers rely on unproven technologies and may never be commercially viable. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said Wednesday in a statement. He has frequently praised SpaceX and attended a test launch of the company’s new Starship rocket earlier this month.

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) trabalha no desenvolvimento de um projeto para facilitar os investimentos em cabos submarinos no Brasil. A intenção é catalogar todas as autorizações necessárias para ancoragem de cabos na costa brasileira, substituindo, assim, o atual modelo marcado por medidas esparsas. A ideia foi comentada pelo diretor do Departamento de Investimento e Inovação do MCom, Marcelo Alves da Silva, nesta quarta-feira, 25, durante o Fórum dig.ia, realizado em Brasília. Em linhas gerais, o projeto chamado de Zona de Interesse de Ancoragem envolve realizar um mapeamento de todas as licenças e autorizações necessárias para a instalação de cabos no litoral brasileiro, incluindo obrigações exigidas por todas as esferas de governo. Com isso em mãos, a pasta acredita que poderá disponibilizar um pré-projeto aos operadores de infraestrutura. A expectativa é de que a modelagem facilite os negócios envolvendo infraestruturas subaquáticas no País. "Isso vai ser resultado de todas as tomadas de subsídios e workshops que fizemos [sobre cabos submarinos]. Ter esse mapeamento é um projeto que estamos trabalhando dentro do ministério", afirmou Silva. Falta de governança Suzana Rodrigues, conselheira substituta da Anatel, comentou que o setor de cabos submarinos carece de governança. Segunda ela, os órgãos públicos envolvidos com o segmento precisam ter uma coordenação para que o operador "não fique correndo atrás de diversos organismos". Na prática, apesar de o Brasil ser atrativo ao segmento, até pelo posicionamento geográfico, o modelo atual atrasa os investimentos. "Fazer esse balanceamento entre segurança jurídica e as necessidades de um setor altamente tecnológico é sempre um desafio. Estamos falando de infraestruturas críticas, e o nosso olhar tem que ser para o operador de uma infraestrutura privada que está pensando em um retorno econômico", avaliou a conselheira substituta da Anatel. Energia para data centers A coordenadora-geral de Planejamento da Transmissão do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), Thais Ingrinde de Souza Araújo, disse que a pasta está adotando um novo modelo de acesso à rede elétrica para facilitar a contratação de energia por data centers. O modelo antigo funcionava como uma fila, com cada solicitação sendo analisada em ordem cronológica pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). Contudo, agora a entidade trabalha com um sistema chamado de "temporada de acesso", no qual diversos pedidos são analisados conjuntamente. "Para os locais em que há muita competição – ou seja, tem mais projetos cadastrados do que a rede consegue absorver –, abre-se um procedimento competitivo com base no sinal econômico: quem der o maior bônus, quilowatt por reais, fica apto a conseguir assinar o seu contrato e seguir com o seu processo de conexão naquele barramento", explicou. De acordo com Thais, a mudança de modelo reduz o tempo de análise e favorece projetos "mais maduros". Além disso, o setor elétrico consegue direcionar investimentos para obras com as quais já tem assinatura de projeto com um provedor de data center. "Com isso, a gente conseguir garantir que nenhuma estrutura de transmissão fique ociosa", resumiu.

artigo.texto: Apresentação de detalhes do data center gera movimento contra sua implantação, com abaixo-assinado digital e análises sobre a falta de consulta à comunidade e questionamento dos impactos socioambientais do empreendimento em Maringá Maringá é mesmo diferente. Enquanto o restante do país e do mundo se preocupam com os efeitos da construção de data centers, aqui anuncia-se para esta sexta-feira o anúncio de detalhes do chamamento público para selecionar um parceiro para implantar um data center de IA na cidade. Em janeiro de 2025 já haviam anunciado, com a presença do CEO Fernando Palamone, que a RT-One iria construir o data center, inclusive reservada grande área nas imediações do Aeroporto Regional Silvio Name Junior. Fala-se em geração de “empregos qualificados”, mas antes a conversa era de que seriam muitas vagas, embora data center só ofereça um pequeno número de empregos após a conclusão da obra física. Não se falou no impacto socioambiental. Ao invés de investimento de R$ 6 bilhões, o que aconteceu foi a criação de mais uma estatal, a Maringá Data e Tecnologia, que vai entrar com até R$ 10 milhões, na condição de parceria da empresa que vencer o chamamento público. Até recentemente a informação era de que o data center seria instalado em uma Zona Especial de Exportação, mas o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, que autoriza a ZPE por meio do Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação, negou que tenha recebido protocolo neste sentido. Em outubro do ano passado, Maringá criou a Zona Especial de Desenvolvimento Econômico (Zede), estabelecendo que um dos objetivos é viabilizar a implantação de uma ZPE. Para que o data center ou outras indústrias operem com os incentivos fiscais e aduaneiros de exportação dentro da Zede, o projeto ainda depende da aprovação federal (CZPE e decreto presidencial) que alfandega o espaço. A Zona Especial de Desenvolvimento Econômico de Maringá ocupa uma área de 2,13 milhões de m² (cerca de 213,5 hectares) na região sudoeste do município, entre a avenida Pioneiro Ângelo Bortolotto, o ribeirão Floriano e o córrego Tatupeba, nas proximidades do aeroporto regional. As regras urbanísticas e ambientais são definidas pela lei complementar nº 1.505/2025 e detalhadas nos anexos gráficos disponíveis no PDF oficial da Prefeitura de Maringá. O projeto cria uma nova via local industrial ligando o prolongamento da avenida Pioneiro Ângelo Bortolotto à rua Cristina Mathias de Souza e prevê uma semirrotatória no cruzamento da avenida Julieta dos Santos Pardini com a Estrada Tatupeba. Os movimentos para a instalação de um data center em Maringá vêm num momento difícil e que pode respingar no poder público, assim como acontece em Uberlândia (MG). Ontem, Bruna Mascote abriu ontem um abaixo-assinado na internet, que está com mais de 400 assinaturas até há pouco, para os contribuintes que se preocupam com a proposta. “Esta questão afeta não só o meio ambiente, mas também o bem-estar de cada um de nós, que escolhemos esta cidade por sua tranquilidade e conexão com a natureza”, explica ela ao apresentar o problema, conclamando os cidadãos a se manifestar contra a proposta. Considera que o projeto do data center em Maringá “deixa muitas perguntas sem respostas, e alimenta nossas apreensões quanto aos impactos ambientais. Sabemos que tais instalações consomem quantidades exorbitantes de água e energia elétrica, recursos que são vitais e devem ser geridos com máxima responsabilidade, especialmente em tempos de escassez hídrica e preocupações crescentes sobre a sustentabilidade ambiental”. Ela reclama da falta de consulta aos maringaenses e apela aos vereadores para que reconsiderem a instalação, embora eles tenham aprovado tudo o que foi enviado pelo Executivo ao Legislativo. Leia mais e assine o abaixo-assinado aqui. O advogado, professor e consultor de negócios Alan Zampieri publicou artigo em que questiona o impacto socioambiental do data center na Cidade Canção. O artigo, que pode ser lido na íntegra aqui, começa com uma conta de escritório: “Pegue toda a energia elétrica que Londrina, a maior cidade do interior do Paraná, consumiu em 2025: 1.639 gigawatts-hora. Agora dobre. É mais ou menos isso que os 400 megawatts de TI anunciados para o data center em Maringá gastariam em um ano, a plena carga”. O tema data center e suas consequências ambientais está em alta em todo o mundo. Dias atrás o presidente Donald Trump, que defende a ideia apesar das manifestações contrárias em vários estados, disse que não permitirá que empresas construam data centers fora dos Estados Unidos. Quem desobedecer receberá um “imposto altíssimo”. Isso poderia influenciar a implantação em Maringá, uma vez que a RT-One se apresenta como uma empresa norte-americana, com atuação multinacional nos Estados Unidos, México, Suíça e Brasil. PS – No mesmo horário em que serão apresentados os detalhes do projeto está marcada uma manifestação de pessoas contrárias à implantação. Foto: Brett Sayles/Pexels

artigo.texto: The midterm elections — with data centers a key issue in many races — helped provide clarity around the environment for data center development, James Burke, Vistra president and CEO, said on an earnings call earlier this month. “Before the elections, in many markets, we were seeing concerns about data centers in the way that the public was reacting to the pace of development, who had control over those decisions, what impact could it have on electric prices, water, all of that,” Burke said on the Nov. 6 call. “Moving past this election is a positive just in terms of being able to understand what's at stake, and now how do we move forward?” So far, the key messages from Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa have been “very similar to some of the key messages that Governor Abbott had expressed and … consistent with messages we've been expressing, which is there has to be some guardrails on this development,” Burke said. Vistra wants tougher requirements for data center interconnection, including higher collateral requirements and take-or-pay agreements for transmission charges, according to Burke. “As we've said for some time, load interconnect queues were overstated across the country and especially in [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas footprint], driven by speculation from developers,” Burke said. Even with the midterm elections and regulatory actions around data centers, through 2030 Vistra expects load to grow by 4% to 6% a year in ERCOT and by 2% to 3% annually in the PJM Interconnection footprint, according to Burke. Despite Vistra’s expectations for load growth in ERCOT, power prices there have been trending lower due to some crypto mining facilities coming offline so they can convert into data centers, and the state’s data center audit and permitting pause, Burke said. “We do not see this as a long-term impact,” he said, noting that ERCOT hit a 91 GW peak demand record this year. Vistra’s fleet has grown to about 50 GW with its Oct. 30 Cogentrix acquisition, Burke said. The fleet includes combined cycle and peaking power plants that are running more often, according to Burke. “As renewable penetration continues throughout the country, you're seeing these assets get called on more,” Burke said in response to an analyst question about potentially selling off parts of the fleet. “So we've been bullish on dispatchable. We've been bullish on flexibility … So as a long-term owner-operator, we like the fleet.”

artigo.texto: Everyone loves a neat david-and-goliath story, especially when a single supplier has charged rent on an entire industry for years. Walk through any auto supply chain briefing right now and you'll hear that CATL's grip on Chinese EV makers is slipping, with automakers like Xpeng pushing hard into battery work of their own. That headline sounds dramatic. Honestly, it also misses how battery manufacturing actually works. Here is the real story upfront. Xpeng isn't trying to out-build CATL in gigawatt-hour commodity cell factories. CEO He Xiaopeng has drawn a sharp line between making raw cells and owning the battery system, pack engineering, software, and multi-supplier procurement. At the same time, CATL isn't collapsingâits global EV battery share sat around 39.1% across JanuaryâSeptember 2026 and hit 40.00% in China's October 2026 power battery installationsâyet its exclusivity is eroding fast as rivals like BYD, CALB, Gotion High-tech, EVE Energy, and Sunwoda grab bigger slices and automakers refuse to rely on one vendor. Why CATL's Grip Looks Different Up Close For years, being an EV startup or mid-sized automaker in China meant begging CATL for allocation, eating price hikes when lithium spiked, and accepting whatever pack roadmap CATL handed down. That leverage came from scale and chemistry leadership. When supply is tight, the biggest cell maker sets the rules. By late 2026, the math changed. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) capacity is plentifulâLFP made up 86.9% of China's October 2026 power battery installationsâand second-tier Chinese cell makers have scaled fast enough to compete on both price and performance. According to SNE Research data cited by CnEVPost and Battery-Tech Network, CATL installed 389.2 GWh globally through September 2026 (39.1% share, up from 37.5% a year earlier), while BYD held 15.2% and seven Chinese suppliers in the top ten combined for 73.0%. Calling CATL "finished" is lazy reporting. Losing monopoly pricing power is very different from losing relevance. Look closely at China's monthly numbers and you'll see two truths at once. In October 2026, CATL still led China's power battery market with 39.60 GWh and a 40.00% share, ahead of BYD at 21.14 GWh (21.36%), CALB at 8.55 GWh (8.64%), and Gotion High-tech at 5.99 GWh (6.05%). Yet CATL's share gap against BYD narrowed for five straight months in China, and more importantly, single-supplier lock-in is out of fashion. Automakers want leverage. When three or four qualified suppliers can hit your spec sheet, nobody can hold your production line hostage over a quarterly price dispute. What Xpeng Means by Battery Production When people hear an automaker is stepping up battery production, they picture giant electrode-coating lines and multi-billion-dollar cell plants. That's not Xpeng's play for mainstream cars. In September 2026, He Xiaopeng explained that Xpeng is bringing battery work in-house starting in 2026 while explicitly distinguishing that from mass-producing standard EV cells. Instead of competing head-on with CATL on commodity cell manufacturing, Xpeng is taking control of pack architecture, battery management software, thermal design, and supplier diversification. It has also invested in battery cell companies and spreads cell sourcing across alternatives such as CALB, Sunwoda, and Svolt rather than putting every egg in CATL's basket. Anyone who has worked on electric vehicle powertrains knows why pack integration matters so much. Two cars can buy similar cells from the same supplier and perform wildly differently on the road. Pack structural efficiency determines how much usable energy fits inside a tight wheelbase without adding dead weight. Thermal plate routing and coolant flow decide whether high-speed charging holds steady or throttles halfway through a session. And the battery management systemâthe Software and hardware that monitors cell voltage, temperature, and state of charge in real time.âcontrols charging curves, state-of-charge accuracy, and long-term cell degradation. There's also a specialized twist in Xpeng's broader roadmap. In late October 2026, reports highlighted that Xpeng started small-batch production of solid-state batteries aimed at its Iron humanoid robot ahead of planned mass production. That's small-batch, niche hardware for roboticsânot a replacement for giga-scale automotive cell suppliers. Confusing pilot or robotics battery work with full-scale EV cell self-sufficiency is one of the biggest mistakes analysts and readers make. How Rivals Are Splitting the Playbook Xpeng isn't doing this in a vacuum. Across China's EV sector, automakers are converging on one conclusionâdon't hand total battery control to one supplierâwhile picking different levels of vertical integration. Take Li Auto. Rather than just buying packs off the shelf, Li Auto has pushed deeper into cell-level alignment, including a strategic stake in Sunwoda Power and self-developed battery systems on newer models. Xiaomi, meanwhile, has leaned on its own pack architectureâsuch as its "Dragon Armour" pack engineeringâpaired with multi-sourcing from cell makers like CALB and Sunwoda. Why are so many automakers splitting up the stack this way? Because cell manufacturing is brutally capital-intensive and unforgiving. A bad yield rate or a shifting chemistry standard can trap billions of dollars in specialized equipment. Owning the pack design, thermal cooling, and software lets a carmaker differentiate the driving and charging experience while keeping cell suppliers hungry and competitive. Let's be fair to CATL, too. In high-margin areas like ternary batteriesâwhere October 2026 data still put CATL at a 63.12% share in ChinaâCATL retains deep technical weight and global scale that smaller challengers haven't matched across every segment. What's changed isn't CATL's engineering talent. What's changed is the buyer's bargaining power. Common Misconceptions About This Shift - Misconception 1: Xpeng is replacing CATL wit

artigo.texto: Governador Clécio entrega o primeiro Data Center da história do Amapá e consolida avanço na modernização da gestão pública Obra marca um novo capítulo na administração estadual ao garantir segurança de dados, eficiência nos sistemas e atendimento mais ágil à população O governador Clécio Luís deu mais um passo decisivo na modernização da administração pública ao inaugurar, na manhã desta quarta-feira, 25, o primeiro Data Center da história do Governo do Amapá. Instalada na sede da Secretaria de Estado da Fazenda (Sefaz), no Centro de Macapá, a nova estrutura marca um avanço inédito na gestão estadual, consolidando o compromisso do chefe do Executivo com a transformação digital, a segurança institucional e a eficiência dos serviços prestados à população. Resultado de um investimento de R$ 14,4 milhões viabilizado por meio do Programa de Modernização da Gestão Fiscal (Profisco II), com financiamento do Banco Interamericano de Desenvolvimento (BID), o projeto foi destravado pela gestão de Clécio Luís. Projetado sob medida para as condições climáticas do Amapá e dentro de padrões internacionais de confiabilidade, o equipamento interliga todas as secretarias estaduais com atenção especial ao fisco, à arrecadação e ao sistema tributário, além de possuir estrutura para dar suporte a outros órgãos públicos. Com autonomia energética, resistência a incêndios e sistemas de redundância, o Data Center foi planejado para suportar situações severas e evitar as quedas de sistema que interrompiam os atendimentos ao público. Durante a entrega, o governador destacou o protagonismo do Estado na adoção de tecnologia de ponta. ”É muito mais do que um sistema, é um cérebro novo, com o que há de mais moderno no mundo, feito especificamente para o Amapá. Ele vai servir a todos os órgãos do Estado, garantindo segurança nos dados, tecnologia avançada e modernização em todos os processos. Hoje, o Amapá está entre os estados brasileiros mais bem equipados com tecnologia de ponta em data center”, afirmou o governador Clécio Luís. Na ponta, o investimento se traduz em mais agilidade para contribuintes e cidadãos na emissão de notas fiscais, certidões negativas e outros documentos essenciais, reduzindo falhas operacionais, paralisações e filas de espera. Para o secretário de Estado da Fazenda, Jesus Vidal, a entrega reflete a visão estratégica do chefe do Executivo para preparar o Amapá para o futuro. ”Esse equipamento vem para dar um ponto de partida, uma transformação nos nossos processos digitais. É um equipamento de última geração, um investimento do Governo do Estado que se preocupa com essa modernização e que vai armazenar e processar todos os dados do governo com velocidade e confiabilidade”, ressaltou Vidal. Durante a visita às instalações guiada pela equipe técnica, o governador também acompanhou o funcionamento dos protocolos rigorosos de proteção do espaço, que possui acesso restrito exclusivamente a profissionais autorizados, portas blindadas, controle por reconhecimento facial, filtragem de ar e sensores automatizados que acionam gás de contenção em caso de abertura indevida. Segundo o coordenador de Tecnologia da Informação da Sefaz, Rivenildo Duarte, a capacidade instalada garante suporte tecnológico ao Estado a longo prazo. ”Hoje o Data Center tem capacidade para 16 racks, e cada rack comporta na faixa de 30 servidores. Com essa configuração, temos estrutura para armazenar mais de 10 a 15 anos de informações com total segurança”, explicou o coordenador. Com a entrada em operação do Data Center, o Amapá e estabelece uma base sólida para a expansão de novos serviços digitais, aproximando o poder público da população por meio de uma gestão mais ágil, segura e preparada para o desenvolvimento do Estado. artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms Skanska Wins Additional Award for New Georgia Data Center Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Key PointsSkanska booked the award as new contracted work rather than revenue already earned. View more - Skanska booked the award as new contracted work rather than revenue already earned. - The latest award mirrors an earlier Georgia project in capacity and footprint. - Skanska's Georgia announcements represent separate awards rather than one cumulative project value. Skanska announced on November 26, 2026 that it had received an additional $275 million award from an existing client to build a new 48 MW data center in Georgia, USA. The award is worth about SEK 2.8 billion and will be included in Skanska’s US order bookings for the fourth quarter of 2026. That classification matters: the announcement adds contracted work to the order book, rather than reporting the full amount as revenue already earned. Building Scope and Delivery Schedule The main facility will total 244,730 square feet, approximately 22,700 square meters. Skanska’s scope covers construction of the shell and interior fit-out for technical spaces, support areas and office functions. An 860-square-foot, approximately 80-square-meter, ancillary water-treatment building is also included. Although small beside the main facility, it places supporting utility infrastructure within the award. Construction began in November 2026, and Skanska expects completion in October 2028, meaning work was already underway when the additional award was announced. September Award Provides a Close Comparison Skanska’s September 22, 2026 announcement described an $84 million contract with an existing client, assigned to US order bookings for the third quarter. It listed the same 48 MW capacity and 244,730-square-foot footprint as the latest project, while specifying five colocation data halls and administrative space. The September project was scheduled to begin in November 2026 and finish in the third quarter of 2028; the latest release gives October 2028 as the expected completion month. September’s delivery scope included civil, structural, utilities, electrical, mechanical, security, interior amenities and fit-out work, plus commissioning of major equipment through completion. Earlier Awards Establish a Sequence of Georgia Work An April 9, 2026 release disclosed a $75 million contract, booked in the first quarter, for a 22,700-square-meter, 244,090-square-foot facility. Its scope included associated site work, underground utilities, administrative space and five data halls. Construction began in March 2026, with completion scheduled for the first quarter of 2028. A June 23, 2026 announcement followed with a $255 million supplemental contract, booked in the second quarter. That project covered approximately 245,000 square feet, associated site work and underground utilities, administrative space and five data halls, with the same stated March 2026 to first-quarter 2028 construction schedule. These releases establish a sequence of Georgia data-center awards during 2026, but not one aggregate project value. Skanska identifies the customers only as existing clients and does not explicitly connect every announcement to the same facility. The values should therefore be read as separate awards, not as a documented cumulative cost for a single project. The latest award’s significance is split between two timelines: a fourth-quarter 2026 booking for Skanska’s US business and a construction program extending to October 2028. The first measures new work secured; the second will track how that booked work becomes a completed 48 MW facility with its supporting water-treatment infrastructure.

artigo.texto: BYD Outsells Tesla in Battery-Electric Vehicles Chinese automaker BYD sold more battery-electric passenger cars than Tesla in 2025, according to reported sales figures. Updated on Nov. 27, 2026 in Electric Vehicles Live Poll Are you planning to buy an electric vehicle in the next year? BYD sold 2,256,714 battery-electric passenger vehicles in 2025, a 27.9% rise from 2024, surpassing Tesla's worldwide deliveries of 1,636,129 vehicles, which fell 8.6% over the same period. The comparison covers only battery-electric vehicles and excludes BYD's plug-in hybrids. Why it matters The result marks a shift in the global electric vehicle market, where a Chinese manufacturer now leads a company that long dominated battery-electric sales. Tesla cut prices twice in China while BYD raised prices there, reflecting diverging competitive strategies in the world's largest auto market. BYD's 2,256,714 battery-electric passenger vehicle sales in 2025 rose 27.9% from 2024, while Tesla's 1,636,129 worldwide deliveries fell 8.6%. Tesla's fourth-quarter 2025 deliveries of 418,227 were down 15.6% year over year, and the comparison excludes plug-in hybrids. The players BYD BYD is a Chinese automaker that produces battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles and is backed in part by Berkshire Hathaway. Tesla Tesla is an American electric vehicle manufacturer founded in 2003 that led global battery-electric sales for years before being overtaken by BYD. The details Tesla cut prices twice in China during the period, while BYD raised prices in the market. Berkshire Hathaway has been a BYD shareholder since 2008, a relationship highlighted in coverage of the sales shift. Timeline - Feb. 15, 2023: Charlie Munger predicted BYD's lead over Tesla at a shareholders meeting. - November 2023: Charlie Munger died. - 2025: BYD surpassed Tesla in battery-electric passenger vehicle sales. - Fourth quarter 2025: Tesla delivered 418,227 vehicles. Roadmap For years Tesla led global battery-electric vehicle sales, a position that defined the early mass-market phase of the industry. BYD's 2025 lead signals that Chinese manufacturers are now setting the pace in the transition to electric vehicles. For buyers comparing electric cars, the sales shift suggests more choice and competitive pricing from BYD in key markets. Price cuts by Tesla in China could also translate into lower purchase costs for shoppers there. The takeaway Battery-electric sales leadership can shift quickly, so buyers and investors should track annual figures rather than assume a fixed market order. Comparing sales data on a like-for-like basis, such as battery-electric only, gives a clearer picture of market share. Further reading Explore more coverage in our Electric Vehicles section. artigo.texto: que são mega data centers de Inteligência Artificial, onde estão projetos no Brasil e por que precisamos de leis rigorosas para conter as Big Techs Por Andressa Santa Cruz – Greenpeace Brasil | A era da Inteligência Artificial (IA) virou uma corrida desenfreada que exige cada vez mais territórios, recursos e dados. No Brasil, mega projetos das gigantes da tecnologia avançam em meio a isenção de impostos, enquanto comunidades e consumidores enfrentam os prejuízos. Mas dá tempo de agir antes que os danos se tornem irreversíveis. “Antes de seguir expandindo os data centers de IA que só aumentam os lucros bilionários das Big Techs, o Brasil deve saber o custo e definir as regras para que o povo brasileiro não pague a conta dos impactos” explica Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. O que são Mega Data Centers de IA? São centros de dados de hiperescala para desenvolver modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA), concentram milhões de servidores para processar, armazenar e transmitir enormes volumes de dados, podendo consumir energia equivalente a países inteiros e milhões de litros de água potável. A diferença está no tamanho e na capacidade: data centers tradicionais operam os serviços digitais que usamos no dia a dia (enviar mensagens, assistir a vídeos e acessar plataformas); já mega data centers de IA são instalações computacionais de escala e impactos industriais e atendem sobretudo às Big Techs. Quais os impactos dos Mega Data Centers de IA? - Aumento na conta de luz: usam a rede local e elevam os custos da energia nas residências – nos EUA, as tarifas chegaram a triplicar para mercados, custo que é repassado aos consumidores. - Consumo de água: apesar de existir “circuito fechado”, há perdas e reposição; nos EUA, o consumo anual chegou a 1 trilhão de litros d’água. - Poluição sonora: geradores fazem ruído insuportável, alto e constante, afetando a qualidade de vida das famílias vizinhas. - Emissões de gases de efeito estufa: a possibilidade de usar fontes fósseis, ampliando as emissões que agravam a crise climática. - Pressão sobre os territórios: ocupam áreas enormes que podem chegar a mais de 100 campos de futebol, disputando terras, água e energia com comunidades locais. - Concentração de poder: domínio de empresas estrangeiras sobre o mercado e as infraestruturas impede o avanço tecnológico no país. Nos EUA, onde mais tem data centers no mundo, a população fez vários protestos contra e o tema foi decisivo nas eleições. Nova York suspendeu novas instalações de hiperescala até ter leis mais rígidas e países europeus também pausaram projetos como Irlanda, Holanda e Dinamarca. Quais são os projetos de Mega Data Center no Brasil? O Brasil já possui data centers (cerca de 225 e quase metade fica no estado de São Paulo), mas os mega projetos para desenvolver IA estão começando a chegar em todo país. O mais avançado está em construção no território indígena do povo Anacé, em Caucaia (CE), região metropolitana de Fortaleza. Segundo o Governo do Ceará, abrigará as tecnologias de IA do TikTok e a previsão é começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Confira abaixo projetos de mega data centers em andamento no Brasil. Lei Redata e a importância de regular data centers no Brasil No Brasil, o Redata (Lei 15.504/2026), sancionada em setembro, criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. Na prática, concede isenções de impostos para atrair centros de dados ao país — uma renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 7 bilhões, segundo Secretaria Especial da Receita Federal, ou seja, recursos públicos que deixam de ser arrecadados. Aprovado sem participação social ou diálogo com as comunidades atingidas, o Redata abre brechas preocupantes, como o incentivo à combustível fóssil. O desenho da lei favorece as Big Techs em detrimento do povo brasileiro e do clima global. Enquanto estados norte-americanos e países europeus discutem limites rígidos, o Brasil se torna alvo da expansão acelerada. O que são Big Techs e quem controla a corrida da Inteligência Artificial? As Big Techs são gigantes da tecnologia que estão entre as empresas mais ricas e influentes do mundo, como Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvdia, Microsoft e TikTok – seus fundadores e administradores ocupam o topo da lista de bilionários da Forbes. São exemplos de como a “inovação” acontece quando é controlada por poucos: lucros recordes, cortes de empregos e a falsa promessa de que automação trará benefícios, porém na prática acumulam infrações trabalhistas, sociais e ambientais. Por que regular Big Techs e Data Centers? Regular não é censurar ou frear o desenvolvimento tecnológico, é assegurar que a população faça parte com salvaguardas que respeitem os ciclos da natureza, o bem-comum e que tragam retorno para a sociedade. Para isso, precisamos de criar regras: - Regulação das Big Techs (ambiente digital e democracia): estabelece limites e responsabilidades para as grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo transparência sobre algoritmos, proteção de dados e direitos digitais. - Regulação de data centers (infraestrutura física e recursos naturais): impõe análise de riscos e leis firmes para a construção e operação desses empreendimentos, considerando os impactos socioambientais. Parem os mega data centers! Nove organizações — Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil – se uniram para frear o avanço de mega data centers de IAs no Brasil até que sejam assegurados: - Consentimento e Transparência: Participação social ativa e consulta livre, prévia e informada para as comunidades tradicionais. - Licenciamento Ambiental completo: Estudo e relatório de impacto assegurando transição energética justa e proibindo instalação em áreas de importância ecológica. - Fim da isenção de impostos: Quem lucra com infraestrutura digital em larga escala deve se responsabilizar pelos custos e impactos, e investi

artigo.texto: A estimativa atribuída à Epoch AI coloca o data center da Huawei em Horinger, na Mongólia Interior, em cerca de 81 mil equivalentes H100 — aproximadamente 7% da capacidade computacional estimada de Colossus 2, associado à xAI. Um equivalente H100 expressa capacidade computacional em relação ao acelerador Nvidia H100. Portanto, os 81 mil equivalentes não representam uma contagem de GPUs Nvidia instaladas. Como Horinger se compara a Colossus 2 As estimativas usam a mesma unidade, o que permite comparar a escala computacional dos dois campi: A estimativa de Horinger equivale a cerca de 7% da estimativa para Colossus 2. É uma comparação entre capacidades computacionais estimadas, não entre contagens verificadas de aceleradores físicos. Para comparar a escala de data centers, use a mesma unidade: equivalentes H100 expressam capacidade computacional estimada, não o número de GPUs instaladas. Como a estimativa foi calculada O método atribuído à análise combina observações de infraestrutura com estimativas de chips. Imagens de satélite permitem identificar equipamentos de refrigeração; a partir deles, estima-se a dissipação de calor e a capacidade do campus. Para estimar a quantidade de aceleradores, o cálculo também considera as vendas de chips da Huawei e o intervalo entre a venda e a implantação. A estimativa atribui ao campus cerca de 105 mil chips Ascend 910C e 8 mil Ascend 910B. Em um relato publicado em novembro de 2026, quatro edifícios de refrigeração densa somavam uma capacidade estimada de 286 MW; três eram descritos como operacionais naquele relato. A mesma análise cita uma subestação de 304 MW e geradores de reserva de 230 MW como referências para conferir a estimativa. Esses valores se referem a infraestruturas distintas dos 286 MW atribuídos aos quatro edifícios.

artigo.texto: Energy Vault Closes $78 Million Financing for Texas Battery Storage Project The financing will support construction of the SOSA Energy Center, with commercial operations expected in Q3 2027 November 24, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Energy Vault, a utility-scale energy storage project developer, has closed $78 million in construction and bridge financing for its 150 MW/300 MWh SOSA Energy Center battery storage project in Madison County, Texas. The bridge financing will be repaid through an $80 million preferred equity investment already committed upon project completion. Energy Vault said the construction financing, preferred equity investment, and a draw on the OIC preferred facility are intended to fund the project through construction and commercial operations on a non-recourse basis. The SOSA Energy Center was the first energy storage asset formally acquired and placed into development under Asset Vault, Energy Vault’s platform for owning and operating energy storage and artificial intelligence infrastructure assets. Once completed, the project will operate on a merchant basis in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas North market. Energy Vault said the project will retain the flexibility to enter into a contracted offtake agreement as market conditions change. Construction began in the fourth quarter of 2025 after the company secured site control and reached environmental and interconnection milestones. Civil work has been completed, and a substation has been installed. Energy Vault is handling the project’s engineering, procurement, and construction. Major equipment is expected to arrive at the site in the coming months. Commercial operations are scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. The company said the SOSA Energy Center represents an investment of approximately $100 million in Madison County. Energy Vault estimates that the project will generate $9.3 million in tax revenue for North Zulch Independent School District and Madison County over 10 years. Construction is also expected to create 65 local jobs. In September 2026, the company acquired more than 2.3 GW of U.S. battery energy storage development projects from Colorado-based developer and operator of utility-scale battery storage projects, Goshe Energy Storage. In the first nine months of 2026, publicly announced energy storage project funding increased by 197% year over year, compared to 9M 2025, according to Mercom’s recently released 9M 2026 Funding and M&A for Energy Storage report.

artigo.texto: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan will receive an US$8.5 million grant from the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) to prepare for trading carbon credits with South Korea. The documents were signed on 25 November during a meeting between Umid Abidkhodjaev, Deputy Minister of Economy and Finance, and representatives of KOICA and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), the ministry said. The grant is being provided under KOICA's technical assistance programme for a project titled "Supporting Uzbekistan's Implementation of the Paris Agreement and Joint Actions with the Republic of Korea under Article 6". The project will be implemented jointly with GGGI. The talks were attended by Kim Myung Jin, head of KOICA's office in Uzbekistan, Stella Seung Yeon Lee, head of GGGI's office in Uzbekistan, and specialists from both organisations. The parties discussed Uzbekistan's transition to a green economy and the regulatory and institutional framework for carbon credit trading. The project will involve developing rules, guidelines and a joint action plan for carbon credit trading between Uzbekistan and South Korea. The grant will also support the establishment of a training centre for specialists involved in preparing and managing carbon projects. The centre will be equipped with the necessary facilities and offer training programmes. Another component will involve pilot projects to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in agriculture, energy and water management. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows countries to cooperate voluntarily in meeting their climate commitments. Under Article 6.2, one country can transfer verified emissions reductions generated by projects within its territory to another country. These transfers are known as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs). The purchasing country can count them towards its national climate targets, while the selling country must exclude the same reductions from its own accounting to prevent double counting. Article 6.4 establishes an international carbon credit mechanism supervised by a United Nations body, while Article 6.8 covers non-market approaches to cooperation. Countries agreed on the main rules for implementing Article 6 at the COP26 climate conference in Glasgow in 2021. In 2025, GGGI, with financial support from KOICA, implemented the Green Restoration of the Aral Sea Region project in Karakalpakstan. It focused on developing climate-resilient agriculture, introducing water-saving technologies and attracting green investment. The new project continues KOICA and GGGI's cooperation in Uzbekistan on green development, climate change adaptation and sustainable finance. According to the ministry, it will expand Uzbekistan's opportunities to participate in the international carbon market and help the country achieve its climate goals.

artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites in space for the creation of data centers critical to powering artificial intelligence. The decision comes as the US races to lead the world in AI, a technology that promises to turbocharge innovation and economic growth. Harnessing AI is also central to SpaceX’s growth ambitions, though the company cautioned in a regulatory filing ahead of its June initial public offering that launching data centers in space relied on “unproven” technologies and “may not achieve commercial viability.” Deploying SpaceX’s “Starmind” constellation – comprised of 1 million orbital compute modules – will help meet “rapidly growing demand” for AI computing power, the FCC said in a statement Wednesday. The deployed satellites will “process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the agency added. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. AI data centers require enormous amounts of energy and Musk has endorsed orbital data centers that can harness the power of the sun. “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX told the FCC when it applied for permission to launch the satellites earlier this year. Musk welcomed the decision, saying on X, his social media platform, that “this will be a great asset to America and the world.” The initiative has drawn criticism from the scientific community, however, who have argued that the technology could disrupt views of the night sky and increase pollution. In a statement Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society said it was “dismayed” by the FCC’s decision, which it had opposed in earlier filings to the agency. The “proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the organization said. It noted that the satellites would be visible as “extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky” and would generate “radio emissions” and “waste heat” that would “threaten… sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research.” It also warned of “atmospheric pollution” from the launches and reentries so many satellites. Under the license, SpaceX must deploy at least one authorized space station by November 2033, deploy 10% of the total – or 100,000 – by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. There are currently around 16,700 operational satellites in space, according to Orbital Radar, a platform providing real-time tracking of objects in orbit. The European Space Agency puts the number of functioning satellites slightly lower, at 15,800. Earlier this month, in a historic test flight, SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft deployed Starlink internet satellites before returning to earth and pulling of an unprecedented landing.

artigo.texto: The European Union (EU) and the United Kingdom (UK) have agreed to link their carbon markets from 2028, bringing together two emissions trading systems that have operated separately since Brexit. The deal aims to create a larger, more liquid carbon market, reduce trade barriers, and support investment in cleaner industries. The agreement could also bring major benefits for businesses. The UK government estimates that linking the markets could add up to £3.8 billion (US$4.9 billion) to the UK economy each year by 2040. It could also help exempt around £6.5 billion (US$8.4 billion) worth of British exports from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The deal marks a major step in carbon market cooperation. However, the link will not take effect immediately. Both sides must complete legal and technical work before the planned launch on January 1, 2028. EU and UK Reconnect Carbon Markets After Brexit The agreement will link the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS). Once operational, companies covered by either system will be able to use emissions allowances issued in the EU or UK to meet their obligations in both markets. The EU ETS began in 2005 and covers major polluting sectors, including power generation, steel, cement, chemicals, and aviation. It sets a cap on emissions and requires companies to hold allowances for the greenhouse gases they release. Companies that cut emissions can sell unused allowances, while those that exceed their limits must buy more. After leaving the EU, the UK launched its own emissions trading scheme in 2021. The two systems have since operated separately, with different rules and carbon prices. The new agreement will reconnect the markets while keeping them legally separate. The UK will retain its own ETS authority and some control over its emissions cap. However, both sides will align key rules to make allowance trading and compliance work across the two systems. The UK and EU first agreed to pursue a link at their May 2025 summit. Negotiations began later that year and concluded with the November 2026 agreement. The news release stated: “This linking will provide the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel.” EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: “The agreement will cut emissions and generate investment in cleaner industries. This will help us advance our shared climate goals.” Linked Carbon Markets Could Boost Trading and Price Stability One of the main goals is to create a deeper market for emissions allowances. Linking the two systems will give companies access to a wider pool of allowances. This could make it easier to buy and sell them, improve market liquidity, and support more stable carbon prices. For businesses, greater access to allowances could also improve planning. Companies operating across the EU and UK will have a more consistent carbon pricing framework. This may help them make longer-term decisions about energy use, industrial upgrades, and investments in lower-carbon technology. The UK government describes the agreement as creating the world’s largest linked carbon market. It also expects the wider market to provide greater price certainty and support a more cost-effective path to net zero. However, a larger market does not guarantee lower carbon prices. Allowance prices will still depend on supply, demand, emissions limits, and policy decisions. The agreement also does not remove the need for companies to reduce their emissions. Instead, it aims to make carbon trading more connected and efficient, giving businesses more flexibility in meeting their climate obligations. £6.5 Billion in UK Exports Could Gain CBAM Relief The agreement could also reduce costs for companies trading between the UK and EU. The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism charges a carbon cost on some imported goods. These include iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity, and hydrogen. The mechanism aims to stop carbon leakage. This happens when companies move production to countries with weaker climate rules to avoid higher carbon costs. The UK has also planned its own CBAM, set to begin in 2027. Without an agreement, businesses could face additional reporting duties and carbon-related costs when trading across the Channel. The UK government estimates that around £6.5 billion worth of British exports could qualify for an exemption from the EU’s CBAM once the linked carbon markets are in place. Mutual exemptions could also reduce administrative costs for companies importing goods from the EU. The government estimates that the agreement could add up to £3.8 billion to the UK economy each year by 2040. These benefits depend on the link becoming operational and the required legal changes being completed. The announcement does not mean that all CBAM charges disappear immediately. Deal Expands Carbon Pricing Across Aviation and Shipping The agreement will also expand the sectors covered by the UK’s carbon market. The country has agreed to align its ETS rules for aviation and maritime activities with the EU system. The European Commission says this expansion will bring more than 10 million tonnes of additional CO₂ emissions into the UK scheme. This will strengthen carbon pricing across transport, including emissions from international aviation and shipping. Airlines and maritime operators that work in both markets could also face fewer separate reporting and compliance requirements. Both systems will also monitor the climate effects of aviation beyond CO₂ emissions. These include other effects that contribute to aviation’s overall warming impact.
