artigo.texto: A new study from the University of Oklahoma puts hard numbers behind a question that planning boards across the country keep asking: what draws data centers to a community? According to the University of Oklahoma announcement, researchers examined 212 U.S. data centers run by 11 major technology companies, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta. Land-use diversity came out as the strongest factor, ahead of the other signals the team tested. The story is dated November 20, 2026, with an update on November 22. It lands at a moment when cloud and AI operators are hunting for sites faster than most local governments can write zoning rules. Our earlier look at an immersion-only data center pitched at under 30,000 square feet showed how much the building itself is changing. The OU work asks a different question: not how to build the hall, but why a given town gets it. This analysis walks through what the study found, what it left out, and what the findings mean for cloud planners, local officials and anyone who has watched a substation upgrade or a rezoning notice appear at the edge of town. We keep to the facts the university has published. Where the record is thin, we say so. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the OU Study Actually Measured Kijin Seong, Ph.D., is an assistant professor in the Division of Planning, Landscape Architecture and Design at OU’s Christopher C. Gibbs College of Architecture. He co-authored the research. The team did not survey executives or ask companies to explain their reasoning. Instead, it looked at where 212 existing facilities sit and tested which local characteristics tracked with those locations. The sample spans 11 major technology companies. Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are named in the announcement, and the other seven are not identified in the material we reviewed. That matters for readers who want company-by-company patterns. The published summary reports aggregate findings, so we cannot say whether Meta favors different communities than Microsoft does. The analysis grouped its explanatory factors into three families: land use, infrastructure and workforce. Land use covers the mix of activities in the surrounding area. Infrastructure covers electrical substations and major roads. Workforce covers concentrations of information technology workers. Those three families gave the researchers a way to compare very different sites on the same terms. Land-Use Diversity: The Strongest Factor in Data Center Site Selection The headline result is the one that surprises people. Land-use diversity, meaning a neighborhood or district that mixes housing, commerce, industry and services, was the strongest factor the analysis identified. Many readers would have guessed that wide-open, single-purpose land wins. The OU team found the reverse pattern holds up better in the data. Why would a mixed area attract a server hall? The study summary does not offer a causal story, and we will not invent one. What we can say is that mixed-use areas tend to come with the things a large facility needs to function: established utility service, road networks, nearby workers and a local government used to permitting different kinds of buildings. A diverse land-use pattern may work as a proxy for all of that. What diversity does and does not mean Diversity here describes the surrounding community, not the data center parcel. A site can sit on a quiet lot and still score high if the district around it mixes uses. For local officials, that distinction changes the pitch. A town does not need to rezone everything for servers. It needs to look like a place where varied development already happens. Practitioners have long published checklists that treat land as a gate. A site selection criteria guide from Base Operations is one example of that genre, which lists the factors developers screen before they commit. The OU analysis adds something those checklists rarely supply: a pattern drawn from where 212 real facilities actually went. Substations, Roads and IT Workers: The Supporting Signals Three more factors helped explain where facilities landed. Proximity to electrical substations, access to major roads and concentrations of information technology workers all showed up in the analysis. None of them beat land-use diversity, but each one added explanatory power. The substation finding fits the physical logic of the business. A data hall is, at its core, a very large electrical load with cooling attached. Sitting close to a substation shortens the path between the grid and the racks. It does not guarantee capacity, and the OU summary reports no megawatt figures, so readers should not read the finding as a statement about how much power any site gets. Major roads matter for less glamorous reasons. Construction crews, generators, cooling equipment and replacement hardware all arrive by truck. Roads also bring staff to the door during shifts. The study treats road access as one measurable proxy for that logistics burden. The IT workforce signal is the most interesting for smaller communities. Facilities cluster where technology workers already live. That suggests that talent, not just land and power, shapes the map. Towns hoping to land a cloud region should ask whether they can supply or attract the people who run it. What Site Selectors Say About Power and Workforce The OU findings line up with how industry practitioners describe the job. Seong himself framed the basics plainly in a report from okcfox.com. He said, “The buildings that hold data centers need land, a lot of electricity, water for cooling and fiber connections.” Note that water and fiber appear in that quote, yet the announcement lists land use, infrastructure (substations and roads) and workforce as the factors the analysis found helpful. artigo.texto: The furor over data centers in Aurora led the City Council to pass a temporary moratorium on projects Monday and one developer to abandon a controversial hyperscale project near the Denver airport. The council adopted a one-year timeout for new data centers in the most developed part of Aurora — south of Interstate 70 and west of Powhaton Road — while more comprehensive data center regulations are developed. At Monday’s council meeting, Mayor Mike Coffman announced that Denver-based Vantage Data Centers has decided to abandon its planned 500-megawatt Trident data center near E-470 and East 48th Avenue. The project was the biggest announced data center in Colorado and it sparked heated opposition by residents, particularly from new residential neighborhoods filling in east of Green Valley Ranch, along Picadilly and Tibet roads. “In response to the recent community concerns, Vantage voluntarily initiated a review of alternative sites, and the examination of viable alternatives continues,” Misty Allen, Vantage vice president for public policy in North America, said in a statement. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state,” Allen said. The announcement brought cheers from the audience at the council meeting. Aurora’s moratorium comes as communities along the Front Range are wrestling with proposed data centers and some, including Denver, Boulder County, Longmont and Thornton, have imposed moratoriums or limited development. Concerns include data centers’ large demands for power and in some cases water, as well as their use of land. Another question is whether power-hungry data centers could drive up electric rates. The Colorado Public Utilities Commission has ordered Xcel Energy, the state’s biggest electricity provider, to develop data center rates that protect other customers. In Aurora, the impact on property values of new homes next near the proposed 108-acre Trident site was a major concern. “Had that Trident center gone forward, the value of your properties would have sunk like a rock,” Coffman told homeowners at Monday’s meeting. “I am just grateful the nightmare is over and you have prevailed.” The council twice failed to pass a more comprehensive moratorium that would have covered the entire city. While the revised moratorium is “limited and imperfect,” Council member Alison Coombs said, “this is the moratorium we can pass.” The moratorium covers approvals for new data centers until October 2027, but there are already projects underway including a 160-MW hyperscale center by Sterling, Virginia-based Quality Technology Services, or QTS. The QTS Aurora facility is the largest data center under construction in the state. “I am against moratoriums of any kind,” Council member Stephanie Hancock said. “What we are in disagreement on is putting a blanket moratorium that would impede the progress of something that is inevitable.” “Data centers are here to stay,” Hancock said. “You’ve got to wrap your heads around it.” Hancock’s remarks were met with a round of boos.

artigo.texto: CATL has unveiled its new 30# Chocolate Battery, a 100 kWh swappable battery designed to extend the driving range of electric vehicles to around 700 km (435 miles) on China’s CLTC test cycle. The new battery expands the company’s standardized battery-swapping portfolio with a higher-capacity option for drivers who need longer range. The battery delivers a peak discharge power of 600 kW and can support vehicle acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h in the three-second range. It can also be exchanged at a battery-swapping station in just 99 seconds, offering an alternative to conventional charging stops. According to CarNewsChina, the battery can add around 400 km of driving range in 10 minutes through fast charging. Its locking mechanism is designed to withstand daily battery swaps for a theoretical lifespan of 27 years. CATL also offers a lifetime warranty for batteries operating within its swapping network. Faster swaps, longer range The 30# Chocolate Battery allows drivers to choose battery capacities according to their travel requirements. CATL is also exploring future upgrade options involving sodium-ion and liquid-solid batteries, potentially allowing the platform to accommodate evolving battery technologies. For users relying on battery swapping, CATL’s system includes the Chocolate Battery Butler, which provides round-the-clock monitoring to manage operational risks. The company says its new-generation swapping stations connect cloud services, stations, and vehicles to coordinate the process. More from Energy See All The system can predict a vehicle’s battery-swapping requirements and schedule resources ahead of its arrival. This is intended to reduce waiting times by ensuring that a station is prepared when a driver reaches it. CATL is also working towards automatic battery swapping that requires minimal input from drivers. CATL expands swapping network CATL currently operates more than 2,500 battery-swapping stations across China and has set a long-term target of expanding the network to 30,000 locations. The company introduced its standardized Chocolate battery-swapping products in December 2024, launching the 20# and 25# versions. The 20# battery comes in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) configurations, with capacities of 42 kWh and 52 kWh, respectively. The 25# offers 56 kWh in its LFP version and 70 kWh in its NMC configuration. The 56 kWh LFP version of the 25# is currently the most widely used battery at CATL’s swapping stations. The new 100 kWh 30# option represents a substantial increase in capacity for the company’s swapping ecosystem. A battery-swapping version of the Xingtan 5X has also appeared in a recent batch of vehicle applications submitted to China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. The model is expected to be a potential candidate for the new 30# battery, although its final battery configuration has not been confirmed. With the 30# Chocolate Battery, CATL is extending its swapping ecosystem beyond smaller-capacity standardized packs, targeting electric vehicles that need longer driving ranges while retaining the convenience of rapid battery replacement.

artigo.texto: Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI. First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power. So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play. Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space. There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field. On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons. For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week. Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center. Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground. But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed. With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center. Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations. But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. artigo.texto: Data centers no espaço: o que a SpaceX ganha com 1 milhão de satélites A FCC autorizou a SpaceX a operar até 1 milhão de satélites para data centers orbitais. O prazo é de 14 anos, mas a corrida por infraestrutura de IA já começou. SpaceX recebe aval para levar IA à órbita terrestre A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC) concedeu autorização condicional para a SpaceX implantar e operar uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites voltados exclusivamente a data centers orbitais. O projeto, batizado de Starmind, pretende posicionar processadores de inteligência artificial em altitudes entre 500 e 1.002 quilômetros. A tese aqui é direta: a aprovação não significa que data centers espaciais estão perto de existir, mas posiciona a SpaceX como o único player com licença regulatória, infraestrutura de lançamento e rede de satélites já operacional para tentar. Isso muda a dinâmica competitiva da infraestrutura de IA nos próximos anos, mesmo que o projeto leve uma década para se materializar. O que a FCC aprovou e o que ainda falta A autorização dá à SpaceX o direito de usar radiofrequências para manter contato e controle dos satélites Starmind a partir da Terra, caso os sistemas primários de comunicação falhem. No dia a dia, a ideia é que os satélites se comuniquem por laser entre si e com a constelação Starlink, já em operação. Mas a aprovação veio com condições relevantes. A FCC ainda não autorizou o plano da SpaceX para lidar com detritos orbitais dos satélites que operarão acima de 600 quilômetros. A empresa pediu uma exceção às regras atuais, que exigem reentrada na atmosfera em até cinco anos após o fim da missão. A SpaceX quer mover satélites aposentados para outras órbitas ao redor da Terra ou até do Sol. O cronograma também é generoso: sete anos para colocar o primeiro satélite operacional em órbita e 14 anos para implantar toda a constelação. Ou seja, a previsão mais otimista coloca o início efetivo da operação por volta de 2033. Por que concorrentes tentaram barrar o projeto A Amazon, que está construindo o Project Kuiper como concorrente direto do Starlink, se opôs formalmente à aprovação. O argumento foi que a proposta carecia de detalhes técnicos básicos e representava uma "ambição grandiosa, não um plano real". A empresa também alertou que, apesar da falta de detalhes, o projeto "oferece risco de dano real" ao ambiente orbital. A Viasat e a Sociedade Astronômica Americana também levantaram objeções sobre congestionamento orbital, interferência de radiofrequência e impactos ambientais. A FCC descartou parte dessas preocupações por considerar que fugiam de sua competência regulatória, o que levanta uma questão: quem fiscaliza os impactos que a FCC não cobre? O presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, classificou a decisão como a abertura de "uma nova fronteira ousada para a infraestrutura de computação necessária à liderança e ao crescimento dos Estados Unidos". Elon Musk agradeceu publicamente. Os obstáculos que a manchete não mostra A aprovação regulatória é apenas o primeiro degrau de uma escadaria longa e cara. A SpaceX enfrenta desafios técnicos que ainda não têm solução comprovada em escala. O principal é a dissipação de calor: processadores de IA geram calor intenso, e o vácuo do espaço dificulta o resfriamento. No solo, data centers consomem volumes enormes de água e energia para refrigeração. No espaço, isso simplesmente não existe. Há também a questão do custo de manufatura e lançamento. Colocar chips de IA em órbita exige que cada componente sobreviva à vibração do lançamento, à radiação cósmica e à ausência de manutenção física. E o financiamento para chips que literalmente saem do planeta é uma categoria de risco que investidores ainda não precificaram com clareza. A corrida por chips de IA no solo já consome dezenas de bilhões de dólares. A versão orbital dessa disputa exige orçamentos ainda maiores e retornos ainda mais incertos. O contraponto: ambição sem cronograma não é vantagem competitiva O melhor argumento contra a relevância imediata desse movimento é o que a própria Amazon levantou: falta substância técnica. Uma licença para operar frequências de rádio não é o mesmo que ter a tecnologia para processar inferência de IA em microgravidade. E 14 anos é tempo suficiente para que a dinâmica inteira do mercado de IA mude várias vezes. Esse argumento tem peso, mas ignora um ponto estratégico. A SpaceX é hoje a única empresa do planeta que fabrica foguetes reutilizáveis, opera a maior constelação de satélites de comunicação do mundo (Starlink, com mais de 6.000 unidades em órbita) e agora detém a licença regulatória para data centers orbitais. Nenhum concorrente reúne essas três peças. Mesmo que o Starmind demore para sair do papel, a vantagem regulatória e logística é real. O Google já sinalizou interesse em data centers orbitais por meio de uma parceria com a Blue Origin, mas está em um estágio ainda mais embrionário. A SpaceX, ao garantir a aprovação da FCC agora, compra tempo e cria barreiras para quem vier depois. O que observar daqui para frente Três sinais importam para acompanhar esse movimento. O primeiro é a decisão da FCC sobre o plano de detritos orbitais: sem essa aprovação, satélites acima de 600 quilômetros ficam travados. O segundo é a evolução da tecnologia de resfriamento em ambiente espacial. Se a SpaceX ou qualquer parceiro demonstrar um protótipo funcional nos próximos dois a três anos, o cronograma pode acelerar. O terceiro sinal é financeiro. Data centers terrestres já custam bilhões por unidade. A versão orbital precisa de um modelo de negócio que justifique o investimento. A aposta provável é que a demanda por processamento de IA cresça tão rápido que a capacidade terrestre, limitada por energia, água e terreno, não dê conta. Nesse cenário, o espaço deixa de ser ficção e vira necessidade. O mercado de data centers cresceu de forma explosiva nos últimos dois anos, impulsionado pela demanda de IA generativa. artigo.texto: As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs. In the study, published Nov. 9 in Nature Energy, Cornell researchers analyzed growth in energy demand and infrastructure projects for four major U.S. power grids from 2020 to 2025 and found that data centers have hiked wholesale energy prices and on average paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth — $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill in 2025. The remaining $5.13 billion, or 62 percent, fell largely on residents, with the lowest income households seeing extra energy costs up to 28 percent of their incomes. “We were trying to answer a very simple question: With the booming of data centers, who pays for that expansion and who benefits?” said Fengqi You, the Roxanne E. and Michael J. Zak Professor in Energy Systems Engineering in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering. “It’s not just a question of generating enough electricity but of whether the rules for paying for the grid are keeping pace with who is driving new demand.” The research is the first multi-region, long-term assessment of how data center development impacts infrastructure growth and how costs are distributed across communities. It comes amidst a boom in data center construction. The researchers found that transmission investment in energy infrastructure projects increased from $2 billion in 2020 to $34 billion in 2025, with data centers driving much of that rise. Debates are ongoing – from local communities to state governments to Congress – about who picks up the bill as growth accelerates; data centers are projected to consume between 8% and 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with 70% to 80% of that attributed to AI. With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site). “In a lot of discussions right now, people take one side or the other, completely yes on data centers or completely no,” said You, director of the Cornell AI for Sustainability Initiative. “But there are benefits and costs, and the key issue in the end is how to balance the trade-offs.” Sharing the cost of power infrastructure The team analyzed data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers, as well as power-price records, rate filings from utilities, power-line plans, and federal household and job data. The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date. State incentives for data centers have provided returns on the investments, if inconsistently, the researchers found. Some states, such as California, reaped $180 in worker income for every dollar spent, while Virginia increased income $2 for every dollar invested. The researchers determined that the presence of an existing, qualified workforce was a stronger indicator of high returns than the amount of incentive spending. Data centers also increased wholesale electricity prices, the amounts utilities pay regional power markets before delivering the electricity to homes. In the most-affected hubs, data center growth raised those prices by nearly 10 percent or more by 2025. In Virginia, the costs jumped 15 percent and in California’s southern Bay Area, 20 percent. In contrast, residents in New York and New England, where data center construction has been limited, have not seen clear price increases due to data center expansion, the researchers found. “I think that means we’re at a good starting point in New York to think about the next steps,” You said. “Economic benefits, job benefits, investment, fairly allocating the costs – these are the dimensions and trade-offs we need to consider.” A key problem is how the costs of new infrastructure projects are currently shared: The allocation is often based on previous patterns of energy consumption. “It’s kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” You said. “Because if you’re going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there’s no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they’re not using energy. So with this model of relying on past consumption, households end up taking on much of the infrastructure costs.” Many more rural and lower-income residents saw proportionally higher bills; the share of rural families shouldering a high energy burden — spending more than 6% of their incomes on energy – rose 76% more than among urban residents. The authors cite a national survey finding that rural residents are also less likely to use AI tools like ChatGPT than urban residents. The impact on energy bills also has a wide geographical reach. For example, residents in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio help pay for grid upgrades linked to data center growth in Virginia, the researchers said. “You do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure,” You said. “The grid connects communities across states, and cost-sharing rules connect them financially.” Using insights from the data, You and Feng recommend changes to cost-sharing rules and strategies to lower burdens. In all four regions, they found that, if data centers cut back power use during 22 of the region’s peak demand hours each year, they would relieve strain on the grid and minimize the need to expand. artigo.texto: St. Charles may get a battery storage system meant to reduce energy costs as part of a pilot program with its electricity provider, even while the city’s future with the Illinois Municipal Electric Agency, or IMEA, remains uncertain. The city is looking to work with IMEA, which would pay for and manage the project, on the construction of a battery storage facility that St. Charles would take over management of in the event the city does not continue to get its energy from the electricity provider past 2035. Generally speaking, a battery energy storage system, or BESS, works by storing electrical energy in batteries so it can be used later, said St. Charles Director of Public Works Peter Suhr at a meeting of the St. Charles City Council’s Committee of the Whole on Nov. 16, at which a measure expressing the city’s support for participating in the pilot program was recommended for approval. Such a system can lower utility bills by storing electrical energy when the energy is least expensive, and then discharging that stored energy when prices are at their highest, Suhr said. It can also improve electricity reliability because a system can act as a backup generator during power outages. The measure recently recommended for approval by the Committee of the Whole is essentially a preliminary step to allow St. Charles to work with IMEA on the proposed battery storage project in the city. At this point, the city is looking for council approval for initial analysis work and participation in a request for proposals with IMEA for the project, Suhr said. The project is set to be formalized in a contract around March, Suhr said. St. Charles is one of 32 municipalities across Illinois that are part of IMEA, a nonprofit joint action agency that sells electric power to municipally-owned utilities, per its website. The city began purchasing partial electric power for its electric utility with IMEA in 1999, and entered into its current contract to get all of its electric power from them in 2004. The city is among those served by PJM Interconnection, the regional grid that includes northern Illinois, 12 other states and the District of Columbia. The downstate area is part of the Midwest Independent System Operator grid, or MISO, which also serves 14 other states from Mississippi to North Dakota as well as Manitoba in Canada. As part of a sustainability plan that details its goal of reducing the power supplied to its member municipalities to net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, IMEA has been looking at the feasibility of utility-scale behind-the-meter battery storage on its member distribution systems, according to its website, and it is now looking to pursue pilot projects for this technology. Several months ago, IMEA sent out requests for proposals to all 32 municipalities, with the goal of having one battery storage pilot in the PJM market, and another in the MISO market, Suhr said. According to Suhr, IMEA received responses from both Naperville and St. Charles, but St. Charles was ultimately selected for the planned pilot. The idea behind the pilot program is to allow city staff and IMEA to “dip (their) toes into this technology,” Suhr said. If successful, it could be scaled up in the future. Being part of the pilot would give the city hands-on experience with battery storage technology and help prepare its electric utility for future power supply decisions, a city memo indicated. The program anticipates systems in the range of 1 MW to 5 MW, with a capacity of about four hours’ worth of energy, or less than 1% of St. Charles’ total peak load, Suhr said. The proposed location of the battery storage system is at a substation between Kirk Road and the East Side Sports Complex. This proposal comes as St. Charles’ long-term relationship with IMEA remains uncertain. Last year, the City Council voted against extending its contract with the electricity provider after its current agreement expires in 2035, though returning to IMEA is not necessarily out of the question for good. Among the major concerns raised about the IMEA contract was the potential environmental impact of the city getting its electricity from the cooperative electric supplier. One of IMEA’s primary suppliers is a downstate coal plant called Prairie State that was one of the top 10 biggest polluters in the country, according to 2023 data from the United States Environmental Protection Agency. How nearby Naperville, another IMEA member, will procure its electricity post-2035 is similarly still playing out. Participating in the battery storage pilot with IMEA would not lead to any direct costs to St. Charles until at least 2035, because IMEA would be handling things like construction and maintenance, Suhr said. But, if the city opts not to continue working with IMEA, St. Charles would be responsible for costs associated with the battery storage system. A system like this is expected to cost the city around $100,000 to $200,000 annually, according to Suhr. The measure recommended for approval at the Nov. 16 Committee of the Whole meeting essentially allows the city to move forward with participating in the pilot program. The measure is expected to come to the City Council for final approval on Dec. 7, per the resolution. From there, IMEA would seek vendors for the project, Suhr said, and an official contract would be expected to come back to the City Council for approval around March. mmorrow@chicagotribune.com

artigo.texto: Duke Energy to build new battery storage system in Goldsboro, its largest in NC Duke Energy is building a new battery storage system in Wayne County — the largest of its kind on Duke's power grid — as North Carolina sees a surge in electricity demand. The utility company expects to spend up to $756 million to build the facility, which will be able to store up to 410 megawatts of backup electricity, the company announced on Nov. 18. It will also receive a 50% federal tax credit for "investing in an energy community with domestic content," according to Duke's announcement. Battery storage systems can store excess electricity that's generated from power plants, and release that electricity onto the grid at times of high demand. In recent years, battery storage has emerged as a way to make electric grids stronger and prevent blackouts when energy use spikes. North Carolina's demand is largely due to data centers, but also from population growth. Duke Energy has been planning to drastically scale up its battery storage capacity, building up to 6,500 megawatts of battery storage by 2035. This new plant is a first step toward that goal. With a capacity of 460 megawatts, it will more than double Duke's current battery storage capacity, which currently adds up to about 308 megawatts across 14 facilities in North Carolina. "We're building new resources to keep the Carolinas' economy thriving, while reinvesting in our existing power plant communities that have powered North Carolina and South Carolina for decades," said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a Nov. 18 news release. The plant will be built next to the H. F. Lee natural gas plant in Goldsboro, about 50 miles southeast of Raleigh, with construction happening in two phases, according to Duke's announcement. The first battery storage system, which will have capacity to store up to 260 megawatts of electricity, will come online in fall 2028. The second system, which will be able to store up to 150 megawatts of electricity, will come online by the end of 2028. Construction is expected to start early in 2027. Economic impact The new system is expected to generate an estimated $2 million in revenue for Wayne County, on top of the $5.8 million that Duke Energy already pays to the county in taxes for the existing H. F. Lee plant. It's also expected to create nine permanent full-time jobs linked to this facility and "other regional battery and solar resources," according to Duke's announcement. County leaders celebrated the investment last week, and Joe Daugherty, chair of the Wayne County board of commissioners, called it a "significant milestone." "This project will provide substantial long-term tax revenue while reinforcing Wayne County's role in meeting the growing energy needs of our state," Daugherty said. The announcement came after the N.C. Utilities Commission authorized Duke Energy to develop about 2,700 additional megawatts of new battery storage capacity as a part of its Carbon Plan, which outlines what type of energy Duke will invest in over the next several years. Along with increasing battery storage capacity, the Utilities Commission also approved heavy investments in gas, nuclear and solar energy as part of the Carbon Plan ruling. artigo.texto: Os carros estão cada vez mais parecidos com smartphones sobre rodas e precisam de conectividade para melhorar a experiência dos motoristas. É de olho nessa transformação que a TIM está ampliando sua presença na indústria automotiva. A operadora acaba de fechar uma parceria com a BYD para oferecer conectividade embarcada inicialmente a cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa nos próximos dois anos. O acordo também prevê a instalação de uma infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da BYD em Camaçari – a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina. A parceria faz parte da estratégia da operadora de ampliar sua atuação no mercado corporativo, através da unidade TIM B2B Solutions, oferecendo portfólio de soluções que vão desde a conectividade a serviços de tecnologia. Detalhe: a iniciativa ganha escala em um momento de expansão da BYD no mercado brasileiro. A montadora ultrapassou a marca de 300 mil veículos em circulação no País em 2026. “Hoje, a tecnologia é um dos principais motores de transformação da indústria automotiva e da mobilidade,” disse Alberto Griselli, CEO da TIM Brasil. Nos veículos da BYD, a tecnologia utilizada será o eSIM – uma espécie de chip digital que facilita a ativação remota de serviços. A solução da TIM permitirá interações com motoristas desenvolvidas pela montadora em seu próprio aplicativo e através das mídias no carro. Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil e head de marketing e comercial da BYD Auto, diz que a ideia é que a experiência digital do consumidor continue evoluindo ao longo da vida útil do automóvel. Segundo o executivo, a parceria com a TIM vai permitir à BYD ampliar a oferta de serviços e funcionalidades e garantir que a experiência de quem escolhe a marca continue evoluindo mesmo depois que o veículo sair da concessionária. “O consumidor brasileiro está cada vez mais exigente, e não basta oferecer um carro com tecnologia de ponta se essa experiência não continuar evoluindo ao longo do tempo,” disse Baldy. A outra frente da parceria está em Camaçari, onde a BYD inaugurou sua maior operação industrial fora da China. O complexo ocupa uma área de 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados, que será atendida pela infraestrutura de conectividade da TIM. O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais da fábrica. A cobertura dedicada foi planejada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e conectar não apenas os colaboradores e visitantes, mas também os sistemas operacionais e os próprios veículos ainda durante a fabricação. Com isso, diz o CEO da TIM, diferentes etapas da operação poderão trocar informações em tempo real, facilitando a integração dos processos industriais e abrindo espaço para novas aplicações digitais. A infraestrutura também foi dimensionada para acompanhar a expansão da capacidade produtiva da montadora, combinando conectividade e digitalização industrial. Para a TIM, o acordo com a BYD representa mais um avanço em um mercado que vem ganhando importância com a digitalização dos veículos e das operações industriais. A companhia já conecta mais de 670 mil veículos por meio de soluções da chamada Internet dos Veículos (Internet of Vehicles, ou IoV): uma tecnologia que permite integrar automóveis a redes e serviços digitais. “Esta parceria com a BYD une a digitalização de uma das mais importantes operações industriais em desenvolvimento no Brasil à evolução da conectividade embarcada dos veículos,” disse Griselli. Segundo Griselli, a operadora também oferece soluções de Internet das Coisas (IoT), computação em nuvem, cibersegurança e aplicações com inteligência artificial para apoiar a transformação digital de empresas de diferentes setores – que já são linhas de negócios relevantes dentro da companhia.

artigo.texto: Norway's transmission system operator Statnett paused new grid reservations for data centers on 9 November, the same day the government announced a licensing scheme that will keep out new crypto mining. The grid reservation halt will last until at least August 2027, when a new system is set to come into effect. Both moves come as data center demand threatens Norway's long-standing power surplus. A queue larger than the country's peak demand Data centers have asked for about 34 gigawatts (GW) of grid capacity in Norway, well above national peak demand of about 25 GW. Only 0.8 GW is connected today. Another 4.2 GW holds reserved capacity, 10.8 GW is in the queue, and 18 GW is still at the inquiry stage. Statnett has stopped granting new reservations and approving facility functionality under the Regulation on System Responsibility (fos) § 14 rule while it sets functional requirements for data centers. These will cover when facilities must stay connected during disturbances, how quickly their load may change and how to limit grid fluctuations. Projects with reserved capacity keep their place but still need approval before connecting, and existing connections are not affected. About half of the queue has asked for power by the end of 2028. With no new reservations until August 2027 at the earliest, and grid build-out still to follow, those dates look out of reach for established operators and newcomers alike. Norway is building faster than most of Europe Norway is not alone. Grid operators across Europe are replacing first-come, first-served queues with rules that favor projects able to show progress. Great Britain, Germany and Denmark have all tightened their connection rules since 2025. Satellite images show how far projects due in 2027-28 have to go. In the UK, almost two-thirds of the 2027-28 capacity has no building under way. In the Nordics, it is just over a third. In Norway, about half of the 1.5 GW due in 2027-28 shows new construction, but a single project accounts for most of it. Crypto is on its way out Norway has six operating crypto data centers with about 0.2 GW combined. Under the licensing scheme, new crypto sites will not be permitted, and existing ones cannot get more grid capacity and could face restrictions once transitional arrangements expire. Some operators are already converting to AI. Data center power use in the NO3 price area fell from late 2025 as one large site stopped mining ahead of its conversion, and is now rising again. Pressure on prices Hydro supplies about 90% of Norway's power, and decades of surplus have kept its electricity prices below those in most of Europe. That advantage is set to erode. Under normal hydrology, rising demand from data centers and other consumers could cut Norway's net exports by 71%, from 14.3 terawatt-hours in 2027 to 4.1 TWh in 2030. In a dry year, Norway could become a net importer and winter prices could reach about €290 per megawatt-hour.

artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network. In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago. “It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He said that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr said. In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.” “This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said. Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris. In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision. The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation. SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040. In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time. SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites. The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.” Among other companies planning data-processing satellite constellations are: - Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, which has proposed a 51,600-satellite constellation for its Project Sunrise initiative. - Redmond-based Starcloud, which has applied to the FCC to operate an 88,000-satellite data center constellation. - Cowboy Space, formerly known as Aetherflux, which has applied to deploy a 20,000-satellite constellation. The California-based company is leasing a 291,035-square-foot facility in Kent to serve as its launch vehicle and satellite design hub. “We will be building our rocket engines and solar [power] systems here too,” the company said. - Google, which is testing satellites for a data-processing constellation called Project Suncatcher. Last week, Google announced that its first Project Suncatcher satellites would be launched by Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, with liftoff planned for no earlier than 2029. - Sophia Space, a California startup with Seattle connections that is planning to create a 10-satellite constellation for high-performance orbital computing. Last week, Sophia Space announced that its orbital operating system was deployed on Kepler Communications’ optical data relay constellation.

artigo.texto: Compass Datacenters pushed back a $380 million asset-backed securities transaction it no longer expects to finish this year, planning to re-enter the ABS market in the coming year. A Nov. 17 cooling-system outage pushed temperatures above contract limits for 148 minutes, breaching the site's environmental service-level agreement. The deal had already slipped after a major investor walked, with price talk on an $85 million slice widening to 2.1 percentage points over the benchmark from about 1.95, and the tranche flagged as potentially smaller or removed before the full offering was delayed. What happened Compass Datacenters put a $380 million ABS sale on hold and now expects to revisit the market next year. The move followed an operational disruption at one facility and investor departures from the offering, which the company addressed on a Wednesday call with investors. The Nov. 17 incident involved a cooling outage that sent temperatures beyond contractual thresholds for 148 minutes, constituting a violation of the facility's environmental SLA. Inside the outage On the call, Compass said a third-party team performing maintenance shut down a cooling unit even though the maximum number of other units already offline had been reached. The company attributed the event to human error and insufficient oversight of third-party personnel rather than equipment or design flaws. Management told investors a senior Compass engineer should have supervised the partner firm's team and stopped the extra unit from being taken offline. The tenant at the affected site was said to be satisfied with Compass's response and handling of the outside technicians. Price talk on an $85 million tranche widened to 2.1 percentage points over the benchmark rate from about 1.95, and investors were later told that the slice could be reduced or removed before Compass ultimately delayed the entire deal. The ABS is backed by six data centers totaling 216 megawatts of capacity, each under its own 15-year lease to a AAA rated tenant. Who said what Guggenheim Securities' spokesperson - the lead bookrunner and structuring adviser - declined to comment. A Compass representative also declined to comment. Compass is owned by Brookfield Infrastructure Partners and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan. The bottom line: a temporary pullback from the ABS market, a contained operational issue chalked up to process and oversight, and collateral tied to long-dated leases with a AAA tenant. artigo.texto: ReData deve ser regulamentado nos próximos dias, diz ministro Frederico de Siqueira Filho prevê políticas de data centers e cabos submarinos para 2027 e defende ampliar o papel do MCom na infraestrutura digital. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou nesta quarta-feira, 25, que a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (ReData) está na fase final de discussão dentro do governo federal e que a expectativa é de que o processo seja resolvido nos próximos dias. Já as políticas nacionais de data centers e de cabos submarinos deverão ficar para 2027. Em entrevista à imprensa durante o Fórum Dig.IA, em Brasília (DF), o ministro disse que as discussões sobre o ReData envolvem a Casa Civil e a Presidência da República. “Mas a gente acredita que nos próximos dias isso será resolvido, perante a importância do tema”, afirmou Siqueira Filho. Durante seu discurso no encerramento do evento, o ministro destacou a participação do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nas articulações para viabilizar os incentivos ao setor de data centers. Segundo ele, o Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) também trabalhou na elaboração do regime em conjunto com a Receita Federal, o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). O objetivo do governo, segundo Siqueira Filho, é transformar o Brasil em um polo de infraestrutura de data centers voltados à inteligência artificial (IA) na América Latina, aproveitando as condições da matriz energética brasileira. Políticas nacionais ficam para 2027 Questionado sobre a possibilidade de publicação das políticas nacionais de data centers e de cabos submarinos ainda em 2026, o ministro descartou a perspectiva. “Não, acredito que não. Isso vai ficar para 2027”, respondeu. Segundo Siqueira Filho, a política nacional de data centers será complementar ao ReData. Entre as medidas em discussão estão a redução da burocracia e a articulação com estados e municípios para simplificar os processos de licenciamento dos empreendimentos. “Balcão único de licenciamento, é isso que a gente está propondo para dar mais visibilidade e segurança jurídica para quem decide investir no Brasil”, afirmou. No caso dos cabos submarinos, o governo trabalha na descentralização das zonas de ancoragem ao longo da costa brasileira, na atualização das cartas náuticas em articulação com a Marinha e na proteção das áreas de chegada dos cabos, considerando seu caráter de infraestrutura crítica. A proposta envolve a participação de órgãos responsáveis pela defesa e pela segurança nacional. O ministro também destacou a necessidade de compatibilizar a presença dos cabos submarinos com as atividades de exploração de petróleo na costa brasileira. Ainda não há definição sobre a necessidade de alterações legislativas para implementar a política. “A gente primeiro está definindo o conceito”, explicou o ministro, acrescentando que o objetivo é reduzir a burocracia e dar agilidade e previsibilidade aos investidores. Infraestrutura digital no próximo governo Lula Siqueira Filho também defendeu que o Ministério das Comunicações amplie sua atuação na agenda de infraestrutura digital durante o próximo mandato do presidente Lula. Na avaliação do ministro, a expansão da inteligência artificial exige investimentos em redes resilientes, tecnologias de comunicação por satélite, cabos submarinos e ampliação da cobertura 5G. “O tema digital está no centro da discussão do governo”, declarou. Segundo o ministro, tratar essas atividades sob a perspectiva da infraestrutura digital contribuirá tanto para o fortalecimento do setor produtivo quanto para o do próprio Ministério das Comunicações. MCom vai ouvir provedores sobre Norma 4 Outro tema abordado pelo ministro foi a discussão sobre a Norma 4. Siqueira Filho afirmou que ainda não tratou pessoalmente do assunto e que pretende conversar com a Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) antes de estabelecer uma posição. O ministro também afirmou que pretende ouvir os provedores de internet e as demais empresas do setor para compreender os impactos da discussão. Funttel destina R$ 150 milhões à inteligência artificial Durante o evento, o Ministério das Comunicações informou a destinação de R$ 150 milhões do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) a projetos relacionados à inteligência artificial e à infraestrutura digital. Desse montante, R$ 46 milhões são destinados ao desenvolvimento de uma plataforma nacional de inteligência artificial que deverá integrar data centers regionais e ampliar a capacidade computacional no interior do país. Outros R$ 104 milhões são destinados a projetos executados em parceria com o CPQD, no triênio de 2026 a 2028. As iniciativas incluem pesquisas sobre redes 6G, ferramentas de inteligência artificial generativa para operadoras de telecomunicações, soluções de segurança e privacidade digital e aplicações de telemedicina. O ministro afirmou ainda que o Brasil atingiu a marca de 1 gigawatt (GW) de energia elétrica contratada para data centers e ocupa a 12ª posição entre os maiores mercados mundiais do segmento. Siqueira Filho também destacou a ampliação das possibilidades de aplicação dos recursos do Fundo de Universalização dos Serviços de Telecomunicações (Fust), incluindo investimentos em data centers e na modernização das redes de telecomunicações. Segundo ele, mais de R$ 300 milhões foram investidos na recuperação das redes de fibra óptica no Rio Grande do Sul. O ministro citou ainda o lançamento, nesta quarta-feira, do Conecta CRAS, iniciativa de conectividade dos Centros de Referência de Assistência Social com recursos do Fust, que se soma às políticas de atendimento a escolas públicas e unidades básicas de saúde.

artigo.texto: According to a MoP proposal, battery storage could be required for rooftop solar systems above 10 kW The proposed requirement is at least 20% of the system's daily energy generation, unless a different proportion is specified The storage provision is expected to take effect from April 1, 2028, under the draft India's Ministry of Power (MoP) has proposed requiring battery energy storage systems (BESS) for rooftop solar installations above 10 kW, with effect from April 1, 2028. The proposal is part of the draft Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2026. It proposes that the storage provision will take effect where State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) have not specified a different capacity threshold. The proposal gives state regulators flexibility to determine the threshold and storage requirements based on local conditions. As per the draft, SERC may prescribe the capacity threshold above which prosumers must install energy storage. The required storage capacity would be at least 20% of the renewable energy system's total daily generation, unless the respective Commission specifies a different proportion. In the absence of a threshold set by a State Commission, the proposed requirement would apply to renewable energy systems with an installed capacity exceeding 10 kW. The ministry said falling battery storage costs, supported by economies of scale, technological innovation and market competition, have improved the economic viability of storage deployment. Integrating batteries with rooftop solar could also help shift surplus electricity to evening hours, support grid stability and ease operational pressure on distribution companies. Additionally, the draft also proposes allowing consumers, including commercial and industrial (C&I) units and MSMEs, to install rooftop solar capacity beyond their sanctioned load. This will be subject to limits set by State Commissions based on local grid capacity and technical requirements. However, consumers would be allowed to feed electricity into the grid only up to their sanctioned load, unless the distribution company approves a higher limit. Power injected beyond the approved limit would not qualify for compensation and could attract penalties. The draft also proposes delaying the rollout of Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs to align it with smart meter installation. Under the proposal, ToD tariffs would apply to consumers with a load of 10 kW and above from April 1, 2028, and to other non-agricultural consumers from April 1, 2029. This will give state regulators the flexibility to decide solar and peak hours based on electricity demand and generation patterns in their respective states, instead of following fixed timings. Earlier, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) proposed making co-located energy storage mandatory for new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned after July 1, 2027 (see India May Mandate Storage For Solar, Wind Projects From 2027).

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are scaling rapidly as power systems integrate more wind and solar. But in markets that moved first, revenue per unit of capacity is falling, ancillary-service markets are saturating, and yesterday’s battery investment assumptions may no longer support tomorrow’s returns. Around 108 GW of battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than the previous year. The investment question is shifting from “Should we invest in battery storage?” to “Which batteries can continue to create value as the market matures?” Our Point of View examines what separates resilient BESS investments from assets at risk of becoming financially stranded. BESS economics are no longer determined by the battery alone. Grid access, market design, contract tenor, operating capability, cybersecurity, data rights and power-conversion-system requirements increasingly determine which assets outperform. Investors and asset owners need to assess these factors across the full asset lifecycle, from the investment decision and commissioning through operations, optimisation and refinancing. The point of view explores: Why BESS market saturation is real but uneven across geographies Which assumptions can make or break a battery storage business case How to identify the risk of a financially stranded battery How market design, operations and contracts change returns How data and AI can turn operational performance into margin Five lifecycle levers investors and asset owners should test The next phase of the BESS market will not be won by batteries alone. It will be won by assets designed, contracted and operated to adapt as markets change. Arthur Arrighi de Casanova Head of Sustainable Futures, Capgemini Invent France Arthur has over 10 years of experience leading exclusively sustainability and energy transition engagements, supporting clients in the development of related strategies. At Capgemini Invent, in recent years, Arthur has applied his expertise to the creation of climate and growth strategies, renewables development, green power sourcing, market analysis, transformational roadmaps, business due diligence, new business model design, and go-to-market support. FAQs What is a battery energy storage system (BESS)? A battery energy storage system stores electricity for later use. Utility-scale BESS assets can earn revenue through energy arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity markets and contracted flexibility, depending on local market rules. Why are BESS revenues coming under pressure? BESS revenues can decline when battery capacity grows faster than the balancing and trading opportunities available. Ancillary-service markets saturate first because system operators procure a limited volume. As more batteries compete, value shifts towards energy trading, optimization and other revenue pools. What is a financially stranded battery? A financially stranded battery is an asset that continues to operate and support the grid but no longer earns the return assumed when capital was committed. It may cover operating costs without paying back its full capital cost. What is the BESS mortality test? The BESS mortality test is a five-question stress test for battery storage investment cases. artigo.texto: Two forces are behind falling energy storage costs, which is a boon for the clean energy industry. The market features growing competition among battery manufacturers and a possible lithium surplus in 2027. Here's what to know As SolarQuarter detailed, InfoLink's Energy Storage Supply Chain Price Forecast Report projects a slight lithium surplus in 2027. Battery-grade lithium carbonate prices could fall to about 99,800–117,900 Chinese yuan ($14,945-$17,656) per U.S. ton in the first half of that year. The forecast comes after declines in storage-cell prices. In July 2026, the tax-inclusive average prices for both 280 amp-hour and 314 amp-hour lithium iron phosphate storage cells dropped 4% to 0.36 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to the outlet. Smaller, 100 amp-hour cells averaged 0.44 yuan per watt-hour, down 2.7% from June 2026. For households facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity rates, whole-home batteries can keep essentials running during outages, while leases can help protect homes without upwards of $20,000 in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace connecting battery shoppers with trusted partners offering unique prices and exclusive deals — another avenue for homeowners exploring backup power as storage-cell costs decline. More background The cost of lithium iron phosphate cathode material used in storage applications declined to approximately 47,800 yuan ($7,158) per U.S. ton, bringing tax-inclusive storage-cell production costs to around 0.31 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to SolarQuarter. These declines can translate to savings down the road for consumers looking to tap into their storage systems. Home batteries can also help reduce energy bills by supplying stored electricity during expensive peak-pricing periods. For households seeking a smaller-scale option, Pila offers plug-and-play battery backup at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. What's being done? Intense competition among battery manufacturers as supply expands is putting additional pressure on storage-cell prices, according to SolarQuarter. Lithium carbonate prices could still rise before the projected surplus in 2027. InfoLink's September and October 2026 price forecast is about 131,500–136,100 yuan ($19,692-20,381) per U.S. ton, above the expected August 2026 average near 127,000 yuan ($19,018) per U.S. ton. The firm expects seasonal demand and restocking to support that increase. According to SolarQuarter, China will begin taxing lithium-ion battery consumption at 2% on September 1, 2026, with the rate rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Meanwhile, the estimated U.S. tariff rate for lithium-ion battery systems originating in China is around 40.9%. China's July 2026 average free-on-board export prices were $50.30 per kilowatt-hour for 280 amp-hour cells, $51 for 306 amp-hour cells, and $50 for 314 amp-hour cells, per the outlet. For shoppers exploring their options, EasyHome works like Groupon for home energy, negotiating special offers for its large audience and providing unique battery deals. It also offers special solar deals. Pairing solar with a battery can increase savings and provide backup power during outages, giving homeowners another way to put energy storage to work. artigo.texto: New solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing new demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The company also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies. From the source grid to the cabinet: an integrated AIDC power architecture During the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management. Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the company describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE. The solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle. The system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life. Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE says the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years. Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications. The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications. Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds. According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less. Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly launched AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the company's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration. The integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when issues arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock. artigo.texto: Data center proposal in Northern New York met with pushback CHAZY, N.Y. (WCAX) - A proposed data center in New York’s North Country is facing resistance from the community. On the shores of Lake Champlain, Chazy is home to large apple orchards and poultry farms. It’s also home to the NorthStar Technology Center. The owners of NorthStar say they are exploring the possibility of building a data center there. While we don’t know much about the project, we do know it would meet state requirements and fall below the threshold of the state’s moratorium, which is 50 megawatts. Despite this, residents in the town say they have concerns and questions about the proposal. “My immediate thoughts were, well, it’s time for action,” said Nelson Pelton of Chazy. Pelton said the prospect of a data center in a place he’s called home for three decades worries him. “Really value things like water for our agriculture, preserving the environment for the amazing habitats we have around here and also keeping our energy bills low for people that are already dealing with already high costs; that’s a big concern to me,” Pelton said. The Rockefeller Institute said New York has around 150 data centers. Molly Ryan, the executive director of the Clinton County Industrial Development Agency, said data centers can bring short-term job creation and potentially lower taxes. “Usually data centers are a couple hundred million dollar investment and therefore property taxes usually end up significantly going down,” Ryan said. But she said data centers also have drawbacks, many of which are top of mind for residents in Chazy. “Concerned about noise pollution, water usage and groundwater contamination, along with energy rates,” said Alex Sweet of Chazy. The owners of the NorthStar Technology Center did not reply to a request for comment. However, WCAX News did obtain a mockup presented to the Chazy Town Board, which shows the preliminary placement of the data center at the existing facility. Neither the town nor the county said they are weighing in just yet. “We believe in local control and every community has to decide what’s right for them and they should be establishing what works in their community,” Ryan said. Town officials have scheduled a public meeting on the proposed data center on Dec. 7. It will be held at the Chazy Central School auditorium at 6 p.m. Copyright 2026 WCAX. All rights reserved.
