artigo.texto: US Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-NC, has introduced bipartisan legislation to prevent Chinese telecommunications companies previously identified as national security threats from accessing American data centers and cloud services. The Digital Infrastructure Security Act of 2026, House Bill 11100, introduced by Harrigan and US Rep. Dave Min, D-CA, seeks to extend existing federal telecommunications restrictions to digital infrastructure that handles sensitive American financial, medical, and military information. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) previously revoked or denied telecommunications licenses for China Telecom Americas, China Unicom Americas, and China Mobile USA over national security concerns. However, those actions did not automatically remove the companies’ equipment and connections from American data centers. According to Harrigan’s office, investigations identified more than 108,000 instances of Chinese-linked networks redirecting internet traffic between 2018 and 2025, raising concerns about foreign interference and the potential exposure of sensitive information. “China has spent years stealing American technology and targeting our communications networks, and we know they’re not going to stop,” Harrigan said in a press release announcing the legislation. Harrigan said the legislation would address gaps in existing federal restrictions by prohibiting the companies from operating domestic data centers or conducting business with Americans through cloud services, including through subsidiaries and other intermediaries. “What concerns me is that we’ve already identified these companies as national security threats, revoked their licenses, and somehow still allowed them to keep a foothold in our data centers,” he said. “When we’re talking about the systems that handle Americans’ financial information, medical records, and sensitive military data, I think that’s a pretty reasonable safeguard.” Under the legislation, the FCC would enforce the restrictions, with fines of up to $1 million per violation or per day for continuing violations. Existing operations and contracts would have 180 days following enactment to comply. It would also establish a waiver process subject to a federal national security assessment. The legislation comes as North Carolina grapples with the rapid expansion of data centers and their impact on electricity demand, water resources, and local infrastructure. More than 30 local governments across the state have enacted temporary moratoriums on data center development, while state lawmakers repealed the sales tax exemption for electricity consumed by data centers earlier this year. Broader legislation, Senate Bill 730, the Ratepayer Protection Act, remains stalled in the Senate and would establish additional ratepayer protections, water-use standards, and restrictions on data center ownership by entities tied to foreign adversaries, including China. Harrigan criticizes Nvidia CEO’s reinstatement The legislation coincides with heightened scrutiny in Washington over the relationship between American technology companies and China, including Monday’s reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected by US officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia’s board of directors unanimously voted to reinstate Huang on Nov. 23 following discussions with Huang and input from senior federal government officials. The company said its board was confident that his reinstatement posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump supported Huang’s reinstatement, while several congressional Republicans, including Harrigan, criticized the decision on X. “For the past two years, I have privately said there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised,” Harrigan wrote in a post on X. “Turns out, well, we all know.” Harrigan argued that Huang’s reinstatement was premature and called for further congressional investigation into the potential national security implications. “His reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake,” he continued. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the company and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.” Harrigan called for investigations by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees. “Today, we sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law,” he said. “That is a dangerous precedent to set, and one I believe will come at a significant cost to our country in the long run.” Harrigan’s Digital Infrastructure Security Act was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on Nov. 19.

artigo.texto: Residents in Sutton and neighboring Central Massachusetts communities worry that the giant data center proposed by the Kraft Group would inflate their energy bills. In reality, it could also raise costs for customers across New England. The computer facility, which would support power-intensive artificial intelligence services across a 10-building campus, likely would require hundreds of millions of dollars in upgrades to electricity infrastructure, according to energy specialists. Those kinds of costs have often been passed on broadly to customers in this region and in other states. Many of Sutton’s 9,700 residents are already up in arms about the magnitude of the proposed $16 billion project by the Kraft family, owners of the New England Patriots. A January town meeting is scheduled at which residents may vote to ban data centers, and stall or kill the Krafts’ massive project. According to the proposal, when fully built, the campus would use as much as 900 megawatts of electricity — comparable to what a medium-sized city requires — and would be among the largest such facilities in the country. “The scale of that certainly made my eyes go wide,” said Dan Dolan, president of the New England Power Generators Association. Dolan, whose group represents power plant owners and energy developers, knows how hard it is to get even smaller projects up and running. Developers usually spend months, if not years, prospecting for sites that check all the regulatory boxes. Then they have to go through rigorous studies by energy agencies to determine how a site could get hooked up to the grid and at what cost. “You put all of those elements together” for the Kraft plan, “and this would be a Herculean task,” Dolan said. As Sutton weighs the Kraft project, efforts are already underway locally and across the country to make data centers pay their own way — part of a campaign to block or slow development of the warehouse-sized campuses that have sparked outrage over their impact on electricity bills as well as air, noise, and water pollution. Governor Maura Healey issued an executive order in September requiring data centers to fund the full cost of energy infrastructure upgrades and provide new clean energy to the grid. The order also imposes a fine if developers can’t meet clean energy requirements. And New England’s grid manager, ISO New England, has just proposed a regulation, currently under review by a federal agency, to make large customers like data centers pay for their own upgrades. In Massachusetts, where electricity rates are already among the highest in the nation, the ISO New England proposal, along with the governor’s order, could potentially prevent rates from going even higher as more data centers are built to support growing AI usage, industry experts say. “The standard business model of the industry is to socialize costs of new infrastructure,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard University’s Law School. There’s now progress in putting pressure on the developers to shoulder the costs, he said. But he warns ratepayers may still end up with higher bills. In the proposal presented at a Select Board meeting this month, Town Manager Austin Cyganiewicz emphasized that the full cost of energy supply, infrastructure, and interconnection should be borne by the project developer. “Massachusetts energy consumers, communities, and residents should not bear the costs or burdens of data center development, operations, or energy and water needs,” he said. Robert Kraft’s companies, the Kraft Group and Unified Global Packaging Group, own a 383-acre parcel in an industrial area of the town, sitting directly under a major transmission line. The Kraft Group has long tried to find a tenant to occupy the largest lot on the property, but to no avail. In late October, executives at the companies approached Sutton’s town manager with a proposal to build a data center campus on the site. The proposal made public by Sutton officials does not disclose details on how the Kraft Group plans to power the data center or handle its costs. The proposal said that the developers was in discussions with ISO New England and the local utility company, National Grid. An ISO spokesperson told the Globe that while “a conversation took place” with the Kraft Group, the organization has not received any formal proposal or launched any studies. A National Grid spokesperson said the utility company discussed the project with the Kraft Group, and has begun studying the site. The study will cover energy demand, available grid capacity, and any potential required infrastructure upgrades. The spokesperson added that the customer, in this case the Krafts, covers the cost of such studies. The Kraft Group did not respond to a request for comment. Given the experience of other communities where electric rates have jumped with the arrival of data centers, it’s no surprise Sutton officials and residents were quick to question who would pay for the upgrades needed for the Kraft project, with many voicing staunch opposition in public meetings. And infrastructure upgrades are not the only way consumers could see bills spike. Data centers also can drive up costs for all customers at peak demand times, such as summer heat waves. “When demand goes up, as it’s going to go up for electricity . . . then prices go up, and we all pay those higher market prices,” said Peskoe, of Harvard’s Electricity Law Initiative. The following month, a state utilities organization created a tariff that requires data centers to pay for most of their own electric capacity. Essas antigas instalações têm tudo o que um data center precisa: espaço de sobra, boas vias de acesso e, o mais importante, uma conexão garantida à rede de transmissão de energia elétrica. artigo.texto: Administration Gives SpaceX OK to Launch 1M Data Centers The Trump administration gave SpaceX the green light on Wednesday to turn orbit into an AI server farm, the Wall Street Journal reports. The FCC authorized the company to deploy up to 1 million "Starmind" satellites—AI-focused orbital data centers that CEO Elon Musk says will tap solar power to cut computing costs and sidestep local fights over land- and energy-hungry installations on Earth. The decision "opens a bold new frontier," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement, per the AP. But it's a high-stakes bet on hardware that doesn't yet exist at scale. And there's already organized opposition to putting data centers in space. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy," saying on Wednesday, "It's not going to happen." He cited difficulties and risks that include in-orbit collisions that could affect other essential satellites and add to the accumulation of space junk. SpaceX must lean on its Starship rocket to build out the constellation through 2040, over objections from Amazon, Viasat, and astronomers worried about light pollution, per the Journal. artigo.texto: Goleta has begun taking steps toward banning data centers in the Good Land. In a 4-1 vote, the Goleta Planning Commission on Monday moved forward an ordinance that would permanently prohibit data centers in the city. The ordinance will now head to the City Council for review. The city currently doesn’t have regulations on data centers, according to Anne Wells, the city’s advance planning manager. Goleta has not permitted any data centers or received applications, supervising planner Andy Newkirk said. He said that while most people think of data centers as large-scale facilities, they can be the size of a “normal office building,” and it’s “certainly possible” that the city could receive a proposal. The drafted permanent ordinance is a way for Goleta to get ahead “of a potential issue” and “not get caught off-guard,” Newkirk said. While the ordinance would be permanent, the city could revisit the details of the prohibition in the future. “I do think it is a good idea to have an ordinance and to get ahead of it,” Commissioner Jennifer Fullerton said. City staff highlighted water, electricity, noise and air pollution as potential data center impacts. “We are very aware that in other jurisdictions around the country, this is becoming a really big issue, and we know that in other areas of regulation we have been caught unprepared,” said Peter Imhof, planning and environmental review director. Commissioner Rita Serotkin had similar sentiments. She referred to Goodland Guns’ relocation next to a preschool and daycare facility as sneaking “around behind.” Goleta’s proposed ordinance defines a data center as a facility that houses a group of networked computer systems used for data storage and processing, to be used for the storage, processing and/or distribution of data. The facilities may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, backup batteries, fire suppression systems, enhanced security features and other associated utility infrastructure to support operations, according to city staff. Goleta’s proposed ordinance also includes a lengthy description of what is not considered a data center. A data center is not, according to the staff report: an enclosed room, suite or other accessory space containing computer servers, data storage and processing equipment, network switching equipment, telecommunications equipment, and related supporting equipment, including cooling, electrical, backup power and security systems, that are used to support and facilitate an allowed on-site principal use that takes up no more than 20% of the floor area of the principal use. The 20% allowance considers businesses that may need data center-like facilities on site, according to the city staff report. However, that 20% allowance brought some concerns Monday night. It was later swapped in favor of an exemption that would allow for data center-like facilities that use less than 3 megawatts of energy. Some commissioners had worried about how it would affect local technology companies. “My only concern is the 20% and not having reached out to the tech companies,” Fullerton said. Commissioner Cary Penniman, who voted against the recommendation Monday night but supports preventing “hyperscale data centers” in Goleta, had similar concerns. He worried about how it would impact small startups coming out of UC Santa Barbara. “I don’t think we want to prevent that from happening,” he said. “There are some unintended consequences.” He advocated that city staff develop a tighter definition of a data center. He posted a question to staff that a public commenter had asked earlier in the night: “What are we exactly trying to prevent?” Others were concerned about the energy use from the allowance. “The primary concern for me is sort of the energy and water usage, and so that’s where I feel like the restriction should be,” Commissioner Katie Maynard said. She asked staff why they decided to go with the floor area instead of “focusing on things that are most (concerning) for data centers such as energy or water.” She advocated for the allowance to be 3 megawatts or less. Newkirk said the decision was made to provide some flexibility. “Thinking (of) it as a proxy, it would be fairly consistent over time, where I think the energy demands may be really a standard today might not make much sense tomorrow,” he said. Wells also told the commissioners that city staff looked at other jurisdictions and floor area is a typical measure. Cherie Cabral spoke Monday on behalf of the California Construction Labor Management Trust and urged the Planning Commission against supporting a “blanket ban.” She also encouraged the commission to look at possible advantages that data centers could bring to the city and other cities’ regulations. “It’s entirely doable to create regulations that would address most of the issues, and in fact, many of the issues that are under discussion at the moment are generated out of social media as opposed to something that comes out of studies,” she said. Commissioner Anne Miller acknowledged the commissioner’s concerns about local impact, but insisted that the timing of establishing an ordinance was important. “I think it’s important to get on top of this now before something really disastrous happens in the meantime,” she said. “It’s moving so quickly, and it’s scary, I think.” Monday night’s discussion comes about a month after the Earl Warren Fairgrounds’ CEO put an end to speculation that the fairgrounds were considering a data center.

artigo.texto: Wayne County issued a stop-work order on November 20, 2026, to Panattoni Development Co. for construction at Google’s planned data center in Van Buren Township, Michigan. The county cited concerns about impacts to county drains, flood risk, permits, stormwater and erosion controls. Why Wayne County stopped construction County officials said construction was affecting multiple county drains at the site, including work in drain easements and obstructions in the channels. The county also cited work in a county road right-of-way without a permit, stormwater-ordinance violations, and missing erosion and sediment controls. Panattoni’s response and the reported steps to resume Panattoni Development Co. was the recipient of the order and the project’s developer for Google, its intended operator. Panattoni Data Centers said it had temporarily paused work and was coordinating with county officials to review the issues, provide clarification and determine next steps. Reports described a county construction permit and agreements with the county drain commissioner or local drainage districts concerning stormwater runoff as prerequisites to resuming construction. They also described erosion-control measures, including silt dams to keep soil runoff out of the drain system, as part of the steps tied to resumption. The reported path back to construction runs through county permitting, drainage agreements and erosion controls. Wayne County communications director Matt Allen said in remarks published November 24 that he did not know how long the permitting process would take.

artigo.texto: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands (PROPUBLICA) - A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies. “Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them. Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth. ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules. Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers. Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land. “These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives. “I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress. Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority. “These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.” Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities. Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes. The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued. Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate. Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.” The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land. artigo.texto: Korean researchers have developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates reliably at room temperature under low pressure. The technology could ease the high-pressure requirements that are one of the barriers to commercializing all-solid-state batteries and could be used to reduce their weight and size. A team led by Park Su-jin, a chemistry professor at Pohang University of Science and Technology POSTECH, said on the 26th that it had developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates at room temperature under pressure of 0.3 megapascals (MPa) or less. The team worked with researchers at Chung-Ang University, Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States. The findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications on the 7th, local time. All-solid-state batteries are attracting attention as a next-generation technology that can reduce fire risks by using a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. Using lithium metal in the anode can increase energy density, but the lithium expands during charging, creating gaps between the electrode and the electrolyte. In this process, branchlike growths called lithium dendrites can penetrate the electrolyte and cause an internal short circuit. High pressure has been applied to batteries to prevent this, but the equipment needed adds weight and bulk. The researchers addressed the problem by preventing cracks in the solid electrolyte and distributing the pressure caused by lithium expansion. They added thioctic acid (TA) to a sulfide-based solid electrolyte to form a polymer network, suppressing cracks in the electrolyte and the penetration of lithium dendrites. They also applied a porous carbon material with many tiny holes to the anode current collector to provide space for lithium to accumulate. The design distributes the force generated by lithium expansion during charging within the current collector, reducing the strain on the electrolyte. The researchers used the Pohang Light Source to observe the inside of the battery in 3D during charging and discharging. They found that stress from expansion was relieved as lithium filled and left the pores of the current collector. A battery using the technology operated reliably at room temperature and under pressure of 0.3 MPa or less, even in a full cell using a ternary cathode material (NCM811) for electric vehicles. The researchers said it was the first time in the world that such low-pressure operation had been achieved in a sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium-metal full cell with an areal capacity of 2.4 mAh/㎠. "We addressed both the limitations of the brittle sulfide-based solid electrolyte with a polymer network and the stress caused by lithium expansion with a porous current collector," Park said. "This result came from close collaboration with Korean researchers." References Nature Communications(2026), DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-79393-w

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump told reporters at a White House news conference on Friday, November 20, 2026, that U.S. companies building artificial-intelligence data centers in other countries would face a “tremendous tax.” The Trump overseas data center tax threat landed on the largest American cloud providers with almost no detail attached. Yahoo Finance ran several stories on the remarks and reported no tax rate, no start date and no legal mechanism. The wording was blunt. According to NBC News, Trump said, “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country.” Yahoo’s coverage recorded the follow-up: “They can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.” Those two sentences are the entire policy, as of today. Six days later, the idea still sits in threat territory rather than law. For governments courting hyperscale capital, that ambiguity is its own problem, as our earlier story on Australia’s $115 billion AI data centre bet and the Trump tax threat showed. This analysis separates what the record confirms from what remains guesswork, then walks through who is exposed, how a tax could work, and what cloud buyers should do while they wait. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Trump Said About Data Centers Abroad on November 20 The remarks came during a White House press briefing, in the middle of a broader discussion about U.S. artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Trump framed overseas construction as something his administration would not simply permit. He then softened the point in the same breath, saying companies could still go ahead, but at a price. That pairing of a prohibition and a toll is typical of how he floats trade measures, and it leaves room to land almost anywhere between a symbolic levy and a hard restriction. NBC News said the president went on to describe substantial penalties for companies that try to build abroad. Yahoo News and AP-syndicated Yahoo coverage described the statement as an open-ended threat. Yahoo’s reporting also said Trump argued that overseas construction could end up benefiting China, a point we return to below. None of the outlets we reviewed found a document, draft bill or executive order behind the remarks. That matters because the phrase “data centers abroad” covers a huge range of activity. A hyperscaler can own a facility outright, lease capacity from a local colocation operator, sign a power deal for a campus it never builds itself, or rent capacity inside a partner’s cloud region. Trump’s comments did not say which of those would trigger a tax. They also did not say whether a facility already under construction counts. What the Reports Confirm and What They Leave Open Readers are seeing a lot of confident takes on this story, so a clean ledger helps. The table below lists what the named outlets support and what they do not. Anything marked unconfirmed has no supporting statement in the coverage we reviewed. Two lessons come out of that ledger. First, every operational question, from rate to enforcement, is still open. Second, anyone quoting a percentage or a start date is guessing. Our fact base holds no number of that kind, and neither do the Yahoo Finance and AP-syndicated reports we reviewed. Which Companies Face Exposure From the Overseas Tax Reports name five U.S. companies with international data-center operations that a tax like this could touch: Amazon.com, Inc., Alphabet Inc., Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms, Inc. and Oracle Corp. The White House has not published its own list, so the grouping reflects journalists’ reading of who has the largest overseas footprint, not an official target list. Amazon and Alphabet Headlines framed the story around Amazon and Google, and Yahoo Finance’s own headline named Amazon, Google and Microsoft. One caution applies. It remains unconfirmed whether Google or Amazon as consumer brands would be the taxpayers, as opposed to the legally registered corporate entities that actually own and operate the facilities. Corporate structure decides who writes the check, and large cloud groups hold their foreign assets through layered subsidiaries. Microsoft, Meta and Oracle Microsoft has been the most visible voice so far, thanks to President Brad Smith’s television comments covered below. Meta and Oracle also appear in the reports as firms with international data-center operations. The coverage we reviewed does not quantify the hit to any single company. Why Hyperscalers Build Data Centers Outside the United States Cloud companies do not go abroad for sport. Latency pushes capacity toward users, because a video call or a trading application runs better when servers sit close by. Data-residency laws push the same way, since many governments require certain records to stay inside national borders. Customers in regulated sectors, such as banking and health care, often refuse to buy from a region they cannot place on a map. Power is the third driver, and it is getting more important. AI training and inference clusters draw enormous electricity, and grid connections in some U.S. markets now take years. Developers therefore look wherever the electrons and the land are available. Our coverage of Goldman’s 52 GW forecast for U.S. data centers in 2028 shows how hard domestic power demand is already climbing, which gives companies an extra reason to look abroad for capacity. Seen through that lens, a tax on foreign sites would not just add a cost line. It would squeeze three strategies at once: serving local customers, meeting local data law and finding spare grid capacity. A company could absorb the levy, shift the build back home, or hand the foreign build to a partner. Each answer carries its own price, and none of them is free. Two L&T verticals – the Renewables business and L&T Electronic Products and Systems (LTEPS) - have jointly won an order to develop a 300 MW / 900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at Khavda in Gujarat. The advanced BESS solution will incorporate liquid-cooling technology to deliver higher power density, enhanced safety and a longer operating life. artigo.texto: Data center emissions are worse than we knew, Harvard study confirms This past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers, voting to restrict new projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create. Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher. You May Also Like The study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries. Researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average. The best tech deal this week Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission. Certain U.S. states are worse off than others in terms of climate pollution from data centers, according to Harvard researchers. For example, Virginia has the most data centers, and fossil fuel-burning power plants are most common there. Other states, such as Oregon, have green-friendly, eclectic grids, so data centers residing there are likely emitting less pollution. Data centers have become a controversial topic across the U.S. Thanks to the AI boom, the tech industry is looking to build more data centers in the U.S. to provide compute for AI models and research. However, data centers are proving unpopular in many communities. Some state legislatures have taken action to restrict data center buildouts and stiffen regulations around the industry. As previously mentioned, 44 ballot measures to restrict data center buildout were passed by voters during the midterm elections. And the movement against AI data centers appears to only be growing. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich launched her own data center tracking initiative earlier this year. The tech and AI industries are currently struggling with a series of other issues. However, based on what studies are finding, it seems the anti-data-center movement will continue to be a thorn in the side of big tech and AI. LONDRES, 26 de novembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — O Concierto AI já está disponível para o público em geral em todos os mercados. A plataforma leva o Concierto, solução de transformação empresarial de nível corporativo já utilizada por governos, universidades e empresas em diversos países, para a era da inteligência artificial: IA de ponta para todos os colaboradores, executada integralmente na nuvem ou no centro de processamento de dados da própria organização, sem que dados, propriedade intelectual ou comandos enviados aos modelos (prompts) saiam do ambiente corporativo. O Concierto garante a soberania dos dados não apenas nas fronteiras nacionais, mas também no nível do próprio rack de servidores. A escolha do momento não é por acaso. Conselhos de administração e CEOs querem resultados concretos da IA desde já. No entanto, as equipes de segurança, jurídica e de conformidade não podem permitir que segredos comerciais, propriedade intelectual, código-fonte ou registros de clientes saiam do ambiente corporativo, além de precisarem atender às novas e rigorosas regulamentações sobre IA. O resultado é uma divisão no uso da IA: sua aplicação fica restrita a algumas equipes e a tarefas de baixo risco, enquanto atividades de alto valor que poderiam ser transformadas pela tecnologia permanecem inacessíveis. Cada trimestre em que essa barreira persiste representa uma oportunidade perdida. O Concierto AI elimina essa barreira. O principal destaque do Concierto, Produtividade Soberana da Força de Trabalho, combina o C/Composer, um assistente de IA para cada profissional do conhecimento, com o C/Code, um agente de programação para cada engenheiro. Ambos operam em uma infraestrutura de IA totalmente controlada, hospedada na própria nuvem privada virtual ou no centro de processamento de dados do cliente, mantendo todas as informações dentro dos limites da organização. O Concierto AI introduz funcionalidades que as empresas nunca tiveram antes. Sua implantação totalmente isolada e soberana mitiga a ameaça de risco sistêmico. Isso torna a IA mais segura, aplicando controles de segurança determinísticos a cada usuário e ativo que exige inferência, independentemente de sua localização, além de oferecer um mecanismo de desativação sob o controle do cliente. Seu design híbrido elimina a necessidade de erguer novos centros de dados para IA, deixando a tecnologia mais sustentável. A plataforma também transfere a propriedade, a visibilidade, o controle e a segurança para o próprio departamento de TI da empresa, fazendo com que eles governem a IA da mesma forma que governam todos os outros sistemas. Acima de tudo, o Concierto elimina a economia baseada em tokens. A plataforma precifica a IA por usuários e cargas de trabalho, fazendo com que os custos sejam claros, fixos e acessíveis, com uso ilimitado. Com o mesmo capital que uma organização investe em IA pública, o Concierto alcança um número bem maior de funcionários, democratizando a IA em toda a empresa. Os testes gratuitos começam hoje em concierto.ai. “Toda mudança tecnológica abre uma falha geológica, e as empresas ou a atravessam ou caem nela”, afirmou Sri Manchala, CEO da Trianz. “A IA é a mais ampla que já vi e a que avança mais rápido. As empresas foram instruídas a escolher entre agir rapidamente e manter o controle; entre a segurança e a aceitação de danos colaterais; entre tornar a IA parte de um sistema mais seguro ou permitir que ela se torne um sistema todo-poderoso em si mesma. Rejeitamos essas falsas dicotomias em todas as camadas. O Concierto AI permite que organizações de qualquer país disponibilizem IA a todos os seus colaboradores, tornando-a mais eficiente, segura, sustentável e acessível. Além da Produtividade Soberana da Força de Trabalho, o Concierto abrange Transformações Soberanas, que avaliam, migram, modernizam e incorporam agentes aos ambientes de aplicações em uma velocidade sem precedentes; IA Agentiva Soberana, que coloca agentes sob governança para atuar em sistemas corporativos, sujeitos à autoridade humana e ao controle externo; e Operações Soberanas, que mantêm todo o ambiente operacional em funcionamento, com cada ação devidamente auditada. Por meio de um plano de controle unificado, as equipes de IA e Segurança conseguem visualizar quem usa a IA e para quê, independentemente de onde a infraestrutura de TI esteja localizada — podendo, ainda, fornecer aos órgãos reguladores a transparência e a conformidade que exigem, de forma sistêmica. O Concierto AI pode ser implementado na Amazon Web Services, no Microsoft Azure, no Google Cloud ou em data centers locais, em qualquer região onde a empresa atue. Está disponível imediatamente, por meio de uma rede crescente de parceiros que atendem clientes que precisam de IA empresarial e não podem mover dados para fora de sua própria infraestrutura. artigo.texto: Socomec, a specialist manufacturer of low-voltage power management and battery energy storage solutions (BESS), has announced it was selected by KALS Energie Kraftwerk to deliver a first-of-its-kind energy storage system in Tyrol, Austria. The project combines hydropower and photovoltaic generation with Socomec’s BESS to increase renewable energy value and make hybrid generation more dispatchable, profitable, and useful to the local grid. KALS Energie Kraftwerk is an Austrian renewable energy producer operating hydroelectric and photovoltaic generation resources in the Tyrol region. With renewable generation rarely aligning with real-time grid demand, the company sought a solution that would allow it to store surplus hydroelectric and solar energy for optimised dispatch, as well as to unlock new revenue opportunities through supporting positive and negative balancing energy services. Given the plant’s location at an altitude of 2400 m, the solution also needed to deliver reliable performance in demanding conditions, including temperatures ranging from -18˚C to +25˚C and humidity levels of up to 100%. To support these objectives, Socomec deployed its SUNSYS HES XXL BESS as part of an integrated hydropower, photovoltaic and energy storage project. The installation combines 847 kW of hydroelectric generation and 400 kW of photovoltaic generation with Socomec's SUNSYS HES XXL BESS, delivering 1.5 MVA of output power and 3.3 MWh of storage capacity, as well as delivering approximately 90% efficiency. Integrated with an external energy management system (EMS), the BESS continuously analyses grid demand and dispatch opportunities, storing surplus renewable electricity and redistributing it within milliseconds according to market conditions and regional energy requirements. Its high-durability design, complete with a UV-resistant coating, ensures reliable performance even in challenging alpine conditions. Since commissioning, the project has demonstrated strong commercial performance and is expected to deliver a payback period of 5 – 6 years. Socomec’s BESS has so far supported the injection of up to 107 MWh of electricity into the grid per month, while ensuring that surplus renewable generation can be stored and utilised when and where it is needed most. KALS can now actively manage renewable energy production and respond rapidly to electricity market opportunities, improving the overall flexibility, profitability, and efficiency of its renewable assets. “This was a particularly challenging project, combining hydropower, photovoltaic generation and battery storage in a demanding mountainous environment,” said Robert Trenkwalder, CEO of KALS Energie Kraftwerk. “Socomec supported us every step of the way – from the initial design phase, through commissioning, and continuing today with the ongoing operation of the system. Their expertise and commitment gave us confidence throughout the project and they continue to deliver value today.” “Our partnership with KALS Energie Kraftwerk for the Tyrol plant clearly demonstrates how battery storage improves the overall business case for renewable generation,” added Michael Stötzner, Project Execution Manager, Socomec Germany. “The unique combination of hydropower, solar generation and intelligent energy storage provides a practical and replicable model for renewable energy producers across Europe seeking to increase the profitability, flexibility, and the value of their existing assets.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: A DSEZA declarou que o projeto da fábrica da Arbin Energy em Da Nang abrange uma área de 5,34 hectares no Parque de Alta Tecnologia de Da Nang, com um investimento total de US$ 117 milhões (equivalente a mais de VND 3,05 trilhões). A fábrica produzirá sistemas de armazenamento de energia alimentados por baterias (BESS), equipamentos para teste de baterias e equipamentos para a produção de baterias. Empresa americana investe US$ 117 milhões na construção de fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em Da Nang. DNVN - O Conselho de Administração do Parque de Alta Tecnologia e Zonas Industriais de Da Nang (DSEZA) emitiu a Decisão 347/QD-BQL aprovando a política de investimento e reconhecendo a Arbin Energy LLC (EUA) como investidora no projeto da usina da Arbin Energy em Da Nang. A construção da usina da Arbin Energy em Da Nang deverá começar em dezembro de 2026 e a produção no terceiro trimestre de 2028. Este é um dos resultados concretos da visita de trabalho aos Estados Unidos realizada pelo presidente do Comitê Popular de Da Nang, Nguyen Manh Hung, em setembro de 2026. Até o momento, somente o Parque de Alta Tecnologia de Da Nang atraiu 14 projetos de investimento estrangeiro direto (IED), com um capital registrado de US$ 830,5 milhões. Segundo o Departamento de Estatísticas de Da Nang, nos primeiros 10 meses de 2026, a cidade atraiu um total de investimento estrangeiro direto (IED) registrado superior a US$ 800 milhões, incluindo novos registros, ajustes e aportes de capital/aquisições de ações, um aumento de mais de 147% em comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior. Desse total, 130 projetos foram recém-registrados, totalizando quase US$ 630 milhões em capital, o que representa um aumento de mais de 17% no número de projetos e de mais de 233% no capital. O capital recém-registrado representou 78,3% do capital total atraído e aumentou em US$ 440,7 milhões em comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior, contribuindo com 92% do aumento total do IED. Em termos de setores econômicos , o capital de investimento estrangeiro direto (IED) recém-registrado em Da Nang durante os primeiros 10 meses de 2026 concentrou-se fortemente no setor imobiliário, com aproximadamente US$ 435,7 milhões, representando 69,2% do total do capital recém-registrado; e nas indústrias de transformação e processamento, com US$ 177,6 milhões, representando 28,2%. Esses dois setores representaram 97,4% do total do capital recém-registrado. No setor imobiliário, os novos aportes de capital estão focados principalmente em projetos de desenvolvimento e operação de infraestrutura para parques industriais e centros comerciais, com destaque para os projetos de infraestrutura dos parques industriais VSIP Da Nang e WHA Da Nang e para o centro comercial AEON MALL Da Nang Hoa Xuan.

artigo.texto: For a decade, the industry met rising energy demand with better efficiency. With the increased rack densities associated with AI and high-performance computing (HPC), however, efficiency alone cannot meet the rising energy demand, and the constraint has moved from the building to the grid. With expert insight from Jeff Gyzen, Global Practice Group Director, Mission Critical, Arcadis Executive summary The rapid growth of AI data centers is driving unprecedented increases in data center energy consumption, power demand, and cooling requirements. While energy efficiency improvements and liquid cooling technologies can reduce the energy required to support higher-density AI workloads, they do not eliminate the industry's primary challenge: securing enough power to support continued growth. As rack densities rise from tens to hundreds of kilowatts per cabinet, grid availability, power procurement, cooling strategy, data center water usage, and long-term infrastructure planning have become critical business decisions. For developers, operators, and investors, the key question is no longer how efficiently a facility uses power, but whether sufficient power and cooling capacity can be delivered when and where they are needed. An operator sets out to convert an existing data center for AI. Everything seems promising: the building is sound, the fiber is in, and the power is already contracted at 50 megawatts (MW), contracted with the utility years ago and paid for ever since. On paper, it is the cheapest AI capacity anyone will find this year. However, when you look closely at the density math, it’s not quite the bargain it seems. That 50 MW is spread across 1,000 racks of existing cloud-era equipment, each drawing 50 kilowatts (kW), but a single AI rack can draw the full 500 kilowatts on its own. The conversion concentrates the capacity already there into 100 cabinets, and the other 900 racks come out. The conversion does not add capacity to the room because the power entering the building never changes. That calculation is where many conversations about AI data center energy demand and AI data center power consumption now end, and it explains why the industry’s habitual answer to rising demand is no longer sufficient. Energy efficiency was the right response when the primary constraint was operating cost. Today, the binding constraint is supply: efficiency can increase the compute delivered by a fixed power allocation, but it cannot create additional grid capacity. “We are currently designing data centers with cabinet densities of 600 kW, and current trends will soon see as much as 1.2 MW per cabinet. The footprints stay the same. It’s the rack densities that increase,” says Jeff Gyzen, Global Practice Group Director, Mission Critical at Arcadis. This shift did not arrive gradually. Rack density is the variable that moved, and a decade of design assumptions built around it—racks at eight to 12 kilowatts, air cooling, a utility connection you could count on—gave way at around the same moment. What replaced them isn’t a bigger version of the old problem, but an entirely new engineering challenge. Behind those megawatts sits something easy to lose sight of: this demand comes from people. Someone waiting on a translation, a diagnosis, a search result—all of it is expected instantly. The facilities serving that demand are built in specific places, alongside communities that experience their noise and pressure on local infrastructure. The actual brief is to meet digital demand without transferring an unacceptable burden to the places that host it. For the people financing these data centers, this shift has a sharp edge: the efficiency case and the power procurement case are now the same case, and both must be settled before design begins in earnest. Why the grid, not the building, sets the limit on AI data center power consumption The first consequence of higher density is obvious: higher power consumption. The second consequence is easier to miss: power becomes heat, the heat becomes cooling load, and the cooling load draws power again. Density never lands in one place but compounds through the whole system. But the constraint that stops projects sits outside the fence line. What clients most often misunderstand is that public utilities operate on a very different timeline. In Tier 1 markets, most of them can’t deliver additional capacity for three to 10 years. Tier 1 markets are the established hubs where most capacity has been built, and where the queue is longest. If a utility cannot serve a site within the project’s viable development window, the project must secure an alternative power route, relocate, or stop. That is why developers and hyperscalers—the largest cloud operators—increasingly treat on-site generation as part of the baseline power strategy rather than as a contingency. It also means the energy conversation can no longer start at design. It now starts at the property search. “When we search for property, we’re looking for available power first. If none is found, we look at the potential for natural gas, which we can use to generate our own,” says Jeff. Leave that question late and you don’t end up with a worse design. You end up with a project that can’t procure the power at all. Where AI data center energy consumption goes Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of a data center’s total energy use to the energy used by its IT equipment alone. As AI data center power consumption increases, operators are paying closer attention to both energy efficiency and the cooling systems responsible for managing the resulting heat load. A PUE of 1.0 would mean every watt reaches compute. PUE can be categorized into three types associated with design and actual operation. Design PUE models expected efficiency from planned equipment loads and design conditions before the data center is constructed and starts running. Request a Free Sample Report - Includes Market Forecasts, Manufacturer Profiles, Competitive Analysis and Quantum Battery Technology Insights: https://www.qyresearch.in/request-sample/energy-power-global-quantum-battery-technology-market-insights-industry-share-sales-projections-and-demand-outlook-2026-2032 Quantum battery technology refers to an emerging class of energy-storage and energy-management devices that use quantum-mechanical effects to absorb, store, retain and release energy. The scope of this study focuses on device concepts, prototype systems, enabling materials and research platforms based on quantum coherence, superposition, entanglement, superabsorption, superradiance and strong light-matter coupling. Typical physical implementations include organic microcavities, quantum dots and inorganic nanostructures, perovskite-related platforms, superconducting quantum circuits and qubit-based architectures. The core value proposition lies in faster charging, more efficient energy transfer, low-interference power management and potential integration with quantum computing, microelectronics, sensors, wireless charging and future high-rate energy systems. At the current stage, the industry should not be measured as a conventional battery-cell market; pricing is more appropriately assessed through prototype R&D contracts, customised experimental devices, enabling material supply and early-stage technology licensing rather than standardised cell-level ASP. Based on our research, quantum batteries should be understood as a pre-commercial quantum energy-storage technology rather than a sub-segment of conventional electrochemical batteries. The industry is currently defined by laboratory-scale prototypes, quantum thermodynamics, advanced materials platforms and device-level proof-of-concept work. Its decisive technical variables are quantum-state lifetime, scalable light-matter coupling, usable energy extraction, device stability and system integration, rather than cell manufacturing capacity or battery-pack cost. The 2026 Australian proof-of-concept marked an important step because it demonstrated a full charge-store-discharge cycle, but the present capacity and storage duration remain far from practical battery deployment. The global supply structure is not yet comparable to the lithium-ion or solid-state battery industries. At this stage, the most credible participants are research organisations and deep-tech entities, while quantum-dot materials suppliers and quantum-computing companies should be treated as adjacent or potential participants only when official product evidence supports their relevance. Planckian remains the most notable corporate name historically associated with quantum battery development, but its current public positioning appears more focused on next-generation quantum processors, which requires caution in revenue modelling and ranking. From a demand perspective, near-term adoption is more likely to emerge from quantum computing, microelectronics, sensors, optical energy conversion and low-interference energy-management systems than from electric vehicles or grid-scale storage. Policy support for quantum technologies in Europe, China and the United States can improve the funding environment, but it should not be interpreted as direct evidence of a mature quantum battery market. The sector's outlook is attractive but highly option-like: a single technical breakthrough in storage lifetime or scalable device manufacturing could materially change the market trajectory, while slow progress would keep the market largely confined to research and prototype revenues. artigo.texto: Resumo - Pela 1ª vez, a FCC liberou que data centers em formato de satélite subam ao espaço - Permissão foi concedida à SpaceX, de Elon Musk, para até 1 milhão de equipamentos - Constelação será chamada de 'Starmind' e deve atender à demanda por IA - Satélites processarão dados em órbita, mas para uso no planeta Terra - FCC diz que medida impulsiona a 'economia de superinteligência' dos EUA A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC, na sigla em inglês) dos Estados Unidos autorizou a SpaceX, empresa aeroespacial de Elon Musk, a desenvolver uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites que funcionarão como data centers espaciais. A decisão, anunciada nesta quarta-feira (25), representa a primeira autorização desse tipo na história do país. Com o aval, a companhia poderá avançar com o projeto batizado de Starmind. A iniciativa prevê instalar módulos de processamento de dados em órbita para atender à crescente demanda por capacidade computacional, especialmente no desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial (IA). A proposta da SpaceX envolve uma infraestrutura que funciona de maneira diferente dos centros de dados terrestres. Em vez de concentrar servidores em grandes instalações no planeta, a empresa pretende distribuir a capacidade de processamento entre milhares de equipamentos no espaço. A estratégia aproveita dois recursos considerados fundamentais para o projeto: a disponibilidade de energia solar fora da atmosfera e o espaço físico disponível em órbita. Embora operem longe da Terra, os módulos continuarão conectados ao planeta. Afinal, eles deverão processar grandes volumes de informações e transmitir os resultados para usuários e sistemas terrestres. O que a FCC pretende impulsionar? A autorização faz parte de uma estratégia dos Estados Unidos para ampliar sua infraestrutura tecnológica e fortalecer a chamada “economia de superinteligência”. O presidente Donald Trump utiliza o termo superinteligência ao tratar da corrida global pelo desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial. Nesse contexto, a FCC considera os data centers uma estrutura essencial para sustentar o avanço da tecnologia. Em comunicado, o presidente da agência, Brendan Carr, afirmou que os Estados Unidos lideram a nova etapa do desenvolvimento tecnológico. “Essa ação abre fronteiras ousadas para a infraestrutura de computação necessária para impulsionar a liderança e o crescimento da América”, declarou. Com a decisão, a SpaceX poderá desenvolver a constelação Starmind, que prevê até 1 milhão de módulos orbitais de processamento. Segundo a FCC, o objetivo é atender à rápida expansão da demanda por capacidade computacional voltada à superinteligência. A autorização também permite que a companhia utilize frequências de rádio como alternativa de comunicação e emergência. Além disso, os equipamentos poderão complementar suas conexões ópticas entre satélites com transmissões por radiofrequência. Economia de energia e civilização Kardashev tipo II Um dos principais argumentos em favor dos data centers espaciais envolve o aproveitamento da energia solar. Fora da atmosfera terrestre, os equipamentos poderão captar energia diretamente do Sol. Segundo a SpaceX, essa estrutura também poderá reduzir a pressão sobre recursos naturais utilizados pelas instalações terrestres, como eletricidade e água. A FCC relacionou o projeto a um conceito da escala de Kardashev. Essa classificação hipotética mede o nível de desenvolvimento tecnológico de uma civilização conforme sua capacidade de aproveitar energia. Uma civilização do tipo II conseguiria captar e utilizar a energia produzida integralmente por sua estrela. No caso da Terra, isso significaria aproveitar toda a energia emitida pelo Sol. A agência americana mencionou esse conceito ao defender a dimensão tecnológica da iniciativa. Entretanto, a classificação representa uma referência teórica, e não uma condição que o projeto da SpaceX já tenha alcançado. Quando os data centers espaciais serão lançados? Apesar da autorização, a construção da constelação não acontecerá imediatamente. A SpaceX ainda precisará desenvolver a infraestrutura, fabricar os equipamentos e organizar os lançamentos. Além disso, a aprovação regulatória não garante que a companhia consiga colocar todos os 1 milhão de módulos em órbita. A própria viabilidade técnica e econômica de uma operação dessa dimensão ainda representa um desafio. A decisão da FCC, portanto, abre caminho para o desenvolvimento do projeto, mas não significa que toda a estrutura já esteja pronta para funcionar. Por fim, a agência informou que continuará analisando solicitações de outras empresas interessadas em desenvolver data centers orbitais. Dessa forma, a autorização também abre espaço para uma nova disputa tecnológica envolvendo a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial no espaço.

artigo.texto: A new study co-authored by a UCLA Fielding School of Public Health researcher has found that over the course of a year, the largest data centers in the United States use four times as much power as the city of Los Angeles. Findings also indicated that such centers’ electricity consumption and carbon emissions rival those of some U.S. states. The study, published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Sustainability, examined hyperscale data centers (HDCs), the largest and most powerful class of data centers that support services such as cloud computing, large language model training and global deployment of artificial intelligence tools. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions since the rise of AI. The authors include researchers from Harvard University and Falco Bargagli Stoffi, an assistant professor in the UCLA Fielding Department of Biostatistics. They compared their findings on power usage to electricity sales by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP), which serves approximately 4 million Angelenos. “Our central estimate suggests that the 403 hyperscale data centers we studied across the United States used nearly four times as much electricity as LADWP sells to its customers in a year,” said Bargagli Stoffi, adding that the analysis attributed more than half, or 54%, of the centers’ electricity use to fossil fuels. The study was one of the first to combine fragmented data, helping to better paint a picture of the emissions of individual facilities. “Better public information on electricity use would help communities and policymakers assess the environmental consequences of this industry’s growth,” Bargagli Stoffi said. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is heavily generated by coal-fired power plants. The study found that four states — Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa —accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied.

artigo.texto: Brewer holds informational meeting on proposed data center rules BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Brewer residents had a chance Tuesday to learn more about proposed rules for data centers in the city. The city held an informational meeting at the Brewer Auditorium to discuss the proposal and hear from residents. What the proposal includes The Planning Board recommended the changes earlier this month. They would increase the allowable size of data centers from 20 to 50 megawatts in an industrial zone primarily located behind the city landfill. The proposal also includes noise standards, requirements for cooling and wastewater, and a community benefit agreement. Citizens weigh in People on both sides of the issue spoke. Vikas Dhiman, a University of Maine professor, said the proposed size would equal the residential electricity use of Penobscot County. “The regulations are up to 50 megawatt data center. The entire consumption of Penobscot residential electricity usage is 60 megawatts. So it’s the same as the entire county of Penobscot residential consumption. I don’t want a big data center, power-hungry, water-hungry, land-hungry, resource-hungry data center in my neighborhood,” Dhiman said. Jim LeBrecque, an engineer and president of Flexware Control Technology, said data centers help him in his work. “I’m an engineer, and data centers help me out tremendously. I can do in just a matter of a few minutes what took me many months to do before. We could not have the standard of living we have today if it was not for electrification. And the next big jump in our standard of living is going to come from data centers,” LeBrecque said. City’s response and next steps The city said it is not negotiating with any data center developers and that the proposed rules do not approve a specific project. The City Council is scheduled to consider the amendments Dec. 8 and again Jan. 12. Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX's request to launch as many as 1 million satellites for the creation of a network of data centers in orbit for complex artificial intelligence computing. The agency's first-ever authorization of data centers in space makes way for a concept that was central to Elon Musk's pitch to investors ahead of SpaceX's initial public offering in June. The company has cautioned that orbital AI data centers rely on unproven technologies and may never be commercially viable. "By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said Wednesday in a statement. He has frequently praised SpaceX and attended a test launch of the company's new Starship rocket earlier this month. The FCC's approval clears a regulatory hurdle to SpaceX's ambitious plan for orbital data centers, which the company says can serve as lower-cost and more environmentally friendly alternatives to land-based compute. SpaceX still faces significant hurdles, since orbital data centers will require engineering extremely large solar panels, technically sophisticated cooling technology and systems for transmitting much larger amounts of data to Earth than exist today. SpaceX didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The company's request to launch its orbital data centers, filed in January, included details about its plans for the new network. Instead of requiring cooling systems that use large volumes of water, the network would rely on radiative cooling that occurs in space, allowing for the dissipation of heat. It would also reduce the need to rely on batteries, since it would acquire energy from the sun, according to the filing. The satellites, which will use laser links to communicate with each other, will be launched between an altitude of 311-1,272 miles (500-2,000 kilometers) in an orbit that would provide them near constant access to the sun, according to the filing. SpaceX's plans to launch so many satellites, however, have raised concerns from scientists and others in the space industry who worry that the tremendous size of the proposed network will overcrowd Earth's orbit, increase satellite collisions and decrease the visibility of stars for astronomers. The proposal received more than 1,500 public comments, with stakeholders including the American Astronomical Society urging the FCC to deny the application. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin has also requested permission with the FCC to launch its own orbital data centers, although that it still awaiting regulatory approval. SpaceX separately announced on Wednesday it plans to contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, the tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children.

artigo.texto: 24 Novembro 2026 Demanda de energia elétrica foi de 82 TWh, cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade do país, com emissões de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. A informação é publicada por ClimaInfo, 24-11-2026. Em um ano, entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, os 403 maiores centros de dados dos Estados Unidos emitiram mais dióxido de carbono do que a Dinamarca, que tem cerca de 6 milhões de habitantes. É o que mostra um estudo publicado na revista Nature Sustainability na semana passada. A pesquisa é uma das primeiras a estimar o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de centros de dados hiperescaláveis (HDCs, sigla em inglês) desde o surgimento da inteligência artificial, segundo a Euronews. Em diferentes cenários de carga, esses HDCs consumiram entre 68 e 99 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade, associados a aproximadamente 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (MtCO₂). No cenário médio, a demanda de eletricidade desses data centers foi de 82 TWh, correspondendo a 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA, com emissões de CO₂ atribuíveis de cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono. Cerca de 54% da geração atribuída foi proveniente de fontes de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás e carvão. A estimativa de emissões é de duas a três vezes maior do que a demonstrada em estudos anteriores, afirmou a autora sênior do estudo, Francesca Dominici, professora de bioestatística de Harvard. “É o equivalente à emissão de CO₂ de um pequeno país europeu”, disse a especialista, acrescentando que os planos para mais 2 mil centros de dados tornam essa quantidade ainda mais preocupante para o futuro, destaca a AP. Os HDCs são a maior classe de centros de dados, sendo o tipo que executa serviços em nuvem e treina grandes modelos de IA. Os edifícios da amostra tinham uma capacidade elétrica média de cerca de 40 megawatts, explica a Earth.com. 🔍 Adicione o Instituto Humanitas Unisinos – IHU às suas fontes favoritas do Google Os pesquisadores começaram o estudo com 675 locais candidatos de um banco de dados comercial e mantiveram os 403 que puderam ser confirmados. Cada endereço foi associado a um telhado, e sua área foi verificada no OpenStreetMap. Em seguida, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite e aéreas em busca de indícios de um centro de dados: grandes telhados uniformes, equipamentos de refrigeração e uma subestação ao lado. Dos HDCs analisados, 142 estão localizados na Virgínia, que abriga mais estruturas desse tipo do que qualquer outro estado dos EUA, 56 no Oregon e 38 em Ohio. Nenhum data center opera em sua capacidade nominal máxima a cada hora, e as empresas não divulgam suas cargas reais. Por isso, a equipe multiplicou a capacidade de cada instalação pelas horas do ano e por um fator de carga. Os pesquisadores executaram quatro versões desse fator, desde uma carga leve até uma destinada a abranger o treinamento pesado de IA, para chegar aos resultados. Agora a equipe planeja examinar os efeitos das emissões associadas aos HDCs na saúde, conta Francesca. “As centrais elétricas movidas a combustíveis fósseis nos sistemas regionais de distribuição de energia, associadas a essa demanda, também liberam outros poluentes, como partículas finas, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, que estão diretamente ligados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura”, disse a especialista. As pessoas que respiram esses poluentes vivem perto das usinas, que podem estar longe de qualquer centro de dados.

artigo.texto: Parcerias B.Grimm e NTT buscam oportunidade de desenvolver um centro de dados de IA de 400 MW na Tailândia Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO memorando apenas compromete os parceiros a buscar uma oportunidade de 400 MW, em vez… Ver mais - O memorando apenas compromete os parceiros a buscar uma oportunidade de 400 MW, em vez de confirmar a construção. - O negócio existente de geração e distribuição de energia da B.Grimm sustenta o seu papel energético no plano do data center. - O acordo separado da NTT com a Bloom Energy mostra que a disponibilidade de energia agora determina a rapidez com que a capacidade de IA pode ser entregue. A B.Grimm anunciou em 24 de novembro de 2026 que a B.Grimm Power havia assinado um memorando de entendimento com a NTT Global Data Center para buscar uma oportunidade de desenvolver um centro de dados de 400 MW na Tailândia, abrangendo infraestrutura digital, um ecossistema de IA e infraestrutura energética, com investimento estimado em aproximadamente 113 bilhões de THB. O memorando é um acordo para buscar a oportunidade, não uma confirmação de que as obras já começaram. Nopadej Karnasuta, presidente da B.Grimm Power para Tailândia, Malásia e Negócios de Soluções de Energia & Industriais, participou da visita ao Japão durante a qual o documento foi assinado. Segundo a B.Grimm, a visita, liderada pelo vice-primeiro-ministro e ministro das Finanças Ekniti Nitithanprapas, ocorreu de 17 a 21 de novembro de 2026. Conversas no Japão conectam infraestrutura de IA e energia Em um comunicado de 23 de novembro de 2026, o Conselho de Investimentos da Tailândia informa que a delegação esteve em Tóquio de 17 a 20 de novembro de 2026. O Diálogo de Investimento e Negócios Tailândia–Japão BOI–Keidanren reuniu 64 executivos japoneses do setor privado, de 38 empresas de nove setores. As discussões abordaram três cadeias de suprimentos: veículos modernos; infraestrutura de IA e eletrônica avançada; e redes elétricas modernas. Essas prioridades correspondem de perto à combinação de computação e energia prevista no MoU. A delegação também visitou o NTT Data Mitaka EAST Data Center para estudar segurança, continuidade dos sistemas e eficiência energética em infraestruturas que dão suporte à IA. Segundo o relato da B.Grimm, Ekniti destacou que as instalações da NTT no Japão são eficientes, silenciosas, respeitam o meio ambiente e conseguem coexistir com as comunidades locais. A B.Grimm Power também pretende manter essas práticas e compartilhar conhecimentos e tecnologia com a população tailandesa no longo prazo. Operações de geração de energia e digitais da B.Grimm A B.Grimm Power leva para a proposta uma operação consolidada no setor de energia. Seu perfil corporativo informa que a empresa tem capacidade instalada de 5.180 MW, fornece energia por meio de suas próprias redes de distribuição a mais de 400 clientes industriais e tem como meta garantir contratos de compra de energia que totalizem 10.000 MW até 2030. Com sede na Tailândia, a empresa desenvolve, financia, constrói e opera usinas de energia em áreas sem instalações anteriores. Essas operações são relevantes porque o MoU inclui explicitamente a infraestrutura energética, além do centro de dados e do ecossistema de IA. A B.Grimm também tem uma iniciativa de infraestrutura digital industrial. Em 18 de junho de 2026, a subsidiária B.Grimm BeyondBridge e a INET criaram a B.Grimm INET para desenvolver e operar plataformas na Tailândia voltadas à gestão de energia, a sistemas ambientais e de serviços públicos inteligentes, ao monitoramento e à gestão de gases de efeito estufa, à segurança na nuvem e a tecnologias de IA. A iniciativa anterior documenta a expansão da B.Grimm para além da geração de energia, com entrada no setor de plataformas digitais industriais, antes do acordo com a NTT. Expansão regional e estratégia energética da NTT A NTT DATA nomeou Yasuhiro Kajiki em 10 de setembro de 2026 para o cargo de diretor-geral para Japão e Ásia-Pacífico da NTT Global Data Centers, com responsabilidade pelas operações regionais e pela estratégia de crescimento. A empresa associou a ampliação das atribuições do cargo ao aumento da demanda dos clientes por infraestrutura digital preparada para IA na região da Ásia-Pacífico. Um acordo com a Bloom Energy, anunciado em 5 de novembro de 2026, prevê que a NTT instale 900 MW de capacidade de geração de energia no local em vários projetos de centros de dados no mundo todo, com os primeiros envios planejados para 2027. A NTT DATA espera que os sistemas modulares de células a combustível da Bloom permitam disponibilizar energia à medida que as obras avançam e ampliar a capacidade para atender às cargas de trabalho de IA, cada vez mais intensivas em energia. “Nossos clientes estão desenvolvendo recursos de IA em um ritmo que a rede elétrica, sozinha, nem sempre consegue acompanhar, e a rapidez para disponibilizar energia tornou-se um dos fatores decisivos para fornecer capacidade onde e quando ela é necessária”, afirmou Doug Adams, CEO da NTT Global Data Centers. Anunciado separadamente do MoU tailandês, o acordo com a Bloom mostra por que o papel da B.Grimm no setor de energia é importante: para os centros de dados de IA, garantir energia escalável é essencial para fornecer capacidade computacional. A questão em aberto é a execução: será que os parceiros conseguirão combinar a expansão dos centros de dados da NTT com as operações de energia e a experiência em infraestrutura digital da B.Grimm para oferecer a eficiência, a operação silenciosa e a convivência com as comunidades destacadas durante a visita ao Japão? Isso transformaria um memorando firmado durante uma missão de investimento na infraestrutura de IA operacional que a Tailândia busca.
