artigo.texto: AI data center opposition now carries a price tag. Reuters reported that community opposition blocked or delayed at least 120 data-center projects worth $198 billion during the first six months of 2026, citing figures from Data Center Watch. That works out to roughly 20 projects a month, on our own arithmetic, and it lands while the industry is trying to build faster than ever. The resistance is not confined to one country or one grid. We have already tracked it in our report on 220+ Tokyo residents fighting a data centre boom, and the Associated Press now describes rising community opposition to large data centers built for AI and cloud computing. The International Energy Agency (IEA) adds a policy layer, saying that governments are responding to worries about electricity prices, emissions and water use. This analysis asks a narrow question. If regulation, local opposition and funding pressure all tighten at once, can AI data center operators survive by running leaner? We sort what the named sources confirm from what they do not, then look at who gains, who loses and what to watch next. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the Latest Reports Confirm About AI Data Center Opposition Four outlets and one global agency supply the facts behind this story. Reuters provided the headline count of blocked and delayed projects. The Associated Press documented the rise in community resistance and showed how it now appears in corporate risk disclosures. Network World relayed a recent NBC News poll and a financial estimate from The Wachters. The IEA framed the policy side, and Data Center Knowledge described what operators can do about grid strain. Every claim below traces to one of those named reports. Where the reports stop, so does this article. The material we worked from does not include a country-by-country or company-by-company breakdown of the blocked projects, so we do not offer one. It also does not name the filer behind the October securities document the AP cited, and we will not guess. That discipline matters because the topic invites overreach. Data center fights generate loud anecdotes, and a single canceled campus can feel like a trend. A tally compiled by a tracker such as Data Center Watch, reported by a wire service like Reuters, gives a firmer base than any one town meeting. It is still a count of what the tracker could find, and Reuters framed the figure as a minimum with the words “at least.” One more caution before the numbers. The phrase triple squeeze, which frames this story, is not independently confirmed by the sources. The three pressures it names (regulation, local opposition and funding) each show up in the reporting, but no source we reviewed calls the combination a squeeze. We treat it as a useful lens and nothing more. The Numbers: 120 Projects, $198 Billion, Six Months Start with the scale. Reuters reported, citing Data Center Watch, that opposition blocked or delayed at least 120 projects worth $198 billion in the first half of 2026. Divide the value by the count and you get about $1.65 billion per project. Treat that as a rough guide only. The count is a floor, the projects almost certainly vary widely in size, and we have no list to check the average against. Stretch the same figures across the half-year and the pace becomes clearer. Roughly $33 billion of planned construction a month ran into blocked or delayed status, again on simple division. For a sector whose business model depends on getting capacity online quickly, a delay can cost nearly as much as a cancellation. Capital sits idle, equipment orders wait, and customers look elsewhere. The table shows how different the evidence types are. One row is a count, one is a poll, one is a modeled estimate, one is corporate disclosure language and one is a policy observation. They point the same way, but they do not add up to a single index. Readers should resist stacking them into one headline number. Why Local Opposition Is Now a Disclosed Business Risk The strongest sign that opposition has moved from nuisance to material risk sits in a securities filing. The Associated Press cited an October filing that listed “community opposition, local moratoriums, and hyper-local dissent that may impede or delay infrastructure development” as operational risks. Companies do not write that language casually. Lawyers add risk factors when a problem is real enough that omitting it could create liability. The AP also reported that technology companies and developers face increasing community opposition to large data centers meant for AI and cloud computing. The word increasing carries weight. It tells us the trend line, not just a snapshot, and it matches the Data Center Watch tally that Reuters reported for the first half of 2026. What a moratorium does to a build schedule A local moratorium is blunt. It pauses new approvals while a town or county writes rules, and the pause can run long. A developer with land, power requests and equipment on order cannot easily shift to another site, because each of those commitments is tied to a place. The filing language names moratoriums and “hyper-local dissent” side by side, which suggests the companies see both formal and informal resistance as schedule threats. Why hyper-local matters for AI specifically AI campuses draw more attention than older cloud sites for a plain reason. They are large, they concentrate power demand, and they are tied in the public mind to a technology many people have mixed feelings about. For a wider view of the field, our AI and machine learning coverage tracks how model makers and infrastructure builders are responding. artigo.texto: FCC autoriza SpaceX a lançar 1 milhão de satélites para data centers Projeto Starmind prevê módulos computacionais alimentados por energia solar e integrados à infraestrutura de comunicação da Starlink. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC) autorizou hoje (25) a SpaceX, de Elon Musk, a implantar uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites destinados ao processamento de dados no espaço. Denominado Starmind, o projeto é voltado ao atendimento da demanda por capacidade computacional para aplicações de IA. Segundo a FCC, trata-se da primeira autorização concedida pelo regulador norte-americano para uma constelação de data centers orbitais. O presidente da agência, Brendan Carr, associou a decisão à estratégia dos Estados Unidos para o desenvolvimento de sistemas avançados de IA. O órgão informou que também examina propostas de constelações concorrentes. A SpaceX apresentou o pedido de autorização em janeiro deste ano. Em 4 de fevereiro, o regulador admitiu formalmente a solicitação e abriu o processo para manifestações de interessados, conforme o documento DA 26-113. Na proposta original, a empresa previa distribuir os módulos computacionais em órbitas não geoestacionárias, a altitudes entre 500 km e 2 mil km. Infraestrutura computacional em órbita De acordo com a documentação técnica divulgada pela SpaceX, os satélites do modelo AI1 terão potência destinada aos sistemas computacionais de até 250 kW de pico e 175 kW em média. A companhia prevê iniciar a produção desses equipamentos no fim de 2027. O projeto contempla o uso de órbitas heliossíncronas para favorecer a exposição dos equipamentos à luz solar e, dessa forma, reduzir a dependência da infraestrutura terrestre de geração e distribuição de eletricidade. A arquitetura da Starmind prevê ainda a utilização de enlaces ópticos entre os módulos computacionais e os satélites da Starlink. Essa integração faz parte da estratégia de comunicação da infraestrutura orbital com sistemas em Terra. Uso do espectro A decisão da FCC contempla também a utilização de duas faixas de radiofrequências para complementar a infraestrutura de comunicação do sistema. A SpaceX recebeu autorização para operar nas frequências de 18,8 GHz a 19,3 GHz, no sentido espaço-Terra (downlink), e de 28,6 GHz a 29,1 GHz, no sentido Terra-espaço (uplink). O uso do espectro inclui operações de contingência e emergência relacionadas à telemetria, ao rastreamento e ao comando dos equipamentos (TT&C, na sigla em inglês). A constelação estará sujeita às regras estabelecidas pela FCC para mitigação de detritos orbitais.

artigo.texto: A new research paper has mapped which states are rolling out the red carpet for data centers and which are putting up roadblocks, based on tax incentives, development conditions and environmental requirements. The researchers analyzed how states across the U.S. are responding to the rapid expansion of data centers, finding stark differences in how strongly state policies encourage or discourage new developments. Why Are Data Centers So Controversial? Supporters argue that data centers are essential infrastructure for the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and cloud computing, bringing investment, jobs and additional tax revenue while helping the U.S. compete with China in AI. Read More on U.S. But opponents have raised concerns about their high electricity demand, water used for cooling, pressure on grid and utility infrastructure, noise and air pollution, and development near homes or agricultural land. A Pew Research Center survey of 10,548 adults conducted from July 20 to August 9 found that 60 percent of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new data center opening in their area. Fifty-four percent said data centers were mostly bad for the environment, while 49 percent said they were mostly bad for nearby residents' quality of life. Half said data centers were mostly bad for household energy costs. Concern about data centers is bipartisan too, with 68 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents and 54 percent of Republicans and Republican leaners saying they would be uncomfortable with a data center opening locally. President Donald Trump has been a prominent supporter of data center construction across the U.S., arguing earlier this year that there are "so many people that want data centers." Several state leaders have also advocated for data-center development. Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn, a Republican, has advocated for data center development. "Data centers are going to be a good and important part of Tennessee’s economic growth," she said. Tennessee has also retained significant incentives for the industry, including sales-and-use tax exemptions and franchise and excise tax credits for qualifying data centers. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, has rejected calls for a moratorium on new data-center development. "Arizona has built one of the strongest AI ecosystems in the country, and our community colleges help power it," she said earlier this year. Other political leaders, however, have moved in the opposite direction as concerns over electricity costs, water use and the pace of development have grown. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, campaigned on pausing new data center construction and, after winning, reiterated that development should stop until stronger safeguards are established. "We need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," she said. Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, has said she intends to issue an executive order pausing new data-center construction after taking office in January, saying the state needs to examine the incentive agreements being used to attract projects. "A lot of data centers are being built in Georgia because of the incentives that have been attached to those data centers. So, of course, we're going to have to take a look at what those agreements entail," she told CBS News. Which States Are Most Friendly to Data Centers? The study, published in Frontiers in Sustainable Cities on October 28, was produced by researchers from Iowa State University, Arizona State University and the University of Kansas. The researchers assigned each state a score based primarily on three criteria: whether it offers tax-based incentives, whether those incentives come with conditions, such as minimum investment or job requirements, and whether environmental assessments are required. States were then grouped into four categories ranging from high incentive, with a score of 1, through moderate incentive at 0 and low or no incentive at -1, to disincentive at -2. Higher scores indicate a policy environment more favorable to data center development. The study classified Nebraska, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island as high-incentive states, citing broad, long-term tax exemptions as a key characteristic of their policies. Most states fell into the moderate-incentive category, generally offering tax exemptions or partial refunds alongside conditions such as minimum capital investment requirements. Examples included Texas, Arizona, Georgia, North Carolina and Utah. Kansas, Montana and Oklahoma were among those classified as offering low or no incentives, a category characterized by limited tax incentives or additional requirements such as grid agreements or infrastructure investment. Minnesota, New Hampshire and Wisconsin were given as examples of states with policies that disincentivize development, including moratoriums, legislative efforts to repeal or roll back exemptions and requirements for developers to bear infrastructure costs. Some States Are Already Shifting State differences extend beyond financial incentives. Researchers also identified states taking different approaches to permitting and local control, with some seeking to accelerate approvals while others considered moratoriums on new development. The study also examined one local jurisdiction in each state. Just 11 of the 50 jurisdictions expressly allowed for data center development in zoning or comprehensive planning documents or on government websites, while more traditional industrial planning rules such as buffers and setbacks were considerably more common. The researchers cautioned that the findings represent a snapshot of policies in late 2025 and early 2026 rather than a live picture of the current landscape. Data center policy has evolved rapidly, with states introducing, reconsidering and reversing incentives and restrictions since the data was collected. (NASDAQ:FNGR), que mudará seu nome para BlueFlare, Inc. e seu símbolo de negociação para BFLR a partir de 25 de novembro de 2026, anunciou uma extensão do período de exclusividade para negociações referentes ao seu empreendimento de colocation Brooks Campus #1 em Alberta, Canadá. A subsidiária integral da empresa, Brooks Campus No. 1 Inc., e a Cascadia Industries Ltd., que opera como Cascadia Power, continuam negociando acordos definitivos após a conclusão do Memorando de Base de Projeto do empreendimento em 18 de novembro. A Cascadia representa um potencial cliente de colocation que busca até 7 MW de capacidade crítica de TI. A FingerMotion espera que o acordo proposto, se finalizado, gere mais de US$ 100 milhões em receita contratada durante um período inicial de cinco anos. O desenvolvimento do campus de Brooks está progredindo O campus tem autorização para até 9,9 MW e foi projetado para fornecer 7,2 MW de capacidade crítica de TI, com o suporte de 9,6 MW de geração de gás natural no local, sem depender da rede elétrica provincial. A empresa pretende disponibilizar o serviço inicial dentro de seis meses após a entrada em vigor de um acordo vinculativo, com a capacidade total prevista para um período de 12 a 14 meses. O Brooks Campus #1 é o primeiro empreendimento dentro do programa planejado de 99 MW da FingerMotion em Alberta, compreendendo dez locais nas zonas de Newell, Coronation, Fox Creek e Vulcan. artigo.texto: Holanda sugere fundo para investimentos em CDNs e micro data centers Conselheiro da Anatel discute contrapartidas de investimentos como alternativa à disputa entre operadoras de telecomunicações e empresas digitais. O conselheiro da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) Edson Holanda levantou nesta quarta-feira, 25, a possibilidade de criação de um fundo setorial para financiar a instalação de redes de distribuição de conteúdo (CDNs) em regiões sem atratividade comercial. Outra alternativa apresentada pelo regulador é a inclusão de obrigações de investimento em infraestrutura digital nos contratos entre operadoras de telecomunicações e empresas de internet. As possibilidades foram discutidas durante o 1º Fórum dig.ia, em Brasília, no painel dedicado ao equilíbrio nas relações entre os agentes do ecossistema digital e aos limites da regulação sobre CDNs e redes de borda (edge computing). Relator na Anatel do processo de regulamentação dos deveres dos usuários, Holanda afirmou buscar uma solução que permita reduzir as divergências entre os setores de telecomunicações e digital em torno do financiamento da infraestrutura. O conselheiro mencionou a possibilidade de estabelecer contrapartidas destinadas a investimentos em localidades que não seriam atendidas exclusivamente por decisões comerciais das empresas. Contrapartidas de investimentos Holanda também levantou a hipótese de que os próprios contratos celebrados entre empresas de telecomunicações e do mercado digital contemplem cláusulas que destinem parte dos recursos envolvidos nas operações comerciais à implantação de CDNs e micro data centers. O conselheiro recorreu a experiências de outros setores regulados, como energia e petróleo e gás, nos quais existem mecanismos de contrapartidas associados a objetivos de políticas públicas. No setor de telecomunicações, citou os investimentos realizados na infraestrutura de conectividade da região amazônica como exemplo de iniciativas destinadas a atender localidades nas quais a implantação de redes não necessariamente apresenta retorno econômico suficiente para justificar a aplicação de recursos privados. Holanda reconheceu que empresas como Meta e Netflix já realizam investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Entretanto, defendeu que a discussão também incorpore objetivos de políticas públicas, para além dos interesses comerciais das companhias. Mediação entre teles e empresas digitais O conselheiro afirmou que a busca de uma solução negociada passa pela necessidade de estabelecer um diálogo entre os agentes envolvidos na discussão sobre o custeio das redes. A possibilidade de construção de metas de investimentos, com a mediação da Anatel, também foi mencionada durante a exposição. Holanda reconheceu que parte das informações sobre os investimentos das empresas está sujeita a questões de confidencialidade comercial. As alternativas apresentadas pelo conselheiro integram suas reflexões como relator do processo sobre deveres dos usuários. Holanda ressaltou que as manifestações representam sua visão sobre o assunto, e não uma posição institucional da agência. Não foram apresentados, durante a exposição, um modelo formal de fundo setorial, valores de contribuição ou cronograma de implementação.

artigo.texto: - Comprising seven advanced-stage battery energy storage (BESS) projects in A Coruña, Almería, Castellón and Navarra, the 380 MW / 1.5 GWh portfolio is expected to come online between 2027 and the first half of 2028. MADRID, November 24, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--SUNGROW RENEWABLES, part of Sungrow Power Supply Group, and ACTUATE ENERGY, an energy storage platform backed by NGP, today announced the largest BESS transaction to date in Spain, comprising 380 MW and 1.5 GWh of storage capacity. The transaction establishes a long-term strategic partnership between Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy, based on the companies' complementary expertise and capabilities and underpinned by a shared commitment to develop, build and bring into operation Spain's first large-scale BESS portfolio, comprising seven advanced-stage projects. The first assets are already under construction, while the remainder of the portfolio is expected to commence construction in the coming months, with the full portfolio expected to reach Ready-to-Build (RtB) status during 2027 and enter commercial operation between 2027 and the first half of 2028. The transaction marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables' pioneering commitment to energy storage in Spain, which it launched several years ago. The portfolio comprises seven stand-alone BESS projects totalling 380 MW / 1.5 GWh. These include the Valencia Cluster, located in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón); Santiago, in Lousame (A Coruña); Berja, in the province of Almería; and the Navarra Cluster, located in Olite and Cordovilla. The agreement also leaves the door open to further collaboration on the development of future assets, reflecting both companies' commitment to continued growth in the energy storage market, strengthening the resilience of Spain's energy system and reinforcing Spain's position as a strategic market within Europe. A landmark transaction for Spain's BESS market The transaction comes at a time when Spain's electricity market is in critical need for energy storage, which is reaching a significant level of maturity, with storage becoming the technology with the largest volume of grid connection applications in Spain, ahead of both solar PV and wind. As Daniel Sánchez, CEO of Sungrow Renewables for Western Europe, noted: "This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain's BESS market. With 380 MW and 1.5 GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution." Sánchez further emphasises: "at Sungrow Renewables, we backed this market when it was still a bet on the future and helped pave the way through the development and commissioning of Sanxenxo, Spain's first stand-alone BESS plant. Today, we are taking a decisive step towards accelerating renewable energy integration and strengthening the stability of the power system, in a transaction that reinforces our long-term commitment to the Spanish market. Energy storage is no longer a promise for Spain: it is strategic infrastructure that we are turning into reality." Ben Skinner, CEO of Actuate Energy, said: "Spain is a market leader in deploying renewable energy, but battery storage has not kept pace. This portfolio marks a real step forward for the Spanish grid, adding flexible assets that respond in seconds to keep the system stable allowing more renewables to come online. For Actuate Energy, this is a landmark transaction that establishes our presence in Spain enabling our growth into Europe. We are delighted to partner with Sungrow Renewables, and we look forward to operating these projects for the benefit of the country and the communities that host them." Sungrow Renewables' continued strategy in Spain This latest milestone marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables' commitment to Spain and to the integration of energy storage. The company was a pioneer in Spain in the development of hybrid solar PV projects from 2022 onward, moved early into stand-alone BESS with its Sanxenxo project, and currently has stand-alone BESS assets already in operation in the country. Spain remains a strategic market for the company, which operates in more than 20 countries. Actuate Energy's entry into Europe with backing from NGP Actuate Energy focuses on dynamic European energy markets and is committed to supporting an accelerated transition toward renewable energy by investing in and operating energy storage assets that provide stability to the power system. Actuate Energy is backed by NGP, a premier energy private equity firm with over $25 billion of cumulative equity commitments. With this agreement, Spain becomes the starting point for Actuate Energy's entry into Europe, driven by the country's high renewable energy penetration, the ongoing need to provide grid stability, and the growth potential of a mature project pipeline. About Sungrow Renewables Sungrow Renewables Development Co., Ltd. is the renewable energy development and investment platform of Sungrow Power Supply Co., Ltd. and a national high-tech enterprise specializing in solar PV, wind power, energy storage, electric vehicle charging and multi-energy integration (wind, solar, storage and hydrogen). It provides integrated solutions covering the full project lifecycle, from R&D and development through design, construction and operations, and positions itself as the world's largest solar PV developer. The company has received recognitions including being named among the world's Top 500 New Energy Enterprises, China's Best ESG Employer and Most Socially Responsible Enterprise. In line with its mission of "Clean power for all," the company aims to become a global leader in new energy generation technology. artigo.texto: A Twenty Four Seven Data Centers, companhia brasileira de infraestrutura de colocation que projeta, constrói e opera data centers na América Latina, anunciou a contratação de Marcelo Issa como seu novo diretor de relações institucionais. Com cerca de 20 anos de experiência em relações governamentais e políticas públicas, o executivo vem da Pulso Público, uma consultoria voltada para formulação de normas e políticas públicas para empresas, organizações e entidades, onde atuou por mais de uma década como sócio diretor. Também no setor, foi supervisor na Patri Políticas Públicas, diretor de operações na e-Stratégia e assessor de gabinete do Governo do Estado de São Paulo. Nos anos 2000, coordenou a área de advocacy do Instituto Akatu e trabalhou como editor do projeto excelências, da Transparência Brasil. Esta última é uma organização não governamental e sem fins lucrativos que Issa cofundou em 2006 ao lado de outros 32 profissionais, entre eles professores, empresários, jornalistas, magistrados e procuradores. Desde 2016, o profissional desempenhava o papel de diretor executivo da instituição e deixou a função em dezembro do ano passado. Hoje, segue no conselho deliberativo da entidade como membro. Graduado em direito pela Universidade Presbiteriana Mackenzie, o profissional possui um mestrado em ciência política pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo (PUC-SP) e um mestrado em relações governamentais pela Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV). Em seu novo cargo, chega para liderar a agenda institucional da Twenty Four Seven em um momento de expansão do mercado de data centers no Brasil, o que exige atenção às questões regulatórias e à articulação com o poder público. “A implantação desses empreendimentos envolve desafios que vão além da construção e da operação, passando por temas como segurança jurídica, previsibilidade regulatória e disponibilidade energética. É uma oportunidade de contribuir para o desenvolvimento de um mercado cada vez mais estratégico para o Brasil”, comenta Issa. A Twenty Four Seven Data Centers foi fundada em 2024 pela Arch Capital, especializada em soluções de colocation, modelo em que empresas alugam espaço e infraestrutura física para hospedar seus servidores e equipamentos. A companhia atua em todo o ciclo de desenvolvimento de data centers, incluindo projeto, construção e operação, com soluções voltadas a provedores de nuvem, grandes players de tecnologia e organizações que demandam alta capacidade de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Seus primeiros empreendimentos estão concentrados no corredor entre São Paulo e Campinas. Em 2026, a empresa recebeu investimentos da gestora internacional Just Climate e de fundos administrados pela Kinea Investimentos, que se juntaram à Arch Capital em sua base acionária.

artigo.texto: O Brasil é responsável por aproximadamente 3% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa, segundo dados oficiais da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima. Essas emissões têm origem majoritariamente em setores como mudança do uso da terra, agropecuária e energia, refletindo o perfil produtivo e territorial do país. Ao mesmo tempo, o Brasil possui uma das matrizes elétricas mais limpas do mundo, conforme dados da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. Esse equilíbrio entre alto potencial de mitigação e relevância global nas emissões explica a adoção do modelo regulado: ele permite alinhar as metas nacionais do Acordo de Paris às oportunidades econômicas e tecnológicas de uma economia de baixo carbono. A criação do mercado regulado responde a três vetores principais: Compromissos internacionais - cumprir as metas do Acordo de Paris e das NDCs atualizadas do Brasil, que preveem redução de 67% das emissões até 2035, em relação aos níveis de 2005; Pressão econômica global – adaptar-se a mecanismos, com alta pegada de carbono; Oportunidade competitiva – atrair investimentos verdes e inovar em cadeias de valor baixas em emissões. O governo brasileiro reconheceu o SBCE como parte central do Plano de Transformação Ecológica, iniciativa coordenada pelo Ministério da Fazenda que prevê a mobilização de bilhões de reais em ativos verdes até 2030, conectando a regulação climática à nova economia sustentável. Em dezembro de 2024, o governo brasileiro sancionou a Lei 15.042/24, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões. O sistema estabelece que cada empresa participante receberá Autorização para Emissão de GEE, unidades que representam o direito de emitir uma quantidade específica de CO₂ equivalente. Essas autorizações poderão ser negociadas, guardadas ou usadas conforme a estratégia de cada organização. As operações e os saldos de créditos de carbono regulados serão registrados no Sistema Nacional de Redução de Emissões de GEE, plataforma pública de rastreabilidade e transparência ambiental mantida pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima.

artigo.texto: A próxima corrida dos data centers não será apenas por infraestrutura A corrida global pela inteligência artificial está redefinindo a importância estratégica da infraestrutura digital e não é uma novidade. Por Ana Cláudia Reis e Michel Hannas* – À medida que a economia digital acelera, liderança, competências e capital humano podem se tornar fatores tão decisivos quanto energia, conectividade e investimento. A corrida global pela inteligência artificial está redefinindo a importância estratégica da infraestrutura digital e não é uma novidade. Mas, o que antes era tratado como uma camada de suporte à atividade econômica passou a ocupar posição central na competitividade de países e organizações. Por exemplo, os Data Centers, conectividade, capacidade computacional e energia tornaram-se ativos fundamentais para viabilizar a próxima geração de crescimento econômico baseada em dados, automação e IA. Neste contexto, é possível observar que o Brasil reúne características raras. Poucos países combinam uma matriz energética predominantemente renovável, disponibilidade territorial, mercado consumidor relevante, conectividade crescente e potencial para expansão em larga escala. Não surpreende, portanto, que o país passe a ser visto como um dos mercados mais promissores para investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Mas, à medida que a conversa amadurece, surge uma questão que vai além da disponibilidade de energia, do acesso à rede ou da atração de capital: quem desenvolverá, operará e liderará essa nova infraestrutura? A ascensão da inteligência artificial transformou os data centers em algo maior do que uma agenda de tecnologia ou infraestrutura imobiliária. Eles passaram a ocupar uma posição estratégica na interseção entre energia, engenharia, conectividade, equipamentos críticos, capital e execução operacional. E, como acontece em toda infraestrutura crítica, a qualidade dos ativos físicos será apenas parte da equação. A capacidade de construir organizações preparadas para operar essa complexidade pode ser igualmente determinante para o sucesso do setor. A infraestrutura digital está criando uma nova demanda por capacidades Durante muitos anos, a discussão sobre talentos em tecnologia esteve concentrada principalmente em engenheiros de software, profissionais de infraestrutura de TI e especialistas em redes. A expansão dos data centers e o avanço da inteligência artificial ampliaram significativamente esse universo. A nova economia digital demanda profissionais capazes de operar ambientes computacionais de alta densidade, gerenciar infraestrutura crítica 24 horas por dia, integrar sistemas complexos de energia e conectividade, proteger ecossistemas digitais contra ameaças crescentes e sustentar operações cuja interrupção pode gerar impactos relevantes para clientes, mercados e cadeias produtivas inteiras. E nisso, ao mesmo tempo, a própria natureza das competências exigidas está mudando. Conhecimentos técnicos continuarão importantes, mas passam a coexistir com habilidades relacionadas à resolução de problemas complexos, gestão de riscos, colaboração interdisciplinar e aprendizagem contínua. Surge também uma demanda crescente por líderes e executivos comerciais capazes de gerir relacionamentos complexos com grandes clientes globais, incluindo hyperscalers, provedores de nuvem e empresas de tecnologia. Esses profissionais precisam reunir uma combinação ainda relativamente rara de competências: compreender os aspectos técnicos da infraestrutura digital, conduzir negociações estratégicas de longo prazo e atuar em ambientes internacionais, nos quais muitas das decisões são tomadas fora do mercado local. Em muitos casos, decisões sobre investimentos e contratação de capacidade são tomadas fora do Brasil, o que exige executivos capazes de atuar em estruturas matriciais, influenciar múltiplos stakeholders e conectar oportunidades locais às prioridades globais de seus clientes. E neste contexto, o conhecimento técnico precisa vir acompanhado de capacidade de relacionamento, negociação e coordenação global. Em um ambiente em que tecnologias, arquiteturas e modelos operacionais evoluem rapidamente, a capacidade de adaptação torna-se tão valiosa quanto o domínio técnico acumulado ao longo da carreira. E a transformação cria uma pressão crescente sobre organizações e sobre o próprio mercado de trabalho. Mas a questão não é apenas a disponibilidade de profissionais qualificados, mas a velocidade com que novas competências precisam ser desenvolvidas. Muitas das funções críticas para a infraestrutura digital da próxima década ainda estão emergindo. Outras sequer estão claramente definidas. Por essa razão, as organizações mais bem posicionadas provavelmente não serão aquelas que simplesmente competirem pelos mesmos talentos disponíveis no mercado, mas aquelas capazes de desenvolver competências internamente e criar mecanismos contínuos de evolução profissional. Em um ambiente marcado por escassez e transformação acelerada, a capacidade de aprender pode se tornar mais relevante do que a capacidade de contratar. *Ana Cláudia Reis é Senior Client Partner na Korn Ferry *Michel Hannas é Senior Client Partner na Korn Ferry

artigo.texto: A One-of-Three Veyron ‘Black Bess’ Sold Quietly in Cologne. Its Lineage Has Never Been Priced in Public. A Cologne dealer has marked as sold one of the three Bugatti Veyron Grand Sport Vitesse 'Black Bess' cars built in 2014. Amian Cars describes a one-owner example, first registered in July 2014, finished in black, showing 2,600 miles and inspected at a Bugatti dealer before handover. The price was "on request." The buyer, the date and the number were never published. That silence matters more than usual this autumn. In September, a 'Jean-Pierre Wimille' Legend sold for CHF 4,505,000 at RM Sotheby's in Zurich, a public auction record for any Veyron. We argued then that Zurich re-rated one chapter of Bugatti's Legends series, not the whole set. The Black Bess is a chapter whose case has never been argued in public, and this sale did nothing to change that. The Black Bess may be the tidiest idea in Les Légendes, and nobody can tell you what one is worth. Quiet dealer trades like this one keep it that way. The Only Legend That Honors a Car Bugatti built six Legends editions of three cars each in 2013 and 2014, all on the open Grand Sport Vitesse. Five honor people: Jean-Pierre Wimille, Jean Bugatti, Meo Costantini, Rembrandt Bugatti and Ettore Bugatti himself. The fifth edition, unveiled at Auto China in Beijing in April 2014, honors a machine. That machine is the Type 18. According to Bugatti's heritage material, only seven were built between 1912 and 1914. Ettore Bugatti drove one to a class win at the 1912 Mont Ventoux hill climb, and that result caught the attention of Roland Garros, the aviator who wanted to travel as fast on the ground as he did in the air. Garros took delivery of chassis 474 on September 18, 1913. Its 5-litre four-cylinder made more than 100 PS and reached about 160 km/h, and Bugatti describes it as the fastest road vehicle of its day. The name 'Black Bess' came later. The car survives as one of three Type 18s still in existence, and Evert Louwman lent it from his museum in The Hague for the 2014 premiere. Read that description again and it could be the Veyron's brief. The Veyron existed to be the fastest road car in the world, and the Grand Sport Vitesse set the roadster record at 408.84 km/h with its roof off. Bugatti's then-president, Wolfgang Schreiber, called the Type 18 the Veyron's "legitimate forerunner." Of the six tributes, this is the only one where the subject and the platform make the same argument. The Wimille car borrows Le Mans. The Black Bess borrows the Veyron's own reason for existing. What Bugatti Actually Built Mechanically, the Black Bess is a standard Grand Sport Vitesse: the 8.0-litre, quad-turbocharged W16 with 1,200 PS and 1,500 Nm. The work is in the finish. The exposed carbon body is painted entirely black, as the Type 18 was. Bugatti then added 24-carat gold to the horseshoe, the rear EB badge and the hub covers, and ran gold stripes from below the headlights across the front wings, tapering out at the door line. Bugatti says it was the first time real gold had been used on a Bugatti body. The fuel and oil caps are engraved 'Black Bess'. Inside, the headliner, seats and centre console are light beige, the dashboard and door trims are Havanna leather, and the steering wheel rim is red Crimson leather with matching stitching. The selector and console panel are rosewood. The door panels carry hand-painted scenes of the Type 18 and Garros's Morane-Saulnier Type H monoplane, made with an ink and impregnation process Bugatti developed for the car. The net price at launch was €2.15 million, slightly below the roughly €2.2 million Bugatti quoted for the first three editions. The Door Panels Are the Fingerprint One detail in Bugatti's 2014 announcement deserves more attention from buyers than it gets. Bugatti says no two of the six door panels across the three cars are identical. That makes the artwork a means of identification as reliable as a chassis plate. Anyone buying a Black Bess should be able to match the panels in the car against factory delivery photography and Bugatti's own records. That matters here because the Amian listing documents very little. It calls the car a "Veyron 16.4" coupe instead of a Grand Sport Vitesse. It quotes 1,250 Nm, the figure for the original Veyron, not the Vitesse's 1,500 Nm, and it describes the W16 as twin-turbocharged, not quad-turbo. It gives no chassis number and describes the interior only as "bespoke." None of this suggests anything wrong with the car. Dealer listings often run on generic templates. But it does mean the public record says nothing a buyer at this level should rely on. For a car like this, the paperwork is the factory file, the Bugatti inspection, the delivery records and a complete service history through Bugatti's network. The listing is also undated. Its gallery images sit in a July 2023 upload folder on the dealer's website, which suggests the car was photographed and offered well before Zurich. We cannot say when it sold, so it should be read as evidence of how these cars trade, not as a post-Wimille price signal. Why Private Trades Keep This Chapter Unpriced The public record for the Legends is thin. Bonhams sold a 'Meo Costantini' car online in August 2020 for $1,750,000, less than its price when new. RM Sotheby's sold the Wimille car this September for more than three times that. Both are racing tributes. We are not aware of a public auction result for a Black Bess, and with only three built, there may not be one for years. When the non-racing Legends change hands through dealers at "price on request," the market learns that demand exists and nothing about how deep it is. Sellers have obvious reasons to prefer it that way: a confidential sale cannot set a public benchmark that disappoints. The cost is borne by everyone else. Price discovery is a choice, and the owners of the quieter Legends keep choosing not to make it. Before You Ask for the Price - The nature of the story. The

artigo.texto: TELF AG on How Public Policies Are Reshaping Energy Storage Strategies TELF AG on public policies and energy transition The expansion of renewable energy is prompting governments to reconsider the scope of their energy policies. While the development of wind and solar power remains a central objective, public institutions are increasingly focusing on the infrastructure required to manage renewable electricity efficiently. A recent example comes from the United Kingdom, where the National Wealth Fund has confirmed its support for two large-scale battery storage projects in southern Scotland. The facilities will have a combined power capacity of 1 GW and an energy storage capacity of 2 GWh. The initiative reflects a broader transformation in public energy strategies, with governments increasingly involved in the development of infrastructure that complements renewable electricity generation. “The expansion of renewable energy is encouraging public institutions to address a wider range of infrastructure needs, particularly those associated with the management and distribution of electricity,” says Stanislav Kondrashov. The Changing Scope of Public Energy Policies For several years, many government initiatives related to the energy transition have focused on encouraging renewable electricity production. Regulatory measures, financial incentives and technological development programs have contributed to the construction of wind farms and photovoltaic facilities. However, the increasing availability of renewable electricity is creating new challenges. Electricity generation from wind and solar sources depends on weather conditions, meaning that production does not always coincide with consumption patterns. Governments are therefore paying greater attention to technologies capable of managing these fluctuations. Energy storage systems represent one of the most promising solutions in this area. The British National Wealth Fund has allocated approximately £87 million to support the development of the two Scottish battery storage projects. Their planned locations along electricity transmission corridors connecting Scotland and England could help address some of the challenges associated with renewable electricity distribution. Energy Storage and the Management of Renewable Electricity Scotland has particularly favorable conditions for wind energy generation. Its geographical characteristics and exposure to strong winds have supported the development of both offshore and onshore renewable energy facilities. However, the expansion of generation capacity can place additional pressure on existing transmission networks. When electricity production exceeds the capacity of the grid to transport it, renewable energy facilities may be required to temporarily reduce their output. This phenomenon, known as curtailment, illustrates the importance of developing infrastructure alongside renewable generation capacity. Battery energy storage systems, commonly referred to as BESS, can help address this issue. These facilities store electricity during periods of abundant generation and release it when demand increases or transmission conditions become more favorable. “The Scottish example illustrates how public policies can address some of the operational challenges emerging from the rapid expansion of renewable electricity generation,” explains Stanislav Kondrashov. Storage technologies can also contribute to grid frequency regulation and provide additional flexibility during periods of fluctuating electricity demand. Their effectiveness in addressing transmission congestion depends on their location, operating strategies and the characteristics of the surrounding electricity network. Public Policies and Critical Raw Material Supply Chains The growing attention devoted to energy storage infrastructure also has implications for industrial supply chains. Large-scale battery systems require various raw materials, each performing a specific function within the technology. Lithium is widely used in lithium-ion batteries, while graphite is commonly employed in battery anodes. Copper and aluminum are also used in electrical connections, current collectors and other system components. As governments expand their energy policies to include storage infrastructure, demand for these resources could be influenced by a broader range of public initiatives. This development highlights the relationship between energy policy, industrial planning and raw material availability. Decisions concerning electricity infrastructure may have repercussions across multiple stages of the supply chain, from mineral extraction and processing to battery manufacturing and system installation. “Public energy strategies are becoming increasingly interconnected with industrial policies, technological development and the availability of the materials needed to build modern electricity infrastructure,” concludes Stanislav Kondrashov. The Scottish projects offer an example of how public institutions can participate in this transformation. Rather than focusing exclusively on increasing renewable generation, governments are beginning to address the technical and infrastructural conditions necessary for its effective integration. The future of renewable energy may therefore depend not only on the number of wind turbines and solar panels installed, but also on the ability of public policies to support more flexible, resilient and efficient electricity systems. artigo.texto: ACME Solar Completes Commissioning of 255.12 MWh Battery Storage System for NHPC Renewable Energy Project ACME Solar has commissioned part of its battery storage project in Rajasthan. Commercial operations are set to begin later this week. Read more. ACME Solar has commissioned a 63.78 MW battery storage facility in Rajasthan, with an energy storage capacity of 255.12 MWh, under its NHPC renewable energy project. The company completed the commissioning on 25 November, with commercial operations scheduled to begin on 27 November. The commissioning was carried out through ACME Hybrid Urja Private Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar. The project is located at Mehar Nagar village in Pokharan tehsil of Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan. The company said the commissioning covers only the battery storage component of the NHPC FDRE project. ACME Solar Share Price Movement Shares of ACME Solar Holdings were trading higher on Thursday following the development. The stock touched an intraday high of ₹419.60, gaining 0.73% from its previous close of ₹416.55. It opened at ₹417.65 and slipped to an intraday low of ₹413.75 during the session. At 12:32 pm, ACME Solar Holdings shares were down 0.66% on the National Stock Exchange (NSE). What is the Total Battery Storage Capacity of the Project? The commissioned component has a discharge capacity of 63.78 MW and an installed capacity of 300 MWh. It forms part of a larger battery storage installation planned under the project. The total BESS component has a discharge capacity of 280 MW/1,120 MWh, against an installed capacity of 280 MW/1,316 MWh. ACME Solar has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with NHPC Ltd for the project. The latest commissioning marks another step in the company's execution of its FDRE project portfolio. However, the exchange filing did not disclose the project cost, expected revenue contribution or the financial impact of the commissioned capacity. How do Battery Energy Storage Systems Support Renewable Energy Projects? Power generation from renewable sources can vary through the day. Battery systems allow companies to store the electricity generated and release it when demand arises. Such systems are an important part of FDRE projects. They aim to provide renewable electricity in line with scheduled power requirements. The commissioned capacity will form part of ACME Solar's battery storage infrastructure for its NHPC project. In 2025, global Vehicle Solid State Battery production reached approximately 9680 MW , with an average global market price of around US$200 per kilowatt. A vehicle solid-state battery is an advanced energy storage system for electric vehicles that replaces the liquid or gel electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte (ceramic, sulfide, or polymer-based materials). This allows lithium ions to move between electrodes through a solid medium, significantly improving energy density, safety, thermal stability, and cycle life, while reducing fire and leakage risks. Solid-state batteries are considered a next-generation EV battery technology, currently transitioning from R&D to early commercialization. The upstream of vehicle solid-state batteries includes lithium resources, cathode materials (high-nickel NCM, LFP variants), anode materials (silicon-carbon, lithium metal), solid electrolytes (oxides, sulfides, polymers), and current collectors, supplied by companies such as Albemarle, SQM, Ganfeng Lithium, Tianqi Lithium, BASF, Umicore, and CATL material ecosystem partners. The midstream consists of battery manufacturers such as Toyota, QuantumScape, Solid Power, CATL, Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Factorial Energy. Downstream applications include electric vehicle OEMs (Tesla, Toyota, Volkswagen, BYD, Mercedes-Benz, NIO) as well as premium energy storage, robotics, and aerospace systems. Vehicle solid-state batteries are currently in a critical transition phase from technology validation to early commercialization. The key drivers include the demand for higher energy density, longer driving range, faster charging, and improved safety in electric vehicles. By replacing liquid electrolytes with solid materials, solid-state batteries fundamentally address safety risks and energy limitations of conventional lithium-ion systems. However, challenges remain, including high interfacial resistance, high material costs, manufacturing scalability issues, and limited cycle stability. The industry is currently adopting a "semi-solid first, full-solid later" roadmap. Future development will focus on lithium-metal anodes, scalable sulfide electrolytes, solid-solid interface engineering, and automotive-grade mass production technologies. artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo Uma reportagem publicada nesta quarta-feira (25) pela Reuters informou que empresas ligadas a Alice Huang, a empresária apontada como espiã chinesa por agências de inteligência dos EUA e com quem o CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, teve um caso, equiparam grandes data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) na China. De acordo com a agência britânica, registros do banco central chinês indicam que tais empresas obtiveram financiamento oferecendo como garantias 764 servidores e módulos de IA avaliados em US$ 270 milhões e equipamentos usados para conectá-los em grandes redes de computação avaliados em US$ 31 milhões. A Reuters apurou que grande parte desse hardware foi alocada em um grande data center em Xangai, associado a um projeto de computação de IA lançado no âmbito de uma parceria estratégica entre a gigante chinesa de tecnologia Tencent e o governo do distrito de Songjiang. A agência britânica disse que os registros do banco central da China não detalham se tais infraestruturas utilizam chips cuja exportação ao país asiático foi vetada pelos Estados Unidos. Na segunda-feira (23), o Departamento de Comércio dos EUA incluiu a Megaspeed, empresa sediada em Singapura e ligada a Alice Huang, em sua lista negra comercial. A empresa negou qualquer irregularidade e afirmou que Alice Huang deixou a empresa em agosto de 2025. Na segunda-feira, onze dias após ter renunciado, Jensen Huang retornou ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia, com a empresa americana e o governo Donald Trump alegando que a recondução dele não representa riscos à segurança nacional. O presidente americano admitiu que intercedeu junto ao Conselho de Administração da gigante dos chips para que Jensen Huang fosse reconduzido ao posto. A volta do CEO fez as ações da Nvidia dispararem. Segundo informações do jornal britânico Financial Times, Trump, que é acionista da empresa, teria ganhado até US$ 15 milhões com essa movimentação de mercado.

artigo.texto: 24 Novembro 2026 Demanda de energia elétrica foi de 82 TWh, cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade do país, com emissões de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. A informação é publicada por ClimaInfo, 24-11-2026. Em um ano, entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, os 403 maiores centros de dados dos Estados Unidos emitiram mais dióxido de carbono do que a Dinamarca, que tem cerca de 6 milhões de habitantes. É o que mostra um estudo publicado na revista Nature Sustainability na semana passada. A pesquisa é uma das primeiras a estimar o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de centros de dados hiperescaláveis (HDCs, sigla em inglês) desde o surgimento da inteligência artificial, segundo a Euronews. Em diferentes cenários de carga, esses HDCs consumiram entre 68 e 99 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade, associados a aproximadamente 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (MtCO₂). No cenário médio, a demanda de eletricidade desses data centers foi de 82 TWh, correspondendo a 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA, com emissões de CO₂ atribuíveis de cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono. Cerca de 54% da geração atribuída foi proveniente de fontes de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás e carvão. A estimativa de emissões é de duas a três vezes maior do que a demonstrada em estudos anteriores, afirmou a autora sênior do estudo, Francesca Dominici, professora de bioestatística de Harvard. “É o equivalente à emissão de CO₂ de um pequeno país europeu”, disse a especialista, acrescentando que os planos para mais 2 mil centros de dados tornam essa quantidade ainda mais preocupante para o futuro, destaca a AP. Os HDCs são a maior classe de centros de dados, sendo o tipo que executa serviços em nuvem e treina grandes modelos de IA. Os edifícios da amostra tinham uma capacidade elétrica média de cerca de 40 megawatts, explica a Earth.com. 🔍 Adicione o Instituto Humanitas Unisinos – IHU às suas fontes favoritas do Google Os pesquisadores começaram o estudo com 675 locais candidatos de um banco de dados comercial e mantiveram os 403 que puderam ser confirmados. Cada endereço foi associado a um telhado, e sua área foi verificada no OpenStreetMap. Em seguida, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite e aéreas em busca de indícios de um centro de dados: grandes telhados uniformes, equipamentos de refrigeração e uma subestação ao lado. Dos HDCs analisados, 142 estão localizados na Virgínia, que abriga mais estruturas desse tipo do que qualquer outro estado dos EUA, 56 no Oregon e 38 em Ohio. Nenhum data center opera em sua capacidade nominal máxima a cada hora, e as empresas não divulgam suas cargas reais. Por isso, a equipe multiplicou a capacidade de cada instalação pelas horas do ano e por um fator de carga. Os pesquisadores executaram quatro versões desse fator, desde uma carga leve até uma destinada a abranger o treinamento pesado de IA, para chegar aos resultados. Agora a equipe planeja examinar os efeitos das emissões associadas aos HDCs na saúde, conta Francesca. “As centrais elétricas movidas a combustíveis fósseis nos sistemas regionais de distribuição de energia, associadas a essa demanda, também liberam outros poluentes, como partículas finas, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, que estão diretamente ligados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura”, disse a especialista. As pessoas que respiram esses poluentes vivem perto das usinas, que podem estar longe de qualquer centro de dados.

artigo.texto: Sky negocia compra de ativos do braço de data centers da V.tal Operação submetida ao Cade envolve empresa ligada a um dos maiores projetos de infraestrutura digital do Nordeste A Sky, tradicionalmente conhecida por sua atuação no mercado de televisão por assinatura, negocia a aquisição de ativos da Tectodigital II, sociedade de propósito específico ligada ao braço de data centers do grupo V.tal. A operação foi submetida à análise do Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) e tornada pública nesta semana. A empresa envolvida na negociação está associada ao Mega Lobster, data center localizado em Fortaleza, no Ceará. O empreendimento é beneficiário de um pacote de financiamento de aproximadamente 233 milhões de reais aprovado pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) para sua expansão. Fortaleza ocupa uma posição estratégica no mercado de infraestrutura digital em razão da concentração de cabos submarinos que conectam o Brasil à América do Norte, à Europa e à África. A negociação ocorre em meio à corrida das empresas de telecomunicações e tecnologia por infraestrutura capaz de atender à crescente demanda por processamento, armazenamento e transmissão de dados. O edital publicado pelo Cade classifica o negócio como uma aquisição de ativos no segmento de tratamento de dados e hospedagem na internet. O valor da transação e o detalhamento dos ativos envolvidos não constam do edital.

artigo.texto: Generali China to use AI in energy storage insurance pricing The partnership will also develop coverage against battery capacity degradation. Generali China Insurance and Beijing Syi Tsing Energy Technology have signed a strategic cooperation agreement to integrate battery safety technology into insurance underwriting and pricing for energy storage power stations. Under the partnership, the two firms will build an artificial intelligence underwriting platform using real-world operating data, historical failure records, and battery safety checks. The system will convert power station operating data into standardised risk scores to calculate insurance premiums, replacing traditional pricing methods with data-led assessments. The companies will also develop performance guarantee insurance for energy storage assets. This coverage will use Syi Tsing Energy’s battery lifespan prediction algorithm—which combines electrochemical models with AI—to compensate asset owners if battery capacity drops below expected levels. According to the firms, the agreement is designed to shift energy storage insurance from paying out after an incident to preventing failures before they happen. The joint framework will cover risk assessment before a policy is issued, real-time safety monitoring while the policy is active, and loss assessment if damage occurs.

artigo.texto: SpaceX has installed more than $250 million worth of Tesla Megapacks at its new data center at Starbase, Texas — a site that was still bare dirt less than 90 days ago. The scale and speed of the buildout, flagged on Wednesday night by Tesla investor Sawyer Merritt, underscore how aggressively Elon Musk's two companies are now co-engineering an independent power grid to feed SpaceX's compute ambitions. The Megapack farm visible in the latest aerial imagery is part of a much larger infrastructure push at the southern tip of Texas, where SpaceX is building a self-contained energy and compute campus alongside its Starship launch operations. It is also the latest confirmation that SpaceX has become one of Tesla Energy's single largest customers — a relationship that is now visible on both companies' financial statements. A data center built in under 90 days Merritt's post emphasized the pace: the parcel hosting the new facility was undeveloped dirt roughly three months ago. Construction tempo at Starbase has consistently outrun traditional industrial timelines — the nearby Gigabay expansion and launch-pad rebuilds have moved on similar cycles — but standing up a data center shell and a nine-figure battery installation inside a quarter is unusual even by SpaceX standards. The energy build is tied to a broader $24 billion initial investment at Starbase for a gas-fired power plant and "super-compute facility," according to filings reviewed by the Texas Tribune. The explicit goal, per planning documents, is for the campus to generate its own electricity and operate independently of the public grid. In that architecture, Megapacks are not a backup — they are the buffer that makes a private, gas-plus-storage grid viable for 24/7 AI workloads. Key figures At current Megapack 2XL specs — roughly 3.9 MWh of storage per unit — $250 million buys on the order of 150–200 units depending on configuration and software bundles. That is consistent with the density visible in the Starbase imagery, and it slots neatly beneath the 1,377-unit combined figure that analysts at SemiAnalysis attributed to SpaceX's "Colossus and Starbase" sites earlier this month. How Starbase fits into SpaceX's compute strategy Starbase has always been a launch facility first, but the campus is quietly being re-pitched as a compute node. Our earlier coverage of the Gigabay expansion showed how the physical footprint has already outgrown what Starship assembly alone needs. The data center visible today is the logical next step: co-locate compute with cheap on-site gas power, a captive battery buffer, and SpaceX's own Starlink backhaul. That mirrors the Memphis playbook. In Q2 2026, SpaceX disclosed $295 million of Megapack purchases to power AI data centers in Memphis — the Colossus cluster xAI is building. As detailed in our Memphis data center breakdown, those sites also depend heavily on Tesla battery storage to smooth gas-turbine output and ride through grid events. Starbase appears to be a direct replication of that model, this time on SpaceX-controlled land with fewer local-grid constraints. Zoom out further and the pattern is consistent. According to SemiAnalysis, SpaceX is now Tesla's largest Megapack customer, with purchases potentially reaching up to roughly 8 GWh across its sites — a significant chunk of which has already been delivered to Colossus 2. A large signed-but-unbilled Megapack order attributed to SpaceX is also expected to show up in future Tesla disclosures. The Starbase installation is another visible piece of that backlog landing on concrete. Why Tesla owners should care Even if you'll never see a Megapack on your driveway, the Starbase install matters for Tesla shareholders and the broader Tesla Energy thesis. Three reasons: - Megapack is no longer a sideshow. SpaceX alone is tracking toward multi-hundred-million-dollar annual spend on Megapacks. That gives Tesla Energy a predictable, high-margin anchor customer independent of utility RFP cycles. - Deployment speed is the product. The sub-90-day Starbase buildout is a demonstration — to hyperscalers watching Colossus, Memphis, and now Starbase — that Megapack can move at AI-datacenter timelines. That's the pitch Tesla has been making to Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon-scale buyers. - Vertical integration is tightening. SpaceX designs the launch vehicles, builds the compute, owns the Starlink backhaul, and now buys the batteries from Tesla. For investors who own both the public stock and SpaceX exposure via secondaries, the capital is increasingly recycling inside the Musk ecosystem. What to watch next - Tesla's Q4 2026 Energy deployment number. A Starbase install of this size should be visible in GWh deployed when Tesla reports in late January. - SpaceX's next financial disclosure. The H2 2026 filing will show whether Megapack spending accelerated from the $329M H1 pace. - Starbase gas plant permits. The Megapacks only make sense paired with on-site generation; watch Texas PUC and TCEQ filings for the gas-plant timeline. - Starmind satellite constellation ramp. As covered in our FCC Starmind clearance piece, orbital compute is coming — but ground-based Starbase is where the first workloads will run. Editor's view The headline here is not really the $250 million — it's the 90 days. Hyperscalers have spent the last decade telling the market that data centers are three-to-five-year projects, gated by transformers, interconnects, and power purchase agreements. SpaceX and Tesla are demonstrating, in public, a parallel stack that doesn't wait for any of that: self-generate the power, self-buffer with Megapacks, self-build the shell. If that model holds, Megapack's addressable market stops looking like a utility product and starts looking like a core piece of AI infrastructure. Starbase is the proof of concept. artigo.texto: On November 26, 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration published a notice of proposed information collection under the Paperwork Reduction Act to launch Form EIA-872, the first federal statistical survey dedicated to measuring facility-level energy consumption across large data centers. The new annual collection directly impacts university high-performance computing centers, national laboratories, and academic energy economists tracking the rapid expansion of power-intensive digital infrastructure. What happened The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA) formally initiated public review for the Data Center Energy Consumption Survey (DCECS), designated as Form EIA-872. The agency placed Federal Register Document 2026-24077 on public inspection on November 26, 2026, ahead of scheduled publication on November 27, 2026. Signed in Washington, D.C., on November 23, 2026, by Pushpal Mukhopadhyay, Director of the EIA Office of Statistical Methods and Research, the notice requests Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval to institute mandatory, facility-level data reporting for high-density computing infrastructure under statutory authorities granted by 15 U.S.C. 772(b) and 42 U.S.C. 7101. According to the official text of Federal Register Document 2026-24077, Form EIA-872 will collect annual operational and physical data from data center facilities across the United States that have an information technology (IT) design capacity of at least 1 megawatt (MW). The survey addresses a critical blind spot in federal statistical programs: while federal statistical agencies track aggregate utility generation and commercial floor-space usage, the government has never collected uniform, facility-level end-use power metrics from large computing installations. Key details The proposed data collection establishes specific structural parameters, operational thresholds, and legal protections that govern which facilities must report and how statistical data will be handled: Qualifying capacity threshold: Mandatory reporting applies to all facilities with an IT design capacity of at least 1 MW. Facilities that fall below this 1 MW design threshold are entirely excluded from the survey scope. Covered facility categories: Eligible sites include enterprise data centers, commercial colocation facilities, hyperscale cloud centers, edge computing hubs, carrier hotels, network gateways, cryptocurrency mining sites, and emerging super intelligence (SI) artificial intelligence computing clusters. Campus definition: The survey defines a data center facility as a dedicated building, multiple buildings, or a delineated portion of a structure whose primary purpose is housing servers, storage, and networking hardware. Functionally integrated multi-building campuses that share common power delivery or cooling infrastructure are treated as unified reporting units. Protection of proprietary data: EIA explicitly stated that it is not proposing to collect confidential business information concerning the commercial customers or computing tenants that these facilities serve. All reported data will be protected under the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act of 2018 (CIPSEA, 44 U.S.C. 3572), which guarantees that individual responses cannot be disclosed in identifiable form and may only be published in aggregate statistical summaries. Reporting schedule: Data collection will commence in 2027, gathering operational and consumption data for the previous 2026 reference year. The notice outlines the substantial administrative scope and estimated compliance burden across the domestic data center industry: Background and context Historically, the federal government monitored commercial energy use through the Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey (CBECS), a sample-based survey conducted every several years that last gathered field data for the 2018 reference cycle. However, EIA concluded that CBECS is structurally inadequate for evaluating modern computational facilities. Data centers exhibit unprecedented power densities—often exceeding standard office buildings by orders of magnitude—and rely on continuous baseline electrical draws, complex uninterruptible power supply (UPS) arrays, and sophisticated air- or liquid-cooling infrastructures that standard real estate surveys cannot capture. The data gap has become acute as artificial intelligence workloads accelerate electricity demand across regional power grids. Recent Department of Energy assessments of data center electricity demand, supported by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory research, estimated that domestic data centers accounted for approximately 176 to 192 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023 and 2024, or roughly 4.4% to 4.7% of total national electricity consumption. Projections suggest this figure could reach nearly 12% of total domestic electricity consumption by 2030, driven by the expansion of hyperscale facilities and academic high-performance computing facilities. Reaction and sector perspectives Independent energy economists and grid policy analysts have welcomed the federal initiative while underscoring the severe forecasting challenges confronting utilities and regional transmission organizations. In an analytical study titled The Hype on Hyperscalers: Data Centers and Growing Electricity Demand, published by Resources for the Future, researchers Molly Robertson and Karen Palmer highlighted the extreme uncertainty clouding power growth forecasts. Robertson and Palmer observed that while corporate announcements project massive energy requirements, data centers can be built in two to three years, whereas constructing transmission lines and clean energy generation assets requires five to ten years. The resulting planning friction has prompted utilities to explore specialized clean transition tariffs to shield residential ratepayers from infrastructure upgrade costs. EIA lead

artigo.texto: ANDERSON — As battery energy storage systems proliferate in the United States, officials have sought to dispel what they say are misconceptions about their safety. Battery energy storage systems, or BESS, help stabilize electrical grids by “providing steady power flow despite fluctuations from inconsistent generation of renewable energy sources and other disruptions,” according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The Clean Coalition, a nonprofit organization “whose mission is to accelerate the transition to renewable energy and a modern grid through technical, policy and project development expertise,” says BESS helps sources like solar panels and wind turbines reach their full potential by storing excess energy produced during times of high generation and dispersing it when those sources are unavailable. The facilities operate by using lithium-ion batteries to receive and store electrical currents, according to the Indiana Office of Energy Development. “Individual battery cells are grouped together to form battery packs,” according to a study commissioned by the IOED. “Each system has cooling and fire systems to manage safety risks. Each battery storage facility is required to provide emergency response plans as a condition of project approval through Indiana Department of Homeland Security. Operators are required to provide training to first responders, offering instruction on proper responses to battery storage system emergencies.” The Clean Coalition goes on to point out several benefits of BESS, including job creation and the generation of tax revenue for local governments. The Clean Coalition’s website also mentions that BESS is essential in reducing the “environmental footprint of energy generation,” and Rebecca TeKolste, the director of climate and energy at the Hoosier Environmental Council, said BESS is an important tool. “You’re really able to leverage those renewable resources throughout all times of the day, regardless of whether or not the wind is blowing and the sun is shining,” TeKolste said. “Batteries can store any kind of energy. It could be they’re storing energy from gas plants, solar — it really just depends on what the utility has in excess.” TeKolste acknowledged that some people hold safety concerns related to BESS, with several fires breaking out at facilities years ago. TeKolste said batteries are considerably safer now than they were in the past. “There’s always going to be some challenges with safety considerations,” TeKolste said. “Largely, those have been mitigated with the improvements of technology over the last couple of decades. I think now what we are seeing is the primary challenges with batteries rather than safety. Now they’re much more in the supply chain. “Batteries rely on rare Earth metals, and in some cases, there are some concerns about labor when it comes to where those metals are being mined.” Currently, there are nine operating utility-scale battery energy storage systems in Indiana. TeKolste said regulating them is difficult because decisions are typically made through local zoning ordinances. With 92 counties in Indiana, that means up to 92 different potential sets of rules. Sean Coffington, a clean energy organizer at Greenlight America, said that “battery energy storage systems, as part of the electrical grid, are a net environmental positive.” When talking about the placement of BESS facilities, Coffington said their installations near population clusters are logical. “You hear a lot about these systems being built near population centers,” Coffington said. “You can think of it like a water tower on top of an apartment building. We need electricity where the people are, and if we’re producing extra electricity, it makes sense to hold it in storage near where it will need to be used.” TeKolste said when looking at other alternatives, BESS is a better option. “If you look at an apples-to-apples comparison between mining, burning and storing coal ash, that is a known, certain risk to communities, whereas the battery technology has lower risk on almost every metric,” TeKolste said. “Everything has some level of risk, but the level of risk to a battery system is a lot lower than the level of risk of running a coal plant for the same amount of energy. “It’s all part of a system where there are trade-offs,” she continued. “From our perspective, batteries are a solution to get some of these more polluting, more expensive and more carbon-intensive resources offline faster and used significantly less.”

artigo.texto: Justiça Federal nega pedido de suspensão do leilão de baterias ABEEólica questionava principalmente o custeio da contratação das baterias, que por definição legal foi imputado aos geradores de energia A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal negou nesta quarta-feira (25) um pedido de tutela de urgência que buscava suspender a realização do primeiro leilão para contratação de baterias para o setor elétrico brasileiro, marcado para a próxima semana. Ao negar o pedido, apresentado pela associação de energia eólica ABEEólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica), o juiz Diego Câmara entendeu que não estavam presentes no caso os requisitos para a concessão da medida, como perigo de dano ou o risco ao resultado útil do processo. Na ação civil pública, a ABEEólica questionava principalmente o custeio da contratação das baterias, que por definição legal foi imputado aos geradores de energia. Segundo a entidade, a lei que impôs o ônus aos geradores é inconstitucional. Em paralelo, a ABEEólica também apontava "vícios" na estruturação do certame de baterias pela Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), citando a falta de uma regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos entre os diferentes geradores. Sobre a questão da inconstitucionalidade, o juiz observou que a entidade também entrou com ação no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) sobre o tema, e avaliou que "não é prudente que este Juízo... antecipe o juízo sobre a validade de lei federal que a própria parte autora submeteu à Corte Constitucional". Já sobre a alegada ilegalidade do certame, por ter sido convocado antes da definição do rateio do encargo entre os geradores, o juiz disse que não há norma legal ou regulamentar que condicione a realização do leilão à definição prévia pela agência reguladora Aneel do rateio do encargo. O juiz considerou ainda que não há dano iminente aos geradores associado ao leilão, já que a disputa marcada para a próxima semana não corresponde ao início da cobrança de encargos -- algo que somente ocorreria com a entrada em operação dos projetos, em 1º de agosto de 2028. O juiz citou ainda em sua decisão elementos trazidos em defesa da manutenção do leilão pelo governo, como o risco de déficit de potência já a partir do próximo ano.
