artigo.texto: Two forces are behind falling energy storage costs, which is a boon for the clean energy industry. The market features growing competition among battery manufacturers and a possible lithium surplus in 2027. Here's what to know As SolarQuarter detailed, InfoLink's Energy Storage Supply Chain Price Forecast Report projects a slight lithium surplus in 2027. Battery-grade lithium carbonate prices could fall to about 99,800–117,900 Chinese yuan ($14,945-$17,656) per U.S. ton in the first half of that year. The forecast comes after declines in storage-cell prices. In July 2026, the tax-inclusive average prices for both 280 amp-hour and 314 amp-hour lithium iron phosphate storage cells dropped 4% to 0.36 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to the outlet. Smaller, 100 amp-hour cells averaged 0.44 yuan per watt-hour, down 2.7% from June 2026. For households facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity rates, whole-home batteries can keep essentials running during outages, while leases can help protect homes without upwards of $20,000 in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace connecting battery shoppers with trusted partners offering unique prices and exclusive deals — another avenue for homeowners exploring backup power as storage-cell costs decline. More background The cost of lithium iron phosphate cathode material used in storage applications declined to approximately 47,800 yuan ($7,158) per U.S. ton, bringing tax-inclusive storage-cell production costs to around 0.31 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to SolarQuarter. These declines can translate to savings down the road for consumers looking to tap into their storage systems. Home batteries can also help reduce energy bills by supplying stored electricity during expensive peak-pricing periods. For households seeking a smaller-scale option, Pila offers plug-and-play battery backup at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. What's being done? Intense competition among battery manufacturers as supply expands is putting additional pressure on storage-cell prices, according to SolarQuarter. Lithium carbonate prices could still rise before the projected surplus in 2027. InfoLink's September and October 2026 price forecast is about 131,500–136,100 yuan ($19,692-20,381) per U.S. ton, above the expected August 2026 average near 127,000 yuan ($19,018) per U.S. ton. The firm expects seasonal demand and restocking to support that increase. According to SolarQuarter, China will begin taxing lithium-ion battery consumption at 2% on September 1, 2026, with the rate rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Meanwhile, the estimated U.S. tariff rate for lithium-ion battery systems originating in China is around 40.9%.

artigo.texto: The 2026 midterm elections that swept Democrats into power in Congress and state legislatures also delivered a stunning rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry. Ballot measures that limited the construction of data centers – from California to Kansas to North Dakota – were approved by voters in 40 of 41 instances. These measures included the Kansas prohibition on construction of a type of battery energy storage system, a 180-day moratorium on data centers in Maine, and the outright ban on data center construction in Ohio. Drawing on recent survey data, we suggest that the Democratic sweep and the nationwide rejection of data centers are related. Republicans’ connections with an unpopular AI industry may have contributed to their poor showing at the polls. We are survey researchers. Our August 2026 survey of a nationally representative sample of 1,000 American adults shows that opposition to data centers is widespread. The survey shows that 65% of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. This opposition is bipartisan, with 76% of Democrats, 67% of independents and 52% of Republicans opposed to the sites. To better understand the sources of this opposition, we asked respondents to explain it in their own words. Twenty-eight percent of respondents voiced concerns about the negative environmental impact of data centers. One respondent stated: “Draining our water reserves significantly with a data center would be catastrophic to our region.” Some respondents, 15%, also expressed concerns about data centers’ negative impact on their quality of life. For example, one respondent said: “Noise issues, energy issues and visual site are three issues that are major concerns for a AI data center to be in the area I live in.” Ten percent of respondents singled out the centers’ connection to increased utility costs. One respondent said that “ever since a data center has been built in my local area the prices of water and electricity have more than doubled.” Finally, 13% of respondents expressed a broad distrust of AI and the industry itself, with one stating, “I think that AI needs to be better regulated and a lot more developed and proven safe before any massive full scale deployment.” Despite mounting public opposition to data centers, President Donald Trump expressed strong support for data center construction before Election Day. He said that if Americans want to live in “crime-infested areas” and “squalor,” they should not have a data center. Days after the midterms, Trump threatened to penalize U.S. companies that build data centers overseas. As widespread opposition to data centers grew through 2026, Republican congressional candidates increasingly had to weigh loyalty to Trump against local backlash. As Election Day neared, many Republican candidates had distanced themselves from unrestricted data center construction. In contrast, many Democrats made opposition to data centers an important theme of their campaigns. Our poll suggests that these efforts may have resonated with voters. Among Americans who expressed opposition to data centers, 48% indicated they would support the local Democratic candidate in the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 25% for the Republican candidate. And 47% of those living in states that held a Senate election were planning on voting for the Democratic candidate, while 28% planned to vote for the Republican Senate candidate. Even taking partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics into account, opposition to data centers was associated with an intention to support Democratic House and Senate candidates. Given widespread public concern about data center construction, Democrats have electoral incentives to make AI regulation a part of their legislative agenda in the new Congress. Whether or not they enact new legislation, popular opposition to data centers is unlikely to abate anytime soon. Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links.

artigo.texto: UK and EU aim to link emissions trading schemes by January 2028 The UK and EU have agreed to link their emissions trading systems, targeting 1 January 2028 for the arrangement to take effect alongside the UK's planned expansion of carbon pricing to international shipping. IMAGE: Flags of the UK and the EU. Getty Images The agreement could simplify compliance for shipping companies operating under both schemes by allowing them to use UK and EU carbon allowances interchangeably, the UK's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in an explainer on 20 November. Under the planned expansion, the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) is set to cover 50% of emissions from international voyages between UK and non-UK ports for vessels of 5,000 GT and above from 1 January 2028. The UK ETS has already covered 100% of emissions from domestic voyages and emissions at berth in UK ports since 1 July 2026. The EU ETS similarly covers 50% of emissions from voyages between EU and non-EU ports, while requiring shipping companies to account for all emissions on voyages between EU ports. The UK ETS will also adopt the EU's approach to neighbouring container transhipment ports. Ports on the European Commission's designated list will not count as UK ports of call when determining which voyage emissions fall under the scheme. The list is updated every two years. Once linked, the two schemes will continue operating separately but allow shipping companies to use allowances from either market to meet their emissions obligations. This could eliminate the need for operators covered by both schemes to purchase UK allowances (UKAs) and EU allowances (EUAs) separately. The arrangement is also intended to cover emissions obligations for 2027, with the first deadline for using allowances interchangeably scheduled for 30 September 2028. The UK and EU are also working towards a common administrative process that could allow shipping companies to manage compliance under both schemes together. The UK also plans to remove its minimum auction price for carbon allowances when the link takes effect. Impact on shipping The agreement aims to bring UK ETS shipping rules more closely in line with those of the EU ETS, including requirements for monitoring, reporting and verifying emissions. The UK plans to end the temporary arrangement that allows shipping companies to surrender allowances for only 50% of emissions on voyages between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. These voyages are expected to face the full 100% requirement from 2028, bringing them in line with other domestic UK routes. Meanwhile, passenger and ro-pax vessels serving islands with fewer than 200,000 residents and no road or rail connection to the mainland are expected to qualify for a temporary surrender derogation until at least 31 December 2030. Ice-class vessels are also set to qualify for a 5% reduction in their allowance surrender obligations until at least the same date. The agreement also addresses how shipping companies can account for lower-emission fuels. Operators would be able to apply a zero-emission factor to eligible biofuels, renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) and recycled carbon fuels, provided they meet the sustainability and greenhouse gas savings requirements under the EU Renewable Energy Directive. The UK government has also said it will review how its carbon pricing rules interact with any future global emissions measure adopted by the IMO. The review would aim to avoid charging shipping companies twice for the same emissions while keeping compliance requirements manageable. “Any review would take into account any relevant changes to the EU ETS, and its outcomes will maintain support for maritime decarbonisation, and remain consistent with net zero,” the department said. The UK and EU are working towards bringing the two carbon markets together by January 2028, with technical preparations and legislative approvals still required. By Konica Bhatt Please get in touch with comments or additional info to news@engine.online

artigo.texto: Residents in a rural community in southern Wisconsin are calling for the rejection of a new data center proposal. But the developer says the project would be much smaller than the massive data center campuses being built in other parts of the state. Radius DC, a Colorado-based developer, hopes to build a 100,000 square-foot data center on nearly 40-acres in the village of Johnson Creek, located between Madison and Milwaukee. The village board had been set to vote on the proposal this week, but decided to put off making a decision after residents spoke out at the meeting. Residents who spoke with WPR shared concerns ranging from what they described as a lack of transparency from the village to negative impacts to the environment and local wildlife. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “Everything came about way too fast, and the community wasn’t notified properly, in my opinion,” said Miranda Taylor, a community organizer. “That has created a lot of distrust in this business and the village board itself, and I think that’s where a lot of the opposition is also coming from.” Lindsay Kinateder, who lives in Johnson Creek, said she had too many unanswered questions about the project. “I think we need to slow down, we need to evaluate all of this and we need to make sure that there’s minimal risk and harm to the wildlife, to the environment and to the people that are living close to this area,” she said. The village board is expected to take up the proposal again on Jan. 11. Johnson Creek is in Jefferson County, which passed an 18-month data center moratorium this summer. But that moratorium doesn’t apply to municipalities in the county with their own zoning codes. Jefferson County Board Chair Steve Nass said the county passed the moratorium to give itself time to craft local zoning and regulations on data centers. “We felt that we didn’t have enough information to write a decent ordinance, or really to feel that we could competently regulate it without doing some more study,” Nass said. Some residents feel the Johnson Creek proposal goes against the intent of the moratorium. “It seems (like) a bad faith action to move forward with that, considering the moratorium,” said Cody Stark, who lives kitty-corner from the development site. “I understand the position that the county is in. They can’t actually make any decisions for cities or villages, but — to me — it does go against what I feel like the public wishes were intended to be on that.” Johnson Creek Village Administrator Kyle Ellefson said the village has already passed an ordinance that sets regulations on these types of developments. He said those rules would prevent a hyperscale data center — like those under construction in Mount Pleasant or Port Washington — from coming to the community. Ellefson said the proposed project would be located in a tax increment financing district created last year to support a separate manufacturing project, but would not receive incentives from the village. The village’s proposed development agreement also includes language that would prevent the data center from expanding beyond its proposed 105,000 square feet. Under the agreement, the developer would commit to creating at least $35 million in assessed property value on the site annually for 15 years. “If they don’t meet that level, they will make it up with a payment in lieu of taxes, or a PILOT payment,” Ellefson said. “They also agree that they will not challenge the assessment if it’s at or below 45 million dollars.” The proposal has come as data centers have become increasingly unpopular in Wisconsin. An October Marquette Law School poll found 75 percent of state voters believe the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits. Recent reports from state regulators have raised concerns about spiking electricity demand tied to the developments, while environmental groups have also raised concerns about water usage. But the project in Johnson Creek would use far less water and electricity than two of the data center projects tied to spiking electricity demand, according to the developer. RadiusDC says their data center would require 20 megawatts of power and would use a closed-loop cooling system that would be filled with 30,000-gallons of water. The company says water would be cycled through the system with only occasional top-offs. For context, Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant is expected to need 8.4 million gallons of water each year and could need 2.1 gigawatts by 2030. Robert Marchant, a spokesperson for the Wisconsin Partnership for Progress, a pro-data center nonprofit that advocates for responsible development, said the type of facility being considered in Johnson Creek would be roughly the size of a Home Depot. “These can go in existing industrial areas within communities, places that are zoned for business and industry already, and they’re really significantly low impact,” he said. “From a land use standpoint, it’s a relatively small development and building.” The project would create 100 construction jobs, as well as 15 permanent jobs on-site once the facility is operational, according to the developer. Keith Klesner, the vice president of development for RadiusDC, said the company began looking into the project over the summer. He said he’s heard the community’s concerns and that he hopes the company can answer as many of those questions as possible before January. “A lot of the challenges that people think about with data centers on the large-scale may not have the same impact for a data center that’s sized like a big box retailer,” he said. “We’re definitely working to make sure that we’re respecting the watershed, we’re managing noise and any other development concerns for the community.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin

artigo.texto: A community’s mixture of developed land, power infrastructure, fiber connections and tech workers may help decide whether it attracts a data center, according to new research examining more than 200 of the facilities. While proponents argue the projects attract investment, create jobs and generate tax revenue, data centers have faced growing backlash across the United States. Residents have cited concerns including their potential impact on electricity bills, water consumption and noise disrupting nearby neighborhoods. The study, published in the academic journal Cities, analyzed 212 data centers operated by 11 major technology companies, according to a release from the University of Oklahoma. The researchers found that land use, infrastructure and workforce were associated with the locations chosen for the facilities. Read More on AI “The buildings that hold data centers need land, a lot of electricity, water for cooling and fiber connections,” said Kijin Seong, an assistant professor in the university’s Division of Planning, Landscape Architecture and Design, and one of the researchers behind the study. “Artificial intelligence has a very real physical footprint and that footprint lands in real communities.” The study compared every data center with four similar census tracts that had no such facility. The researchers found that the variety of land uses in an area was the most important factor separating data center locations from other sites. Facilities were also more commonly associated with nearby electrical substations and major roads, as well as areas with larger information technology workforces. Locations with extensive fiber networks had nearly triple the odds of containing a data center, the university said. “We expected climate to matter a lot because cooling is one of the biggest costs of running a data center,” Seong added. While climate conditions may still factor into a company’s initial choice of a state or wider region, the availability of suitable land and essential infrastructure may carry greater weight when companies move on to evaluating specific properties, Seong suggested. The study also found that roughly 85 percent of the facilities examined were in states that offered incentives. However, the comparison with similar locations did not establish whether those incentives affected companies’ choices of particular sites. Newsweek contacted the researchers for comment by email via the University of Oklahoma on Thursday. Largest Data Centers Use As Much Power As Entire Countries Separately, a Harvard-led study found that the largest data centers in America combined consume as much electricity as some countries. That research, published in Nature Sustainability, identified 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S. and estimated how much electricity each consumed annually from May 2024 through April 2025. Under its central scenario, the study’s researchers estimated that demand from the behemoth facilities was roughly 82 terawatt-hours, which equated to around 1.8 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption. This was more electricity than countries including Denmark, Finland, Nigeria and Venezuela consumed in 2024, according to statistics website Worldometer. Data Centers Linked to Premature US Deaths Meanwhile, another recent study suggested that air pollution associated with data centers’ electricity use contributed to an estimated hundreds of premature deaths across the country. Massachusetts Institute of Technology researchers estimated that data center electricity demand resulted in 513 premature deaths associated with fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, and another 137 with ozone, or smog, for a combined total of 650 in 2023. artigo.texto: The FCC has broken new ground, granting SpaceX the first US authorization to launch up to one million satellites as part of the company's Starmind plan to establish orbital data centers that sidestep the physical and regulatory limitations of terrestrial facilities. Modern data centers are the backbone of the world's digital infrastructure, the foundation on which AI, software, communications, commerce, scientific computing, and almost everything we do online depends. They are also central to future computing advances, tomorrow's economy, and even international relations as well. So it's small wonder they sit at the epicenter of economic, social, political, and diplomatic ruckuses, disrupting industries on a scale not seen since Gutenberg rolled out his printing press. Much of this friction stems from the technical and regulatory bottlenecks of building and operating terrestrial facilities. Data centers require continuous, reliable power on a gigawatt scale. Meeting that demand requires not only the power plants to generate the electricity, but also an upgraded grid – right down to the cables and substations – to deliver it. That requires a lot of planning and engineering. It also means developers can't simply plop a data center down anywhere. Facilities must be sited where massive power and water supplies are available, as conventional air cooling is no longer sufficient for modern AI chips. Even when utilities are secured, projects face strict regulations, environmental impact studies, land-use permits, and all manner of local or ideological opposition that can grind construction to a halt. SpaceX's strategy is to bypass these terrestrial hurdles by placing compute capacity in orbit, at altitudes between 310 and 622 miles (500 to 1,002 km), using up to one million satellites linked back to Earth via the Starlink network. Each satellite, spanning 230 to 246 feet (70 to 75 m) when deployed, houses a central rack of radiation-hardened compute modules flanked by two sets of panels. A smaller 1,184-square-foot (110 m²) array circulates liquid through double-sided radiators angled edge-on to the Sun to vent heat into deep space. A larger solar array generates up to 250 kW of peak electrical power. Because the satellites will operate in both 30-degree inclinations and near-polar, sun-synchronous orbits, much of the constellation can harvest near-continuous sunlight while radiating heat away. A modular design also allows SpaceX to upgrade hardware quickly as chip technology evolves. By putting data centers in orbit, Starmind aims to solve terrestrial infrastructure bottlenecks while avoiding local zoning and permitting battles. In a way, it takes moving the factory out of town to avoid the zoning ordinances to a whole new level. The FCC's conditional authorization sets out Starmind's orbital parameters, backup radio frequencies, orbital debris requirements, and deployment milestones through 2040. Under the terms of the license, SpaceX must deploy and operate its first Starmind satellite by November 25, 2033, or forfeit the authorization. Source: FCC

artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr. e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA O governo está confiante na realização do leilão de baterias na próxima semana, segundo fontes relataram à Agência iNFRA. A convicção vem na esteira da decisão da Justiça Federal em Brasília, que negou, na quarta-feira (25), o pedido de suspensão do certame em ação movida pela Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias). Além disso, o governo espera uma decisão favorável do STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) em ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) também apresentada pela associação. No caso da ADI, o pedido é para suspender a aplicação da regra de custeio exclusivo pelos geradores para contratação das baterias. À Agência iNFRA, interlocutores a par do assunto afirmam que a decisão, qualquer que seja, não deve prejudicar a realização do leilão. A presidente da Abeeólica, Elbia Gannoum, afirmou que a entidade vai recorrer da decisão desta quarta. Segundo ela, deve ser protocolado agravo de instrumento no TRF-1 (Tribunal Regional Federal da 1ª Região) para contestar a decisão de primeira instância e pedir a revisão do indeferimento da liminar. Elbia destacou que a associação ainda espera o pronunciamento do STF, cuja relatoria está com o ministro Cristiano Zanin. Segundo ela, o objetivo da associação não é travar o certame, mas garantir a mudança na forma de custeio. “A gente não quer parar o leilão, só não quer pagar o encargo. O leilão em si a gente quer muito”, disse. Expectativas no setor No setor, fontes afirmam que os agentes que estão se preparando para disputar o leilão trabalham com o cenário de que as sessões públicas na próxima quarta-feira (2) e sexta-feira (4) serão realizadas normalmente. Ou seja, não acreditam que a Justiça paralise o certame. No caso do processo no STF, relatado pelo ministro Cristiano Zanin, um interlocutor a par do assunto disse que há dois caminhos com maior probabilidade: o primeiro de negar a liminar e manter a discussão do mérito, e o segundo de conceder a liminar suspendendo a eficácia do trecho da lei que atribui o encargo aos geradores, mas sem adiar o leilão. Paralelamente às ações judiciais, fontes também veem chances de ser votado na semana que vem o PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que inclui os consumidores no rateio do encargo. A medida é defendida pelos geradores como a saída ideal, posição compartilhada pela Abeeólica. Elbia afirmou que os processos na Justiça só foram iniciados pela demora na aprovação do texto. Processos judiciais Na decisão de quarta-feira (25), o juiz Diego Câmara, da 17ª Vara Federal da Seção Judiciária do Distrito Federal, negou o pedido de liminar da Abeeólica que solicitava a suspensão do leilão. Ele destacou que as consequências práticas desaconselham a paralisação, como o risco de déficit de potência no sistema elétrico. Na prática, o juiz acolheu argumentos da defesa da União e da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), afirmando que nenhuma norma exige a regulamentação do rateio antes da realização do leilão e que não há urgência, uma vez que nenhum valor será cobrado antes de agosto de 2028. A decisão trata apenas do pedido de urgência e a ação segue em tramitação. No STF, a discussão é mais abrangente e trata da constitucionalidade de um trecho da Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (15.269/2025), que atribui os custos da contratação de baterias exclusivamente aos geradores. Na última semana, o relator da ação, ministro Cristiano Zanin, pediu informações à Presidência da República, ao Congresso Nacional, ao MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) e à ANEEL. Em manifestação assinada no último dia 17, a consultoria jurídica do MME defendeu a legalidade dos certames e a importância da continuidade do cronograma. A pasta informou ainda que não há necessidade de regulamentação prévia sobre o custeio que remunerará as baterias, uma vez que a cobrança só seria iniciada em agosto de 2028. Controvérsia sobre custos Para além da realização ou não do leilão e da forma de custeio, o próprio custo do certame tem causado controvérsia entre entidades do setor. A Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia divulgou um estudo segundo o qual o PL 3.716/2026 pode acrescentar até R$ 6,2 bilhões por ano à conta de luz. Em 15 anos, segundo a Frente dos Consumidores, o custo pode chegar a R$ 94 bilhões, considerando a receita fixa anual que seria cobrada pelos armazenadores. A entidade defendeu que a proposta seja rejeitada pelo Congresso. Elbia afirmou que o número não considera o custo da alternativa, que seria a contratação de novas térmicas, mais caras. Ela ponderou que, no leilão de baterias, o preço-teto ficou em R$ 1,58 milhão/MW/ano (sem conteúdo local), enquanto no LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na Forma de Potência) de térmicas, em março, o preço de novas termelétricas foi de R$ 2,9 milhões/MW/ano. “Bateria atende a essa necessidade de potência a custos menores e reduz o curtailment, além de entregar energia só no horário que precisa e sem precisar ser ligada antes como é a térmica, algo que piora o curtailment e traz mais custos”, disse Elbia. Em nota, a Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) ressaltou que o custo de R$ 6 bilhões para contratar baterias existe com ou sem o PL, mas que não se trata de um valor adicional. A entidade também defendeu as baterias como “solução de menor custo” e disse ainda que a cobrança do encargo via geradores encarece a conta, recaindo de toda forma sobre os consumidores “acrescido de tributos, custos financeiros e prêmio de risco”.

artigo.texto: New solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing new demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The company also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies. People are also reading… From the source grid to the cabinet: an integrated AIDC power architecture During the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management. Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the company describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE. The solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle. The system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life. Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE says the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years. Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications. The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications. Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds. According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less. Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly launched AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the company's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration. The integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when issues arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock. EVE says it ranked No. 2 globally in energy-storage cell shipments in the first half of 2026. The company reports cumulative global shipments of 230 GWh and inclusion in S&P Global's Tier 1 list of energy storage system integrators. Building on its strategy of "global manufacturing, global cooperation and global service," EVE says it will continue developing grid-forming capabilities and energy storage products for the full range of AIDC applications. artigo.texto: The Tennessee Valley Authority is set to receive $1.7 billion in aggregate payments from an unnamed data center customer under its new tariff for data centers above 5 MW, the federal utility said in a Nov. 12 U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. “Capacity commitment charges under the agreement are based on a rate of approximately $1.5 million per MW of requested capacity above 5 MW,” the filing said. “This rate reflects TVA's current cohort-based pricing methodology, which may be revised for future customer cohorts.” The new tariff took effect Oct. 1 and will be phased in through 2029, the filing said. That phase-in period will apply to existing customers to allow them to retain their existing rate structure for a period of time, the Nashville Scene reported in August. TVA CEO Mike Skaggs said during a Nov. 13 earnings call that the change to data center rates has supported the utility’s investments. Those investments include extending the lives of the utility’s existing nuclear units and “helping expand the nuclear fuel and supply hub in the East Tennessee area,” he said. The utility recently received the first small modular reactor construction permit from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission for a BWRX-300 reactor at the Clinch River Site in Oak Ridge, “although TVA has not yet decided whether to construct a reactor at the site,” its filing said. Skaggs came out of retirement to serve as interim CEO following the retirement of former CEO Don Moul and was instated as TVA’s permanent CEO following a Nov. 10 board meeting, TVA’s vice president of financial planning and investor relations Clifton Lowry said on the call. TVA’s filing also noted that in August, the utility’s board approved 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation, “targeted to be online in 2032.” As of Sept. 30, TVA said it “had spent $463 million on long-lead-time equipment associated with previously approved projects, which will now be utilized in connection with the project. TVA could spend up to an additional $3.1 billion on this project.” That previously approved project is TVA’s defunct Middle Tennessee Energy Solution project. In August, TVA said its approval of the new 1.5 GW gas facility “closes out” the previous project, “and all funding has been transferred to the New Gas Facility 2032.” TVA’s President and CFO Tom Rice said that the utility is in a “strong financial position” to executive its $13 billion capital investment plan over the next three years. That investment comes on top of the more than $23 billion in investments since 2020, Rice said. However, TVA’s filing notes that it “continues to experience supply chain pressures resulting from inflation, tariffs and other trade restrictions, material constraints, and labor availability.” “These factors have contributed to project delays, limited availability of critical materials, and increased costs for both materials and labor,” the utility said. “TVA anticipates that inflationary and tariff pressures will persist into 2027. Although these challenges have been managed with limited disruption to business operations thus far, continued or escalating pressures could result in more substantial operational impacts and increased pressure on power rates.”

artigo.texto: Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power Co. has entered into agreements to build distribution and transmission infrastructure to serve three Microsoft data centers planned for Wyoming, the company said Tuesday in a filing at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The redacted agreements require Microsoft to pay for the infrastructure through “contribution in aid of construction” payments, according to the filing. Cheyenne Light — a subsidiary of Bright Horizon Energy Corp., a utility holding company created by the Nov. 13 merger of Black Hills Corp. and NorthWestern Energy Group — doesn’t believe FERC has jurisdiction over the retail agreements but filed them for review “out of an abundance of caution” due to the agency’s recent statements related to cost recovery agreements for transmission costs caused by large load customers. The Microsoft agreements reflect a massive data center buildout that is underway in southeast Wyoming where Cheyenne Light operates. The utility is executing on a 3-GW data center pipeline, including 600 MW of Microsoft and Meta projects, Black Hills officials said during a Nov. 5 earnings conference call. It is also in initial talks on an additional 2.5 GW of early-stage data center opportunities. Cheyenne Light has about 46,000 retail electric customers in the Cheyenne area and set a peak load record of 439 MW in July, according to Black Hills’ most recent U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission earnings report. The utility in September agreed to supply a Google data center project in Cheyenne with 590 MW and manage 2.1 GW of third-party power supply in a microgrid, Black Hills said in its earnings presentation. The agreements with Google contain cost pass-through mechanisms that protect customers from costs related to the planned data center while protecting utility returns from inflation, interest rate volatility and other cost pressures, Black Hills noted in the SEC filing. Cheyenne Light intends to serve the data centers through its Large Power Contract Service tariff and a proposed Large Customer Transmission Cost Adjustment Mechanism, which are designed to insulate the utility’s customers from the infrastructure costs related to data centers. Black Hills expects the Wyoming Public Service Commission will make a decision on the transmission tariff proposal by mid-2027. Cheyenne Light plans to use the transmission tariff to recover the costs of two recently proposed transmission projects totaling $686 million needed to serve large loads, including the Google data center. Under the tariff, large load customers would pay their share of the transmission expansion. The Google data center is set to begin operating late next year and ramp up to its full load by the end of 2030, according to the SEC filing. To serve it, Cheyenne Light plans to build a $1.8 billion, utility-owned 564-MW gas-fired power plant between 2027 and 2029, through an unregulated affiliate. The company expects the deal with Google will boost its net income by $150 million a year starting in 2030. In its SEC filing, Black Hills warned that the Google deal increases its risk by making it more reliant on one customer. “Our agreements with Google represent a significant long-term growth opportunity and are expected to contribute meaningfully to future revenues, earnings, cash flows and capital investment,” the company said. “As a result, we will have increased exposure to a single large customer and to trends affecting the data center, cloud computing and artificial intelligence industries.” Also, Black Hills said that large load demand forecasts face “significant uncertainty” and could be affected by technological advancements, economic conditions and regulatory developments. “Although the agreements contain customer credit support, termination payment and other investment recovery provisions, those protections may not fully mitigate the impact of reduced customer demand, contract disputes, non-renewal or customer default,” Black Hills said.

artigo.texto: Trending WARREN TOWNSHIP – The township is the latest community to address data centers, approving a six-month moratorium to allow zoning board members to have time to review and prepare guidelines if a center were to locate in the community. Trustees on Tuesday voted 3-0 on the six-month moratorium. The decision comes weeks after Champion and Warren Township officials met with the public about the former Copperweld Steel property located in both communities. Champion Township has placed a three‑month moratorium on issuing data center permits, while both Champion and Warren trustees are working together to set matching zoning rules for the former steel site off Mahoning Avenue. The property has 65% of the land in Warren Township, and 35% is in Champion. Warren Township Trustee Ed Anthony said the township has had no requests to build a data center there or anywhere else in the township. Anthony said that any zoning regulations must address residential, agricultural and environmentally sensitive areas; adequate infrastructure; traffic and noise impacts; and preserving public health, safety and welfare. Darryl Parker of the township zoning commission said the board will discuss data centers and their impact as a land use on the community at the Dec. 7 meeting. The current zoning does regulate data center uses. Parker said the commission will review the matter and then make recommendations on zoning regulations or text amendments related to data centers. Trustee Tyler Wilson said the moratorium is on any zoning applications relating to data centers. “The moratorium provides the time for the zoning board to do a review of current zoning and what regulations should be in place,” Wilson said. Anthony said an extension beyond the six months can be approved later if more time is needed. Also, Resident Art Williams said he was concerned with open burning issues in the township. He asked if fire officials can cite people. Anthony said most fire officials do not cite, but police officials can and do for open burning. In other business, trustees: * Approved a new three-year agreement with the road department union, which represent three full-time workers and one part-time worker. * Approved a cell-tower lease with Vertical Bridge for the fire station on Dover Avenue. * Declared properties at 146 and 158 Park Road, 341 Forest Road and 4109 Turner Road as unfit for habitation and structurally defective, with plans for demolition. * Approved the promotion of Daniel Barbe as a full-time patrolman. * Accepted the resignations of Adam Scott, a part-time patrolman, and Jamie Hoffman, a full-time patrolman, from the police department. * Announced Christmas with Santa will be at 6 p.m. Dec. 6 at the Johnson Community Center. The event is sponsored by the trustees. * Heard from fire Chief Joseph Natali that the fire department had 73% coverage for October because of assistance from off duty response. He said the department received mutual aid for emergency medical service 32 times and provided mutual aid to other departments two times. * Canceled the December trustees meeting because of the holidays.

artigo.texto: A comprehensive bibliometric survey examining approximately 3,060 peer-reviewed publications published between 2015 and 2024 has established a unified electrochemical framework that explains how transition metal oxide electrodes transition between surface-dominated pseudocapacitive charge storage and bulk diffusion-controlled battery reactions. Rather than treating rechargeable batteries and electrochemical capacitors as entirely disconnected technological domains with isolated operating principles, the decadal synthesis reveals that transition metal oxides operate along a continuous charge-storage continuum governed by fundamental physicochemical descriptors. These governing descriptors include intrinsic electronic conductivity, solid-state ion diffusion kinetics, the spatial density of electrochemically accessible redox-active sites, surface adsorption energetics, defect chemistry, and crystallographic phase stability under repeated cycling. By evaluating material modifications across both device architectures simultaneously, the unified model demonstrates how structural engineering, morphologic tailoring, and chemical doping systematically shift an electrode’s charge-storage mechanism toward either rapid surface-confined power delivery or high-capacity bulk energy storage, resolving longstanding fragmentation in literature. The extensive analysis underscores that pristine transition metal oxides face an inherent performance trade-off between delivering high theoretical capacitance through multi-electron Faradaic redox transformations and suffering from severe kinetic and mechanical limitations. While conventional graphite anodes in commercial lithium-ion batteries are constrained to a theoretical capacity of 372 milliampere-hours per gram through reversible lithium intercalation, transition metal oxides undergoing multi-electron conversion mechanisms, such as hematite and cobalt oxide, boast theoretical capacities exceeding 800 to 1,000 milliampere-hours per gram. Similarly, single and mixed-valence metal oxides offer specific capacitance values that far outstrip traditional carbon-based electric double-layer capacitors, which rely exclusively on electrostatic charge separation. However, pristine oxides typically exhibit poor intrinsic electronic conductivity, sluggish solid-state ion transport kinetics, substantial volume expansion during repeated cycling, and structural degradation. These interconnected physical constraints induce rapid electrode pulverization, severe capacity fading, and high charge-transfer resistance, preventing pristine bulk oxides from realizing their full theoretical electrochemical capabilities without targeted structural modifications. Within the established framework, electrochemical energy storage systems are distinguished by the kinetic nature of their charge-transfer processes, which can be quantitatively mapped using technique-specific electroanalytical signatures. In electrical double-layer capacitors, energy is stored via electrostatic ion accumulation at the electrode-electrolyte interface without electron transfer, yielding superior cycling stability and elevated power densities but modest energy density. In contrast, battery-type materials undergo diffusion-controlled Faradaic ion intercalation or conversion reactions within the bulk crystalline lattice, producing nonlinear galvanostatic charge-discharge profiles with distinct voltage plateaus and sharp redox peaks in cyclic voltammetry. These physical mechanisms are evaluated through the power-law relationship relating current to voltage scan rate, where a power-law exponent b approaching 1.0 identifies an ideal surface-confined capacitive response, whereas an exponent near 0.5 indicates diffusion-limited bulk storage. Transition metal oxides uniquely span this boundary, frequently exhibiting intermediate exponents between 0.6 and 0.9 that reflect hybrid electrochemical behavior. To overcome the intrinsic conductivity-capacitance trade-off, material synthesis routes dictate the resulting crystal architecture, defect distribution, and electroactive surface area of transition metal oxide electrodes. Hydrothermal and solvothermal synthesis methods typically yield two-dimensional nanosheets or elongated nanorods that provide high specific surface areas and short ion diffusion paths, which facilitate rapid ion transport and elevate pseudocapacitive contributions. Template-assisted synthesis produces hollow, mesoporous structures capable of accommodating mechanical strain during cycling to enhance durability, though often at the cost of synthetic complexity. Chemical vapor deposition deposits high-purity thin films with precisely controlled thicknesses that reduce internal resistance, while electrochemical deposition enables direct electrode growth on conductive substrates to minimize interfacial contact resistance. Complementing these synthesis routes, advanced engineering strategies—such as inducing oxygen vacancies through defect engineering, incorporating conductive carbon frameworks, creating multi-component heterostructures, and introducing aliovalent dopants—alter the underlying electronic band structures, raise charge-carrier concentrations, and lower activation energy barriers. Nickel oxide functions as a prototypical hybrid material in alkaline electrolytes, where charge storage is governed by reversible Faradaic redox transitions involving the divalent and trivalent nickel redox couple. At elevated scan rates or within nanostructured architectures, nickel oxide displays surface-confined pseudocapacitive kinetics with power-law exponents between 0.6 and 0.9, while at lower operating rates, deeper proton diffusion into the bulk crystalline lattice triggers battery-type storage. artigo.texto: Data Centers, AI, and the Growing Demand for Energy: Impacts, Risks, and Solutions Learn how the rapid growth of data centers is affecting electricity bills, public health, communities, and the environment and what can be done about it. Data centers, the physical infrastructure powering the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and our increasingly digital lives, are expanding at an unprecedented pace and scale around the world. This growth is creating enormous new demand for electricity and other resources, with consequences for communities and the environment. In the United States, where data center development is surging, unchecked growth could raise electricity bills for families and small businesses, strain power grids and water supplies, increase pollution, and slow progress toward a clean energy future. Communities should not be left to bear the costs of this expansion without a meaningful voice in the decisions that affect them. People deserve transparency and a real say in whether and how data centers are built. The wealthy technology companies driving this growth should pay for the infrastructure their facilities require rather than shifting those costs onto the public, bring new clean energy to meet new electricity demand, and meet strong protections for public health and the environment. Linked below are fact sheets, expert blogs, guides, and other resources that explore the impacts of data center development in the United States and around the world as well as solutions that can help ensure people and the planet remain at the center of the decisions ahead. AI Has an Energy Problem Asking ChatGPT a quick question might feel innocuous, but you might end up paying for it in the long run. The massive data centers that are popping up around the country to support the AI boom are using up enormous amounts of energy and water and creating noise and air pollution. NRDC’s Ben Schaefer, senior manager of strategic communications, and Jackson Morris, director of state power sector policy, dive into how these centers can impact nearby communities and your energy bill. artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday announced it has given permission to SpaceX to launch 1 million data centers into space. The agency said its decision authorizes SpaceX to “deploy at an unprecedented scale.” It comes as battles brew across the U.S. over where data centers are being built, with residents protesting against construction over noise, environmental and other concerns. The FCC added that the approval will “bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun.” The Kardashev scale, according to Encyclopedia Britannica, is a “hypothetical measure of an alien civilization’s level of technological advancement,” first coined by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev. It proposes three levels of civilization, and a Type II civilization — the FCC’s goal — has the capability of using the entire energy output of its star. “Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI (super intelligence),” FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the movement. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.” “Much appreciated,” SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said on X in response to Carr’s announcement. “This will be a great asset to America and the world.” In July, a coalition of environmental and scientific organizations petitioned the FCC to conduct an environmental review on the effects of data centers in space. The groups, represented by Earthjustice, said that sending that many data centers into space could change the atmosphere and disrupt other satellites already in orbit. “Allowing a million orbiting data centers with no environmental review isn’t just irresponsible — it’s reckless,” Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, said at the time. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.” In its authorization, the FCC wrote that it expects SpaceX to launch its first data center into space by November 2033, with all of them being deployed by November 2040. As of July, there are 15,000 active satellites in space, according to Earthjustice. In order for SpaceX to complete its goal, it would be required to launch 5,000 rockets into space a year, or 13 to 14 a day, according to a paper by scientists Eloise A. Marais and Connor R. Barker published in the journal Earth and Space Chemistry.

artigo.texto: Capital Deployment & Mexico's Data Center Competitiveness Mexico could capture part of the US$82.5 billion in projected data center investment through 2031, but global infrastructure capital remains selective due to transmission bottlenecks, permitting delays, and regulatory uncertainty. Developers must deliver energized substations, long-haul fiber connectivity, and clear 20- to 30-year legal frameworks to compete for institutional capital. Global infrastructure funds hold ample capital for digital infrastructure, yet Mexico faces a competitive bottleneck because investors prioritize large-scale projects with ready power and predictable regulations. During his keynote address at the Mexico Data Center Summit 2026 on Nov. 25, 2026, Simón Masri, President and CEO, C3NTRO Telecom, outlined the structural requirements Mexico must meet to convert announced capacity into operational megawatts. While global data center demand is projected to nearly triple from 82 GW in 2025 to 219 GW by 2030, Mexico operates an installed base of 279 MW, with 250 MW concentrated in Queretaro. According to industry data cited by Masri from the Mexican Data Center Association (MEXDC), total capacity could expand roughly eightfold to 2,214 MW over the next five years if announced and under-construction projects materialize, representing an estimated US$82.5 billion investment window between 2026 and 2031. However, Masri warned that capital is not scarce, it is occupied elsewhere. The 10 largest global infrastructure funds hold US$209.4 billion in commitments, while five major technology companies—Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle—are projected to spend US$791 billion in capital expenditures in 2026 alone. That annual hyperscaler spending equals roughly 48 times Mexico's five-year data center investment projection. Furthermore, US debt markets closed US$223 billion in data center loans through September 2026, absorbing institutional bandwidth with single-campus transactions such as Meta's US$12 billion debt package in El Paso, Texas. "The capital is not scarce; it is occupied. Mexico has to be easy to understand and easy to approve," says Masri. Substation Readiness and Fiber Bottlenecks Within the five-layer artificial intelligence stack—spanning digital energy, digital infrastructure, chips, models, and applications—Masri noted that Mexico competes in the two physical foundational layers: power generation and transmission, and physical facilities such as data centers, fiber networks, and edge nodes. To attract hyperscalers and neocloud operators, Masri argued that preliminary feasibility letters from the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) or the National Energy Control Center (CENACE) are insufficient. Institutional investors and cloud buyers require substations that are either under construction with confirmed energization dates or already energized. High-voltage substation construction requires significant upfront capital and specialized engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractors, which remain limited in Mexico. Connectivity presents a parallel constraint. High-density AI workloads require extensive long-haul and metropolitan fiber networks, with US metropolitan fiber deployments scaling from four strands in 2004 to 16,000 strands by 2026. Major US operators and technology firms have pre-ordered massive fiber volumes from manufacturers such as Corning, pushing equipment lead times to 52 weeks. Without dedicated fiber routes, Masri noted, available power capacity cannot be commercialized. Cross-Border Dynamics and Execution Milestones Geopolitical shifts in the United States create both an opening and a policy risk for Mexican operators. Local opposition led to rejections in 40 of 41 US municipal data center ballot measures during the November 2026 midterm elections, alongside calls from congressional leaders for a national moratorium. While stricter US permitting could push demand south under the USMCA framework, Masri highlighted a Nov. 20, 2026 White House proposal to impose tariffs on US firms building data centers abroad, leaving cross-border tax rules undefined. To demonstrate execution viability in Mexico, Masri cited C3NTRO Telecom's Tikva project, a 2,500 km terrestrial fiber backbone connecting Queretaro to Phoenix, Arizona. Financed by European development banks after domestic lenders hesitated over non-real-estate digital assets, the corridor is 84% complete—spanning 2,100 km—and scheduled to be ready for service in the first quarter of 2027. The route integrates 30 carrier-neutral edge data centers across Mexican municipalities from Nogales to Queretaro, providing 10 MW of initial capacity scalable to 60 MW. Looking ahead, Masri identified four priorities to capture long-term compute investment: mixed CFE and private-sector transmission schemes, specialized infrastructure capital, single-window permitting with binding timelines for rights-of-way, and public communication clarifying water and clean-energy management. If Mexico executes on its current 2 GW pipeline by 2030, Masri concluded, the sector should aim for 10 GW of installed capacity by 2035.

artigo.texto: Schneider Electric industrializes European liquid cooling manufacturing capacity to underpin AI & data center demand AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 26 de novembro de 2026 - Schneider Electric is increasing Cooling Distribution Unit (CDU) manufacturing capacity by 100% at its Conselve facility in Italy, with expanded production capacity expected from January 2027 - Chiller manufacturing capacity will increase by 50% by the end of 2026, supporting growing demand for AI and high-density data center cooling across Europe - A new advanced cooling test laboratory will triple existing testing capacity by December 2027, strengthening Schneider Electrics European leadership in cooling innovation, R&D and product validation CONSELVE, Italy, Nov. 26, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Schneider Electric, a global energy technology leader, has today announced a major expansion of its European cooling manufacturing capabilities at its Conselve facility in Italy, doubling production capacity for advanced liquid cooling technologies to support the rapid growth of AI and high-density data centers across Europe. The expansion, which follows the acquisition of Motivair last year, will increase CDU manufacturing capacity by 100% from January 2027, alongside a 50% increase in Big Chiller manufacturing capacity by the end of 2026. The development strengthens Schneider Electric’s European industrial footprint, industrializing its advanced cooling manufacturing capabilities, and bringing both engineering and technical expertise closer to customers while supporting the deployment of AI-ready digital infrastructure. As part of this expansion, Schneider Electric is investing in a new advanced cooling test laboratory, targeted for completion in December 2027. The facility will triple existing testing capacity, strengthening R&D, product validation and quality assurance for next-generation air and liquid cooling technologies. This investment further accelerates innovation by providing advanced validation capabilities for chillers up to 4 MW, Motivair by Schneider Electric CDUs up to 5 MW and CRAH and fan wall systems up to 800 kW. Located in the Veneto region of Italy, Conselve remains Schneider Electric’s largest cooling manufacturing facility in Europe and a central hub for research and development, engineering and technical training. “AI is fundamentally transforming the way in which our customers design and operate data centers, creating unprecedented demand for advanced liquid cooling technologies that can support increasingly powerful computing systems,” said Damien Dhellemmes, senior vice president of the Secure Power and Data Center Business in Europe at Schneider Electric. “By doubling our liquid cooling manufacturing capacity in Conselve, we’re strengthening our ability to deploy resilient, scalable and energy-efficient AI infrastructure, while bringing critical technologies and expertise closer to our customers in Europe.” Accelerating European cooling innovation As AI workloads drive higher rack densities and increasingly complex thermal requirements, liquid cooling is becoming essential to the next generation of data center infrastructure. Schneider Electric’s expansion at Conselve will strengthen its ability to meet these demands through increased manufacturing capacity, greater supply-chain resilience and closer collaboration with European customers. The development also complements Schneider Electric’s broader liquid cooling portfolio, including Motivair by Schneider Electric, combining specialist cooling expertise with the company’s end-to-end capabilities across power, cooling, software and services. Investing in Europe’s industrial future The expansion reflects Schneider Electric’s continued investment in European manufacturing and specialist technical skills. Over the past five years, Conselve’s workforce has nearly doubled, supporting growth across engineering, production, quality assurance and technical functions. Through its expanded manufacturing and innovation capabilities, Schneider Electric is reinforcing its commitment to delivering the resilient, efficient and scalable infrastructure needed to support Europe’s rapidly growing digital economy. Its technologies enable buildings, data centers, factories, infrastructure, and grids tooperateas open, interconnected ecosystems, enhancing performance, resilience, and sustainability. The portfolio includes intelligent devices, software-defined architectures, AI-powered systems, digital services, and expert advisory. With 160,000 employees and 1 million partners in over 100 countries, Schneider Electric is consistently ranked among the worlds most sustainable companies. artigo.texto: A Korean research team has developed a next-generation battery technology that allows all-solid-state batteries — often called the "dream battery" — to run for extended periods at room temperature without heavy pressurizing equipment. POSTECH said on the 26th that a team led by Park Soo-jin, a professor of chemistry, along with Lee Hyung-seok and doctoral candidate Sung Ji-hoon, has built an all-solid-state lithium metal battery that operates stably at room temperature and under low pressure. The findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications. Moon Jang-hyuk, a professor at Chung-Ang University, Lee Young-joo of the Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and a team led by Donghai Wang, a professor at Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States, also took part in the research. All-solid-state batteries use a solid electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid, making them safer, and applying lithium metal to the anode can sharply increase energy storage capacity. The problem is that lithium builds up during charging and swells significantly in volume. Gaps then open between the solid electrolyte and the electrode, and when sharp, branch-like lithium crystals known as dendrites grow through those gaps, they cause internal short circuits. Existing technology has prevented such gaps by pressing the battery hard with large equipment at high temperatures. The team found its solution in an electrolyte that resists cracking and in "empty rooms" for the swelling lithium to occupy. The researchers first added thioctic acid (TA), which links together into chains on its own, to a sulfide-based solid electrolyte that is vulnerable to impact. Tests confirmed that a dense polymer network formed by thioctic acid was firmly bound to the electrolyte. Much like automotive safety glass that holds fragments together instead of shattering, the network flexibly held the electrolyte in place, blocking cracks and the penetration of lithium crystals. The team addressed the volume expansion problem by using a porous carbon material, riddled with fine pores like a sponge, as the anode current collector, the component that gathers and transmits electricity. Buffer space was prepared in advance underneath to accommodate lithium that swells during charging. As a result, the stress generated as lithium expands was not concentrated solely toward the electrolyte but was distributed evenly across the empty pores of the current collector. The team verified the mechanism directly by capturing real-time three-dimensional images of the inside of an operating battery with the Pohang Light Source II (PLS-II), in a manner similar to a hospital CT scan. Repeated charging and discharging produced no short circuits and no distortion at the boundary between the electrode and the electrolyte. The images also captured the fine pores of the current collector filling and emptying of lithium to absorb expansion pressure. The battery also operated stably at room temperature and at pressure of 0.3 megapascals or less in a full-cell configuration using NCM811, a nickel-cobalt-manganese cathode material widely used in electric vehicles. Park said the team "resolved the limits of brittle sulfide-based solid electrolytes with a polymer network and the expansion stress of lithium with a porous current collector," adding that the result came from "close collaboration with domestic research teams." Lee Hyung-seok, a co-first author, said: "By eliminating the large pressurizing equipment, we can reduce the volume and weight of the battery pack. This will come to be used as a core mechanism for accelerating the commercialization of all-solid-state batteries."

artigo.texto: Buscando expansão no Nordeste, Tecto anuncia data center no Recife Empreendimento de plataforma controla pelo BTG Pactual terá capacidade escalável de até seis megawatts e integra plano da companhia de investimentos de US$ 2 bilhões até 2028 A Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, anunciou nesta terça-feira (24) seu primeiro data center em Pernambuco, o segundo no Nordeste. O empreendimento, batizado de TREC1, será instalado no Recife e terá capacidade inicial de 1 MW (megawatt), com possibilidade de expansão de até 6 MW. Segundo a companhia, com a expansão, a ideia é montar uma estratégia "AI Grid", criando uma rede de data centers regionais, conectando polos do Brasil a pontos estratégicos no exterior. "A estratégia da empresa combina duas camadas: a AI Factory reúne instalações de grande porte e alta densidade, voltadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial e ao processamento intensivo de dados. E AI Grid distribui a infraestrutura de processamento por meio de data centers regionais interligados, aproximando-a dos locais onde os dados são gerados e consumidos", afirmou em comunicado. A operação está prevista para inicar no primeiro trimestre do ano que vem e atenderá as chamadas "hyperscales", que são operadoras, provedores de nuvem e de conteúdo e empresas do segmento enterprise, oferecendo serviços de colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados para operações que demandam alta disponibilidade, segurança e baixa latência. Como mostrou a CNN, com alta demanda do setor e oferta abundante de energia renovável, o Nordeste segue avançando como um forte polo de data centers no país, ampliando a presença do setor para além do eixo Rio-São Paulo. Atualmente, a Tecto opera em Fortaleza (CE) o TFOR3, que é o maior centro de dados em operação da região. Conhecido como "Mega Lobster", o empreendimento fica na Praia do Futuro, e foi inaugurado em outubro do ano passado. Para o CRO da companhia, Tito Costa, a região reúne a conectividade internacional e uma demanda crescente por infraestrutura digital, tendo papel estratégico na expansão da empresa. “Acreditamos que Recife está para Fortaleza, assim como o Rio de Janeiro está para São Paulo. Essa é a lógica da nossa estratégia AI Grid, que conecta data centers, levando capacidade de processamento para perto das empresas e complementando as grandes estruturas do AI Factory”, acrescentou. Com os dois polos conectados (Recife e Fortaleza), os clientes da companhia poderão distribuir suas operações entre diferentes localidades, inclusive para estratégias de recuperação de desastres e continuidade dos negócios, sem sair da região. A capacidade final é de 20 MW (megawatts), com a expansão ocorre em etapas, acompanhando a demanda dos clientes. A previsão da empresa é de aumentar a capacidade inicial de 4 MW para 8 MW até o começo de 2027. A partir da chegada do TREC1, a empresa passará a contar com oito data centers operacionais até 2027, sendo cinco no Brasil (incluindo o de Recife, três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro) outros três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Além dessas unidades, a companhia segue com o desenvolvimento do TGRU1, em Santana de Parnaíba (SP), com 200 MW, um dos maiores do país em capacidade, que será voltado para aplicações que empregam inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Há também o TPOA1, em Porto Alegre (RS), com 20 MW. Ao todo, o plano de investimentos da companhia é estimado em US$ 2 bilhões, previstos entre 2026 e 2028, para acelerar a expansão na América Latina. Brasil deve dobrar capacidade até 2030 Ao todo, dos 660 MW que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados, segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL. Ainda segundo a consultoria, a ocupação dos data centers brasileiros chegou a 96% no primeiro semestre deste ano. Para a colunista da CNN Infra, Joísa Dutra, o setor busca acelerar os investimentos de forma mais eficiente, buscando alianças internacionais, ao mencionar o lanlamento da AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), da qual fazem parte empresas como Emerald AI, Google e NVIDIA, além de outras quase 20 companhias. O objetivo da aliança é criar protocolos e melhores práticas os investimentos. Os esforços dessas empresas são para criar condições para que esses investimentos em data centers possam ocorrer de modo eficiente, possam ocorrer mais rápido no tempo", avaliou a colunista. A iniciativa surge em resposta a um fenômeno já observado em diferentes países, inclusive no Brasil: a resistência de comunidades locais à instalação desses empreendimentos. Joísa descreveu esse comportamento como "nimby" — expressão em inglês que significa "not in my backyard", ou seja, "aqui não, não no meu quintal". Segundo ela, esse tipo de reação, antes associado a plantas de energia ou projetos de transmissão, começa a aparecer também no segmento de data centers. Atualmente, São Paulo concentra o setor, mas a expansão deve alcançar outras regiões, como no Nordeste, impulsionado por incentivos do Redata e pela abundância de energia renovável na região. Para Tito Costa, a concentração paulista decorre da proximidade entre clientes, redes e outros data centers, mas avalia que disponibilidade de energia e terrenos levará o mercado a novos polos à medida que os atuais se saturarem.
