artigo.texto: Google, Blue Origin Plan Orbital AI Compute Test The 2029 mission will deploy rack-scale computing satellites, with cooling, autonomous recovery, and hardware longevity likely to determine whether orbital infrastructure can support commercial workloads. Google has booked a Blue Origin New Glenn launch for the first quarter of 2029 to advance Project Suncatcher, a test of solar-powered computing satellites designed to evaluate whether space-based infrastructure can support AI workloads at roughly the scale of individual data center racks. The companies announced the agreement Nov. 19, outlining a dedicated heavy-lift mission to place satellites equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units into sun-synchronous orbit. Google has described the project as a long-term effort to expand AI infrastructure by tapping solar energy in space. For data center operators and investors, the more immediate questions are how much useful computing the satellites can sustain, how they recover from failures, and whether their operating lives can justify launch and replacement costs. Proving Orbital Reliability Dave McCarthy, IDC’s group vice president for cloud and datacenters, enterprise infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that successful deployments will need to demonstrate sustained uptime, autonomous fault recovery, and optical communications capable of keeping pace with the processors. “A server rack in orbit has to prove it can run for long periods of time because you can’t send a technician to swap a failed GPU at 500 kilometers,” he said. Those requirements sharpen the technical and economic questions surrounding Orbital’s planned AI satellites, including radiation resilience and the ability to sustain GPU operations over time. Rob DeMillo, CEO and cofounder of orbital computing company Sophia Space, said the demonstrations must also show that multiple nodes can compute together and run useful customer workloads. “An operator doesn’t necessarily need a demonstration to be large. They need it to demonstrate that the underlying architecture works and can scale,” DeMillo told Data Center Knowledge. “There is a significant difference between putting a computer in space and building computing infrastructure in space.” Cooling May Set the Limits Heat rejection remains the largest engineering obstacle. Because space has no atmosphere to carry heat away, operators must rely on radiators, which add weight and complexity and compete with processors and other components for launch capacity. Bill Ray, distinguished vice president analyst at Gartner, said cooling is only part of the challenge. Radiation protection, micrometeorite shielding, and maneuvering capability to avoid debris in the heavily used sun-synchronous orbital environment are also critical. “Heat is the primary barrier, but not the only one,” Ray told Data Center Knowledge. “Micrometeorite shielding will be essential, along with redundancy to provide radiation resistance.” These constraints also surfaced in orbital infrastructure discussions at September’s AI Infra Summit, where executives highlighted the tradeoffs among radiator size, weight, and launch requirements. DeMillo said designs that simply replicate enclosed terrestrial server racks could create substantial cooling burdens, including the need for pumps and fluid loops. A more viable approach, he said, is to integrate power generation and heat rejection with computing capacity. “Radiation is also a system-level engineering problem,” he said. “Shielding is part of the answer, but so are hardware error correction, fault detection and software that can recover or redistribute workloads when components encounter problems.” The First Workloads Will Follow the Data One of the clearest early commercial applications is processing data already collected in space, reducing the amount of raw information that must be transmitted back to Earth. DeMillo identified wildfire detection, disaster response, weather analysis, and maritime tracking as potential uses for orbital image processing. “Earth observation satellites can collect enormous amounts of imagery,” he said. “Processing that information in orbit and sending down the answer rather than all of the raw data saves bandwidth and, in many cases, more importantly, time.” If more advanced AI workloads move into orbit, ground-to-space communications capacity will become even more important. McCarthy pointed to asynchronous model training and synthetic data generation as possible use cases where computing demand is high but data movement is relatively limited. Ray took a narrower view, saying he expects orbital edge computing to focus on tasks such as screening imagery before transmission and providing security services. Replacement Costs May Decide the Business Case Commercial viability will also depend on how long satellites can provide useful computing before they need to be replaced. The long development timeline for space-based data centers leaves operators balancing potential energy advantages against launch, communications, and maintenance costs. McCarthy said falling launch prices will need to coincide with hardware that can survive at least five years, roughly matching standard data center depreciation cycles. “Abundant solar power in orbit doesn’t automatically offset a steep launch bill,” he said. Radiation damage and thermal wear could shorten that lifespan, increasing the frequency with which operators would need to launch replacement capacity. “If radiation or thermal wear forces operators to replace satellites every two or three years, the unit economics won’t work,” McCarthy said.

artigo.texto: Trump quer os data centers em casa. E o Brasil com isso? Ameaças do líder americano sobre o tema colocam investimentos e a soberania digital do Brasil em xeque Ao retornar da Ásia, Donald Trump disse que empresas americanas que construírem data centers fora dos Estados Unidos poderão pagar impostos muito mais altos. Operadores globais como Equinix e Digital Realty estão na mira, mesmo boa parte da imprensa internacional tendo lido o recado como mais um capítulo da disputa com a China pelo controle da IA. A lei ainda não mudou, mas sim a natureza da decisão. Escolher onde construir um data center era uma conta de engenharia e de custo que mirava energia barata, água, terreno, proximidade dos clientes, dos cabos e fibras óticas. Com a fala de Trump, essa escolha entra na agenda de segurança nacional, ao lado dos chips e dos minerais estratégicos. O volume de dinheiro em jogo explica o interesse. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft e Oracle devem investir juntas cerca de US$ 800 bilhões em 2026 e mais de US$ 1,2 trilhão em 2027, segundo estimativas do Morgan Stanley. Nem tudo isso é data center, mas uma parte grande é. Quem decide onde esse dinheiro vai parar decide também quem fica com os empregos, os impostos e o poder tecnológico da próxima década. As próprias big techs já esbarram em limites de infra e custo dentro dos EUA. As empresas precisam estar perto de clientes no mundo inteiro, para responder rápido, ter cópias de segurança em outros locais e cumprir leis de países que exigem que certos dados fiquem em seu território. O cenário mais provável não é o fim da expansão internacional, mas uma expansão mais seletiva, lenta e negociada, em que cada projeto fora dos Estados Unidos passa a carregar um custo político. Para o Brasil, isso pesa mais do que parece. Boa parte da nuvem que bancos, varejistas, startups e órgãos públicos usam aqui pertence a empresas americanas, que vinham anunciando bilhões em data centers no país. Se cada novo investimento no exterior virar alvo em Washington, alguns desses projetos podem ser adiados ou encolhidos. Na prática, isso significaria menos capacidade instalada no país, serviços de IA mais caros ou mais lentos para empresas brasileiras e mais dados nossos processados no exterior, sob leis de outros países. É uma questão de soberania digital, e também de competitividade. Empresas que pagarão mais pela computação podem vir a inovar menos. O outro lado da moeda é a disputa por capital. Se as americanas hesitarem, o espaço tende a ser ocupado por investidores de outras origens. O país já tem um exemplo dessa diversificação no complexo que a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, constrói no Pecém, no Ceará. Mesmo trazendo dinheiro, coloca o Brasil no meio da rivalidade entre EUA e China, e a escolha de quem constrói e opera um data center pode virar tema diplomático. É nesse cenário que ganham fôlego ideias que pareciam distantes, como os data centers flutuantes — a coreana Samsung Heavy Industries e a cingapuriana Seatrium já têm projetos de dezenas de megawatts —, e pesquisas com resfriamento por água do mar mostram economia relevante de energia, por enquanto apenas em simulações. Nada disso está provado em escala comercial. O Brasil tem litoral, portos já estudados pelo governo para receber a cadeia da energia eólica no mar — Pecém, Suape e Açu — e uma indústria naval e de petróleo que sabe trabalhar offshore. Essas competências podem servir à infraestrutura digital mesmo em terra, com data centers perto de portos, de cabos submarinos e de energia renovável. Nessa esfera, grandes projetos de construção de novos data centers governamentais e privados aqui no país, redundantes ou não, ganham nova pauta para discussões de locais previamente já definidos, uma vez que apenas o terreno se torna parte pequena na conta, e ganham celeridade para serem executados. Provavelmente o caso com que tive muito contato em Vitória, no estado do Espírito Santo, e no Triângulo Mineiro. Para empresas e investidores, a lição é tratar a localização da computação como risco geopolítico, e não apenas técnico. Quem contrata nuvem deve perguntar onde ficam seus dados, o que aconteceria se o fornecedor congelasse a expansão no país e se existe alternativa. Quem investe tem o olhar além das big techs, sendo energia contratada no longo prazo, transmissão, refrigeração, cabos, construção e financiamento de projetos os elos que ganham em qualquer cenário, porque alguém terá de construir, alimentar e resfriar essas máquinas, aqui ou lá. E, para governos, o recado é que atrair data centers exige previsibilidade, regras tributárias estáveis, licenciamento claro e energia firme. Como princípio claro da inteligência vir antes do dinheiro, a ameaça de Trump ainda é só uma frase, mas mostra que o mapa da IA será também orquestrado geopoliticamente. O dinheiro inteligente não vai esperar a regra sair para se reposicionar. O Brasil quer ser apenas um endereço onde outros constroem ou um país que participa da construção? *Marcela Costa é CEO da SM Partner, um ecossistema de investimentos, estrategista, conselheira e engenheira de telecomunicações. Tem mais de 18 anos de experiência executiva em tecnologia, com passagens por IBM e Oracle, e atua com governança, Smart Money e construção de valor em empresas.

artigo.texto: I’m a momentum trader, and I’m always looking for stocks where the potential reward outweighs the risk. Today I’ve got my eye on Vertiv Holdings . I already own a position in Vertiv and I'm looking to buy more. The Ohio-based company provides essential equipment for data centers, including power management and cooling systems that keep servers running. Key points Strong third-quarter earnings and surging orders show demand is still high. Local restrictions could delay data center construction, but they haven't translated into canceled orders. Vertiv generates free cash flow without taking on the same financial risks as its customers. Vertiv shares plunged 25% in the first two trading days after the November midterms amid growing concerns that opposition to data center development could lead to construction restrictions. Shares have continued to slide and are now trading roughly 55% below their May high of $379.94. What's interesting is that while the political rhetoric is getting worse, Vertiv's underlying business is getting stronger. This creates the kind of asymmetric trade I'm looking for. Why I'm buying Business is booming despite the backlash In Vertiv's third-quarter results, revenue surged 61% from a year earlier to $4.31 billion, while adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.21, beating Wall Street's estimate of $1.82 by roughly 21%. Adjusted operating margin reached 25.2%, and organic orders more than doubled from a year earlier. Management also raised its full-year guidance. Those are impressive numbers for a company whose shares have been cut nearly in half. A delay doesn't mean a cancellation There is political opposition to data centers, but there's a key distinction between local opposition and a nationwide slowdown in data center construction. So far, restrictions have been limited to the local level, with bans in towns across six states. There are no statewide bans. I think states and communities that don't want data centers may ultimately reject them, while those that welcome the investment will attract more development. That could change where data centers get built, but it doesn't necessarily eliminate the demand for them. An overlooked advantage Vertiv sells the power and cooling infrastructure that those companies need. It doesn't carry the same construction-related debt burden as the customers financing these massive projects. The company generates positive free cash flow and receives advance payments from customers. That matters in an environment where investors are increasingly questioning the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv Holdings, YTD Management also raised its dividend by 60% on November 16, another sign of confidence in the company's cash generation. Why now? Wall Street's consensus price target for Vertiv is approximately $329, implying roughly 92% potential upside from current levels. Given the stock's recent volatility however, I would use stops to protect capital if shares continue to weaken. Bottom line The biggest risk is that the political backlash gains enough traction to produce statewide restrictions or more widespread delays in data center construction. Vertiv's stock is also trading well below its major moving averages, so the technical damage is real. But right now, the company's results aren't showing the deterioration that its stock price suggests. Steven Grasso is the CEO of Grasso Global Inc. artigo.texto: 247 – O juiz Diego Câmara, da 17ª Vara Federal da Seção Judiciária do Distrito Federal, rejeitou nesta quarta-feira (25) um pedido de liminar impetrado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica). A entidade buscava suspender o leilão de baterias programado para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. Ao fundamentar a decisão, o magistrado destacou que as consequências práticas desaconselham a paralisação da disputa. De acordo com o juiz, a interrupção do certame poderia gerar o risco de déficit de potência no sistema elétrico do país. Com isso, a Justiça acolheu a argumentação formulada pela defesa da União e da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL). O julgador registrou que nenhuma norma impõe a obrigação de regulamentar o rateio antes da realização do leilão, apontando ainda a falta de urgência da medida, visto que nenhum valor será cobrado antes de agosto de 2028.

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O armazenamento de energia é mais do que uma alternativa tecnológica, é uma questão estratégica para a operação e a expansão dos sistemas elétricos. À medida que cresce a participação de fontes renováveis variáveis, como a solar e a eólica, aumenta também a necessidade de recursos capazes de oferecer flexibilidade, equilibrar geração e consumo e garantir suprimento nos momentos críticos. Na prática, o armazenamento desloca energia no tempo, absorvendo eletricidade em períodos de excedente de geração para disponibilizá-la quando a demanda ou o valor da energia forem maiores. Isso contribui para mitigar cortes de geração renovável (curtailment), atender às rampas de carga e ampliar a segurança operativa. Armazenamento, porém, não é sinônimo de bateria. Existem diferentes tecnologias capazes de estocar energia, cada qual com características técnicas, econômicas e operativas próprias. O debate não deve ser a defesa de uma solução específica, mas o reconhecimento do papel de cada uma na matriz de flexibilidade do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Além disso, o armazenamento não é a única resposta aos novos desafios: expansão da transmissão, resposta da demanda, maior flexibilidade de hidrelétricas e termelétricas e aperfeiçoamento dos sinais econômicos também fazem parte da solução. A escolha deve partir, portanto, da necessidade do sistema: potência, capacidade, duração, tempo de resposta, localização, disponibilidade, vida útil e custo total. No cenário internacional, as Usinas Hidrelétricas Reversíveis (UHR) ocupam posição de destaque no armazenamento em grande escala e longa duração. Segundo a International Hydropower Association (IHA), a capacidade instalada mundial da tecnologia ultrapassou 200 GW ao final de 2025, com recorde de 11,7 GW adicionados naquele ano. Embora seja uma tecnologia madura, o armazenamento hidrelétrico reversível recuperou relevância estratégica diante das transformações dos sistemas elétricos. Uma UHR armazena eletricidade por meio da transferência de água entre dois reservatórios em diferentes altitudes. Durante o bombeamento, a energia da rede leva água do reservatório inferior para o superior. Quando há necessidade de geração, a água retorna ao reservatório inferior pelas turbinas, acionando geradores. Trata-se de armazenamento mecânico de energia potencial gravitacional, capaz de viabilizar projetos de elevada potência e capacidade. Como toda tecnologia de armazenamento, a UHR não é uma fonte primária, mas um sistema que consome mais energia no bombeamento do que devolve na geração, devido às perdas do ciclo. Essa relação, chamada de eficiência de ciclo completo, costuma situar entre 70% e 85%, conforme a configuração, equipamentos e condições operativas. Para compreender a dimensão de um projeto, é fundamental distinguir potência (em MW, capacidade instantânea de absorver ou entregar energia), capacidade de armazenamento (em MWh, volume de energia estocada) e duração (em horas). Uma UHR de 500 MW e 5.000 MWh, por exemplo, gera durante dez horas à potência nominal, desconsideradas restrições operativas e reservas. Se a capacidade fosse de 2.000 MWh para os mesmos 500 MW, a duração cairia para quatro horas. Usinas de mesma potência prestam, portanto, serviços distintos conforme sua capacidade. Quanto à relação com os recursos hídricos, as UHR classificam-se em circuito aberto (ao menos um reservatório conectado a um sistema hídrico natural), híbridas ou circuito fechado, em que a água circula entre dois reservatórios sem conexão contínua com cursos d’água naturais, reduzindo interferências sobre o regime de vazões dos rios. No Brasil, o circuito fechado ganhou relevância regulatória após a Aneel estabelecer tratamento específico para essa modalidade na Resolução Normativa nº 1.161/2026, enquadrando-a como Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia Elétrica (SAE) autônomo. Outra classificação importante é a configuração eletromecânica, que define como a água é bombeada e como a eletricidade é gerada: - Bomba-turbina reversível de velocidade fixa: solução tradicional em que uma mesma máquina atua como bomba no armazenamento e como turbina na geração. - Bomba-turbina reversível de velocidade variável: opera com diferentes rotações, ampliando a flexibilidade. - Sistema ternário: utiliza equipamentos separados para bombeamento e geração, garantindo maior rapidez e flexibilidade na transição entre modos. A escolha dessas configurações depende das características do local, dos serviços que se pretende oferecer e da avaliação técnico-econômica. A diferença de altitude entre reservatórios é fundamental para determinar o potencial energético de uma UHR, mas é apenas o primeiro filtro. A viabilidade concreta depende de fatores geográficos, geológicos, hídricos, elétricos, ambientais e econômicos. Por envolverem obras de grande porte, como túneis subterrâneos, escavações e barragens, a qualidade da rocha e a estabilidade do terreno são determinantes. Trajetos hidráulicos longos encarecem a obra e elevam perdas de energia. Além disso, mesmo no circuito fechado, é preciso garantir disponibilidade hídrica para o enchimento inicial e para repor perdas por evaporação e infiltração. A conexão elétrica e a localização também são essenciais. É necessário avaliar capacidade da rede, requisitos de acesso e eventuais reforços de transmissão. Uma usina próxima a regiões com excedente renovável absorve energia que seria cortada; já outra perto de centros de carga ou gargalos de transmissão entrega alívio operativo. Soma-se a isso a dimensão socioambiental, que exige avaliar supressão vegetal, movimentação de terra e eventual deslocamento de atividades ou comunidades. artigo.texto: EU, UK Agree to Link Emissions Trading Systems The EU and UK have agreed to link their Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), a statement posted on the European Commission’s (EC) website recently announced. The parties committed to applying this agreement as of January 1, 2028, subject to the ratification process and entry into force in the EU and UK, a separate statement posted on the EC site noted. It highlighted that the intention to link the two systems was announced at the first EU-UK Summit in May 2025. This EC statement pointed out that the UK will expand its ETS, including for aviation and maritime. As a result, over 10 million tons of additional CO2 emissions will be included in the system, “incentivizing decarbonization,” it noted, adding that both the EU and UK ETSs will apply monitoring for aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects. “This linking will provide the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel,” the statement highlighted. The statement pointed out that the EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland’s ETS since January 1, 2020. It revealed that this link will remain in place. “Linking the EU and the UK ETS’ brings benefits for both sides,” the EC statement said. “The agreement will ensure that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK, creating a level playing field for businesses on both sides of the Channel,” it added. “It will also create a larger, more liquid carbon market with a more stable carbon price, supporting the EU and the UK on our paths to climate neutrality,” it continued. “A larger carbon market also enables more efficient investment decisions, supporting the sustainable development of the EU and UK economies,” it went on to state. A release posted on the UK government website on November 20 announced that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had agreed a “landmark package” with the European Union at the UK-EU Summit in Brussels and confirmed the linking of the UK and EU’s ETS. “Linking the UK and EU’s emissions trading schemes creates the world’s largest linked carbon market,” this release stated. “It will exempt GBP 6.5 billion [$8.4 billion] of British exports, including steel and aluminum, from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), removing a major post-Brexit barrier to trade,” it added. “Linking our emissions markets is expected to add up to GBP 3.8 billion [$4.9 billion] a year to the UK economy by 2040,” it continued. A policy paper explaining the EU-UK ETS linking agreement, which was published on the UK government website and pointed out “key features” of the deal, noted that the UK ETS and EU ETS will continue to operate as two separate but linked systems. Industry Reaction In a statement sent to Rigzone, industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) said plans to link the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems “should only be taken forward on terms that prioritize competitiveness of UK industry, reduce trade barriers, and provide investment certainty”. “Any agreement must also guard against higher UK charges for industrial carbon emitters that could disadvantage domestic operations against international competitors facing lower or no equivalent costs,” OEUK added. OEUK said in its statement that UK industrial competitiveness “must be at the core of any agreement with the EU”, noting that the UK’s oil and gas and renewable energy sectors “are critical to European energy security and are underpinned by closely connected markets, infrastructure, and supply chains”. The industry body also emphasized in the statement that cooperation on energy, carbon markets, and security “must promote increased investment across the UK and Europe”. Enrique Cornejo, OEUK Energy Policy Director, highlighted in OEUK’s statement that “the competitiveness of UK industry must be at the heart of any agreement with the EU”. “Our oil and gas and renewable energy sectors are critical to European energy security,” he added. “Any closer carbon market alignment must strengthen competitiveness, reduce trade barriers and support investment, alongside continued cooperation on energy security and resilience,” he continued. In a separate statement sent to Rigzone, an Ineos spokesperson said linking the UK and EU Emissions Trading Schemes “risks imposing yet another financial burden on British manufacturing at a time when industry is already struggling to survive”. “Linking the EU and UK ETS schemes will add further cost to businesses in addition to sky-high energy prices,” the spokesperson added. “Based on current costs, linking the Emission Trading Scheme to the EU ETS, will mean an additional 10 percent increase in carbon tax for UK businesses who are already paying a 70 percent premium due to speculation of linkage,” the spokesperson continued. This spokesperson highlighted that the EU is reviewing its emissions trading system and said “it makes little sense for Britain to commit to alignment before knowing what the future rules will be, or what influence the UK will have over them”. “This will add to uncertainty for UK industry and further undermine investment confidence,” the spokesperson noted. This spokesperson went on to state that “any agreement must protect the long-term competitiveness of British industry, maintain effective safeguards against carbon leakage and address the growing threat from cheap, high-carbon imports from China and the USA”. “The government argues that closer alignment with Europe will deliver economic growth. But if the result is higher costs, factory closures and the loss of British jobs, in practice the opposite is true,” the spokesperson warned. artigo.texto: Data centers, geopolítica e IA: a ameaça de Trump à expansão global da nuvem Empresas como Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Oracle sustentam seus serviços em infraestruturas distribuídas globalmente. Por Alessandra Montini* – A inteligência artificial depende de uma base física: data centers, energia, água e chips avançados. Por isso, decisões políticas sobre onde essa infraestrutura pode ser construída têm efeito direto sobre quem consegue desenvolver e usar IA. Em 20 de novembro de 2026, o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou em coletiva na Casa Branca que não permitirá que empresas americanas construam data centers fora do país e ameaçou aplicar um imposto elevado e outras penalidades severas a quem descumprir a diretriz. A justificativa apresentada foi evitar que a China assuma o controle dessas estruturas no exterior. Quero analisar aqui com vocês os possíveis impactos dessa ameaça sobre a cadeia global de computação em nuvem e IA, com atenção especial às economias emergentes, como o Brasil. Vale ressaltar que, segundo a análise da revista Veja, trata-se de uma intenção política ainda sem regras detalhadas, e o próprio presidente admitiu que não havia discutido o plano formalmente com sua equipe. As consequências descritas abaixo são, portanto, cenários possíveis, e não efeitos já consolidados. Risco para o modelo de expansão das Big Techs Empresas como Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Oracle, além de operadoras como Equinix e Digital Realty, sustentam seus serviços em infraestruturas distribuídas globalmente. Essa distribuição serve a dois objetivos: reduzir a latência, aproximando o processamento do usuário, e cumprir leis locais que exigem o armazenamento de dados dentro do território nacional. O caso mais imediato citado pela reportagem é o plano do Google de investir cerca de US$ 15 bilhões em data centers e infraestrutura de IA na Finlândia entre 2027 e 2028, que Trump disse pretender bloquear. Além do impacto sobre projetos específicos, a ameaça de penalidades cria insegurança jurídica para contratos internacionais já firmados e obriga as empresas a reavaliar cronogramas de investimento em escala global. Geopolítica: infraestrutura como ativo de segurança nacional Ao justificar a medida pela necessidade de conter a China, Washington trata a infraestrutura física da internet como ativo estratégico de segurança nacional. Esse movimento se insere em uma disputa tecnológica mais ampla, frequentemente descrita como uma nova “Guerra Fria” e que tende a fragmentar a rede global em blocos. Há, porém, um efeito potencialmente contraditório. Se empresas americanas forem impedidas de investir fora dos Estados Unidos, países em desenvolvimento e mercados emergentes podem passar a depender mais de alternativas chinesas, como Huawei Cloud, Alibaba e Tencent, para atender à sua demanda por processamento de dados. A medida, pensada para limitar a influência chinesa, poderia assim abrir espaço para ela. Impactos sobre economias emergentes e o caso brasileiro Vários países buscavam se posicionar como polos regionais de data centers, atraindo investimentos com energia limpa e incentivos fiscais. O Brasil, com sua matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, é um exemplo. Esses países enfrentariam agora um duplo obstáculo: a possível proibição de investimentos diretos de empresas americanas e as restrições recentes à exportação de chips avançados de IA. Na mesma semana do anúncio, o Departamento de Comércio dos EUA incluiu o Brasil em uma lista que exige licença prévia para a exportação desses chips, medida que, segundo o material analisado, também atinge Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. Sem infraestrutura local de ponta, empresas e governos teriam de processar dados a longa distância, o que encarece os serviços de nuvem e retarda a adoção de ferramentas avançadas de IA. Em termos acadêmicos, trata-se de um risco de ampliação da desigualdade tecnológica entre os países que concentram capacidade computacional e os que dependem dela. Gargalo energético e oposição interna nos EUA Concentrar toda a expansão global de data centers em território americano também esbarra em limites internos. De acordo com a reportagem, a resistência de comunidades locais, motivada pelo alto consumo de energia e água e pelo impacto ambiental, já levou ao cancelamento de cerca de US$ 260 bilhões em projetos em 2026. Na própria coletiva, Trump pediu que essas comunidades parem de barrar novos empreendimentos e negociem compensações financeiras com as empresas. O ponto revela uma tensão central: a política de “manter tudo em casa” exige que o país absorva os custos ambientais e energéticos de uma expansão que, até aqui, vinha sendo parcialmente distribuída pelo mundo. A ameaça de Trump evidencia que a computação em nuvem e a IA deixaram de ser apenas questões de mercado e passaram a ocupar o centro da estratégia geopolítica. Entre os efeitos possíveis estão a paralisação de investimentos bilionários, a fragmentação da infraestrutura global, o fortalecimento de concorrentes chineses em mercados emergentes e o aumento de custos e atrasos tecnológicos para países como o Brasil, além de tensões energéticas dentro dos próprios EUA. Como a medida ainda não foi detalhada, o acompanhamento de sua regulamentação é essencial. Para a área de IA, a lição é clara: o desenvolvimento da tecnologia depende de decisões sobre energia, território e soberania digital, e não apenas de avanços em algoritmos. *Alessandra Montini é Diretora do LabData, da FIA Business School

artigo.texto: The Department of the Army recently began soliciting data center proposals for Fort Rucker. The Wiregrass site is one of nine military bases listed in a request for proposals (RFP) released on Friday. “The Department of the Army (“DA”) is issuing this Request for Proposals ('RFP' or 'Solicitation') to solicit competitive proposals from private, public and/or not-for-profit entities interested in leasing non-excess DA land ('Properties') for development of commercial power generation facilities and data centers under a long-term lease agreement(s) ('Enhanced Use Lease' or 'EUL') at Blue Grass Army Depot, Pine Bluff Arsenal, Tooele Army Depot, Sierra Army Depot, Fort McCoy, Fort Bragg, Fort Hood, Fort Rucker, and Joint Base Lewis-McChord ('Installations')," the RFP states. “The EUL(s) that would result from this RFP would be for the purpose of the selected Offeror(s) designing, financing, permitting, developing, constructing, installing, owning, maintaining, operating, securing, and decommissioning a commercial power generation facility and a data center ('Project'). DA’s preference is for integrated power generation facility and commercial data center Projects, but an Offeror can elect to propose power generation only. DA may elect to award one or more EULs pursuant to this RFP.” The 1819 Newsletter Enter your email below to get our top stories delivered straight to your inbox every weekday morning. When asked about the Army's RFP, U.S. Rep. and Sen.-elect Barry Moore (R-Enterprise) told 1819 News in a statement on Tuesday, “My priority is ensuring Fort Rucker remains well-positioned to carry out its critical role in our national defense.” “As the Army moves through this process, I look forward to learning more about the potential opportunities and impacts for both the installation and the surrounding communities,” Moore said. “Any proposed development should be carefully evaluated to ensure it serves the best interests of our military and the people of Alabama.” According to the Army, “Power Generation Facility and Data Center Project” applicants may submit proposals for both power generation and a data center. Proposals are not restricted to any particular data center size or capacity. However, the Army’s preference is for the following data center frameworks: Profile 1: Hardened, physically isolated campuses built to ICD 705 standards for Top Secret/IL6 workloads. Profile 2: Large-scale hyperscale and AI/HPC facilities targeting PUE ≤ 1.15. Offerors electing to integrate commercial data centers alongside generation assets may do so within a unified campus master plan. “Proposed Projects must provide energy resilience capabilities to the DA that will be part of the lease consideration to be provided to DA by the Leassee,” the RFP states. “These capabilities must include the provision of resilient power within one (1) hour of a grid outage and fora minimum of fourteen (14) continuous days, and providing any required improvements to DA’s utility infrastructure that may be required to enable the Installation to accept delivery of the resilient power. For purposes of this RFP, a grid outage is defined as any loss of power from the grid serving the Installation. Preference will be given to Offerors whose Proposal is for the provision of contingency power in excess of fourteen (14) continuous days.” According to the RFP, “projects must avoid draws on water aquifers and must prioritize industrial greywater,treated municipal effluent, or closed-loop cooling towers. Water usage must be net-neutral or better. Offeror shall, at its sole expense, source all industrial process water from non-potable alternative sources, which may include brackish groundwater,reclaimed municipal wastewater (graywater), or treated industrial/agricultural runoff,subject to DA approval and regulatory compliance. DA expects that all power generated and data center capacity (where applicable) will be sold to third-party off-taker(s). The selected Offeror will be responsible for identifying and securing off-taker(s).” Proposals are due by January 18, according to the Army. artigo.texto: MHI and SAKURA sign agreement to explore Japan-based AI data centers The proposed alliance pairs industrial power and cooling technology with cloud operations. Faster construction and greater domestic control remain goals, not delivered results. Loading page… Listen to this story The November 18, 2026 memorandum pairs Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ engineering capabilities with SAKURA internet’s cloud and data-center operations to examine a strategic alliance. The work could produce Japanese-built infrastructure and modular facility designs, but the agreement funds no announced deployment or new capacity. For AI operators, the proposal addresses dependence on overseas platforms and the practical bottlenecks of power, cooling, construction time, and resilience; any expansion into Asia and Oceania depends on what the exploratory work delivers. The companies will study two workstreams: a domestic computing and service foundation, and reference architectures and modular methods for mechanical and electrical systems. SAKURA already operates data centers in Tokyo, Osaka, and Hokkaido; those facilities are existing capacity, not an outcome of the MOU. Japan’s Digital Agency selected SAKURA as a Government Cloud provider for fiscal year 2026; the companies describe it as the first domestic provider selected. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and SAKURA internet want to give Japan AI infrastructure that is domestically controlled and faster to build. Their November 18, 2026 announcement establishes an earlier step: a memorandum of understanding to explore collaboration toward a strategic alliance, including modular AI data centers. It is an agreement to investigate development, not a completed deployment. The companies describe their objective as sovereign AI and sovereign cloud: keeping data and AI platforms under a country’s own laws and control. Their proposed collaboration reaches beyond cloud services to the equipment and construction methods needed to support them. They want infrastructure designed, built and operated in Japan, with resilience against disruption as a central requirement. The partners frame overseas cloud dependence as one reason for the effort. They say much of Japan’s AI processing runs on platforms operated by foreign providers, leaving users exposed to sudden service changes or suspensions. Their case for domestic infrastructure is therefore about continued access to computing as well as control over the rules governing its use. Their joint release also identifies a more physical obstacle: AI data centers require large power supplies and advanced cooling. Securing electricity and completing construction can delay operations. The companies say facilities must also withstand disasters and geopolitical uncertainty. Rapid construction and reliable operation are linked goals in the proposal, rather than speed being its only stated measure of success. SAKURA’s announcement divides the exploratory work into two connected areas. One concerns the domestic computing and service foundation; the other concerns how the facilities themselves would be designed and assembled: As AI becomes national infrastructure, that infrastructure has to be resilient in both how it is built and how it is operated. With SAKURA internet, we want to give Japan a sovereign AI foundation that is secure, available when it matters, and fast enough to keep pace with demand. Masayuki Suematsu, executive vice president and chief strategy officer, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries MHI brings engineering capabilities spanning design, manufacturing, controls, simulation and maintenance. Its existing work covers social infrastructure, aviation, defense and space. The company says it is strengthening a data-center business that integrates cooling, power, controls and high-security technologies, with resilience already one of the pillars of its growth strategy. SAKURA supplies the cloud and data-center operating experience. It runs facilities in Tokyo, Osaka and Hokkaido and provides cloud and computing services from its own domestic data centers. That operating footprint is existing background to the agreement, rather than new capacity created by signing it. The announcement also points to SAKURA’s selection by Japan’s Digital Agency as a Government Cloud service provider for fiscal year 2026. The companies describe it as the first domestic cloud provider selected. They present that public-sector credential alongside its facility operations as relevant experience for the proposed domestic infrastructure work. Japan is the initial focus, but the intended market is not exclusively domestic. The companies aim to take products and solutions established through the collaboration into global markets, including Asia and Oceania. That overseas ambition depends on what the exploratory work produces. Loading discussion... Join the conversation Explain how much ownership should matter compared with a provider’s track record. artigo.texto: IQM Quantum Computers Partners with QAI, a South Korean Quantum-AI company to Deploy a Quantum Computer in Their Private AI Data Center in Korea - IQM will deliver an IQM Radiance R3, a 54-qubit quantum computer, to QAI, a South Korean quantum-AI data center and cloud infrastructure company, by the end of 2027. - Once operational, QAI expects to offer the system to its customers through its Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) offering to explore industry use cases. - The order is IQM’s second quantum computer sale in South Korea , following the IQM Spark system atChungbuk National University . SEOUL, South Korea & ESPOO, Finland--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 25, 2026-- IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX), a global leader in superconducting quantum computers, is partnering with QAI Co., Ltd., a South Korean quantum-AI data center and cloud infrastructure company, to deliver an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer. The order covers a complete on-premises quantum computing solution for QAI’s data center, including an IQM Radiance R3 system and associated services. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261125732569/en/ IQM Quantum Computers partners with QAI, a South Korean quantum-AI company to deploy a quantum computer in their private AI data center in Korea. The 54-qubit quantum computer will be the first IQM quantum computer deployed to a private data center in Asia. The deal brings on-premises quantum computing into QAI’s commercial data center environment, where it will help build applications and a resilient, competitive infrastructure within South Korea’s quantum ecosystem. The IQM Radiance R3 is expected to be delivered and installed on-premises at QAI’s data center in Seoul by the end of 2027. "We are proud to partner with QAI as they bring an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer to their data center in Seoul," said Sylwia Barthel de Weydenthal, Chief Commercial Officer at IQM Quantum Computers. "This sale marks an important milestone for quantum computing in South Korea. With on-premises access to IQM Radiance, QAI will be able to accelerate research, develop commercial applications for businesses and support sovereign quantum capabilities that keep critical technology and data under national control. We look forward to working closely with QAI to build a thriving quantum ecosystem in Korea and across the Asia-Pacific region." QAI builds data centers that combine GPU-based AI computing with quantum computing resources. Once the system is operational, QAI plans to make it available to its customers through its Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) offering. This would give Korean enterprises, research institutions and public organizations access to the IQM Radiance R3 quantum computer hosted in South Korea. The system will initially be used to explore industry use cases in compute-intensive fields such as drug discovery, next-generation materials, including batteries, financial portfolio optimization and scheduling optimization for logistics and energy infrastructure. "By bringing IQM Radiance R3 into our data center in Seoul, we are creating a place where Korean companies and researchers can use GPUs and a quantum computer together to solve real problems,” said Ui-tae Kim, Co-CEO and CTO of QAI. “Together with IQM, we will build an environment where Korea’s industry and research community can work with quantum computing hands-on." IQM Radiance is IQM's most powerful on-premises quantum computer, designed for integration into high-performance computing (HPC) environments, where installing it on site reduces latency for hybrid quantum-classical workloads. The 54-qubit system offers high-fidelity gates and tunable couplers between the qubits, arranged in a square lattice with the highest connectivity available at this scale. Its layout natively supports surface-code error correction. Customers own and operate the system on site, with pulse-level access and the option to upgrade with the latest chips and components as IQM's technology develops. South Korea has made quantum technology a national priority. Under its Sixth Basic Plan for Science and Technology, the government plans to invest more than 200 trillion South Korean won (approximately EUR 135 billion) in research and development between 2026 and 2030, with quantum named as one of ten national strategic technology fields. In January 2026, the Ministry of Science and ICT also set out its first comprehensive plan for the quantum science, technology and industry, which aims to give Korea the world's highest utilization rate of quantum computers by 2035, alongside training 10,000 quantum professionals and fostering 2,000 quantum companies. Reaching those goals will require businesses and researchers in Korea to have hands-on access to quantum computers. With IQM's quantum computer installed on-premises and integrated into its data center offering, QAI will be able to provide that access as a service to customers across Korea. IQM's first quantum computer in South Korea, an IQM Spark at Chungbuk National University, was the first commercial quantum computer installed through the Korean government's official procurement process. IQM opened its Seoul office in June 2025. The QAI order will further extend IQM's installed base across Asia-Pacific, following systems already delivered in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan. About IQM Quantum Computers IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX) is a global leader in integrated quantum computing, delivering full-stack superconducting quantum computers to enterprises, research institutions, universities, high-performance computing centers and national laboratories worldwide. With more on-premises systems sold than any other manufacturer, IQM gives customers direct ownership and control of quantum computers that integrate with their supercomputing and AI infrastructure, with cloud access also available through IQM Resonance. artigo.texto: To their backers, data centers dangle a tantalizing golden ticket to financially strapped communities: the promise of hefty tax revenues to plug gaping budget gaps. Critics condemn them as landscape-chewing behemoths that consume massive amounts of electricity, generate noise, and guzzle water. Frank Mand puts himself somewhere in between those positions, at least for now. That may come as a surprise to those aware of the Planning Board member’s longtime mission to protect Plymouth’s environment, notably through his affiliation with the Southeastern Massachusetts Pine Barrens Alliance. Mand is skeptical of the benefits of having a data center in town but says he needs to learn more about the pros and cons before cementing a position. He’s watched with alarm as data centers have spread across the country at breakneck speed. It’s a high-stakes race to meet the demand of an artificial intelligence revolution that offers the potential for seismic advances in medicine and other fields, along with one whopper of a potential downside: an existential threat to humanity. According to the website US Data Center Map, as of October there were 3,172 operating centers nationwide. Four hundred are under construction, with another 1,199 in the planning stage. Data Center Census, an independent website, says a typical building is 250,000 square feet (about 38,000 square feet larger than the Walmart Supercenter in Plymouth). But some facilities are much bigger – so vast they make Amazon warehouses look like mom-and-pop stores by comparison The Stratos Center in Utah, for example, would cover 40,000 acres – that’s about 47 Central Parks. No one has proposed building a data center in Plymouth. Mand, realizing the town doesn’t have regulations in place to deal with them, decided to take pre-emptive action. Earlier this year, he proposed a one-year moratorium on the complexes, which are essentially warehouses stacked with rows of humming computer servers. The Planning Board recommended a Town Meeting warrant article to that effect and in October the legislative body approved it without discussion by a 149-0 vote. Pending state approval, hitting the pause button buys time – until the fall of 2027. “Where we’re at now is that the moratorium’s passed, but we don’t have any sort of a path forward,” Mand said in an interview. The next step, he said, is to create “some kind of a citizen committee” that can study the issue and propose a set of rules to put in place before a company or developer advances a plan to build a data center in Plymouth. “I use the metaphor ‘the eye of the needle,’” he said. “The regulations have to be so strict and so refined and so protective that the likelihood of a data center coming would be very low because it just would be not what (a company) would want … I don’t even know if something that truly protects the environment and reduces noise, doesn’t use too much electricity, and doesn’t cost the town a lot of land is even a reality.” But if “all those things were in place,” Mand added, he could conceive of Plymouth hosting a modest-size data center, with the emphasis on “conceive.” With A.I. advances accelerating at a pace inconceivable just a year ago, officials here and across the country are scrambling to assess the pros and cons of data center plans that can morph from theory to reality seemingly overnight. “Plymouth has shown its stripes as the rube in the country that always is looking for that solution that’s going to solve all our problems,” said Planning Board member Frank Mand, who came up with the idea for a one-year moratorium on data centers. In October, Westfield’s Planning Board refused to issue a permit for a data center that was in the final stretch of the approval process. Earlier this month, Dedham Town Meeting approved its own 12-month moratorium. Other cities and towns in Massachusetts are considering similar moves. And nationwide, voters in the midterm elections expressed alarm over the centers’ proliferation, even as an increasing number of people rely on A.I.-powered tools daily. Locally, the subject has taken on heightened urgency with news of plans for a center in Sutton, a central Massachusetts town with a population under 10,000. The proposal by New England Patriots owners Robert Kraft and his family is anything but modest. It calls for a $16 billion, 10-building campus on 383 acres. Operating it at full capacity would gobble 900 megawatts of electricity, or about 7% of the power used statewide on a sweltering summer day. The proposal, which Sutton officials had been quietly discussing for a year, has caused a furor among most residents. A minority view it as a way out of a burgeoning fiscal crisis, one not unlike the financial challenges facing Plymouth in coming years. Once fully operational, the Kraft data center could pay a staggering $27.8 million in annual taxes. Sutton’s entire budget is $40 million. Mand said Plymouth has an unfortunate history of looking for a single answer to a broad set of challenges. He cited its embrace of the troubled Pilgrim nuclear power plant; “Hollywood East,” a far-fetched 2008 scheme to put a $300 million movie and television production campus on the site of the Waverly Oaks Golf Club; and four years ago, a similarly suspect idea to build a horse racing track and casino on county land. “Plymouth has shown its stripes as the rube in the country that always is looking for that solution that’s going to solve all our problems,” he said. “But usually, these things come with so many other problems.” Planning Board Chair Steve Bolotin credits Mand with calling attention to the data center issue. He is also quick to note that Plymouth – contrary to popular belief – does not have wide-open tracts of land to accommodate the kind of giant center that would fill town coffers with tens of millions of dollars. artigo.texto: Indian solar manufacturer Kosol Energie is looking to make a bigger play in India's battery energy storage system (BESS) market through its subsidiary KoBESS, bringing a portfolio of storage solutions spanning residential, commercial and industrial (C&I), and utility-scale applications to the country. The company is leveraging more than a decade of experience in battery energy storage deployments, with its solutions having been in the market since 2015, primarily catering to the US market. It is now looking to replicate that experience in India, as renewable energy integration, round-the-clock power requirements and energy cost optimisation increasingly drive demand for storage. Speaking to Saur Energy International, Kayan Kalthia, Executive Director – Business Development at KoBESS, said the company sees battery storage playing a critical role in transitioning renewable energy from an intermittent source to firm power. “Renewable energy plus BESS is what gives a firm load and RTC power, round-the-clock power,” Kalthia said, outlining the company's vision for energy storage in the Indian market. A portfolio spanning multiple segments KoBESS is positioning itself across three major market segments, with a manufacturing facility having a capacity of 6 GW, according to Kalthia. Its portfolio includes residential storage solutions ranging from 5 kW to 25 kW, C&I offerings including 250 kWh, 500 kW and 1 MWh systems, and utility-scale battery storage containers with capacities of 5 MWh and 6.2 MWh. The company is seeking to differentiate its offerings through quality assurance and reliability testing, with Kalthia stating that every product and bill of materials used has undergone reliability testing. He also pointed to the company's existing deployments and projects with more than a decade of operating experience as evidence of the technology's maturity. Indigenous EMS at the centre of its offering. A key part of KoBESS's strategy is its energy management system (EMS), which Kalthia described as the company's primary differentiator. Both the hardware and software for its energy management platform have been developed in-house in India, and the technology has been deployed for more than a decade. The EMS is designed to optimise energy consumption, power sourcing and storage utilisation based on a customer's requirements. KoBESS aims to use the software capabilities and historical deployment data to demonstrate the economics of storage to prospective customers, including potential returns on investment. Moving beyond standard BESS sizing KoBESS is also focusing on customised storage solutions rather than recommending battery capacity based on standardised configurations. Kalthia said the company first studies a customer's energy consumption and load profile through a data acquisition system installed at the facility. The data is then analysed through its software to determine the required BESS capacity, the most suitable application, potential savings and the expected payback period. The approach is intended to help customers better understand the economics of battery storage before committing to an investment. Autonomous energy optimisation and market participation The company is also pitching its storage systems as part of a broader energy optimisation platform that can factor in consumption patterns, weather forecasts and holidays to determine the most economical energy mix. Kalthia cited Kosol Energie’s own captive power plant as an example of the approach, describing a planned hybrid installation comprising approximately 12 MW of solar DC capacity and 25 MWh of BESS. The system is intended to match the factory's consumption at 15-minute intervals, moving it towards near-100% renewable power supply. He added that the platform can also support revenue stacking and autonomous energy market participation, including buying and trading electricity in the open market, depending on the applicable market framework and customer requirements. Betting on India's growing storage market KoBESS is introducing its existing international product portfolio to India rather than developing a separate range exclusively for the domestic market. Kalthia said the company sees Indian entrepreneurs and businesses becoming increasingly receptive to new technologies and believes energy storage investments can deliver meaningful returns. With its focus on residential, C&I and utility-scale systems, indigenous energy management technology, and experience in international deployments, Kosol Energie is looking to establish KoBESS as a broader player in India's evolving energy storage market. The company's pitch is that BESS is no longer merely an add-on to renewable energy installations, but increasingly a tool for firming power, optimising energy costs and enabling greater renewable energy integration. artigo.texto: The transaction establishes a long-term strategic partnership between Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy, based on the companies’ complementary expertise and capabilities and underpinned by a shared commitment to develop, build and bring into operation Spain’s first large-scale BESS portfolio, comprising seven advanced-stage projects. The first assets are already under construction, while the remainder of the portfolio is expected to commence construction in the coming months, with the full portfolio expected to reach Ready-to-Build (RtB) status during 2027 and enter commercial operation between 2027 and the first half of 2028. The transaction marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables’ pioneering commitment to energy storage in Spain, which it launched several years ago. The portfolio comprises seven stand-alone BESS projects totalling 380 MW / 1.5 GWh. These include the Valencia Cluster, located in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón); Santiago, in Lousame (A Coruña); Berja, in the province of Almería; and the Navarra Cluster, located in Olite and Cordovilla. The agreement also leaves the door open to further collaboration on the development of future assets, reflecting both companies’ commitment to continued growth in the energy storage market, strengthening the resilience of Spain’s energy system and reinforcing Spain’s position as a strategic market within Europe. The transaction comes at a time when Spain’s electricity market is in critical need for energy storage, which is reaching a significant level of maturity, with storage becoming the technology with the largest volume of grid connection applications in Spain, ahead of both solar PV and wind. As Daniel Sánchez, CEO of Sungrow Renewables for Western Europe, noted, “This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain’s BESS market. With 380 MW and 1.5 GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution. “At Sungrow Renewables, we backed this market when it was still a bet on the future and helped pave the way through the development and commissioning of Sanxenxo, Spain’s first stand-alone BESS plant. Today, we are taking a decisive step towards accelerating renewable energy integration and strengthening the stability of the power system, in a transaction that reinforces our long-term commitment to the Spanish market. Energy storage is no longer a promise for Spain: it is strategic infrastructure that we are turning into reality.” Sungrow Renewables’ continued strategy in Spain This latest milestone marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables’ commitment to Spain and to the integration of energy storage. The company was a pioneer in Spain in the development of hybrid solar PV projects from 2022 onward, moved early into stand-alone BESS with its Sanxenxo project, and currently has stand-alone BESS assets already in operation in the country. Spain remains a strategic market for the company, which operates in more than 20 countries. Actuate Energy focuses on dynamic European energy markets and is committed to supporting an accelerated transition toward renewable energy by investing in and operating energy storage assets that provide stability to the power system. Actuate Energy is backed by NGP, a premier energy private equity firm with over $25 billion of cumulative equity commitments. With this agreement, Spain becomes the starting point for Actuate Energy’s entry into Europe, driven by the country’s high renewable energy penetration, the ongoing need to provide grid stability, and the growth potential of a mature project pipeline.

artigo.texto: Renewable Energy Strategies for Mexico’s Data Center Expansion Panelists at Mexico Data Center Summit 2026 say renewables with storage are becoming a competitive foundation for data center power but must operate within grid-connected hybrid architectures. Atera Energy says about 1,800MW of CENACE's 7,000MW in new demand requests come from data centers, too much for solar alone. GE Vernova identifies transmission as the main bottleneck, while Atlas Renewable Energy says solutions must be designed at the system level. Panelists highlight Mexico's gas price advantage for cogeneration, EMS integration, and Energy-as-a-Service models, while warning that rapidly shifting capacity requirements complicate planning. Renewable generation paired with battery storage is becoming an increasingly competitive foundation for powering Mexico's data centers, but it will not be the only solution. Panelists at Mexico Data Center Summit 2026 say grid-connected hybrid architectures, gas cogeneration, and specialized financing models such as Energy-as-a-Service (EaaS) will be required to meet the sector's demand for stable, continuous electricity. "They are not the definitive solution, and they are not the only solution," says Daniel García, Commercial Director, Atlas Renewable Energy, referring to solar and storage. "Renewable sources are key, and they are among the main solutions, because with the integration of storage they can already be economically competitive." The discussion comes as CFE and MEXDC have established a joint power planning framework to identify the energy and infrastructure needs of new data centers. MBN has also reported that developers must evaluate energy availability and transmission capacity before purchasing land. Luis Felipe Vélez, CEO, Atera Energy, says CENACE currently holds about 7,000MW in requests for new demand, of which close to 1,800MW correspond to data centers alone. A centralized response will not be enough, he says, which strengthens the case for decentralized generation. Solar is the most advanced renewable option in Mexico and gains stability when paired with batteries, but covering that demand with solar alone would require very large installations that may not be economically attractive. Vélez sees solar and storage as a complement that stabilizes systems and reduces pressure on the centralized grid, with nuclear microreactors as a possible future option. Vanessa Varela, Sales Manager GSI – Grid System Integration, GE Vernova, says the right mix depends on the type of facility, since hyperscale, colocation, and edge data centers have different demand profiles. The data center ecosystem has embraced solar and wind partly because combined cycle turbines are not available until 2032, she says, while solar is the fastest technology to deploy. Its challenges include stability, which requires batteries, and supply chains for components such as transformers. The most important challenge, however, is transmission. Even if mixed-investment projects add about 8GW of generation by 2030, that energy must reach the sites where data centers need it, she says. García says the question should be framed at the system level. Isolated on-site renewable systems cannot yet guarantee year-round supply without backup, but most projects plan to remain grid-connected. From a financial standpoint, solar or hybrid solar-wind projects integrated with storage can deliver reliable products compatible with data center demand. "The problem is not that data centers consume energy every hour of the year. The problem is that the system is not like that," he says, adding that high renewable penetration must be complemented by expanded transmission and a broader technology mix. Jimena Ortiz, Commercial Director, Solfium, says diesel backup cannot yet be fully replaced, although battery energy storage systems (BESS) can improve power quality and reduce dependence on it. Scale also matters: each megawatt of solar requires roughly the area of a soccer field, she says. Ortiz adds that operators should start by understanding their consumption profile, and that thermal storage offers an advantage, since cooling, the largest load in a data center, can be shifted across hours. On the demand side, Vélez says Germany now requires new data centers to reach a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2, compared with a global average of about 1.5 to 1.6, which forces designs built around efficiency from the start. On the supply side, the grid will remain the main stabilizer for years, and Mexico holds a competitive advantage in natural gas. Vélez says Atera recently signed gas contracts at about US25/MMBtu in other markets,while gas in Mexico costs about US4.50/MMBtu. Self-generation alone does not compete with grid tariffs once CAPEX, OPEX, and fuel are included, but cogeneration makes projects financially viable, he says. Mexico's fast-track approval process for projects of up to 20MW is working in most cases, and larger projects can still obtain authorization through a longer process, he adds. Managing these combined sources requires energy management systems (EMS) that coordinate generation forecasts, battery dispatch, and demand, which García says are now far simpler to integrate than five to 10 years ago. Vélez says operators also need hardware, such as flywheels or batteries, to isolate their self-generation systems from grid disturbances and vice versa. Varela says AI loads, which generate power peaks unlike the stable loads of colocation facilities, are leading some governments to require AI data centers to build their own generation to protect the grid. She adds that microgrids and digital twins will be needed to simulate load and electrical behavior. Financing models are also shifting. García says EaaS goes a step beyond PPAs by allowing operators to invest in their core business while transferring risk management to energy specialists. artigo.texto: Two communities in Texas and Arizona are holding votes next month to determine the future of SpaceX data center plans in their areas. On December 9, the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission in Arizona and the Starbase City Commission are both scheduled to vote on proposals related to the data center project. The two votes center around a special land use authorization and a tax incentive package for the data centers. SpaceX plans to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing campuses, making them two of the largest data center projects in the country. Read More on AI "These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," SpaceX said on its website. SpaceX Data Center in Texas In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a 444-acre plot in Brownsville, near its own Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. SpaceX said the project has already created more than 3,000 construction jobs, with more than 500 permanent jobs coming once its operations begin. It also pledged $200 million to expand Brownsville's water and wastewater infrastructure. The company added that the facility is designed to "stand on its own" by generating its own electricity rather than pulling from the public power grid. The City Commission of the City of Starbase will convene on December 9 to consider approval of a 10-year, 100 percent property tax abatement. Starbase City officials declined to comment to Newsweek. Last week, the Cameron County commission voted against a tax break for the SpaceX data center. The company sought a tax break in Starbase, where two of the three City Commission members are current SpaceX employees. "As Texas communities consider major supercomputing investments, careful long-term tax planning is essential," SpaceX said. "The proposed abatement was designed to address this challenge: provide the County with substantial, predictable new revenue through payments in lieu of taxes (PILOTs), incentivize continued investment and meet the County’s economic development goals." The project was granted an air pollution permit by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) after outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott directed the regulatory agency to pause all data center permits until it completes its impact evaluations. Newly-elected Governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, made halting data center construction a pillar of her campaign to ensure lawmakers can provide adequate protections for Texans. SpaceX Data Center in Arizona SpaceX also plans to build a $50 billion, 747-acre data center in Cochise County, Arizona, about 80 miles east of Tucson. According to the proposal, SpaceX said the plan would reduce electricity bills by up to 20 percent and create 1,000 permanent jobs. This facility would also use a dry cooling system and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, but local residents worry about the already strained aquifer. The Cochise County Planning and Zoning board will vote on the special use authorization for Tombstone Resource LCC, the company building the SpaceX data center. This vote will determine if the project is allowed to proceed under current zoning rules. On November 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the county to postpone the December 9 vote until state and federal agencies could provide a full review of the project. "The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude," Mayes said in a statement. "The company’s proposal raises serious unanswered questions about energy reliability, water use, emergency response capabilities, traffic impacts and effects on surrounding communities. Those issues must be fully examined by the appropriate state and federal agencies before any local approval moves forward." In her letter, Mayes said the project could consume up to six gigawatts of electricity, which is nearly 20 percent of the state's current power-generating capacity, and could strain the local groundwater supplies. She also highlighted concerns about traffic, strains on local emergency service resources and the impact on local wildlife. She said the company's proposal leaves a lot about the project uncertain, saying that "the sheer scale of its power demand and physical size presents exorbitant risks," and reminded the commission of its duty to ensure the development is feasible before construction is approved. Mayes will host a town hall scheduled for Thursday, December 3, for residents to voice concerns. Newsweek reached out to Cochise County officials, Attorney General Mayes and SpaceX for comment. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas

artigo.texto: Tennessee Valley Authority filing references $1.7 billion data center deal It would appear the Tennessee Valley Authority’s new data center rates are paying off. What This Story Is About - A Securities and Exchange Commission filing hints at a major data center project within the Tennessee Valley Authority’s service area. Why It Matters - The deal describes a data center customer prepared to pay the utility almost $2 billion for power. What Happens Next - Many of the details of the project aren’t public, like when the project will begin. For Context - The TVA announced new rates for data centers in September. KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT) - It would appear the Tennessee Valley Authority’s new data center rates are paying off; a new Securities and Exchange Commission filing from the utility implies a large-scale data center may soon be built within the TVA’s service area, netting the country’s largest utility provider a $1.7 billion payday. An annual report form publicly available makes reference to the deal, saying the TVA would see a $31 million primary payment when the agreement is finalized, with the rest to come in 59 installments. That total payoff — $1.7 billion in “aggregate payments” — is important, since it’s the first agreement to fall under the TVA’s new rates. In September, TVA officials announced the new dollar amount data centers would pay for power: $1.5 million per megawatt over five megawatts. Breaking down the numbers — $1.7 trillion worth of megawatts that cost $1.5 million each — the new data center could have a power draw in the neighborhood of 1,100 megawatts. TVA Spokesperson Scott Brooks confirmed the math checked out, but he didn’t go so far as confirming the center’s capacity. Since the TVA is a partially private operation, not all information about the utility is publicly available. “Your understanding is correct, but we wouldn’t speculate on the capacity,” Brooks said. The TVA’s status as a public-private body also means some details of the deal are still under wraps, like which company wants to build the data center and where. Brooks wasn’t able to confirm the information either. “TVA does not disclose confidential business information regarding individual customers or prospective economic development projects,” he said. “Consistent with longstanding practice, we protect commercially sensitive information while working with customers, local power companies and economic development partners.” The filing also doesn’t say when a facility could begin construction, but it does say the TVA expects to log that first $31 million payment in November. artigo.texto: Add military veterans to the growing force demanding a data center reckoning. A national coalition called Veterans for Public Lands is calling on federal powers to immediately pause data center development on public lands until safeguards are in place. “These are our lands,” said Gregg Bafundo, a senior advisor of the coalition and former ranger of the Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest. “If the government’s going to do anything with these, they have to ask the permission of the American people. And right now, the American people don’t want data centers on our public lands.” The coalition launched on Veterans Day, a week after the November midterm elections where at least 69 veterans won election to Congress. “The reality is that veterans themselves … we’re not just a piece of the American pie, we are the American pie,” Bafundo said. “We’re here to protect (public lands) just like we protected (them) in the United States when we were on active duty. The mission, in many regards, hasn’t changed.” The coalition is calling on U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to begin an immediate moratorium. Burgum, a former North Dakota governor, reportedly has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies, according to a Propublica investigation. Burgum’s department recently vowed to sell off public lands to states or tribes in a five-year strategic plan. “Of course he wants to sell them. I mean, the corruption is absolutely blatant,” Bafundo said, noting that Burgum has not responded to the veterans’ request. “They want to dump these lands to the states knowing full well that states have to balance a budget,” he said. Veterans for Public Lands is also calling on the upcoming Congress to advance moratorium legislation on federal public lands within its first 100 days in office. It also wants guardrails in place during development, which include public input, environmental review and tribal consultation. A bipartisan bill slated for a passage vote in the U.S. Senate this week would weaken those protections. Veterans for Public Lands is opening the doors for other veterans to get involved in advocacy work. It is now accepting applications for its Defenders Corps, which trains veterans how to use their voices to help protect and tell the story of America’s public lands.
