artigo.texto: Proposed Colleton County data center raises questions amid moratorium COLLETON COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — A proposed data center development in Colleton County is raising questions about the county’s moratorium and drawing continued opposition from some residents. The first data center development was proposed in the county about a year ago, triggering a lawsuit and a moratorium. The lawsuit was settled last month, establishing restrictions on where data centers can be built. Two more developments have since been proposed. Lighthouse DC plans to purchase approximately 315 acres from Coastal Electric Cooperative near Interstate 95 Exit 62. The property includes the 99-acre site of the former Pomega Battery Systems project and adjacent land. Construction on the first phase is planned for 2027, with delivery targeted for 2028. “Wait, which one? Because there’s so many different things going on at all times and you want to claim that we have a moratorium, then why are we having these conversations right now?” Colleton County resident Alice Banwart said. The county says its moratorium does not affect the two developers considering data centers because both have expressed interest in areas excluded from the moratorium. The moratorium remains in place until the county’s comprehensive plan is updated to reflect areas where digital infrastructure will not be allowed. Under the lawsuit settlement, a new overlay district bans data centers across most of the county’s portion of the ACE Basin and directs development toward industrial areas. Some residents remain concerned about the potential effects on their homes. “It’s still a data center which, you know, none of us really want, but if it’s going to happen, the county is doing the right things and putting it in the right locations,” said Jennifer Singleton, a Colleton County resident and plaintiff in the settled lawsuit. “I would hate to see a situation where we can’t raise our animals, our kids are having problems sleeping and it forces us to the point that we couldn’t even live at the place that we want to call home and if I could be buried there, I would,” Banwart said. Proposed investment, jobs and taxes The county is considering a fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement, or FILOT, for the redevelopment of the Colleton Industrial Campus. County officials say the project would bring more than $600 million in combined investment, making it the largest capital investment in county history. The county also projects that, at full energization, the project will pay more than $600 million in taxes over the course of the agreement, including more than $288 million to the Colleton County School District. “If we can’t afford the basics of, you know, fire protection, 911, like that’s pretty bad, right? artigo.texto: Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) alertou para o risco de déficit de potência no SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional) já em 2027 caso a Justiça suspenda o leilão de baterias, previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Esse risco existe mesmo após a realização do LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência) de março e reforça a necessidade da contratação de baterias, segundo manifestação. O documento, ao qual a Agência iNFRA teve acesso, teve por objetivo subsidiar a defesa da União na ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) movida pela Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal). A entidade questiona a regra de custeio do certame e pediu, cautelarmente, a suspensão da realização. Na manifestação, assinada no último dia 17, a consultoria jurídica do MME defendeu a legalidade dos certames de baterias e a importância de continuidade do cronograma. A pasta afirmou ainda que não há necessidade de regulamentação prévia sobre o custeio que remunerará as baterias, uma vez que a cobrança só seria iniciada em agosto de 2028. Esse mesmo entendimento foi levado pela ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) no outro processo movido pela Abeeólica, este na Justiça Federal em Brasília. A reguladora também disse que não há necessidade de urgência para definir o encargo e afirmou que uma suspensão do certame atrasaria a entrada das baterias e afetaria os mais de 5 mil projetos cadastrados.

artigo.texto: SpaceX gets approval for 1 million data center satellites - Click here to listen to this article - Share via See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred - The Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch 1 million satellites for solar-powered data centers, advancing the company’s push to build artificial intelligence infrastructure in orbit. - SpaceX says the project could help meet growing demand for computing power while easing pressure on Earth’s electricity and water supplies. - Amazon’s Kuiper Systems, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society opposed the application, citing collision risks and other concerns about debris and satellite disposal. SpaceX won U.S. government approval to launch 1 million satellites for data centers in space, clearing a regulatory hurdle as the company charges forward with its artificial intelligence ambitions. The Federal Communications Commission, which announced the authorization Wednesday, said in a statement that the go-ahead will help fuel the United States’ efforts to advance AI. The world’s largest tech companies have been investing hundreds of billions of dollars into building data centers, which house computer servers and other infrastructure used to help train and run AI models. The creation of the data centers also has prompted concern that they are draining valuable resources on Earth such as electricity and water. SpaceX’s data center constellation, known as “Starmind,” will harness solar power, the FCC said. Other companies including Google, which announced a project this year to explore the possibility of hosting AI infrastructure in space, are also looking to the skies as part of new moonshot projects. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement posted on X. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership and expand prosperity here at home.” Some of SpaceX’s rivals, such as Amazon, have expressed skepticism about SpaceX’s Starlink effort, calling it a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Amazon’s Kuiper Systems, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society are among the companies that filed petitions to deny SpaceX’s application, according to a new government filing released Wednesday. The filing said concerns about SpaceX’s project in part centered on “collision risk, disposal failures, and casualty risk.” But the company, which relocated its headquarters from California to Texas, committed to “additional measures as core design criteria to ensure the long-term sustainability of space while upholding the highest standards of debris mitigation.” Those measures include deploying satellites at lower altitudes to make sure they’re working before moving to higher altitudes, according to the filing. SpaceX’s Starship is back on Earth, captured in midair by giant mechanical arms at its Texas launchpad. A day earlier its booster exploded, foiling its plans for a double capture. SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. In a post on X, SpaceX founder and Chief Executive Elon Musk provided brief remarks in response to Carr’s announcement. “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk wrote. SpaceX shares rose 1.3% on Wednesday to $127.44.

artigo.texto: O primeiro certame de baterias do setor elétrico brasileiro está na agenda para 2 e 4 de dezembro, mas a conta que ele gera para as geradoras só chega em 2028. Foi nessa distância entre as datas que a Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal se apoiou para negar, na quarta-feira (25), o pedido de paralisação apresentado pela ABEEólica, associação dos geradores de energia eólica. Na avaliação do juiz federal Diego Câmara, titular da 17ª Vara Federal do Distrito Federal, parar o leilão agora traria consequências práticas indesejáveis. Segundo a Agência iNFRA, ele citou como consequência prática o risco de déficit de potência no sistema elétrico, alerta do Ministério de Minas e Energia, que o situa já em 2027. O magistrado entendeu que o pedido não preenche os requisitos legais para a suspensão. Não enxergou, no caso, perigo de dano iminente nem ameaça ao resultado útil do processo. O perigo de dano, segundo o juízo, se dissolve diante do calendário. Leiloar em dezembro não ativa cobrança nenhuma para as geradoras, porque o encargo só nasce em 1º de agosto de 2028, quando os projetos de armazenamento começarem a operar. A ação civil pública questiona o custeio da contratação das baterias, imputado por lei às geradoras de energia. Na visão da ABEEólica, essa lei é inconstitucional, e o certame também saiu irregular por ter sido convocado antes de a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) regulamentar como os custos serão rateados. A tese de inconstitucionalidade, porém, não chegou a ser examinada. Como a associação já levou ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) a discussão sobre a validade da lei, o magistrado concluiu que “não é prudente que este Juízo… antecipe o juízo sobre a validade de lei federal que a própria parte autora submeteu à Corte Constitucional”. Também caiu por terra a alegação de ilegalidade do certame. Segundo a decisão, não existe norma legal ou regulamentar que obrigue a Aneel a definir previamente o rateio do encargo entre os geradores como condição para o leilão.

artigo.texto: FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million Starmind data centers in space Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit. Issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.” “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.” Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.” Under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command. The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan. A request from the company to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information. To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license. Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” According to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license. SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk. The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August. Shares of SpaceX closed up 1.3% today. artigo.texto: VAN BUREN TOWNSHIP — Wayne County ordered construction to stop at a data center campus being built for Google after inspectors found that work was affecting several county drains and creating a risk of flooding. The county issued the Nov. 20 order to Panattoni Development Company, citing work without a required county construction permit and violations of its stormwater rules. Wayne County Public Services Director Oladayo Akinyemi said inspectors found obstructions in drains and work in areas reserved for drainage access. The developer had a soil erosion permit that allowed limited work such as tree trimming and grading. The county said crews failed to install adequate erosion controls, including silt fencing, allowing sediment to enter county drains. The order also cited unpermitted work within a county road right-of-way. The Van Buren Township Planning Commission approved the project’s final site plan in October. County spokesperson Matt Allen said work next to a county drain also requires a plan to manage runoff, particularly during heavy rain, when mud and silt can wash into the drainage system. The county said Panattoni must obtain a county construction permit, address the erosion-control violations and reach an agreement with the relevant drainage districts or the Wayne County drain commissioner before work can resume. Panattoni said it is working with county officials to address the issues raised in the order. Allen confirmed on Nov. 24 that construction had stopped. He gave no timetable for when it might resume. The development, known as Project Cannoli, spans about 282 acres east of Haggerty Road and north of the Interstate 94 North Service Drive. The developer estimates the campus could use 2 million to 3.6 million gallons of water per day and require about one gigawatt of electricity once operational. Google is slated to use the campus.

artigo.texto: A EDP condiciona a sua participação no primeiro leilão de baterias do Brasil, a ocorrer nos dias 02 e 04 dezembro, à alteração das regras de pagamento do encargo financeiro decorrente da contratação. Sem a garantia de que o custo seja assumido pelo sistema elétrico global é “muito difícil” licitar, considerou o presidente da EDP América do Sul, João Brito Martins, em conversa com jornalistas em São Paulo. Apesar de ter inscrito 700 MW de projetos para o leilão, a empresa aponta barreiras regulatórias que geram uma dupla penalização aos geradores do mercado livre. “Há uma condição que é crítica para nós podermos ir a leilão, que é a clarificação de como fica o pagamento do encargo”, afirmou o presidente da EDP América do Sul, João Brito Martins. O impasse tem origem na lei aprovada em novembro do ano passado, após uma medida provisória do Governo brasileiro, que atribuiu aos geradores a responsabilidade pelo pagamento dos custos do leilão de baterias. No mercado regulado, esse encargo é repassado automaticamente para os consumidores finais, explicou Brito Martins. Contudo, para os geradores com contratos no mercado livre de energia, como a EDP, não existe qualquer repasse desse custo, segundo explicou. O gestor alertou que os operadores do mercado livre já sofrem com o “curtailment” — a limitação da produção renovável por excesso de oferta ou restrições de rede — e seriam novamente onerados. “Eu já sou penalizado porque tenho curtailment e passo ainda a ser penalizado por suportar um encargo não previsto no momento da decisão de investimento”, explicou Brito Martins. A EDP defende que as baterias trazem estabilidade, flexibilidade e resiliência a toda a rede elétrica, devendo o custo ser repartido pelo sistema como um todo. Um projeto de lei em tramitação no Congresso brasileiro propõe essa alteração, o que poderia exigir o adiamento do leilão para adaptação do edital. No entanto, avalia o gestor, a empresa não conta com aprovação da proposta antes do leilão acontecer na próxima semana. A multinacional reitera que a disciplina de capital sobrepõe-se à assunção de riscos regulatórios que comprometam a receita necessária para cobrir os investimentos. Caso as regras atuais se mantenham, a obrigação de entrega dos equipamentos até agosto de 2028, sob pena de sanções, torna a participação inviável. A EDP já opera 550 MW em baterias globalmente, com presença consolidada nos Estados Unidos e um parque recente de 60 MW no Chile. “Sem a clarificação de que o encargo é suportado pelo sistema, é muito difícil podermos participar nesse leilão”, concluiu o líder da EDP na América do Sul. Para tentar atrair ainda mais empresas a participarem, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) reduziu o investimento de referência de 9,8 milhões de reais/MW para 6 milhões de reais/MW, o equivalente a 1,39 milhões de euros/MW para 931 mil euros/MW. Na última terça-feira, a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) defendeu a manutenção dos leilões de baterias já na próxima semana, considerando que é “urgente”. O posicionamento da entidade foi em reação a duas ações judiciais apresentadas na semana passada contra o edital na Justiça brasileira pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica). Abeeólica pede que o leilão não se realize antes da definição das regras sobre a divisão dos encargos de contratação das tecnologias.

artigo.texto: FCC Approves SpaceX Request to Launch One Million Data Centers into Space The approval comes without any environmental review needed to ensure the project will not cause irreparable harm to the planet Contacts Elizabeth Manning, emanning@earthjustice.org; 907-277-2555 In a stunning decision posted on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, the Federal Communications Commission has approved a request by SpaceX to deploy a million data center satellites into orbit. The decision was finalized without any environmental review, as required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Organizations had previously petitioned the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for a comprehensive review of the environmental risks, impacts, and costs of satellite-based data centers. The petition asks the FCC to pause granting any licenses for these “orbital data centers” until it conducts a programmatic environmental review. The SpaceX proposal is one of several that have in recent months sought a license from the FCC to deploy massive numbers of data centers into space. Putting an unprecedented number of satellites in space risks changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky. “These projects could permanently alter the night sky as we know it,” said Ruskin Hartley, executive director of DarkSky International. “The FCC needs to take seriously its obligation to ensure these projects do not cause unnecessary harm to naturally dark skies, and to our overall environment.” “Allowing a million orbiting data centers with no environmental review isn’t just irresponsible — it’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.” “Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.” The number of satellites in space has grown exponentially in the last several years. In 2015, there were about 1,400 active satellites; as of 2026, there are 15,000 satellites, and that number is projected to grow to an additional 58,000 by 2030. SpaceX’s proposal seeks permission to launch up to a million space-based data centers. Satellites have several known environmental impacts, including emissions from rocket launches and reentries, debris from potential collisions, degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution that would disrupt and harm our wildlife and negatively affect humans. The Federal Aviation Administration (“FAA”) is following a similar trajectory as the FCC, and recently proposed a rule to exempt space launches from every environmental and resource protection law. Another factor to consider with this authorization is that under the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (“BAAJA”), the proposed permitting reform legislation, a future administration would not be able to revoke the license except in narrow situations. Worse, it would block judges from enforcing environmental review laws even if they found they’d been violated. “This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of Trump,” said Sam Sankar, Senior Vice President of Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.” Additional Resources About Earthjustice Earthjustice is the premier nonprofit environmental law organization. We wield the power of law and the strength of partnership to protect people's health, to preserve magnificent places and wildlife, to advance clean energy, and to combat climate change. We are here because the earth needs a good lawyer.

artigo.texto: Principais pontos - Em cerca de 90% do ano, a maioria dos data centers da Amazon usa o ar externo para refrigeração, sem usar nenhuma água. - Os data centers da Amazon são mais de sete vezes mais eficientes no uso de água do que a média do setor. - A Amazon melhorou em 52% a eficiência hídrica de seus data centers desde 2021, mesmo com o crescimento do uso de IA. À medida que cresce a demanda por computação em nuvem e IA, crescem também as dúvidas sobre como os data centers afetam os recursos hídricos locais. Quanta água eles realmente usam? De onde vem essa água? E o que acontece com ela depois? O acesso à água potável é um direito humano básico, e levamos a sério nossa responsabilidade com as comunidades onde atuamos. É por isso que projetamos nossos data centers para usar o mínimo possível de água e nos comprometemos a devolver às comunidades e ao meio ambiente mais água do que usamos nas operações diretas dos nossos data centers. Do uso de água e das contas domésticas às tecnologias de refrigeração e à reposição hídrica, confira as respostas para as perguntas mais frequentes sobre os data centers da Amazon e a água, e o que os dados mostram. Quanta água os data centers da Amazon usam? Em cerca de 90% do tempo, a maioria dos nossos data centers não usa água para refrigeração. Em vez disso, eles usam o "free air cooling" (resfriamento por ar livre), que capta o ar externo e o faz passar pelos servidores para absorver o calor, devolvendo-o depois para fora, sem envolver água. Usamos água para refrigeração apenas em cerca de 10% do ano. O data center médio da Amazon usa menos de 13.000 galões de água por dia (cerca de 49.000 litros), o mesmo que aproximadamente 42 residências nos EUA, em comparação com uma média do setor de cerca de 170.000 galões por dia. Considerando toda a nossa estrutura global de data centers, captamos cerca de 2,5 bilhões de galões em 2025. Para efeito de comparação, os norte-americanos usam cerca de 3,3 trilhões de galões por ano só para regar gramados e jardins, segundo a U.S. EPA. Ou seja, todos os anos a irrigação paisagística usa mais de 1.300 vezes mais água do que nossos data centers. Quanta água os data centers usam em comparação com outros setores? Embora os data centers tenham estado recentemente em evidência pelo uso de água, eles respondem por apenas 0,5% do uso industrial de água (e a Amazon representa uma pequena parte disso, cerca de 2%), e vêm melhorando continuamente sua eficiência com tecnologias inovadoras de refrigeração e sistemas de reciclagem de água. Um único prédio de data center em Indiana, por exemplo, usa cerca de um terço da água que um lava-rápido comercial usa em um ano. Um estudo comparativo intersetorial de 2026 da AECOM comparou os data centers com outros oito grandes setores industriais dos EUA (de químicos e mineração a alimentos e papel) e concluiu que os data centers foram os que menos captaram água entre todos eles. O mesmo estudo mostrou que os data centers geram mais valor econômico por galão do que qualquer outro setor analisado, incluindo cerca de US$ 12,5 milhões em PIB e 86 empregos para cada milhão de galões captados. Enquanto isso, os campos de golfe dos EUA usam cerca de 200 vezes mais água do que toda a frota de data centers da Amazon, consumindo em cerca de dois dias mais do que os data centers da Amazon consomem em um ano. Os data centers tiram água potável das comunidades vizinhas? Priorizamos fontes de água que não concorram com as comunidades. Sempre que possível, usamos água de reúso em vez de água potável para refrigeração, e usamos 100% de água de reúso em mais prédios do que qualquer outra empresa. Antes de construir, trabalhamos com as concessionárias locais para entender as necessidades hídricas da região e investimos na modernização da infraestrutura local sem onerar os consumidores atuais. Quando usamos água da rede municipal, nosso compromisso water positive significa que investimos em projetos que devolvem mais água do que usamos nas operações diretas dos nossos data centers, nas mesmas bacias hidrográficas onde atuamos. O que é água de reúso e quanto dela os data centers da Amazon usam? Água de reúso é esgoto tratado. É a água residual do dia a dia, da pia, do chuveiro, do vaso sanitário e da lava-louças, que segue para uma estação de tratamento municipal. Depois de tratada conforme o padrão exigido para uma finalidade não potável específica, como irrigação ou refrigeração industrial, ela pode ser reaproveitada em vez de descartada. Muitas cidades a distribuem por uma infraestrutura dedicada, muitas vezes chamada de sistema de "tubulação roxa" (purple pipe), para diferenciá-la das redes de água potável. A Amazon já usa mais água de reúso do que qualquer outra grande operadora de data centers, segundo uma análise de pesquisa divulgada recentemente. Temos 26 instalações que usam 100% de água de reúso e outras 130 instalações com contrato para usar água de reúso no mundo até 2030, o que ajudará a preservar 1,6 bilhão de galões de água doce por ano. Também estamos ajudando as comunidades a criar esses programas. Na Virgínia, trabalhamos com a Loudoun Water para nos tornarmos a primeira operadora de data centers do estado autorizada a usar água reciclada em sistemas de resfriamento evaporativo direto. No Mississippi, em Hong Kong e na Indonésia, a Amazon também financiou infraestrutura e ajudou no licenciamento para criar novos programas de água de reúso. Como a Amazon está melhorando a eficiência hídrica? Medimos a eficiência no uso de água (quanta água uma empresa usa por unidade de computação) em litros por quilowatt-hora, ou L/kWh. Em 2025, as operações globais de data centers da Amazon usaram apenas 0,12 L/kWh, mais de sete vezes mais eficiente que a média do setor, de 0,84 L/kWh, e uma melhoria de 52% desde 2021. artigo.texto: A site built to bury waste is now generating electricity. Holliston, Massachusetts has activated the Marshall Street solar-plus-storage project on its capped municipal landfill, pairing nearly 5,700 solar panels with a 2.75-megawatt-hour battery system. A capped landfill is a closed disposal site sealed with a protective containment layer over buried waste. That design makes it poorly suited for housing or conventional construction, but structurally compatible with solar infrastructure. Nearly 5,700 panels sit on a ballasted mounting system, meaning the equipment is anchored with weight rather than driven stakes, so the protective cap beneath stays intact. Keeping that layer undisturbed is essential: penetrating it would risk compromising the containment separating buried waste from the surrounding environment. Onyx Renewables developed, owns, and operates the project. Town Meeting approval set off roughly seven years of permitting, utility interconnection reviews, financing, and construction before the facility reached activation. The battery carries a 2.75-megawatt-hour rating, a measure of stored energy capacity. That figure is distinct from the array’s 3.4-megawatt generation rating, which describes how much power the panels can produce at a given moment. Storage allows electricity generated during daylight to be dispatched later, adding flexibility to when and how the power reaches the grid. Holliston will receive lease payments and payments in lieu of taxes under agreements running up to 25 years. PILOT, as the latter arrangement is known, is a negotiated fee that replaces standard property taxes on the facility. Specific revenue figures have not been disclosed in the cited project materials. The project sits beside the town recycling center and soccer fields. Closed landfills can become difficult-to-use parcels in communities with limited available land, and placing solar development on them avoids competing with undeveloped forests, farmland, or recreational space. Six completed U.S. landfill-solar projects totaling more than 14 megawatts DC across Connecticut, New York, and Massachusetts make up the company’s current portfolio, according to Onyx. Project cost, annual municipal revenue, power pricing, and participation in Massachusetts’ SMART incentive program were not disclosed in the cited project materials. Holliston Town Manager Frank Gervasio called the installation “a meaningful contribution to our community’s environmental goals,” according to Resource Recycling. The project illustrates how Massachusetts communities can redirect closed waste sites toward productive municipal use, a model that may apply to dozens of similarly capped parcels across the state.

artigo.texto: EUA autorizam SpaceX a lançar 1 milhão de satélites para data centers Decisão permite à empresa de Elon Musk instalar data centers em órbita até 2038; projeto enfrenta críticas A FCC (Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos) autorizou a SpaceX, empresa de Elon Musk, a lançar 1 milhão de satélites para formar uma rede de data centers em órbita. A decisão foi confirmada nesta 4ª feira (25.nov.2026). Batizada de Starmind, a constelação deverá atender à demanda por capacidade computacional para sistemas de inteligência artificial. A autorização estabelece prazos para a implantação da rede. A SpaceX deverá iniciar as operações até novembro de 2033 e colocar 100 mil satélites em órbita até novembro de 2035. A meta é atingir 500 mil unidades até novembro de 2038. As informações são da Reuters. ENERGIA SOLAR A SpaceX afirma que os data centers em órbita terão acesso direto à energia solar, o que reduziria os custos de operação e o impacto ambiental em comparação com as estruturas terrestres. Segundo a big tech, a exposição quase contínua à luz solar permitirá melhorar a eficiência energética dos equipamentos e diminuir os gastos com manutenção. A execução do projeto depende, em parte, da redução dos custos de lançamento da Starship, foguete reutilizável da empresa que ainda está em desenvolvimento. O veículo deverá ser utilizado para transportar os módulos dos data centers ao espaço. CRÍTICAS A unidade de satélites Leo, da Amazon, e outras empresas se opuseram ao projeto. Elas afirmam que a SpaceX dificilmente conseguirá colocar todas as unidades previstas em órbita e que a implantação poderia levar séculos. A SpaceX pediu licença para lançar 42.000 satélites Starlink, mas a rede conta com pouco mais de 11.000 unidades em operação. Atualmente, há cerca de 17.000 satélites em órbita, segundo a FCC. A agência também autorizou pedidos da big tech para ampliar os recursos de comunicação de sua rede óptica.

artigo.texto: The Santa Barbara Independent republishes stories from CalMatters.org on state and local issues impacting readers in Santa Barbara County. On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products. College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives to ChatGPT are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system — the largest higher education system in the country — is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network that would, according to the proposal, be a “fraction of the cost of commercial solutions.” The University of California is considering doing something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having “initial conversations” with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn’t finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. University-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy, but they’re “not quite necessarily as intuitive,” said Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor’s office on AI. “Your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them.” Locally, individual universities are already moving forward with their own AI plans. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. The most advanced, university-controlled AI platform is at UC San Diego, where university IT services collaborated with its supercomputing center to create TritonGPT, a nod to the campus mascot and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. UCSD was also cited as a partner in the community college system’s AI proposal. “This is the model that the higher education system in the state of California is trying to expand,” said Zachary Johnson, the senior director of AI strategy for UCSD. Why sovereign AI is gaining popularity For the community college system, developing an independent or sovereign AI system comes with three main benefits, Hayward said. The first is cost. While tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are the most popular examples of AI, they’re expensive, with individual plans reaching $200 per month and incurring further costs to go beyond usage limits. To develop their own AI systems, colleges don’t work from scratch — they use other AI tools, known as open-weight models, including Chinese products such as Kimi or DeepSeek or American ones such as Llama and Gemma. Getting these products up and running can be costly, but once operational, they are often not only cheaper than ChatGPT or Claude but also give schools more control. The code behind these low-cost models is typically free to use or change, allowing colleges to rename and rebrand the AI or even repurpose it entirely. The second benefit is control. The Cal State contract with OpenAI specifically says that the company cannot use student data to train its models, but Hayward said these kinds of agreements still have risks and unknowns. “There’s just this concern that somehow it’s going to leak,” he said, adding that internally developed AI tools give colleges “end-to-end control” over the data. That control is helpful for research and for operations. Campuses can develop AI uses that are tailored to help with other projects that commercial models like ChatGPT or Claude aren’t necessarily built for, such as using AI to help with admissions or course enrollment. Lupo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo said these more independent AI models also allow computer science professors and students to design their own AI experiments without having to worry that a third-party might change its model in the middle of an experiment. Hayward said the last benefit is environmental. The community college system has lofty climate goals, including reducing potable water usage by 50%. He said that by adapting open-access or open-weight AI models, colleges take on more of the burden of AI computing internally, which means they can more closely track the power and water demands of these systems. “We can better monitor and know our AI footprint,” Hayward said. “It’s somewhat obscured when you use big vendors like Anthropic and Google.” Pushback to OpenAI For many UC and Cal State leaders, however, big vendors still hold a lot of sway. “OpenAI models are more advanced than open-weight models,” said Holbrook, with the UC. artigo.texto: Kalshi traders put odds of data-center pauses in at least four states at 57% The November 25 snapshot marks a rebound from Sunday, but remains below the post-election peak. New York’s existing permit pause shows what one such restriction covers. Loading page… Listen to this story New York’s temporary permit pause gives traders a real policy example, but it applies to certain permits for new hyperscale data centers—not operating facilities or every proposed project. Kalshi’s contract put the chance of at least four states adopting moratoriums in 2026 at 57% on the morning of Nov. 25, up from 52% three days earlier. That is still below the roughly 75% peak after the midterm elections, and reflects market expectations rather than confirmed state action. The contract counts states adopting moratoriums and is to be verified using state governments; it does not measure projects halted or computing capacity affected. Governor Kathy Hochul signed New York’s pause on July 14; it can last up to one year while the state develops environmental standards. During the review, New York’s Department of Environmental Conservation will withhold discretionary permits not already deemed complete; the state says projects can proceed after standards are set if they meet state and local requirements. Kalshi traders put the chance of at least four states adopting data-center moratoriums in 2026 at about 57% on November 25, CNBC reported. That puts the prospect of wider state-level restrictions above even odds in the market—not confirmation of new limits on developers. The probability rose from 52% on November 22, a five-percentage-point increase by Wednesday morning. But traders were less convinced than immediately after the midterm elections, when the odds reached about 75%. The latest move is a partial rebound, rather than a new high in expectations for state action. The contract asks, “How many states will adopt data center moratoriums this year?” CNBC says the result will be verified using state governments. Its scope is the number of states adopting moratoriums—not the number of individual projects stopped or the amount of computing capacity affected. CNBC disclosed a commercial relationship with Kalshi that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment. New York provides an existing example of the policy traders are betting will spread. Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order on July 14 temporarily pausing certain state environmental permits for new hyperscale data centers—large facilities housing thousands of computer servers—while regulators develop standards. The state described a pause lasting up to one year, tied to preparation of a Generic Environmental Impact Statement, a review of data centers’ potential environmental effects. During that work, the Department of Environmental Conservation would withhold discretionary permits not already deemed complete. That is a specific permitting restriction, rather than an order to shut operating facilities. The review is intended to assess effects from construction and operation, including energy demand, water use and quality, and air quality. Hochul’s administration said the pause would give the state time to establish consistent standards while protecting utility customers, the grid, the environment and communities. New York’s announced route back to development is completion of those standards. The state said it would then lift the moratorium, allowing projects to proceed if they meet state requirements, zoning rules and other local approvals. Loading discussion... artigo.texto: US company to invest $117 mln in battery storage project in central Vietnam U.S.-based Arbin Energy LLC will invest $117 million in a factory producing battery energy storage systems and battery testing equipment at the Danang Hi-Tech Park in Danang city, central Vietnam. The Danang Hi-Tech Park and Industrial Zones Authority (DSEZA) has approved the investment policy and Arbin Energy LLC as the investor for the Arbin Energy Danang Factory project. The project will cover 5.34 hectares at the Danang Hi-Tech Park, with total investment exceeding VND3.05 trillion ($117 million). The factory will focus on manufacturing battery energy storage systems (BESS), battery testing equipment and machinery used in battery production. Its BESS production line will have a designed capacity of 5,000 containers per year, equivalent to 5 GWh annually. The project will add energy storage equipment manufacturing to the hi-tech park's industrial portfolio and create opportunities to connect with supply chains involving companies in power electronics, measurement and automation. Construction is scheduled to begin in December 2026, with production expected to start in the third quarter of 2028. With the latest project, the Danang Hi-Tech Park has attracted a total of 14 foreign direct investment (FDI) projects, with combined registered capital of $830.5 million. In September 2026, during a working visit to the United States, Chairman of the Danang People's Committee Nguyen Manh Hung held a meeting with Arbin Instruments, chaired by its chairman, Chaojiong Zhang. The two sides discussed and updated the company's investment plans in Danang, focusing on project scale, technology, products, infrastructure requirements and implementation timelines. In addition to manufacturing operations, the discussions covered potential cooperation in research and development (R&D), technical training and partnerships with universities and technology companies in the city. The two sides also reviewed investment procedures and agreed on the next steps for implementation. Founded in 1991, Arbin Instruments is headquartered and operates its manufacturing facilities in College Station, Texas, in the United States. Over its 35 years of operations, the company has grown into one of the world's leading manufacturers of battery testing equipment and energy storage system testing solutions. Its core business focuses on researching, designing and manufacturing high-precision battery testing equipment, electric vehicle battery pack testing systems, solutions for industrial-scale battery production, and software systems for data management and analysis. According to the company, its equipment systems are currently used in more than 55 countries. In addition to its approximately 6,000-square-meter headquarters and manufacturing complex in Texas, Arbin Instruments has expanded its operations to Germany, China, India, South Korea, Vietnam and other markets. Its customers include electric vehicle manufacturers, battery producers, consumer electronics companies, universities and research institutes worldwide. In Vietnam, Arbin Energy LLC was established in August 2026, with its registered office at Lot A10, Danang Hi-Tech Park, Lien Chieu ward. The company has initial charter capital of VND52.14 billion ($2 million), and is wholly owned by Chaojiong Zhang, a U.S. citizen born in 1945, who also serves as its chairman. As of August 2026, the United States was one of Danang's key investment partners, with 87 FDI projects worth more than $346 million, ranking seventh among more than 70 countries and territories investing in the city. With support from U.S. diplomatic missions and investment promotion programs, Da Nang has gradually established ties with several leading global technology corporations, including Synopsys, Marvell, Nvidia and Qualcomm. Já são 87 impostos e sistemas de comércio de emissões em vigor no mundo, cobrindo 29% das emissões globais. A Europa começou a cobrar pelo carbono embutido nas importações. E o Brasil está regulamentando o seu próprio mercado, o SBCE, que deve estar em plena operação em 2031. O tema se tornou pauta econômica. Hoje influencia decisões de investimento, financiamento e competitividade. Mas, quanto mais ele avança, mais difícil fica entender como as peças se encaixam. - Por que, exatamente, colocar um preço no carbono? - Qual a diferença entre o mercado regulado e o voluntário, e onde eles se cruzam? - Quem será obrigado a reduzir emissões no SBCE, e a partir de quando? - O que são CBE e CRVE? - Como o CBAM europeu e o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris afetam as empresas brasileiras? - Por que um crédito jurisdicional pode valer três vezes mais que um crédito de projeto? O Guia Reset de Mercados de Carbono responde a essas e outras perguntas de forma didática, mas com a profundidade de quem precisa entender esses mercados na prática. Em quatro capítulos, o guia passa pelos sistemas internacionais, pelo mercado regulado brasileiro e pelo mercado voluntário. No fim, mapeia as oportunidades em sete frentes, do Corsia ao setor financeiro. Muitas dessas oportunidades têm prazo. A aviação internacional entra na fase obrigatória do Corsia em 2027. Os créditos florestais brasileiros têm vantagem enquanto as tecnologias de remoção não ganham escala. E as regras do SBCE ainda estão sendo escritas. Quem se posicionar agora tende a influenciar as regras e os preços do que vem depois. O planeta tem pressa, os negócios também. Clique aqui para baixar.

artigo.texto: Coweta County voters to decide Jan. 12 on $17 billion data center project Probate judge orders special election after petition seeks to repeal county’s approval NEWNAN, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Coweta County voters will take part in a special election Jan. 12 to decide the fate of a $17 billion data center project and whether data centers should be zoned in the county. Coweta County Probate Judge Carrie B. Markham ordered the election Monday after opponents to the project gathered more than 10,000 signatures seeking to repeal the county’s decision. The county initially approved zoning the project in rural Coweta County. Signs and voices in Newnan Yard signs line home after home along Wagers Mill Road in Newnan, calling to keep data centers out of Coweta County. The project’s future is uncertain as voters will have a chance to weigh in. “I think it’s a good idea, an excellent idea,” Leroy Kenner, who lives in Coweta County, said of the special election. “The voters should have the right to decide whether or not the data centers come to Coweta County or anywhere, period.” Jennifer Tedder said she signed the petition. “I just think it’s not a good thing for us to have in our community here,” Tedder said. What the court order says The petition was filed Oct. 16 in Coweta County Probate Court under the Home Rule provision of the Georgia Constitution, according to Markham’s order dated Nov. 23. The order said the petition seeks an election on whether to repeal one Coweta County zoning ordinance and amend another. The order said 10,971 signatures were required, which is 10% of the 109,703 active electors in Coweta County in the last general election. The county’s director of elections certified in a written report Nov. 20 that 11,065 signatures were verified. Markham found the petition valid. The order directs the Coweta County Board of Elections and director of elections to place this question on the ballot: “Shall the action of the Coweta County Board of Commissioners on April 7, 2026 approving REZONE 24-019 be repealed, and Appendix A. Zoning and Development of the Coweta County Code of Ordinances be amended to delete data centers and data center campuses as permitted and conditional uses in all zoning districts and to prohibit data centers, data center campuses, cryptocurrency data centers, and cryptocurrency mining operations in all zoning districts of Coweta County?” The election will be held Tuesday, Jan. 12, 2027. The order says the Board of Elections and director of elections will administer it under Georgia laws governing special elections. The county will pay for the election, and the court will declare and certify the results, according to the order. “We are thrilled with the Judge’s order,” Vivian Allen, a Citizens for Rural Coweta volunteer, said in a press release. “Thousands of our neighbors signed because they wanted a say, and we can’t wait to see Coweta County turn out on January 12.” “This happened because people stood in parking lots, on sidewalks, and at local events collecting signatures in the summer heat,” Donna Boles, also a volunteer with the group, said in the release. “This vote belongs to them.” About Project Sail Project Sail is a data center proposed by Atlas Development, LLC, according to Development of Regional Impact filings for the project with the Georgia Department of Community Affairs. The filings describe a data center of 13 buildings of about 378,000 square feet each, plus substations. They list the location as “Welcome To Sargent Rd & Wagers Mill” and an estimated completion date of Dec. 31, 2036. The filings estimate the project’s value at build-out at $17,161,900,000. They estimate local tax revenue at $163 million per year. PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Coweta County commissioners approve rezoning for massive data center The filings estimate water demand at 9.1 million gallons per day, sewage flow at 3.03 million gallons per day and solid waste at 800 tons per year. They list the Coweta County Water & Sewer Authority as the water and wastewater provider. According to its website, Atlas Development is based in Buford. The company filed an objection to the petition, which the court received Oct. 23. Markham dismissed the objection in a separate order Nov. 23. The order said the Georgia Supreme Court has made clear that no party has legal standing to object to a petition filed under that provision of the Georgia Constitution. The order also said the objection was not verified. Atlas representatives did not respond to our requests for comment. County response Cathy Wickey, communications manager for Coweta County Government, said in a statement that the county is still assessing the potential implications of the ruling. “The County became aware of this news at the same time as our citizens,” the statement said. “Given the unique nature of this situation, we are still assessing its potential implications. We anticipate that legal questions and challenges may arise among the entities involved.” The statement said the Elections Department will conduct the special election in accordance with state election laws, using normal election equipment and precincts. The election is scheduled for Jan. 12. Copyright 2026 WANF. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Four new municipal ordinances topped discussion at the Delaware County Planning Commission’s November meeting. Marcus Hook, Chester and Radnor and Edgmont townships all presented plans to amend their zoning codes to address the technology. Other county municipalities that have recently presented data center ordinances this year include Chester Heights and Newtown, Marple, Concord, Upper Chichester and Chadds Ford townships. No data center has been officially proposed, however a developer in Trainer is discussing plans in that town and has listed community projects that it would perform and estimated how much tax revenue there is to gain for the taxing bodies. The nine-member commission works with the county Planning Department staff to oversee development. Chairman at Large John Gillespie pointed out that while Pennsylvania requires all subdivision and land development proposals to be submitted to a county planning commission the county review is advisory only and final approval for any proposal is made by the municipality. Planning commission members said that as more municipalities update zoning to include data centers they are learning from one another and copying requirements. Michael Leventry, manager of the planning department, reviewed the four proposed ordinances, which he said had similar language. The county also has also compiled a guide regarding land use code approaches and factors for best practices addressing data centers and their related impacts. First up was Marcus Hook, which includes a 20-acre lot size, 250,000-square-foot size maximum, with a height restriction of 60 feet. Leventry said that the town is requiring a 1,000-foot separation from other data centers and a 500-foot separation from residential properties. He said has seen in other municipalities, requirements that include utilities, aesthetics and emergency response plans. The planning department recommended adding fire isolation zones within the building as well as requiring a utility curtailment agreement from the developer as well as an annual compliance report. Leventry said the department highly recommends not allowing storage of treated wastewater due to the potential for a spill or contamination. Marcus Hook Borough Manager Andrew Weldon was on hand for the meeting. He said one issue that drove the borough to develop a plan was anticipating data centers getting smaller and from a zoning perspective they don’t want them encroaching on downtown businesses. “You could potentially see a data center in a retail shop and then another data center in another retail shop,” Weldon said. Weldon said Marcus Hook’s ordinance calls for the facilities to be the heavy industrial district, with a buffer, an industrial transmission district, between that and the residential district. Edgmont’s data center ordinance would put them in the C-3 and L-I zones and would have minimum lot sizes. For data centers under 100,000 square feet the township would require a 5-acre minimum lot size and for over 100,000 then 10 acres minimum. Leventry said Edgmont’s ordinance has common language addressing utilities, aesthetics, emergency response and standard definitions. The planning department recommended considerations to the maximum building requirements with coverage of 70 percent. He said that requirement could yield a very large building as much as 7 acres. They also suggested taking another look at stormwater management requirements. One board member asked that if the data center roof does not hold solar panels, could it be converted to a green roof. Leventry said an ordinance may not address that but it could be suggested. Radnor proposes any data center be in the planned laboratory office zoning district. They would require setbacks of 200 feet, with 300 feet in some areas and with a 38-foot maximum height. Leventry said Radnor’s ordinance has standard requirements for utilities, building size, lighting, wastewater management, and site decommissioning is addressed. He said they have very specific requirements for a data center to meet. He pointed out the ordinance needs to have the underlay district comply. He said isolation zones, firefighter training, and any specialized firefighting equipment would need to be provided and maintained by the data center operator. Chester’s ordinance is similar to the other municipalities. The city is proposing data centers be located in the heavy industrial commercial district with 200 foot setbacks from sensitive areas such as homes, hospitals, daycares, nursing homes, schools, places of worship, art and community centers, landscaping, buffering requirements, emergency power, wastewater electric waste and decommissioning. The planning commission recommended isolation zones, a utility curtailment agreement and annual utility compliance reporting. Members also recommended that utility improvements are paid for by the applicant. Gillespie pointed out the commission had seen a half dozen data center ordinances, but no land development for a data center. Leventry said the planning department believes it could eventually see a plan. “Or the ordinances will be strong enough that they will chase people into some other town,” said one board member. Other projects The planning commission heard a number of other projects, including a proposed car wash at 1251 Haverford Road in Ridley Township as well as plans to subdivide a portion of the Springfield Mall parking lot near Macy’s to allow a freestanding restaurant with seating, and a drive-thru beverage shop in Springfield. The names of the businesses were not announced. Planning officials were pleased with the mall plan, stating it was a good use of otherwise wasted space that is rarely full. A final land development plan was also brought before the board for a Brandywine Conservancy Museum building off Baltimore Pike and East Creek Road near Harvey Run in Chadds Ford Township. artigo.texto: Justiça rejeita pedido de eólicas para suspender leilão de baterias Entidade quer revisão da divisão de custos antes do certame, cuja conta deve ser atribuída aos geradores A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal rejeitou nesta 4ª feira (25.nov.2026) o pedido de liminar da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) para suspender os leilões de armazenamento de energia em baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A decisão é do juiz Diego Câmara Alves, da 17ª Vara Federal Cível do DF. Eis a íntegra (PDF – 57 kB). A entidade –que representa empresas de geração de energia eólica– havia ajuizado uma ação civil pública contra a União e a Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) em 16 de novembro. A associação argumenta que a contratação de baterias beneficia todo o sistema elétrico e que a atribuição dos custos exclusivamente aos geradores é inconstitucional. Questiona também a realização dos leilões antes da definição dos critérios de rateio dos encargos. O magistrado entendeu, porém, que a realização dos leilões não está condicionada à regulamentação da divisão de custos pela Aneel –que, ao atribuir a conta aos geradores, seguiu o que está determinado na lei. A decisão argumenta que não há risco de dano iminente aos geradores, uma vez que a cobrança do encargo terá início só em agosto de 2028. A suspensão dos leilões, por outro lado, poderia comprometer a segurança do fornecimento de energia elétrica. DISPUTA SOBRE QUEM PAGA A CONTA O impasse em torno dos leilões decorre da reforma do setor elétrico, sancionada em 2025, que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores os custos da contratação de baterias. Associações do setor elétrico articulam a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026 antes dos certames. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o texto retira a obrigação dos geradores e transfere os custos aos consumidores de energia. A proposta tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara dos Deputados e foi designada ao relator Danilo Forte (PP-CE) em 28 de outubro. Entidades que representam os consumidores são contrárias à mudança. A FNCE (Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia) publicou estudo em que estima que a aprovação do projeto possa acrescentar até R$ 6,26 bilhões por ano à conta de luz. Paralelamente à articulação no Congresso, a Abeeólica acionou o STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) em 19 de novembro. Diferentemente da ação civil pública, que busca impedir a realização dos leilões sob as regras atuais, a ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) questiona diretamente a validade do dispositivo legal que atribui os custos aos geradores. O relator do processo, ministro Cristiano Zanin, ainda não analisou o pedido de liminar, segundo a decisão da Justiça Federal.

artigo.texto: Hawaii lawmakers discuss AI safeguards as county weighs data center ban HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii lawmakers are weighing the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence as they consider how to promote the technology while protecting the public. State House and Senate committees held a joint briefing on Wednesday to discuss the development and application of AI, its role in government operations and opportunities for the workforce. The meeting came as Hawaii County lawmakers consider a ban on large-scale data centers that run AI models. “Hawaii is not behind when it comes to AI, and we are actually leading the pack considering other states across the country,” Trung Lam of the Hawaii Technology Development Corporation said. Lam added that Hawaii ranks eighth out of 51 in AI usage nationwide. AI and the workforce Experts have estimated that AI could replace or eliminate up to 15% of U.S. jobs in the next five to 10 years. “One of the concerns in AI is workforce, we definitely need to be mindful of how it’s going to affect our community, especially jobs,” said state Rep. Greggor Ilagan, who attended the briefing. After the briefing, Lam said, “I think that for Hawaii, we need to understand that we don’t have a shortage of jobs, we have a shortage of high-paying jobs.” Government use and data security Government entities in Hawaii have been using AI for virtual assistance, to minimize administrative work amid a transition from paper to digital formats, and to monitor and safeguard their data systems. “I’d like to reassure the public that we have safety as one of our top priorities. We understand that the state government has a breadth of data in service of the public,” said Christine Maii Sakuda, state chief information officer and administrator of the Office of Enterprise Technology Services. “How can we understand the breadth of the work that we do within state government by leveraging AI to do it faster.” Proposed data center ban State Sen. Brandon Elefante is drafting legislation to protect government information from data breaches. Elefante also supports Hawaii County Council Bill 170, which proposes a ban on large-scale AI data centers on Hawaii Island. The proposal is distinct from smaller data centers that already exist. “What we’re hearing across the country is these big data centers, consuming electricity, consuming water in our communities, and that is a serious concern,” Elefante said. Lam added, “I think that the concern about these hyper-scale data centers is valid. I do think in Hawaii, it’s less of a concern because our energy costs and water supply is so low.” Bill 170 is set to be heard by the full council on Dec. 2. Copyright 2026 Hawaii News Now. artigo.texto: As communities across Pennsylvania face growing questions about proposed data center developments, Baker, R-Lehman Township, announced she will introduce legislation to strengthen transparency and increase public input, while ensuring residents have access to information before decisions are made regarding projects. "These decisions should be made at the local level, where officials understand the character of their communities and the concerns of their residents," Baker said. "We should be looking carefully at the availability of water and electricity and the capacity for emergency response, along with the suitability of the proposed site. We should also be prioritizing locations such as brownfields and former industrial properties, rather than sacrificing productive farmland and valuable natural resources." Baker's proposed legislation would address several concerns surrounding the development of data centers, including: —Greater transparency: Prohibit public agencies from entering into nondisclosure agreements that prevent the release of information about proposed data center developments. —Meaningful public input: Require at least two public meetings before a municipality approves a data center application, giving residents an opportunity to ask questions and provide comments. —Infrastructure accountability: Require documentation that a data center applicant has applied for electric service and paid the associated application fees and costs before the required public meetings are scheduled. —Protection of ratepayers: Strengthen reporting requirements to ensure data center development does not shift electricity costs onto other classes of customers. Baker also expressed concern about the potential effects of large-scale data center development on rural water supplies, high-value streams and electricity rates, particularly in communities where residents rely on private wells. "Developers should be responsible for the infrastructure necessary to support their projects. Families and small businesses should not be left paying higher utility bills because of the demands of a new data center," she said. "We can support responsible economic development and technological advancement while protecting our natural resources and the quality of life that makes our communities special." Baker said she will be introducing the legislation in the coming weeks. © 2026 The Times Leader (Wilkes-Barre, Pa.). Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

artigo.texto: MEGAWIDE Construction Corp. has completed the structural framework of the main building of Cebu City’s Carbon Public Market redevelopment in 10 months, with the facility scheduled to open in April 2027. The company on Thursday said interior fit-out and finishing works were now underway at the B2 building, which will replace aging market facilities as part of efforts to modernize one of Cebu City’s major commercial districts. The completion was marked by a topping-off ceremony attended by representatives of the Cebu City government, Megawide executives, project partners, contractors, market stakeholders and members of the Carbon community. B2 will house wet market vendors on the lower ground floor, while flower vendors, native crafts and select dry goods retailers would occupy the upper ground floor. Stall assignments shall be based on product categories and the list maintained by the Office of the City Markets. “B2 will give Carbon’s vendors the comfort and dignity they deserve. Consumers will enjoy a cleaner, more organized market, better facilities, and stall rates in line with the government-prescribed Market Code,” Cebu2World President Louie Ferrer said. The building will feature modern drainage, sanitation and utility systems, as well as passenger and cargo elevators, escalators and loading ramps for users of karumata — the two-wheeled carts or wagons used for loading vegetables and other goods. The upper floors are also being developed to accommodate cafés, specialty retail shops, wellness concepts and an eight-court pickleball center. Megawide said B2 was the first of several major developments under the Carbon Redevelopment Project, which aims to transform the district while preserving its role as a center of commerce and community activity. “We believe B2 can become an icon for Cebu — a world-class public market that honors Carbon’s heritage and serves its people,” Ferrer said. Shares of Megawide on Thursday added P0.01 or 0.19 percent, to close at P5.31 each.

artigo.texto: Two business verticals of Larsen & Toubro (L&T) – its Renewables business and L&T Electronic Products & Systems (LTEPS) – have jointly secured an order to develop a 300 MW / 900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at Khavda in Gujarat. The project will comprise a three-hour battery energy storage facility with a power capacity of 300 MW and an energy storage capacity of 900 MWh. The system will store surplus electricity generated during periods of high renewable energy production and release it when demand peaks. This will help improve the utilisation of clean energy, support grid stability and provide greater flexibility and reliability to the power supply network. The BESS will incorporate advanced liquid-cooling technology, designed to support higher power density, improve safety and extend the operating life of the system. The technology will help maintain operating conditions across the battery installation while supporting efficient performance during charging and discharging cycles. Located at Khavda, the facility will contribute to strengthening India’s power network as renewable energy capacity continues to expand. Energy storage systems are increasingly important for managing variations in solar and wind power generation and matching electricity supply with demand. By storing energy when generation is high and making it available when required, the project will support the integration of a larger share of renewable power into the grid. The order brings together the capabilities of L&T’s Renewables business and LTEPS for the development of a large-scale energy storage facility. It also adds to the company’s work in the energy storage sector and reflects its ability to undertake complex projects involving advanced technologies and integrated execution. The Khavda project is part of the wider development of renewable energy infrastructure in Gujarat, where large-scale generation capacity requires supporting systems to ensure reliable power transmission and distribution. Battery storage can help address fluctuations in renewable generation, improve the use of available electricity and provide additional support during periods of peak consumption. L&T continues to expand its activities across energy and infrastructure, with a focus on engineering, procurement and construction, high-technology manufacturing and specialised products and services. Larsen & Toubro is a USD 32 billion Indian multinational engaged in EPC projects, high-tech manufacturing, products and services. The company operates across diverse business domains and geographies. Its focus on technology, artificial intelligence, customer requirements and quality has supported its leadership across major business segments for eight decades.

artigo.texto: 5 Things You Didn't Know About BAAJA and Data Centers Key Highlights - Beyond hyperscale: Removal of the original 20-MW threshold potentially extends BAAJA's retail ratepayer protections to smaller data center developments. - Competition for power: States could prioritize electricity service opportunities according to the economic benefits projects deliver to other ratepayers. - Monetizing flexibility: Qualifying behind-the-meter energy resources could gain greater access to wholesale electricity markets. - Measuring actual demand: Federal electricity reporting would begin separately accounting for data center loads. - Community empowerment: DOE would provide local governments with technical assistance and opportunities for independent project analysis. For an industry increasingly accustomed to measuring its growth prospects in gigawatts, the most consequential development in American data center infrastructure this November may have come not from a hyperscaler, a semiconductor manufacturer or an electric utility, but from the floor of the U.S. Senate. On Nov. 19, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, better known as BAAJA, by a vote of 62-33. The sweeping legislative package seeks to accelerate the development of American energy and transmission infrastructure through changes to federal permitting, environmental review, judicial proceedings and electricity regulation. The legislation now faces consideration in the House. For the data center industry, the appeal of permitting reform is readily apparent. As DCF has reported, transmission infrastructure is emerging as a defining constraint on AI data center development, with the timelines required to construct new electrical infrastructure increasingly at odds with the deployment schedules envisioned by AI infrastructure investors and developers. But a closer reading of the Senate-passed legislation reveals something more consequential than an attempt to accelerate the construction of power plants and transmission lines. BAAJA is also an attempt to establish the economic and regulatory terms under which America's rapidly expanding computational infrastructure will interact with the nation's electricity system and the communities that host it. Here are five provisions that warrant particularly close attention from data center developers, operators, investors and technology suppliers. 1. BAAJA is no longer just about hyperscale data centers One of the more significant changes between the legislation introduced on Sept. 30 and the version passed by the Senate concerns the size of the data centers subject to its ratepayer protection provisions. The original legislation established a 20-megawatt threshold for its retail ratepayer protections, as outlined in an October analysis by attorneys at Foley Hoag. That threshold is absent from the Senate-passed version of Section 2107, which instead defines covered computational facilities primarily by their function. Computing equipment supporting an otherwise unrelated commercial or industrial operation is excluded. The change potentially brings a much broader segment of the industry into the scope of these provisions, including regional colocation facilities, emerging AI infrastructure providers and smaller inference-oriented developments. For new data center interconnections following enactment, the legislation would protect other utility customers against the incremental costs of serving those facilities. Utilities would require financial assurances or contributions ahead of necessary infrastructure investments, while service agreements would provide for continued cost recovery even if a data center customer ceases purchasing electricity before those investments have been recovered. The implications extend beyond electricity pricing. A hyperscaler with an investment-grade balance sheet may be considerably better positioned to accommodate such requirements than an independent developer pursuing a speculative campus or an emerging neocloud seeking to finance its next phase of expansion. As Metlen's Lillian Kasa discussed in a recent interview on the DCF Show, the distinction between announced infrastructure capacity and capacity that can actually be delivered is becoming increasingly important to the industry's investment calculus. BAAJA could add another dimension to that distinction: the ability of a developer or its customers to financially stand behind the electrical infrastructure their projects require. 2. Data centers could find themselves bidding against one another for electricity Perhaps the most striking language in Section 2107 concerns how states could allocate access to electricity among competing data center projects. The legislation explicitly recognizes state authority to use competitive solicitations or open seasons to award electric service opportunities according to the financial benefits projects would provide to other ratepayers, measured on a net present value basis, rather than simply according to the order in which applications were received. States could also establish distinct retail electricity customer classifications for data centers, offer them less favorable service terms or priorities than traditional industrial and manufacturing customers, and condition electric service on commitments to secure additional generation or accept restrictions on grid withdrawals. These provisions would not establish a mandatory national bidding system for data center power. They instead affirm existing state authority and provide a framework that individual jurisdictions could elect to employ. At the federal level, BAAJA would also direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to revise its transmission pricing policy so that eligible data center loads bear both a share of existing transmission costs and an assessment of the additional costs attributable to serving them.
