artigo.texto: SpaceX ganha autorização para colocar 1 milhão de satélites para data centers no espaço Além de estrelas, planetas, objetos voadores não identificados – para quem acredita-, foguetes e estações, o espaço poderá ficar ainda mais ocupado. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC, na sigla em inglês) concedeu hoje a primeira autorização na história dos EUA para uma constelação de satélites para centros de dados no espaço. O aval foi concedido à SpaceX, que poderá implantar 1.000.000 módulos computacionais orbitais, destinados ao processamento de volumes massivos de dados que serão utilizados aqui na Terra. “Mais fundamentalmente, a iniciativa promete aproximar a raça humana de uma civilização de Tipo II na escala de Kardashev – uma civilização capaz de aproveitar todo o potencial energético do Sol”, diz o comunicado da FCC. O sistema também operará em conformidade com as normas da FCC relativas a detritos orbitais. “Os Estados Unidos estão conduzindo o mundo rumo à era da superinteligência. Sob a liderança do presidente Trump, o país avança de forma decisiva para garantir que essa tecnologia revolucionária gere oportunidades, impulsione investimentos e proporcione benefícios duradouros ao povo americano”, disse o presidente do FCC, Brendan Carr. Com a autorização, a SpaceX poderá estabelecer a constelação “Starmind”, composta por até 1 milhão de centros de dados orbitais, para ajudar a atender à demanda, em rápido crescimento, por computação de superinteligência. A companhia também poderá manter capacidades resilientes de comando e controle, utilizando links de radiofrequência para telemetria, rastreamento e comando (TT&C) de backup e de emergência em todo o sistema de satélites.

artigo.texto: Projeto do data center que será instalado em Belém do Pará. Foto: Reprodução A implantação do mega data center BEL1 em Belém e seus possíveis impactos ambientais serão tema de uma sessão especial proposta pela vereadora Marinor Brito. O debate será realizado nesta quinta-feira (26), às 9h, no auditório da Superintendência do Desenvolvimento da Amazônia (Sudam), com o objetivo de ampliar a discussão pública sobre os efeitos da instalação de um empreendimento dessa dimensão na capital paraense. Entre as principais questões que serão discutidas estão o volume de água e energia necessário para o funcionamento da estrutura, os possíveis impactos sobre o meio ambiente e as comunidades do entorno, além dos benefícios econômicos e sociais que o empreendimento poderá trazer para Belém e sua população. Para a vereadora Marinor Brito, a chegada de um empreendimento dessa dimensão exige transparência e participação popular. “Não somos contra a tecnologia ou o desenvolvimento. O que queremos saber é quais são os custos ambientais e sociais de um projeto desse porte para Belém. Quanto de água e energia será consumido? Quais impactos poderão atingir o nosso território e as comunidades do entorno? E, principalmente, o que a população paraense vai ganhar o que ela vai perder com esse empreendimento? Essas perguntas precisam ser respondidas com clareza”, afirma. A iniciativa também busca garantir que a implantação de grandes empreendimentos tecnológicos na Amazônia seja acompanhada de informações acessíveis e debate público. “A Amazônia não pode ser tratada apenas como um território de exploração de recursos. O desenvolvimento precisa respeitar nossos rios, nossas florestas e as pessoas que vivem aqui. Não podemos aceitar que decisões com consequências para toda a cidade sejam tomadas sem transparência e sem ouvir a população”, destaca a vereadora. A sessão será aberta ao público e contará com espaço para perguntas, manifestações e esclarecimentos. A expectativa é reunir representantes da empresa, da sociedade, especialistas e pessoas interessadas em discutir os impactos e as responsabilidades socioambientais relacionados à implantação do BEL1 em Belém.

artigo.texto: The BMX brand, along with its distributor HDGROUP, officially introduced BMX solid-state battery technology to the Vietnamese market at the THE NEXT STATE showcase event in Ho Chi Minh City. The core of the technology is the use of a solid electrolyte instead of the traditional liquid form, aiming to raise the safety standards for power banks. BMX SolidSafe solid-state batteries arrive in Vietnam: solid electrolyte reduces the risk of fire and explosion for power banks. BMX and HDGROUP introduced the SolidSafe solid-state battery at THE NEXT STATE event in Ho Chi Minh City, featuring a solid electrolyte and two live battery nailing and cutting tests. BMX solid-state battery technology utilizes the SolidSafe solution, using a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid or gel electrolyte. According to the manufacturer, this improvement increases the stability of the battery cell and reduces the risk of overheating during operation. The context for this change is quite clear. For many years, the mobile accessory market has been highly competitive in terms of charging power and capacity. However, the risks of short circuits and overheating have led users to increasingly prioritize safety. Furthermore, the optimized internal structure not only enhances safety but also lays the groundwork for more compact, slimmer, and lighter accessory designs in the future. Nailing and cutting the battery: two tests conducted in real life. At the event, BMX directly performed two rigorous physical tests on solid-state batteries: nailing through battery cells and directly cutting the battery sample. Both aimed to demonstrate the stable properties of the new material. The Nail Penetration Test is a standard method in the energy storage research industry, used to evaluate the response of devices to severe mechanical damage. According to BMX, when pierced by a nail, solid-state battery cells maintain stability and do not experience thermal instability. Furthermore, the live cutting of the battery sample in front of the guests further highlighted the advantages of solid electrolytes. The battery structure did not leak chemicals and limited the risk of fire even when the protective casing was completely destroyed. Important note regarding the scope of the tests. The manufacturer's representative emphasized that the tests were conducted under controlled conditions to illustrate the material's properties. Users should absolutely not attempt similar tests at home to avoid danger. HDGROUP and the BMX charging ecosystem in Vietnam BMX is partnering with HDGROUP to develop the market and expand its distribution network. This collaboration brings solid-state batteries and the next-generation charging ecosystem closer to consumers. At the exhibition space, BMX showcased various power bank models and tech accessories. Content creators and tech experts such as Cu Hiep and Tony Phung also participated in discussions, providing practical assessments of the development trends in the charging accessories industry. According to sources, HDGROUP plays a role in building the sales network, providing after-sales service, and raising user awareness about choosing safe charging devices. The emergence of BMX solid-state batteries is expected to promote new safety standards for the mobile accessory market in Vietnam in the near future.

artigo.texto: Por: Ana Paula De Raeffray e Louis Henri Frederic De Raeffray O Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) da União Europeia alterou em definitivo a segurança jurídica e a dogmática do comércio internacional, alçando a intensidade de carbono à condição de elemento tributário e regulatório decisivo para o acesso de bens ao mercado comunitário. Com a consolidação de sua fase plena, a carga de emissões incorporada aos produtos deixa de figurar como mero parâmetro socioambiental para assumir a natureza de encargo financeiro cogente na aduana europeia. Essa exigência regulatória gera impactos diretos sobre setores fundamentais da indústria de transformação nacional, como o siderúrgico, de alumínio, cimento, fertilizantes e hidrogênio. A principal complexidade jurídica dessa transição reside na assimetria das metodologias de mensuração e valoração das emissões perante o mercado europeu (EU ETS). Produtos com especificações técnicas idênticas sofrerão valoração tributária desequilibrada na Europa a depender da higidez das provas documentais, do rigor das auditorias do processo fabril e da capacidade de comprovar o tributo ou preço de carbono já recolhido no país de origem. É sob a ótica dessa assimetria que a regulamentação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, adquire centralidade jurídica. A consulta pública aberta pelo Ministério da Fazenda em julho de 2026 — destinada a regulamentar as regras de Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação (MRV) — evidenciou a urgência do alinhamento normativo. Embora a legislação comunitária europeia preveja o abatimento dos valores de carbono quitados no Brasil, o exercício dessa compensação condiciona-se à estrita equivalência metodológica e à validação documental perante as autoridades em Bruxelas. A ausência de uma célere interoperabilidade regulatória entre os padrões brasileiros e europeus expõe o setor produtivo ao risco iminente de dupla oneração econômica. Trata-se de um gargalo em que a indústria nacional arrisca suportar o encargo doméstico de carbono sem a devida dedutibilidade nas exportações para a Europa, sofrendo nítida perda de competitividade no cenário global. A relevância da matéria ultrapassou o âmbito normativo interno e ingressou na esfera do contencioso internacional. Em setembro de 2026, o Órgão de Solução de Controvérsias da Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC) acolheu a abertura de painel para aferir a conformidade do CBAM e do EU ETS com os acordos multilaterais. A participação do Brasil como terceiro interessado — ao lado de jurisdições como China, Índia, Estados Unidos e Japão — evidencia que a compatibilidade do mecanismo europeu com o princípio da não discriminação é objeto de profunda controvérsia jurídica internacional. No âmbito privado, o avanço desse regramento redefine os parâmetros da elaboração contratual em operações de exportação. Cláusulas de fornecimento que se limitavam a disciplinar tarifas aduaneiras e Incoterms passam a exigir disciplinas expressas sobre a alocação do risco tributário do carbono, deveres de transparência probatória e garantias de auditoria. A estruturação de instrumentos contratuais juridicamente blindados contra contenciosos internacionais — seja na arbitragem comercial exterior ou perante jurisdições estrangeiras — tornou-se pressuposto indispensável à higidez das operações. O cenário exige atuação institucional e corporativa diligente. O Brasil detém uma matriz energética de matriz limpa, mas arrisca sofrer restrições de mercado por assimetrias de integração regulatória. Cumpre acelerar a consolidação normativa do SBCE com foco no direito diplomático e comercial, cabendo às bancas e aos departamentos jurídicos tratar a contabilidade de carbono e a gestão de prova documental como matéria prioritária de governança e compliance. Sob a perspectiva da advocacia de negócios, essa adequação pode ser convertida em vantagem competitiva. Diante de uma matriz altamente descarbonizada, a indústria brasileira reúne condições para transformar o rigor probatório em diferencial de mercado em relação a concorrentes de matrizes fósseis, desde que assegurada a validade jurídica dos certificados perante os organismos internacionais. A carga de emissões incorporou-se de forma definitiva ao cálculo do custo de exportação, alinhando-se aos encargos freteiros, cambiais e alfandegários. Para o exportador nacional, o cumprimento rigoroso e autônomo dessas exigências não constitui tema prospectivo, mas condição imperativa de segurança jurídica e sobrevivência comercial. Ana Paula De Raeffray Doutora em Direito pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo (PUC-SP). Professora dos cursos de pós-graduação da PUC-SP. Sócia do escritório Raeffray Brugioni Advogados. Louis Henri Frederic De Raeffray Graduado em Business Administration pela IE University. Atuante na área de Relações Governamentais perante o Parlamento Europeu. Consultor do escritório Raeffray Brugioni Advogados.

artigo.texto: While the blue wave that swept across the South during this month’s midterm elections crested without overturning Louisiana’s electoral politics, it may have created more favorable conditions for AI data center projects in the state. Voters in more than two dozen jurisdictions approved restrictions on new data centers, and the Democratic governors-elect in Texas, Georgia and Ohio all campaigned on pausing or limiting their expansion. That’s left Louisiana looking increasingly attractive to those looking to build what Republican Gov. Jeff Landry has dubbed “digital factories.” “We think Louisiana has a significant advantage in the market," Venture Global CEO Michael Sabel said on an earnings call earlier this month. "For the moment, it seems like they might be the only store open on Sunday here for data centers." Days later, Ned Fleming, executive chairman of Suncrete, told investors his firm had met with the governors of both Louisiana and Oklahoma, states where his Tulsa-based concrete logistics company has a backlog of business building data centers. “They would love for every data center that Texas doesn't want to come to Louisiana and Oklahoma,” Fleming said. Gigawatts in pipeline Landry has made attracting large industrial projects to the state, including AI data centers, a key priority of his administration. Meta's Hyperion facility under construction in Richland Parish will be among the largest in the world. While other states have moved to limit data center construction over the past year, with help from opponents on both sides of the political aisle, there's been little organized opposition to the facilities in Louisiana, though that is starting to change. Still, Landry has remained supportive of data center development. Two weeks after the election, the governor rolled out a new ad campaign aimed at luring investment from Texas. “Elections have consequences, and business leaders pay attention to the direction a state is headed," Landry said, announcing the campaign. The recent comments come as developers are lined up waiting to build new AI data centers — and the massive power plants needed to run them. Entergy executives, in earnings calls and investor presentations over the past year, have predicted there will be up to 12 gigawatts of additional new data center power demand over the next two years across its entire service area, which includes most of Louisiana, Arkansas and Mississippi, as well as parts of east Texas. The LSU Energy Institute forecasts up to 19 gigawatts of data center investment in Louisiana through 2033. But more than 20 times that much data center capacity was already in the queue awaiting approval from Texas grid operators and regulators ahead of the election. Now, some developers are nervous their plans may never materialize in the Lone Star State. Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said that dynamic is creating new opportunities for Louisiana. She said her office was already fielding an “aggressive amount” of interest from prospective developers prior to the election. She is expecting more interest in the months to come. “Now, the more the tea leaves lay out the way they are, fewer states are interested. Fewer states have the ability to do it,” Bourgeois said in an interview following the election. Last month, Bourgeois' department finalized a framework requiring developers to submit an “attestation” as to how their projects will help the state in more than a half-dozen ways before they can receive sales tax exemption on data center equipment. “It also does allow us to negotiate from a very strong position,” Bourgeois said. “It allows us to continue to raise what that return is for Louisiana as we have those conversations, because fewer states are having them.” Power play With an abundance of natural gas pipelines and an amenable state government, Louisiana’s largest bottleneck to continued data center expansion will become generating enough electricity. “Everybody may want to relocate to Louisiana, but there's not enough power for them to do so. The power is not available for them to relocate,” said analyst Gordon Johnson, of GLJ Research. Louisiana electrical utility regulators have, so far, fast-tracked approval for new power needed for megaprojects like Meta's Richland Parish data center. Last year, the Public Service Commission implemented a "lightning directive" that lets utilities skip some rules when building new electrical infrastructure, a move recently challenged in state court by a group of advocacy organizations. Some data center developers are looking to sidestep grid regulators by generating their own power. One Florida startup is pitching multiple "permitted campuses" near the border between Ascension and Iberville parishes with up to 4 gigawatts of on-site natural gas plants — and potentially even a new nuclear plant. Venture Global, which is already on track to become the world's largest liquified natural gas producer with the expansion of its facilities in Calcasieu and Plaquemines parishes, is also seeking to get in on the data center game. Company officials last month announced they had inked deals to buy up to 16 gas turbines in order to build facilities with up to 10 gigawatts of power generation capacity on spec. The new power plants would be operate in what's called "island mode," independent of the public grid. “We think Louisiana has a great opportunity to significantly add to their existing gas businesses in the state and become a major supplier of compute in the United States,” Sabel told analysts.

artigo.texto: Sioux City Planning & Zoning Commission advances rules governing future data center projects SIOUX CITY (KTIV) - Sioux City is moving forward with an ordinance governing projects like data centers and cryptocurrency mining farms. On Tuesday, Nov. 24, the city’s Planning and Zoning commission voted 5-0 to approve the language of a new ordinance setting out rules for those kinds of projects. Two members of the commission abstained from the vote. The city’s planning manager says it addresses what the city would require from any future projects, like noise limits, property setbacks and water use rules. It also gives the public opportunities to weigh in on any possible projects. “The Planning and Zoning Commission did put in their recommendation of a site plan requirement, so that site plan would have to go through Planning and Zoning Commission and City Council, if City Council decide they also want to keep that requirement, and so there would be that public notification with what was approved tonight,” said Chris Madsen, Planning Manager for the City of Sioux City. The draft ordinance will go before Sioux City’s City Council at its next meeting on Monday, December 7th. Want to get the latest news and weather from Siouxland’s News Source? artigo.texto: Virginia has two serious problems that ought to be considered together. We need enormous amounts of new electricity to meet growing demand, and much of rural Virginia desperately needs new industry and jobs. Data centers offer an opportunity to address both. Yet instead of figuring out how to take advantage of that opportunity, we seem increasingly focused on making it harder for them to locate here. I’ve spent much of my career in the coal industry and later worked on redeveloping former mining properties for new industrial uses in Southwest Virginia. I’ve seen what happens when communities lose the industries that supported them, and I know how difficult it is to attract new investment. Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and place demands on local infrastructure. Developers should address those concerns and pay their own way. But these facilities support everything from banking and medical research to manufacturing and national security. With artificial intelligence expanding rapidly, demand isn’t going away. The question is whether Virginia intends to benefit from that investment or watch it go somewhere else. Two proposed projects illustrate what’s at stake. STACK Infrastructure is planning a large data center campus in Pittsylvania County, near Danville. At full buildout, it could require 3,000 megawatts of electricity. According to its permit application reported by Cardinal News, the developer expects to generate most of that power on-site, likely using substantial amounts of natural gas. The final generating technology has not been determined. Separately, Dominion Energy is proposing a 3,000-megawatt natural gas power plant in Cumberland County. That plant would supply Dominion’s utility customers, not the STACK project. Think about that. One proposed data center campus could require as much generating capacity as Dominion’s entire new power plant. That’s an extraordinary amount of electricity. It’s also an extraordinary economic opportunity. Virginia needs dependable electricity Virginia already imports a substantial portion of its electricity. In 2023, net imports accounted for 36% of our electricity supply. Meanwhile, PJM, the regional grid operator, projects that peak electricity demand in Dominion’s service territory could more than double by 2046. There’s nothing inherently wrong with importing electricity. But depending heavily on other states becomes a concern when severe weather strains the entire region. There’s an economic cost as well. When Virginia imports electricity, much of the economic benefit of producing it goes somewhere else. Other states get the construction jobs, permanent employment, supporting businesses and tax revenue. Virginia’s energy policies make it harder to change that. The Virginia Clean Economy Act requires major utilities to move toward carbon-free electricity and retire certain fossil-fuel plants, subject to reliability protections. The Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative also adds a cost to emissions from covered power plants. Reducing emissions is a legitimate objective. But so are affordable electricity, a reliable grid and economic development. We can’t pursue one while ignoring the others. Wind and solar have a role, but neither can be counted on whenever electricity is needed. Batteries help for shorter periods, but several days of severe weather require dependable generation. Modern natural gas combined-cycle plants are highly efficient and can operate around the clock. Nuclear power should also play a much larger role in our long-term energy plans. After a career in energy production, one thing I know is that reliable electricity isn’t optional. Factories, hospitals and businesses need power regardless of the weather. With demand growing so rapidly, why make it harder to build the generating capacity we need? Make data centers part of the solution Data centers need dependable electricity around the clock. Developers should help finance the generation and infrastructure they require, rather than leaving existing utility customers with the bill. But we should go further. Large data centers should also contribute to grid reliability during emergencies. Depending on their design, they could provide surplus generation, use backup power where feasible or temporarily reduce demand. Some AI computing can be delayed or shifted elsewhere, reducing demand during a grid emergency. Consider what happens to electricity prices during severe conditions. Wholesale electricity might ordinarily cost $40 to $60 per megawatt-hour. During extreme demand, prices can exceed $1,000 or even $2,500. The last few megawatts needed to keep the system operating can become extraordinarily expensive. If data centers could reliably reduce demand during those critical hours, they could help avoid some of those costs. These arrangements would require firm commitments, proper engineering and reasonable compensation. But the principle is simple: establish the reliability requirements and let developers find the most economical way to meet them. That’s better than dictating the technology they must use. artigo.texto: Madison moves toward hyperscale data center ban as advocates call for statewide protections MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Madison is looking to ban hyperscale data centers within city limits as its temporary moratorium on larger facilities nears its expiration. A proposed ordinance on Tuesday’s Common Council agenda would establish long-term restrictions on the size, location and operation of data centers following months of research and public feedback. While the proposed regulations aim to protect Madison residents, environmental advocacy group Clean Wisconsin says addressing the broader impacts of large-scale data centers will require action at the state level. According to the city, there are currently no active proposals or applications for new data centers in Madison. What is Madison proposing? In January, the Common Council approved a temporary moratorium on zoning approvals for new data centers larger than 10,000 square feet as a property’s primary use, giving city staff time to study potential impacts and develop regulations. Without new regulations in place when the moratorium expires, the city says its existing zoning code would not adequately regulate the size or location of modern data centers. The proposed ordinance, sponsored by Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Alder Derek Field, would replace that moratorium with new zoning regulations. According to a Nov. 19 Planning Division staff report, public feedback prompted several changes to the initial proposal, including reducing the maximum allowable size from 100,000 to 75,000 square feet. Under the proposed ordinance: - Data centers would be capped at 75,000 square feet per zoning lot, with no exceptions to exceed that limit. - Data centers would be prohibited in residential zoning districts. - Facilities between 50,000 and 75,000 square feet would only be allowed in designated industrial and airport zoning districts. - The largest permitted facilities would require a 500-foot buffer from areas zoned for housing and a 300-foot buffer from certain other nonindustrial districts. - Data centers 10,000 square feet or larger would require noise mitigation plans, solid walls surrounding mechanical equipment and emergency generators, and at least 1,000 feet of separation from parcels occupied by another data center of that size or larger. The combination of size and separation requirements would also effectively ban large data center campuses. A separate proposed ordinance would increase fines for violations of the city’s existing noise control ordinance. The city says all existing data centers in Madison would be permitted under the proposed regulations. In a statement Friday, Rhodes-Conway said the proposal would protect residents from potential negative impacts while continuing to allow responsible and legitimate uses of computing power. “With this proposal, the City is effectively exercising its authority, and I strongly urge State lawmakers to enact sensible data center regulation so local communities have additional tools to protect residents,” Rhodes-Conway said. Environmental advocates call for statewide action Clean Wisconsin Communications Director Amy Barrilleaux said Madison’s proposed regulations could help protect nearby residents, but the environmental impacts of large-scale artificial intelligence data centers extend beyond city limits. According to the city, Wisconsin municipalities have authority over land use and zoning but cannot regulate water consumption, energy use, energy sources or utility rates. Barrilleaux said three AI data center projects in Wisconsin are expected to collectively use more energy than four million homes. “Our energy utilities are racing to meet that need by building a large number of new gas plants,” Barrilleaux said. “This appears to be easily one of the largest, if not the largest, increases in fossil fuel energy generation in the history of Wisconsin.” She said the growing demand for electricity raises concerns about air pollution, public health, water use and potentially higher utility bills. “We can’t have Madison or Sun Prairie or Middleton all racing to figure this out,” Barrilleaux said. “There need to be statewide protections that protect every community in Wisconsin because this sort of like piecemeal approach isn’t working for the whole state.” Clean Wisconsin is calling for a statewide pause on AI data center development until additional protections are in place. The organization is advocating for greater energy efficiency, the use of clean energy, increased transparency surrounding water use and pollution, and measures to ensure technology companies cover the cost of energy infrastructure built to meet their needs. Barrilleaux said the organization has been working with state lawmakers and other advocates in hopes of seeing legislative action in the new year. “Local lawmakers do their work at the local level. That’s what they do. And so, if they feel like an ordinance is needed to protect their community, then that’s what their job is,” Barrilleaux said. “State lawmakers have that job too. It’s on the state level. And we can’t expect every community to in the next six months be able to fully protect communities as these huge projects roll out.” What comes next? A City of Madison spokesperson told WMTV Tuesday’s introduction is the first step in the legislative process. The Common Council does not discuss ordinances when they are first introduced. Several city committees will review the proposal and gather public feedback before making recommendations to the Common Council. The proposed timeline includes: - Nov. 30: Plan Commission - Dec. 16: Business and Economic Resources Committee - Dec. 21: Sustainable Madison Committee - Jan. 11: Plan Commission public hearing - Jan. 12: Common Council discussion and anticipated vote Jan. 12 is the last scheduled Common Council meeting before the city’s temporary moratorium expires on Jan. 24, 2027. artigo.texto: O mercado de créditos de carbono ganhou espaço nas discussões da COP31, com avanços nas regras para comercialização internacional e na estruturação de mecanismos de financiamento voltados à preservação ambiental. Embora as negociações sobre combustíveis fósseis tenham enfrentado impasses e impedido um acordo final mais abrangente, a aprovação do artigo 6 representou um dos principais resultados da conferência nesse campo. O mecanismo permite que a conservação de florestas e a adoção de práticas produtivas sustentáveis também tenham valor econômico. Cada tonelada de dióxido de carbono (CO₂) retirada da atmosfera ou cuja emissão é evitada, por meio da manutenção da vegetação nativa e de sistemas como a agrofloresta cabruca, pode dar origem a um crédito de carbono, negociado para compensar emissões. O cenário entre a COP30 e a COP31 aponta mudanças importantes na governança climática e na destinação de recursos para projetos ambientais. Entre os avanços está a aprovação do comércio internacional de créditos de carbono com base no artigo 6, enquanto outros temas da agenda climática permaneceram sob impasse, especialmente aqueles relacionados aos combustíveis fósseis e à resistência de grandes países produtores. Outro destaque é o desenvolvimento do mercado regulado de carbono no Brasil. De acordo com a Secretaria Extraordinária de Mercado de Carbono, vinculada ao Ministério da Fazenda, o intervalo entre as duas conferências foi marcado pelo avanço na implementação desse sistema e pela consolidação de uma coalizão global voltada à cooperação internacional. Na área de financiamento, o presidente do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), Aloizio Mercadante, mencionou a expectativa de captar aproximadamente 39 bilhões em investimentos destinados a iniciativas climáticas e projetos ambientais. Impactos para reservas ambientais e áreas de cabruca O fortalecimento dos instrumentos de financiamento climático também pode ampliar as oportunidades para proprietários de áreas protegidas, especialmente na Mata Atlântica. Nesse contexto, iniciativas de Pagamento por Serviços Ambientais (PSA) e ações de gestão territorial ganham relevância. A Reservas Votorantim, por exemplo, destaca benefícios associados à conservação de áreas de Mata Atlântica e Cerrado. Além da proteção contra invasões, desmatamentos e incêndios, os proprietários podem contar com suporte técnico e jurídico, isenções no Imposto sobre a Propriedade Territorial Rural (ITR) e participação em iniciativas como o PSA Carbonflor. Para acessar essas possibilidades, entretanto, é necessário que as áreas estejam organizadas do ponto de vista técnico e ambiental. Um exemplo é a Reserva Particular do Patrimônio Natural (RPPN) Serra dos Teiús, localizada em Ipiaú, no sul da Bahia. Reconhecida como unidade de conservação de interesse público e caráter perpétuo, a reserva possui 1,5649 hectare no bioma Mata Atlântica. Sua criação foi oficializada pela Portaria nº 007, de 29 de janeiro de 2026. Para propriedades com esse perfil, especialmente aquelas que desenvolvem ou têm potencial para sistemas agroflorestais de cabruca, a elaboração de um plano de manejo é uma etapa importante. O documento deve reunir informações sobre as condições ambientais da área, recursos hídricos, medidas de prevenção de ameaças, cronograma de atividades e indicadores de acompanhamento. Além de orientar a administração permanente da reserva, esse planejamento pode facilitar o acesso a programas de conservação e a iniciativas de financiamento climático.

artigo.texto: Global oil markets are heading… A TVA construction permit and… Data center proliferation will drive demand for natural gas in the United States over the next two years, Goldman Sachs has forecast, estimating that some 52 GW of new data center capacity could be added to the grid in 2028 alone. “Year-to-date, data-center power capacity and demand have increased by nearly 30% in the US, contributing to more than one third of US total power demand growth,” the bank’s analysts wrote in a note this week, as cited by Reuters. “We expect growth acceleration in data centers to be driven not only by a higher volume of facilities, but by increasingly larger physical footprints and higher power density,” they said. This will drive stronger growth in demand for electricity and, by extension, for natural gas, which has become the preferred method for data center operators to source reliable, baseload electricity since nuclear takes too long to build. That data centers are massive energy demand sources is no news. Indeed, data centers are the primary reason for upbeat demand growth projections in the natural gas industry. U.S. gas-fired power generation capacity in development directly tied to data centers nearly doubled to 189 GW in the first half of the year, and chances are the momentum continued in the second half as well. Data center operators like natural gas. And natural gas producers like data centers. No wonder, then, that U.S. natural gas production is on track to close a second consecutive year with record-high natural gas output as producers respond to demand signs both at home and overseas. Soaring demand for powering data centers combined with rising liquefied natural gas exports amid expanding liquefaction capacity, as well as surging global demand for spot LNG cargoes in the absence of Qatar’s gas due to the Iran war, is pushing American natural gas production higher this year. artigo.texto: 247 – A empresa aeroespacial SpaceX, do bilionário Elon Musk, recebeu autorização da Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC) para implantar uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites destinados ao funcionamento de centros de processamento de dados no espaço. A iniciativa busca ampliar a infraestrutura necessária ao desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial (IA), utilizando a energia solar disponível em órbita terrestre. Segundo a CNN Brasil, trata-se da primeira autorização desse tipo concedida pela agência reguladora estadunidense. O projeto, denominado Starmind, pretende transferir parte da capacidade de processamento computacional para o espaço, com equipamentos capazes de atender à crescente demanda por serviços de inteligência artificial utilizados na Terra. A decisão representa um avanço nos planos da companhia de Musk de desenvolver centros de dados orbitais. A SpaceX defende que a instalação dessas estruturas fora do planeta permitirá aproveitar a energia solar e reduzir a pressão sobre recursos terrestres, especialmente água e eletricidade, empregados no funcionamento dos centros convencionais. Embora os equipamentos sejam instalados em órbita, sua finalidade será processar grandes volumes de informações destinados a aplicações terrestres. A proposta prevê a utilização de satélites como parte de uma infraestrutura computacional voltada ao atendimento das necessidades de processamento de sistemas avançados de IA. Governo dos EUA aposta em infraestrutura espacial para inteligência artificial A FCC apresentou a autorização como uma medida destinada a fortalecer a posição dos Estados Unidos no desenvolvimento de tecnologias avançadas. O órgão relacionou a expansão da infraestrutura computacional ao conceito de “superinteligência”, expressão utilizada pelo presidente Donald Trump para se referir à inteligência artificial. O presidente da comissão, Brendan Carr, afirmou que os Estados Unidos “lideram o mundo na era da superinteligência” e destacou a importância dos centros de processamento de dados para sustentar o avanço dessa tecnologia. “Essa ação abre fronteiras ousadas para a infraestrutura de computação necessária para impulsionar a liderança e o crescimento da América”, declarou Carr em comunicado divulgado pela agência. De acordo com a FCC, a autorização permitirá à SpaceX estabelecer a constelação Starmind com até 1 milhão de satélites de centros de dados, com o objetivo de “ajudar a atender à demanda em rápido crescimento por computação de superinteligência”. A dimensão do projeto coloca a infraestrutura espacial no centro da estratégia americana de expansão da capacidade computacional. A proposta da SpaceX é utilizar uma rede de equipamentos em órbita para realizar operações de processamento que atendam às necessidades de sistemas de inteligência artificial no planeta. SpaceX promete reduzir consumo de água e eletricidade na Terra Um dos principais argumentos apresentados pela companhia para justificar a instalação dos centros de dados no espaço é a possibilidade de aproveitar recursos energéticos disponíveis fora da superfície terrestre. A empresa sustenta que a utilização de energia solar em órbita poderá diminuir a necessidade de recursos empregados por instalações convencionais. Entre os benefícios anunciados estão a economia de eletricidade e a redução do consumo de água, recurso utilizado em sistemas de resfriamento de centros de processamento de dados. A iniciativa também pretende aproveitar o espaço disponível em órbita para ampliar a capacidade computacional. Os satélites funcionariam como unidades de processamento de informações, integradas a uma estrutura destinada a fornecer serviços para aplicações terrestres. Esses benefícios, entretanto, são apresentados como objetivos do projeto e não incluem resultados operacionais que permitam quantificar a economia de recursos ou demonstrar a eficiência da infraestrutura proposta. FCC relaciona projeto à civilização Kardashev tipo II Além dos argumentos econômicos e tecnológicos, a agência reguladora americana associou a autorização à possibilidade de avanço da humanidade em direção a uma civilização Kardashev tipo II. O conceito faz parte de uma classificação hipotética de civilizações segundo sua capacidade de aproveitar recursos energéticos. Nesse modelo, uma civilização do tipo II seria capaz de captar e utilizar a energia emitida por sua própria estrela, como o Sol. Ao mencionar essa classificação, a FCC vinculou o projeto da SpaceX a uma perspectiva de expansão do aproveitamento da energia solar para além da superfície terrestre. A referência, contudo, não significa que a implantação da constelação orbital permitiria alcançar esse estágio de desenvolvimento. Trata-se de uma associação feita pela agência entre a utilização de energia espacial e uma hipótese teórica sobre a evolução tecnológica das civilizações. Agência dos EUA poderá autorizar outros projetos A autorização concedida à SpaceX também abre um precedente regulatório para outras empresas interessadas em desenvolver infraestrutura de processamento de dados no espaço. Segundo a FCC, novos pedidos para o lançamento de satélites destinados a essa finalidade poderão ser analisados pela comissão. A decisão, portanto, não estabelece exclusividade para a companhia de Elon Musk nesse segmento. Embora o projeto Starmind tenha recebido autorização para uma constelação de até 1 milhão de equipamentos, as informações divulgadas não apresentam um cronograma detalhado para a implantação integral da rede.

artigo.texto: Green Energy Storage (GES), an Italy-based maker of flow batteries for stationary storage, has received €10 million (~ $10.92 million) in financing from Intesa Sanpaolo. The bank has arranged it as a structured finance transaction through its Banca dei Territori division, which has worked with its IMI Corporate & Investment Banking division. The funds are to pay for the staff, materials and facilities that GES needs in order to scale up its hydrogen-manganese battery under the IPCEI programme. They are also to let the company run its first large-scale installations under real operating conditions, before the product is certified and industrialised. According to GES, the battery works at room temperature, and its power and energy modules can be sized independently of each other. The company, which is based in Povo in the province of Trento, has set itself the aim of reaching technology readiness level (TRL) 6 by the end of 2026. Intesa Sanpaolo lends €10 million to flow battery maker GES With €10 million from Intesa Sanpaolo, the Trentino SME Green Energy Storage is to scale up its hydrogen-manganese flow battery and to run its first large units. artigo.texto: A Odata Brasil recebeu autorização do Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) para comprar uma empresa responsável pelo projeto de implantação do Data Center Anhanguera, localizado em Osasco, São Paulo. O ativo é atualmente controlado pela GP Participações Empresariais e pela Tattva, do grupo BEP Energia. A operação ainda depende do aval de outros órgãos antitruste. Ao Cade, as companhias informaram que o data center ainda não entrou em operação e que ainda não possui capacidade instalada. Atualmente, o data center detém apenas o parecer de acesso emitido pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), documento necessário para a conexão do empreendimento à Rede Básica do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Caso a aquisição seja concluída e o projeto entre em operação, a empresa desenvolverá as mesmas atividades já exercidas pela Odata Brasil. Em manifestação ao Cade, a Odata destacou que a operação representa uma oportunidade de negócio alinhada à sua estratégia de desenvolvimento e expansão no mercado de data centers no Brasil. No momento, a companhia é responsável por oferecer colocation a clientes do segmento atacadista, incluindo provedores de nuvem em modelo hyperscale, empresas dos setores financeiro, de telecomunicações e diversas outras áreas com atuação em múltiplos segmentos. No Brasil, a Odata possui data centers nos estados de São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro, além de unidades na Colômbia, Chile e México. Já os vendedores destacaram que a venda pode contribuir para o desenvolvimento de seus negócios.

artigo.texto: Hindustan Zinc Limited (BSE: 500188; NSE: HINDZINC), the world’s largest integrated zinc producer, and the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) have unveiled an electric three-wheeler prototype fitted with an approximately 1 kWh zinc-air battery designed to function as a range extender. Unveiled at the recently held IIT Madras Energy Summit 2026, the prototype marks a key stage in the research collaboration between the two institutions to develop indigenous zinc-based energy storage technologies for emerging applications. The unveiling was attended by Guest of Honour Praveen Chakravarthy, Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha); Amarendu Prakash, CEO and Whole-time Director, Hindustan Zinc; Prof. Manu Santhanam, Dean (ICSR), IIT Madras; and Dr. Aravind Kumar Chandiran of the Department of Chemical Engineering, IIT Madras, who led the project, along with other stakeholders. The three-wheeler uses a dual-battery configuration in which the zinc-air battery supplies nearly 10% of the vehicle’s total energy requirements. The lithium-ion battery supports acceleration and peak power demands, while the zinc-air unit provides a steady supply of energy during operation. The demonstration highlights how zinc-based batteries could complement existing energy storage systems in electric mobility. Zinc-air batteries generate electricity using zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. The technology uses a non-flammable, water-based electrolyte and an abundant, recyclable metal, offering potential advantages in safety, affordability and environmental sustainability. India’s zinc resources also provide an opportunity to develop domestic energy storage capabilities and support the country’s energy self-reliance. The collaboration, initiated in 2024, has progressed from laboratory research to a vehicle-level demonstration. Amarendu Prakash, CEO and Whole-time Director, Hindustan Zinc, said, “At Hindustan Zinc, we are constantly exploring opportunities to expand the applications of zinc and unlock greater value from this versatile metal. With zinc being abundantly available in India, there is an opportunity to explore indigenous energy storage solutions that can contribute to the vision of Viksit Bharat. Our collaboration with IIT Madras reflects our commitment to translating scientific research into practical applications, creating new demand avenues for zinc and strengthening its role in the global clean energy transition.” Congratulating the research team, Prof V Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras, said, “Energy is the major focus of discussion globally, be it artificial intelligence, agriculture all the way to advanced manufacturing. Ensuring generation, storage and distribution of energy from different sources, specifically the renewable ones is the most important topic for research, development and commercialization. Our collaboration with Hindustan Zinc is yet another important effort towards this goal.” For Hindustan Zinc, a Vedanta Group company, the project forms part of its wider effort to develop new applications for zinc and expand its value-added product portfolio. Under its HZL 2.0 growth and diversification strategy, the company is exploring zinc-based battery technologies for renewable energy storage and electric mobility. Hindustan Zinc Limited (BSE: 500188; NSE: HINDZINC), a Vedanta Group company, is the world’s largest integrated zinc producer and among the top 10 silver producers globally. The company supplies more than 30 countries and holds approximately 74% of India’s primary zinc market. It was recognised as the world’s most sustainable company in the metals and mining category for the third consecutive year in the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment 2025 and became the first Indian company to join the International Council on Mining & Metals in 2025. Its initiatives include EcoZen, Asia’s first low-carbon green zinc brand, a 3.32-times water-positive certification and a Net Zero emissions target by 2050 or sooner. Its social welfare programmes reach 2.6 million people. Established in 1959, IIT Madras is an Institute of National Importance with 18 academic departments and several interdisciplinary research centres. It offers undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes across science and technology disciplines. Recognised as an Institution of Eminence in 2019, it ranked first in the Overall category for the seventh consecutive year and in the Engineering category for the tenth consecutive year in the NIRF India Rankings 2025.

artigo.texto: The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has extended the bid submission deadline for its 800 MW/3,200 MWh standalone Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) tender through Amendment 03. According to the revised schedule, developers can now submit their online bids until December 3, 2026, at 6 PM. The deadline for offline bid submissions has been extended to December 7, 2026, at 6 PM. SECI will open the bids on December 8, 2026, at 10 AM. The extension gives prospective developers additional time to participate in the competitive bidding process. The latest amendment revises the earlier bidding schedule, under which online bid submissions were scheduled to close on November 24, while offline submissions were due by November 27. The bid opening, initially scheduled for November 30, has also been pushed to December 8. The amendment follows two earlier revisions issued on October 31 and November 3, 2026. The latest extension provides prospective bidders with additional time to complete their submissions for the storage procurement programme. What are the new requirements? Under the SECI-ESS-IV initiative, the agency aims to select developers for setting up 800 MW of standalone BESS capacity, equivalent to 3,200 MWh, with a four-hour discharge duration. The projects will be developed under the Build, Own and Operate (BOO) model. Developers will be selected through tariff-based competitive bidding, followed by an e-reverse auction. The tender also requires at least 51% of the energy used to charge the battery storage systems to be sourced from renewable energy. The procurement is aimed at facilitating the deployment of standalone battery storage capacity to support renewable energy integration and improve grid flexibility.

artigo.texto: Publicidade A Petrobras avalia a possibilidade de entrar no setor de minerais críticos destinados à produção de baterias, com atuação que poderá incluir desde a prospecção e extração até o processamento e refino desses recursos. A iniciativa aparece no Plano de Negócios 2027-2031 da estatal, divulgado nesta semana, e integra sua estratégia de diversificação das atividades ligadas à transição energética. A novidade está no detalhamento das oportunidades que a Petrobras poderá explorar ao longo da cadeia produtiva de baterias, em um cenário de crescimento da demanda por veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A empresa, no entanto, deixou claro que ainda não tomou uma decisão definitiva sobre sua entrada no setor mineral, e também não anunciou projetos ou investimentos específicos para essas atividades. O interesse da estatal por minerais críticos não é novo. No planejamento anterior, o tema aparecia entre as iniciativas de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Agora, a companhia amplia o escopo de sua avaliação, incluindo possíveis negócios comerciais relacionados à exploração mineral e ao processamento de matérias-primas utilizadas em baterias. Em entrevista coletiva sobre o novo plano, William Vella Nozaki, diretor executivo de Transição Energética e Sustentabilidade da Petrobras, destacou a experiência da companhia em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e a importância de acompanhar a evolução dessas novas oportunidades de negócios. O executivo ressaltou, porém, que a eventual entrada da Petrobras nesse mercado ainda dependerá de avaliações futuras. Baterias em diversas frentes Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em larga escala impulsionam a procura por minerais críticos, como o lítio, e sustentam a transição energética e as metas ESG (Foto: Zhu Difeng/ Shutterstock) Continua depois da publicidade A Petrobras considera oportunidades em diferentes etapas da cadeia de baterias. Além da prospecção, extração e refino de minerais críticos, a companhia estuda a possibilidade de atuar na montagem de conjuntos de baterias, em sistemas de armazenamento estacionário de energia, na infraestrutura de recarga de veículos elétricos e em atividades de reuso e reciclagem. A fabricação de células de baterias, por sua vez, permanece como uma frente de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Entre os principais minerais empregados na produção de baterias estão o lítio, o níquel e a grafita, recursos dos quais o Brasil possui reservas relevantes. O novo plano, entretanto, não especifica quais matérias-primas poderão ser priorizadas pela Petrobras. A companhia pretende concentrar suas avaliações em oportunidades que apresentem maior relação com suas atividades no setor energético. Continua depois da publicidade Uma das possibilidades está no mercado de baterias de grande escala, utilizadas para armazenar eletricidade e disponibilizá-la conforme a demanda. Esses sistemas ganham importância com a expansão das fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, cuja geração varia de acordo com as condições climáticas. A entrada nesse segmento permitiria à Petrobras ampliar sua presença em atividades relacionadas à transição energética, um de seus principais alvos para os próximos anos. Uma das maiores empresas de energia da América Latina Fundada em 1953, durante o governo de Getúlio Vargas, a Petrobras é uma das maiores empresas de energia da América Latina e uma referência internacional na exploração de petróleo em águas profundas e ultraprofundas. Continua depois da publicidade Ao longo de seus 73 anos, a companhia consolidou sua atuação principalmente na exploração e produção de petróleo e gás natural, no refino e na comercialização de combustíveis e derivados. O desenvolvimento de tecnologias para a produção em águas profundas, especialmente nas reservas do pré-sal brasileiro, é um dos principais marcos de sua trajetória. A empresa amplia investimentos em biocombustíveis e tecnologias de baixo carbono, enquanto avalia diversificar sua atuação para minerais críticos voltados à transição energética (Foto: Divulgação/ PBio) Embora o petróleo e o gás natural continuem sendo o centro de seus negócios, a companhia vem ampliando investimentos em descarbonização, biocombustíveis e tecnologias de baixo carbono. A possível entrada na cadeia de minerais críticos para baterias representaria, portanto, uma diversificação de suas atividades tradicionais. A iniciativa também poderia aproximar a Petrobras de um segmento interessante para a eletrificação dos transportes e o armazenamento de energia renovável. Continua depois da publicidade Plano prevê US$ 13,5 bilhões para transição energética O Plano de Negócios 2027-2031 da Petrobras prevê investimentos totais de US$ 122 bilhões nos próximos cinco anos. Desse montante, aproximadamente US$ 13,5 bilhões estão relacionados a iniciativas de transição energética. Os recursos incluem US$ 6,7 bilhões para diversificação de negócios de baixo carbono, US$ 4,8 bilhões para descarbonização das operações e US$ 2 bilhões para pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. No segmento de baixo carbono, a companhia contempla investimentos em biocombustíveis, geração renovável e armazenamento de energia, além de estudos para outras atividades. A eventual atuação em minerais críticos para baterias faz parte desse movimento de diversificação, mas ainda não possui orçamento específico anunciado. Para o setor mineral brasileiro, a inclusão dessas possibilidades no planejamento da Petrobras sinaliza o interesse de uma das maiores empresas do país em participar de uma cadeia produtiva estratégica para a transição energética. A concretização dos investimentos, entretanto, dependerá da viabilidade técnica e econômica das oportunidades identificadas e de futuras decisões da companhia.

artigo.texto: Pathways for reforming the New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) are available and feasible, but the window to act is closing and deferring policy change beyond 2030 could forgo $11 billion to $12 billion in auction revenue through to 2035, a group of researchers say. “Our concern is that within a few years, we’re going to reach a stage where the NZ ETS really doesn’t serve anyone’s interests. It’s not going to work for high emitters, for low emitters, for foresters, for iwi and Māori, for taxpayers, for future generations - and if it doesn’t work for them, then it doesn’t work for government,” Catherine Leining, policy fellow at economics organisation Motu Research, said in a webinar on Thursday morning. Alongside Leining, Motu Research analyst Ikerne Aguirre, Kapiti Climate director Kristen Green and Victoria University of Wellington associate professor Julia Talbot-Jones, produced a working paper called ‘Scoping NZ ETS and removals pathways for better climate and nature outcomes.’ Publicly released on Thursday, the researchers said through their working paper, they were interested in finding solutions that would work better than the status quo for everyone. Leining made clear that she and other researchers were not presenting an implementation plan, proposal or recommended pathway at this time. “We’re hoping that this work will lead to deeper research and to dialogue.” ETS ‘must evolve to deliver on NZ’s climate targets’ The ETS prices emissions by requiring certain sectors of the economy to have "surrender obligations" for the greenhouse gases they release into the atmosphere. These sectors include forestry, liquid fossil fuels, stationary energy, industrial processes, synthetic greenhouse gases, and waste. The ETS was initially set up to help NZ meet its 2050 net emissions target and international obligations under the Paris Agreement. Changes to climate change law removed a provision which stated the ETS unit volumes and price control regulations must "accord with" Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) under the Paris Agreement. In the working paper, the researchers said the ETS was based on outdated assumptions “and must evolve to deliver on New Zealand’s climate targets and send clear long-term investment signals to emitters and foresters." “By the mid-2030s, the Government will progressively lose control over unit supply and prices, placing market stability and climate targets at risk. The substitution of forestry removals for feasible emissions reductions is delaying decarbonisation and creating intergenerational risks.” Alongside this, the paper said "deferring policy change beyond 2030 could forgo around $11 billion to $12 billion in auction revenue through 2035". Calls for ETS reform are not new, with Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment Simon Upton saying in August that it was a question of ‘when’ not ‘if’ reform happens. A Removals Investment Mechanism The researchers said a complementary Removals Investment Mechanism (RIM) alongside ETS reforms could improve outcomes. “Under current settings, a single price signal cannot deliver both the decarbonisation and removals New Zealand needs in the long term. A RIM would combine government- and market-driven incentives with policies and regulations to value removals for their climate and wider benefits, such as biodiversity and resilience. “A RIM could be used alongside any NZ ETS pathway to boost and diversify investment in forestry and other removals without displacing emissions reductions. This would help with meeting current climate targets - and more ambitious future targets in response to temperature overshoot.” Scenarios were modelled for alternative ETS pathways - this included how the status quo, a pathway with constrained removals in the ETS, and a pathway with no removals in the ETS could impact emissions prices, climate targets, afforestation and fiscal outcomes with and without a RIM. The paper said the RIM could operate independently from a NZ ETS, trading only in gross emissions or in conjunction with an ETS trading in both gross emissions and removals. The role of the RIM would increase with greater constraints on removals in the NZ ETS and the role of supporting policies would increase alongside greater reliance on "least-cost" forestry removals to achieve climate targets, the paper said. “Depending on design, a RIM could be used to help maintain government control over climate targets and NZ ETS market stability, send clearer investment signals for emitters and foresters, generate net revenue for the Crown, and improve outcomes for climate and nature.” “It could be designed in ways that maintain or increase the value of existing and new removals investments relative to the status quo NZ ETS. The RIM modelled in this paper is a hypothetical illustration for demonstrating proof of concept, not a proposal or recommendation, and additional approaches should be considered," the paper said. Policy development should start now, researchers say Leining said the window to act was closing and the policy development process needs to start now as it was slow and took time. “We need inclusive processes and well-signaled outcomes that maintain investment value and market confidence.” The working paper said to avoid market disruption, government decision-making on introducing a RIM would need to be staged carefully and be "shaped and informed by inclusive processes with full regards to the rights, interests, and aspirations of iwi and Māori; and concluded well in advance of implementation.” “Process guardrails would be essential to build confidence in policy change and ensure a just transition for NZ ETS participants, iwi and Māori, broader stakeholders, and communities.” Policy development should start now, the paper said. “Given the lead time required, the process of policy development should begin as soon as possible, while the Government still holds the lever of auctioning and before misdirected investme

artigo.texto: Botetourt County says Google data center construction could wind down over next week BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. (WSET) — Construction activity at Google's proposed data center in Botetourt County could continue for several more days, even after a judge voided the county's agreement with the company. Botetourt County Communications Coordinator Brent Watts says the county learned from its board chair that activity at the site could continue for the next several days, possibly another week. Watts says crews need time to wind down construction and secure equipment already at the site. "They have to wind down construction. They can't just pack up and leave because there's a lot of things that are there that have to be kind of buttoned up," Watts said. The update comes as nearby residents continue looking for answers about what the court ruling means for the project. RELATED: Judge rules Botetourt County Google data center deal violated law, halts construction Courtney Pritt lives about 1,500 feet from the proposed data center site. She says her family thought they had found their forever home, but the project has already brought concerns about noise. "The first time we heard the blasting, I ran outside to get the dogs, who just froze in place, and I took them inside. That was not a great experience," Pritt said. Even after the judge's ruling, Pritt says she noticed activity at the property, including pallets being brought onto the site. She contacted the sheriff's office for answers but says she was directed elsewhere. "I'm just wondering who will be enforcing this?" she asked. Her son, Cooper Pritt, has seen data centers firsthand while training in Leesville. He worries about what the development could mean for the surrounding landscape. "They honestly look like prisons. They're gated- barbed wire fences, just really dark. I feel like this here is a really bright land, and it's just going to drain everything out of it. All of the color, all of the life," Cooper said. ABC13 went to the construction site to ask workers whether construction was still underway. They declined to comment. We also took questions directly to members of the Board of Supervisors. Board member Brandon Nicely said the county is still weighing its options following the judge's decision. "What will you do to make sure you're more transparent with people from now on?" ABC 13 asked. "Well, it's up to our attorneys and all that to make sure we don't get out of line. We felt like we were, so, you know, we acted what we thought was perfectly legal. I think we still have a little bit of... We don't really care for the judgment that much, as anybody would, but we're trying to decide which way we want to go now, so we're going to do our best," Nicely said. But several major questions remain unanswered. ABC13 asked county leaders what will happen to Google's money that has already been spent on capital improvements, whether the county plans to appeal the ruling and what Google's next steps will be. We also asked whether the county plans to hold another vote on the agreement. Board members declined to comment on those questions. For families like the Pritts, the uncertainty continues as they wait to learn what will happen next with the project just down the road from their home. ABC13 will continue following the county's response and Google's next steps.

artigo.texto: JASPER – Artificial Intelligence data centers are cropping up around the nation, bringing many questions from residents who live in highly sought after locations for their construction. Citizen Action Coalition (CAC) hosted an informative program to educate the public with a forum titled “How Data Centers Impact Communities,” held Monday, November 9, at the Astra Theater in Jasper. Projects are rumored in the southwest region, said host Bryce Gustafson, program organizer with CAC, to an ample crowd gathered at the theater. “They're trying to put these things in the pathway of least resistance,” he said. “We’re known as the Crossroads of America,” Gustafson continued, explaining Indiana has a lot of national infrastructure crisscrossing Indiana, such as interstate highways, electric lines, natural gas lines, fibre optics and complimented by cheap land. “Low cost of labor and our taxes are low,” he added. “Pretty much everywhere [in Indiana] is close to a large population,” Gustafson continued, noting Indianapolis, Detroit, Chicago, Columbus and others. “For the most part, we don’t have a lot of natural disaster risks,” he said. Indiana is at low risk for hurricanes and wildfires. Addressing the impacts of AI data Centers to communities and infrastructure, Gustafson started with the lack of transparency and accountability. “This has happened in many places across the state,” he said, “when you have elected officials signing NDAs [non disclosure agreements] … having meetings behind closed doors, when all of a sudden, we have a data center coming.” Gustafson used the town of Monrovia in Indiana, where about 550 acres of farmland and woods were rezoned and plans were revealed for six buildings and a substation, according to the Indiana Daily Student out of Bloomington, Indiana. At the forum Gustafson revealed the project was a Google AI data center. “The developer turned out to be Google,” he said. “They had their lawyer do a town hall one week. Two weeks later it was in front of the planning commission. A week after that, it was in front of the commissioners and they passed it through,” he said. “The public had three weeks to understand what was going on.” “If you’re so keen on these data centers, these projects, you have to have community community buy-in,” Gustafson said. According to wfwyi.org, CAC has publicly raised concerns about confidential information associated with the Monrovia project. Energy and water consumption for one data center project uses a little less than 10% of what the state uses, Gustafson said. “Water consumption is a big thing,” he continued. He explained about a data center project in 2023 in New Carlisle, Indiana, where the county commissioners said the project could take up to 24 millions gallons of water out of the aquifer. The industry response, he said, was “Don’t worry about it, we’re going to do a closed [water] system,” though Gustafson said no one from the industry explained the system. Moving on to air pollution, Gustafson said data centers had backup power generators, which were typically diesel powered generators. “If the power grid goes down, they will have to fire those things up,” he said, explaining that generators produce greater noise and pollution than the data center does on a daily basis. Data center noise can reach 65 decibels, he said. According to the Environmental Resilience Institute at Indiana University, “External noise levels can range from 55 to 85 A-weighted decibels (dBA) … comparable to a busy street. “Noise levels exceeding 85 dBA are harmful to hearing, creating a risk for surrounding communities and wildlife,” as read in the article, “Data centers: An overview for Hoosier communities,” found at https://eri.iu.edu/resources/fact-sheets/data-centers.html. Memory chips are in high demand due to data centers. Chips are used in common digital devices, such as phones and personal computers. The demand for chips have made them hard to get, Gustafson explained, which drives up the costs of our consumer products. “We have chips in our phones and computers, and those costs are being shouldered by us,” he said. Data centers create a “heat island effect,” he said. “You have servers that are running very hot and that heat is going to dissipate into the community around it.” Gustafson said Indiana utilities as a whole are spending tens of millions of dollars on infrastructure to service data centers. The industry, he said is looking to use gas powered energy plants to power data centers. Small modular reactors, or nuclear power, is being considered but no such facilities are operating in the United States. Indiana Senate Enrollment Act 425 was signed into law May 6, 2025, which defines an energy production zone. According to IN Code 8-1-8.2-2, an "energy production zone" means a premise of land on which any of the following was located as of January 1, 2025: “An electric generation facility with a generating capacity of at least eighty (80) megawatts, regardless of whether the electric generation facility is operational; A surface or underground mine at which mining operations are no longer occurring. “The term does not include a premise of land on which either of the following was located as of January 1, 2025: “One (1) or more wind power devices (as defined in IC 8-1-41-7 ) that are integrated into an electric generation facility; One (1) or more commercial solar energy systems (as defined in IC 8-1-42-2 ),” according to https://law.justia.com/codes/indiana/title-8/article-1/chapter-8-2/section-8-1-8-2-2/. Gustafson stated, “If you’re on energy production zones, then the locals have no say.” He noted Spencer County has energy production zones. According to wfyi.org, “Utilities that want to build a new power plant on the site of an old one — or a former coal mine — could bypass local zoning and land use laws under an Indiana Senate bill,” from their February 24, 2025 article, “Bill would let new power plants … override some local laws.” Gust

artigo.texto: SCOTTSDALE, AZ — The Scottsdale City Council has directed its attorney to explore regulation for large-scale data centers. Scottsdale officials wants to make the city is ready if a massive data center ever comes knocking. "The three concerns are the noise, the water usage and the energy demands," Scottsdale City Councilwoman Solange Whitehead said at a recent council meeting. Scottsdale's current city ordinances do not specifically define or regulate data centers. Data centers power cloud computing and artificial intelligence, and they have become a flashpoint for communities across Arizona. Scottsdale already has two smaller data centers — both in place since around 2000 near the Scottsdale Airport. City staff say they operate much like a large office or warehouse and have never been a problem. But the scale of new facilities being built elsewhere is far different. We're all about Scottsdale — the schools, the neighborhoods, the businesses, the decisions being made at City Hall and in the community that affect your daily life. Connect with your community by joining the Your Scottsdale News Facebook Group! "Where those projects, like the ones that we have existing in the community, are between say five and 15 megawatts, now the smallest of the hyper-scale data centers that are coming into these communities would be 200 megawatts," said Kevin Burke, Scottsdale's senior director of economic development. Out in the community, data centers are on the minds of residents. Scottsdale resident Malcolm Sebal was out for a walk near his home this week. He worried about what would go in the space of an elementary school that's closing at the end of the school year. "There's some trepidation from neighbors as to what they're going to lease it out for. We don't want an AI data center sitting here," Sebal said. City officials say Scottsdale is unlikely to attract those massive facilities. "We simply don't have the site availability that some of the other communities across the region have," Burke said. Not every council member sees the urgency. "Can we all just admit that this is not an issue in Scottsdale and close this right now? Because now it's just grandstanding," said Adam Kwasman, Scottsdale city councilman, at a recent council meeting. But Kwasman ultimately supported a motion to have the city attorney explore regulations. Scottsdale Mayor Lisa Borowsky said the city needs to be prepared if an application comes in. "I'm in favor of having our city attorney look at what is appropriate and is relied upon by other communities to put safeguards for our residents." No timeline has been set for when the City Council will discuss data center restrictions.

artigo.texto: Larsen & Toubro (L&T), through two of its verticals, namely its Renewables business and L&T Electronic Products & Systems (LTEPS), has jointly secured a 300 MW/900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) order. According to an L&T press release, the order is for a BESS project at Khavda in Gujarat, with a three-hour storage duration. The project will have a power capacity of 300 MW and an energy storage capacity of 900 MWh. By storing surplus renewable energy during periods of high generation and releasing it during peak demand, the system will help maximise clean energy utilisation, strengthen grid stability, and enhance the flexibility and reliability of power supply. L&T Uses Liquid-Cooling Technology The advanced BESS solution will incorporate liquid-cooling technology to deliver higher power density, enhanced safety, and a longer operating life. The facility will play a crucial role in improving grid flexibility and enabling greater integration of renewable energy into India's power network. The order further strengthens L&T's position in the energy storage sector and reflects the trust and confidence that clients place in the Company's ability to deliver complex projects at scale. Building L&T's BESS Business Since Larsen & Toubro (L&T) carved out a separate renewable energy vertical within its infrastructure segment in 2024, the company has seen rapid growth in its renewable energy and energy storage businesses. artigo.texto: From AI data centers to energy storage, Posco bets on steel's next frontier Artificial Transformation is reshaping every industry. As future sectors such as AI data centers (AIDC), power grids and energy storage systems (ESS) grow, demand for steel that delivers on multiple fronts—superior corrosion resistance, EMI shielding, high energy efficiency and low-carbon manufacturing— is increasing. 2026 Posco sustainable materials forum at Incheon’s Songdo ConvensiAPOSCO Artificial Transformation is reshaping every industry. As future sectors such as AI data centers (AIDC), power grids and energy storage systems (ESS) grow, demand for steel that delivers on multiple fronts—superior corrosion resistance, EMI shielding, high energy efficiency and low-carbon manufacturing— is increasing. Responding to these shifting demands, Posco hosted its 2026 Sustainable Forum in Incheon from Nov. 16 to 18 under the theme “The Path to AI and Green Transformation (AX & GX) — Sustainable Materials Leading New Growth.” The steelmaker unveiled its joint initiative strategy to drive sustainable growth and deliver tangible business results at the event, which drew about 1,000 participants, including 450 representatives from domestic and international partner companies. The forum, featuring a keynote by the futurist Jonathan Brill and presentations from leaders like Google Cloud and UBTECH Robotics, included 31 sessions exploring how AI and green transformations are reshaping manufacturing innovation and industrial dynamics. Posco also signed more than 26 memorandums of understanding (MOU) with partners across AIDCs, shipbuilding and low-carbon materials, shifting from conventional steel supply toward closer collaboration on joint development, supply chain resilience and low-carbon transitions. As AIDCs require powerful cooling, structural durability, safe ESS operation and electromagnetic shielding, Posco’s Early Vendor Involvement model brings steel specifications into the planning process from the initial design stage, aligning material selection with structural and equipment requirements and procurement schedules. On Nov. 11, Posco signed an MOU with GS Group for strategic AIDC cooperation, with the steelmaker supplying specialized materials and customized solutionsand GS Group overseeing infrastructure development and operations, including business planning, power supply, engineering and liquid cooling. The collaboration is expected to improve construction reliability and operational efficiency by strengthening steel supply capabilities A key component of Posco's tailored offerings is PosMAC SHIELD, a specialized shielding steel that combines electromagnetic shielding performance with corrosion resistance through a triple-layer bonded structure. Tests based on electromagnetic shielding measurement standards developed jointly with Korea Electric Power Corporation showed that the material achieved a shielding rate of 79 percent, compared with 24 percent for conventional galvanized steel, 67 percent for nickel-alloy steel and 70 percent for aluminum. Posco's proprietary PosMAC coating technology is also being applied to data centers and power infrastructure to enhance durability and reduce maintenance costs. Posco will also expand production and sales of POCEL, a specialized battery-case material used in electric vehicles and electronic products. As demand grows in the EV and ESS markets, global demand for EV batteries is projected to reach about 3 TWh by 2030. Against this backdrop, Posco plans to bolster its reliable POCEL supply to support the battery industry and help ensure power stability for AI infrastructure. More broadly, Posco is building an integrated materials ecosystem for the AI era, connecting future demand forecasts and its AIDC and ESS business teams with group-wide sales, research and development, and production capabilities.
